title: CEOs of Meta, X, Discord, TikTok and Snap testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee
content: What we covered hereWhat happened:The Senate Judiciary Committeegrilled the chief executivesof five big tech companies, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, about potential harms from their products on teens.Zuckerberg apologized:Zuckerberg stood to apologize to the families in the hearing room, saying: “I’m sorry for everything you have all been through. No one should go through the things that your families have suffered and this is why we invest so much and we are going to continue doing industry wide efforts to make sure no one has to go through the things your families have had to suffer.”What safety advocates are saying:With growingclaims that social media can hurt young users, including worries that it risks driving them to depression or even suicide, some online safety advocates at the hearing said the apologies from tech executives fell far short.Our coverage of the hearing has wrapped. For more on what we learned,click here.Read more AllCatch Up41 PostsLink Copied!Mom whose son died from fentanyl-laced pill ordered on Snapchat slams CEO apology as ‘fake’From CNN's Catherine ThorbeckeBridgette Norring, a mother whose son died from an accidental fentanyl overdose after ordering a pill off of Snapchat, slammed the apology she received today from Snapchat CEO Evan Spiegel as “fake.”“It lacked any heart,” Norring told CNN after the hearing wrapped on Wednesday afternoon. “I think he could have done better in his apology to us.”When asked what was going through her mind as she listened to the tech CEOs defend themselves, Norring said that it was “very frustrating to sit and listen to them.”“I just feel like for them, our children are just casualties, pawns, in this game to make money,” Norring said.Norring appeared on CNN News Central shortly after the hearing concluded alongside Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat from Minnesota. She held a picture of her son, Devin Norring, as she spoke, with the emotion apparent in her voice.Klobuchar was visibly shaken during the hearing, calling for lawmakers to finally enact change after what she said was decades of inaction on legislation aimed at reeling in social media companies.“I just want to get this stuff done, I’m so tired of this,” Klobuchar told CNN News Central. “It’s been 28 years, what since the internet? We haven’t passed any of these bills … it’s time to actually pass them.”Read moreLink Copied!Here's why it's hard to sue social media platformsFrom CNN's Clare DuffyDuring Wednesday’s hearing, several lawmakers lamented the fact that it’s nearly impossible to successfully sue the social media giants to hold them accountable for problematic content on their platforms.“I am tired of talking. I’m tired of having discussions,” South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham said. “Open up the courthouse door. Until you do that, nothing will change. Until these people can be sued for the damage they’re doing, it is all talk.”The reason it’s so hard to sue social media platforms is a 28-year-old federal law called “Section 230,” which holds that tech companies cannot be held liable for the content that users post to their platforms.The statute has for years been criticized by both Republicans and Democrats. But tech companies and digital rights groups have defended as vital to a functioning internet.On Wednesday, lawmakers called for the repeal of Section 230.“It is now time to make sure that the people who are holding up the signs can sue on behalf of their loved ones. Nothing will change until the courtroom door is open to victims and social media,” Graham said.Read moreLink Copied!Sen. Ed Markey blasts tech CEO “excuses”From CNN's Brian FungMassachusetts Democratic Sen. Ed Markey went after tech CEOs following Wednesday’s hearing, saying the executives had little to offer besides “excuses.”“Their CEOs showed up today with even more excuses. It was outrageous,” Markey said.Markey who pioneered the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act, a 1998 law that bars the nonconsensual collection of data of kids under age 13, urged his congressional colleagues to pass an update to the law extending those protections to teens.“An apology by Mark Zuckerberg is not enough,” Markey said. “We need action. We need laws. We need protections …. we’re fed up with apologies.“As he concluded his remarks and walked away, onlookers shouted after him urging Markey to support the Kids Online Safety Act, another hot-button bill backed by Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Marsha Blackburn.Read moreLink Copied!New Mexico attorney general says Zuckerberg “needs to start acting like a parent”From CNN's Brian FungIn a press conference on the Capitol grounds, New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described testimony by Zuckerberg and other tech CEOs as a “command performance” but said that parents can attest that the platforms “aren’t living up to their promises.”Zuckerberg, he said, “needs to start acting like a parent. He has kids himself. He needs to start acting like that.”“When he builds these platforms, when he makes these decisions, he needs to think about what it would be like to have his son or daughter exposed to this,” Torrez continued. “He needs to think about what it would be like to live through the pain and heartbreak that these parents have had to endure. He needs to really take a step back and evaluate his priorities and start helping us build a better future and stop fighting, real change.”Torrezfiled a lawsuit against Metain December, which accuses the company ofcreating a “breeding ground” for child predators.Read moreLink Copied!Meta whistleblower Arturo Béjar expresses disappointmentFrom CNN's Brian FungArturo Béjar, a Meta whistleblower whowent public last yearalleging Mark Zuckerberg ignored internal warnings about child safety, told CNN the company’s behavior in the hearing made clear Zuckerberg does not prioritize the issue.Internal documents released by two US lawmakers today highlighted how Zuckerberg did not respond to senior executives’ warnings that inaction could create major risks for the company.“The emails the Senate made available today, and his responses during testimony, show that Mark Zuckerberg and Meta do not care about the harm teens experience on their products,” Béjar said. “[Meta President of Global Affairs] Clegg writes about profound gaps with addiction, self-harm, bullying and harassment to Mark. Mark did not respond, and those gaps are unaddressed today … Children are not his priority.”Read moreLink Copied!Families and victims were a massive force in today’s hearingFrom CNN's Brian FungPeople held up photographs and placards during the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersThe families of people harmed by social media proved to be an immense force in Wednesday’s hearing.Through applause, laughter at CEO testimony, hisses and moments of silence, the parents who say their children suffered or died as a result of social media served as a key foil. They drove tensions higher and in some cases appeared to fuel the attacks of lawmakers against the CEOs.Congress has held many tech CEO hearings. But more than any other, the presence of so many parents in the room transformed the hearing and injected an unprecedented sense of urgency.Read moreLink Copied!Zuckerberg apology was "mindblowing," Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen tells CNNFrom CNN's Brian FungFacebook whistleblower Frances Haugen in 2022 during an Unfinished Live event at The Shed in New York City.Craig Barritt/Getty ImagesThe Facebook whistleblower who kicked off years of scrutiny on the impact of social media on teens said Mark Zuckerberg’s apology to parents was “mindblowing.”Today’s hearing would have been inconceivable just a handful of years ago, she said, when lawmakers were asking Zuckerberg basic questions about how his company makes money.“Almost every hearing since has been substantially more meaningful, and they’ve asked more insightful questions, more relevant questions. This was four hours long, and there were maybe 20 minutes where I was like, ‘Do you really know what you’re asking?’ And that’s amazing.”Asked about the potential for legislation to move forward, Haugen said she would be surprised if “we make it through another [electoral] cycle where we don’t see something.”Read moreLink Copied!Here's a recap of the key moments from the hearingFrom CNN's Brian Fung and Clare DuffyThe Senate Judiciary Committee’s grilling of four social media executives produced some notable moments. Here are a few:Zuckerberg, Spiegel personally apologize to families:Meta CEO Zuckerberg stood to apologize to the families in the hearing room. “I’m sorry for everything you have all been through,” he said. “No one should go through the things that your families have suffered and this is why we invest so much and we are going to continue doing industry-wide efforts to make sure no one has to go through the things your families have had to suffer.”Mark Zuckerberg spoke to victims and their family members as he testified during the US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, "Big Tech and the Online Child Sexual Exploitation Crisis."Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesSnap CEO Evan Spiegel also apologized to families whose children have died after they purchased drugs on Snapchat. “I’m so sorry that we have not been able to prevent these tragedies,” Spiegel said, before detailing some of the efforts the company takes to protect young users.(L-R) Jason Citron, CEO of Discord, Evan Spiegel, CEO of Snap, Shou Zi Chew, CEO of TikTok, Linda Yaccarino, CEO of X during the hearing today.Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images“The dark side” of social media products “is too great”:Social media companies have created products that have an upside, but they also have a dark side that is “too great to live with,” Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham said Wednesday while grilling chief executives of four such companies. Until social media companies are sued for the damage they are doing, Graham warned that there will be no change.Judiciary Committee Ranking Member U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham (R-SC) spoke during the Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on online child sexual exploitation at the U.S. Capitol today.Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersHating social media companies is a rare unifying force on Capitol Hill:Wednesday’s hearing again demonstrates the breadth of criticism for social media companies among lawmakers, a rare bipartisan topic on Capitol Hill. Despite both parties’ appetite for going after tech platforms, however, Congress has yet to pass meaningful legislation to regulate social media companies. Most of the action has taken place in state legislatures and in the courts, which have become battlegrounds for new policies including age minimums for social media.(L-R) Jason Citron, CEO of Discord; Evan Spiegel, CEO of Snap; Shou Zi Chew, CEO of TikTok; Linda Yaccarino, CEO of X; and Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta, watched a video of victims before testifying at the US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesRead the fullrundown of key hearing moments here.Read moreLink Copied!The hearing has wrappedThe Senate Judiciary Committee has wrapped its hearing where lawmakers grilled four tech executives — Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, TikTok’s Shou Chew, X’s Linda Yaccarino and Discord’s Jason Citron — on the online child sexual exploitation crisis.Read moreLink Copied!Sen. Marsha Blackburn expresses horror at Meta’s valuation of teen users at $270From CNN's Brian FungSenator Marsha Blackburn speaking during the hearing today.From U.S. Senate Committee on the JudiciaryTennessee Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn confronted Zuckerberg on internal Meta documents suggesting that the company estimates the lifetime value of a teen user at $270.“How could you possibly even have that thought? It is astounding to me,” Blackburn said, before recognizing a group of youth advocates in the audience and inviting them to stand.When they did so, the advocates revealed that they were wearing T-shirts emblazoned with the slogan, “I am worth more than $270.”“Children are not your priority. Children are your product,” Blackburn told Zuckerberg in the tense exchange.Audience members attending the US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, "Big Tech and the Online Child Sexual Exploitation Crisis," in Washington, DC, on January 31.Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesRead moreLink Copied!Meta platforms have become "killing field for the truth," GOP Sen. Kennedy saysFrom CNN's Aditi SangalSenator John Kennedy during the US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing "Big Tech and the Online Child Sexual Exploitation Crisis" in Washington, DC, today.From U.S. Senate Committee on the JudiciaryLouisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy said Meta platforms have become a “killing field of information” where users “see only one side of an issue.”“You have convinced over 2 billion people to give up all of their personal information — every bit of it — in exchange for getting to see what their high school friends had for dinner Saturday night,” he said. “And you take this information, this abundance of personal information and then you develop algorithms to punch people’s hot buttons … again and again and again, to keep them coming back and to keep them staying longer. He did not immediately put himself forward as a candidate to succeed President Volodymyr Zelensky.Credit...Jędrzej Nowicki for The New York TimesByKim BarkerReporting from Kyiv, UkraineAug. 19, 2026,5:36 a.m. ETUkraine’s popular former defense minister has called for wartime elections in Ukraine, setting up a potential confrontation with President Volodymyr Zelensky, the man who fired him last month.After Russiainvaded in February 2022, elections in Ukraine were suspended under martial law. Opposing political parties and some Ukrainians have grumbled about Mr. Zelensky’s hold on power, which has extended for more than seven years, but rallied behind him because of the war.The first major crack in that largely unified front appeared on Tuesday evening, when the former defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, whose firing prompted sustained protests against Mr. Zelensky, posteda nine-minute videoon social media. In it, Mr. Fedorov argued that Ukraine was facing a systemic crisis of governance.Ukrainians, Mr. Fedorov said, need to be able to exercise their democratic rights despite the war with Russia. He did not directly put himself forward as a candidate to succeed Mr. Zelensky. But the video of Mr. Fedorov, dressed in a black military-style shirt, dramatically spotlighted at a wooden desk, had the feel of a campaign declaration.“Can Russia effectively be given the right to dictate when Ukrainians can choose their government again?” Mr. Fedorov said. “I am convinced that the answer is no. Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia. title: Chinese Comic Investigated After Singing a Riff of a Patriotic Song

The comedy genre, also known as xiangsheng, mixes scripted and improvised sketches.Credit...Shiho Fukada for The New York TimesByYan ZhuangAug. 19, 2026,5:15 a.m. ETAd-libbing during a routine is standard for many comedians. But in China, it can land performers in hot water. That was the case for one of the country’s most famous comics, Guo Degang, who is under official investigation for riffing on the lyrics of a famous patriotic song during a show.Mr. Guo has drawn comparisons to the likes of Ricky Gervais, and has starred in movies and hosted TV shows in China. After a show in Wuhan in July, he was reported to city’s culture and tourism bureau for singing a modified version of the song, which hails the bravery of Chinese soldiers during a historic battle against Japan.His case highlights the delicate line comedians must tread in a heavily censored creative landscape. The comedy scene provides a rare venue for indirect criticisms about contemporary life in China; but the space for self-expression is becoming increasingly narrow as China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, has made arts and culture a focus for ideological crackdowns.The bureau launched an investigation into Mr. Guo last week after receiving a complaint, according to The Paper, a popular Shanghai-based state-backed newspaper. The bureau said it was looking into whether he had violated a regulation under which performers must have their sets vetted by officials in advance, the outlet reported.An official who answered the phone at the Hubei Culture and Tourism Bureau, in the province encompassing Wuhan, confirmed the investigation against Mr. Guo on Tuesday. He described the matter as sensitive, but did not provide more details. A show Mr. Guo was scheduled to perform in the city of Xi’an was postponed, according to asocial media postby the theater that was going to host it. Organizers have not announced if it will be rescheduled.Mr. Guo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Mr. Guo, 53, is credited with reviving cross talk, or xiangsheng, a comedy genre that mixes scripted and improvised sketches that originated in the Qing dynasty. Mr. Amro said that his customers owed him around $155,000 and that he was struggling to pay suppliers.Credit...Samar Hazboun for The New York TimesByAdam RasgonDavid M. HalbfingerandFatima AbdulKarimReporting from Ramallah, West BankAug. 18, 2026Israeli pressure on the West Bank has sent the occupied territory to the brink of financial collapse as severe restrictions have touched every part of daily life and caused an economic crisis.Sincethe Hamas-led attackon Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has stopped thousands of Palestinians from working in Israel, withheld billions of dollars of tax revenues and enforced banking restrictions that have harmed business.The Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the West Bank, has been forced to cut spending on salaries and public services because of the sharp fall in revenues. The reductions have been felt acutely in sectors such as health care, with pharmacies routinely running out of medicines as the government allocates less money to buy them. The budget cuts have also forced clinics to open only a few days a week and hospitals to operate with fewer doctors and nurses.Ibtisam Hammad, 54, was diagnosed with breast cancer three months ago. After a hospital appointment in the West Bank city of Ramallah, she made her way to a pharmacy to collect her medications. Only three of her six prescriptions were in stock.“I’m lucky,” Ms. Hammad said, smiling despite her exhaustion. “Last time, they only had one.”Ms. Hammad’s trouble getting medicines was indicative of wider economic problems. The Palestinian Authority has often warned of a financial collapse that never materialized, but there are growing concerns about how long it can remain solvent.“We’re facing a huge problem,” Mohammed Mustafa, the authority’s prime minister, said in an interview. “Everyone has been affected.”Unemployment rate in the West BankSource: Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics.Adina Renner/The New York TimesWe are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. title: At Ex-Premier Zhu Rongji’s Funeral, China’s Past Shadows Its Present
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTAt Ex-Premier’s Funeral, China’s Past Shadows Its PresentBeijing wants to portray today’s China as carrying forward Zhu Rongji’s era of growth, but for many Chinese, the optimism of that time has since faded.Listen· 6:24 minShare full article26The Chinese flag flying at half-staff at Tiananmen Square in Beijing on Tuesday for the former premier Zhu Rongji.Credit...Maxim Shemetov/ReutersByYan ZhuangAug. 18, 2026阅读简体中文版閱讀繁體中文版China lowered flags to half-staff across the country on Tuesday to mourn the former premier Zhu Rongji, the last of a generation of politicians who guided China toward a market-based economy, fueling extraordinary growth but also leaving behind deep inequalities.The country’s top leaders, including President Xi Jinping, paid their respects to Mr. Zhu, who died last Wednesday at 97, at his official funeral in Beijing, according to the state news media. Mr. Zhu’s body was cremated.Deaths of senior leaders are delicate occasions in Chinese politics because they can be used to express veiled criticisms of the current leadership. Mr. Zhu’s funeral has an additional element of sensitivity: Just a day earlier, Beijing celebrated the centenary of the birth of Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader whom Mr. Zhu worked under in the 1990s. Mr. Jiang died in 2022.Mr. Jiang’s commemoration and Mr. Zhu’s funeral, together, have prompted nostalgia for their era, which saw some of China’s most consequential economic change, experts said. That can invite comparisons the Chinese Communist Party probably wants to avoid, they said, between a past that felt more optimistic and purposeful and a present sense of malaise and uncertainty.Under Mr. Xi’s leadership, the party has invested heavily in certain tech industries, supporting factories that churn out semiconductors and electric cars to feed a global boom. But many ordinary Chinese are feeling squeezed. A long-running property crisis has dragged down the economy, and job prospects for young people have shrunk. The party has also tightened its grip on private companies, adding to the uncertainty facing the entrepreneurs and investors who once drove China’s growth.Referring to Mr. Xi, Joseph Torigian, an associate professor at American University who studies China’s political elite, said, “He doesn’t want this moment to raise questions about what he’s doing.”We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. title: Queen Camilla Says It Was ‘Difficult’ to Keep Charles’s Cancer a Secret
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTQueen Camilla Says It Was ‘Difficult’ to Keep Charles’s Cancer a Secret“I was just longing to let it out,” Camilla said in rare public comments about the king’s 2024 diagnosis, which was not immediately revealed. “But obviously I couldn’t.”Listen· 2:14 minShare full articleQueen Camilla in 2024, visiting a London support center run by Maggie’s, a cancer charity where she serves as president.Credit...Pool photo by Paul GroverByAmelia NierenbergReporting from LondonAug. 19, 2026,7:28 a.m. ETIn a video released on Wednesday, Queen Camilla made rare public comments about King Charles III’scancer, talking about how difficult his diagnosis had been for her, especially in the days before Buckingham Palace made the news public.“I was just longing to let it out,” Camilla said in thevideo, which was released by the British royal family and by a leading U.K. cancer charity,Maggie’s, of which Camilla is the president.“But, obviously, I couldn’t,” she added.Camilla was reflecting on a 2024 visit with cancer patients and their families, which she made shortly after Charles’s cancer was diagnosed — but before the palace had made an official announcement.The queen, who has been involved with Maggie’s for years, had often made such visits. But this time was different, she said: She was there not just as a figurehead, but as another worried spouse.“I was almost questioning them,” Camilla said. She held back, she said, because she “didn’t want to pry too deeply.”With Charles’s condition still a secret, she could not tell the others that they were all experiencing the fear and uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis. Holding back was “quite difficult,” she said in the video, which was released to mark the charity’s 30th anniversary.“I almost said something,” she added, “but I felt that it wasn’t the time.”It is rare for members of the royal family to speak publicly about their private lives. Since 2024, they have dealt not just with Charles’s diagnosis but with that ofCatherine, the Princess of Wales, who announced weeks later that she, too, was battling cancer.Neither royal has disclosed what type of cancer they have. Both have since returned to public life and have used their diagnoses toadvocate for cancer patientsand speak about the emotional challenges of facing the disease.In December, when Charles told the British public that he was doing well and could scale back his treatment, he said it was “a testimony to the remarkable advances that have been made in cancer care in recent years.”Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.Share full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

title: Barred From Ballot, a Party Becomes a Vessel for Russians’ Discontent

He added: “Are you really going to take the metro? Wow!”It was Friday, and Mr. Rybakov had just filed an appeal of a court decision to remove his party, Yabloko, from the ballot for next month’s parliamentary elections — a decision that the country’s Supreme Court would go on to uphold on Monday. Putin’s presidency.Yabloko’s last-minute disqualification suggested that the Kremlin had belatedly realized not only how unpopular the war was but also that the party could become a vessel for that discontent.A recent pollfound that Russians wanting peace negotiations outnumbered those who favor continued fighting by more than two to one.Mr. Rybakov said the reason for the party’s newfound popularity was people’s growing fatigue with what looked like an endless and fruitless war. title: American Hiker Dies After Lightning Strike on Mount Etna in Italy
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTAmerican Hiker Dies After Lightning Strike on Mount Etna in ItalyRescuers found a 29-year-old man in serious condition on the volcano’s eastern slope on Sunday. He was later pronounced dead at a hospital in Catania.Listen· 2:58 minShare full articleVolcanic activity at Mount Etna as seen from Mareneve near Catania in Italy last week. Italian authorities say a 29-year-old American hiker was killed by lightning while hiking on Europe’s most active volcano.Credit...Salvatore Allegra/Associated PressByLeo SandsandJosephine de La BruyèreJosephine de La Bruyère reported from Rome.PublishedAug. 17, 2026UpdatedAug. 19, 2026,4:45 a.m. ETAn American man died after being struck by lightning while hiking on Mount Etna in Italy, emergency officials said on Monday.Rescuers found the 29-year-old man in serious condition on Sunday on the eastern side of Mount Etna, Europe’s largest active volcano, the local fire department said in a statement. Firefighters transported him by helicopter to Cannizzaro Hospital in Catania, the nearest major city, on the east coast of Sicily.The hospital identified the man as Dylan Standfast of Wichita, Kan. Relatives of Mr. Standfast could not immediately be reached.The man arrived at the hospital in a state of cardiac arrest and was declared dead about an hour later, hospital officials said in a statement.According to local fire officials, the hiker was found alone in an area known as Valle del Bove that was closed to the public. The valley had been rocked by an unusually heavy bout of volcanic activity in recent days, prompting the local authorities to close some of the area.On Monday, Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanologyreported that another volcanic vent had openedin the valley, with fresh lava flowing overnight.Theinternational airport in Catania saidearly Monday that it was imposing limits on the number of flights arriving until Tuesday afternoon as a result of the volume of ash being released into the atmosphere by Mount Etna. Seismic activity at the volcano — which is just 30 miles, or about 48 kilometers, from the airport — hadforced hundreds of cancellations and delaysfor more than 10 days.While thunderstorms had been forecast for Sicily on Sunday, lightning can be generated by volcanic eruptions, according to theNational Weather Service. During a volcanic eruption, tiny collisions among the rising particles of ash can create static electricity, which may in turn produce volcanic lightning. During an eruption of Mount Etna in August 2023,Italy’s National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanologyreported lightning within the ash clouds.According to the Italian health authorities, lightning strikes in the country are particularly common in July and August. Arecent studyshowed that some 89 people were killed by lightning strikes in Italy from 2001 to 2020.During thunderstorms, people in elevated areas such as mountain ridges and summits can be particularly exposed to lightning,according to the National Weather Service.The U.S. consulate in Naples, which has jurisdiction over the region of Sicily, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Nazaneen Ghaffarcontributed reporting.Leo Sands is a correspondent for the Breaking News Hub of The New York Times based in London.Share full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTLiechtenstein Changes Its Law to Allow Women to Ascend the ThroneThe move puts the principality in the majority among nearby nations with royal families.Listen· 3:39 minShare full articleHereditary Prince Alois of Liechtenstein, arriving at the country’s National Day celebrations in Vaduz, the capital, on Saturday.Credit...Romina Amato/ReutersByEphrat LivniAug. 16, 2026Of the roughly four dozen countries where royal families reign, two have wrestled this summer with questions of gender and succession in the modern era, taking starkly different approaches.Liechtenstein, a tiny nation of about 40,000 people wedged between Switzerland and Austria in the Alps, took one route: On Saturday, it announced that women would now be able to become the monarch and wield the broad political power of the throne.The Princely House of Liechtenstein said in a statement that it was shifting from male-only succession to absolute primogeniture, making the future firstborn child of the ruling royal family heir to the throne, regardless of gender.“With this legislative amendment, we wish to ensure that both the Principality of Liechtenstein and the Princely House are governed by the person best prepared for this task,” said Hereditary Prince Alois, the country’s de facto leader. The sons and daughters of the reigning royal “are familiarized from their youth with the unique characteristics of the Principality and the Princely House,” and will “in principle,” be best suited for the ruling role, he said.Prince Alois, 58, is theson of the reigning Prince Hans-Adam, 81, and he has for more than two decades served as his father’s deputy, handling the duties of head of state in his place. He is a father of four, with an elder son, a daughter and two younger sons, but the rule change does not apply to them or anyone already born. It will apply to all future births, Prince Alois told the local news media.Liechtenstein’s move to adopt equal succession rights puts it in the majority among nearby nations with royal families.We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. A vast army of online trolls has stalked her since.They called it a play for attention by Ms. Ahir, 27, a Mumbai-based model and actor. They insinuated that she sold sexually explicit content behind a paywall on Instagram. They circulated a video of her diving into the sea in a bikini. They flooded her social media accounts with slurs and rape threats.Ms. Ahir has chosen to rise above it.“You’re not scared of someone who is telling you online that ‘I’m going to rip you apart the day I see you,’” she said. “I’m trying not to reply to any of them, just letting them do their thing and show their face to the world.”Thousands of young womenhave participated in nationwide protestsdemanding accountability from the government for a flawed education system. But in the two months since the demonstrations started, they have been doxxed and bombarded online by people who have called them immoral, threatened sexual abuse and acid attacks, and used artificial intelligence to create demeaning images. A majority of the attacks have come from accounts, many anonymous, that push Hindu right-wing ideology and pitch themselves as custodians of religious morality. He has served for 15 years as a Roman Catholic priest in the mountainous region of Italy.Credit...Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTListen· 13:23 minShare full article101ByMotoko RichandJosephine de La BruyèrePhotographs byAlessandro GrassaniMotoko Rich and Josephine de La Bruyère spent a weekend with the Rev. Vincent Souly as he toured his parishes.Aug. 16, 2026Leer en españolThe priest stepped into the bedroom where his 90-year-old parishioner lay sleeping in a hospital bed, flanked by oxygen tanks. The pastor towered over the bed and leaned down to move close to the patient, Carlo Martini, as the old man’s eyes fluttered open briefly.“How are you?” the priest, the Rev. Vincent Souly, asked, a bit too loudly.Mr. Martini’s wife, Renza Giagnoni, stood to the side and watched. “It looks like we’re the United Nations!” she said, also a bit too loudly.Father Souly is one of the few Black faces in the province of Prato, a mountainous region of Tuscany, in central Italy, where he has served for 15 years as a Roman Catholic priest. He has built warm relationships with his predominantly Italian flocks and is embraced by many parishioners. Born in Burkina Faso, and raised and ordained in the Ivory Coast, he is now an Italian citizen and is committed to staying in Prato as long as he is needed. Yet, he said, his Italian passport does not necessarily make others see him as Italian.“Where I’m from, we say, ‘A piece of wood, no matter how long it stays in water, will never become a crocodile,’” he said. “You’re accepted, up to a point. But there’s this unspoken part, right? You remain what you are.”He felt a flash of that otherness when Ms. Giagnoni referred to the United Nations, he told us later, or when parishioners referred to him as a “prete di colore” or “priest of color.”He would prefer that people refer to him by his country of origin rather than by the color of his skin, he said. “When you say, ‘He is an African priest,’ it’s already more elegant, it’s more cultured,” he said. “That means that you’ve tried to locate where Africa is on the world map. If you say, ‘He is from the Ivory Coast,’ that’s even better. Using the color is a shortcut.”We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. title: Bou Meng, Rare Survivor of Khmer Rouge Torture House, Dies at 85
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTBou Meng, Rare Survivor of Khmer Rouge Torture House, Dies at 85Saved by his ability to paint, he was one of only a handful of prisoners to make it out of the brutal prison Tuol Sleng.Listen· 5:53 minShare full articleBou Meng, who was imprisoned at the notorious Khmer Rouge interrogation and torture facility Tuol Sleng, in 2009 at the prison, which became a genocide museum.Credit...Seth Mydans/The New York TimesBySeth MydansPublishedAug. 15, 2026UpdatedAug. 17, 2026Bou Meng, a Cambodian painter who was one of only a handful of prisoners to survive the Khmer Rouge interrogation and torture house Tuol Sleng, and who later became a fixture at the genocide museum on the site, died on Friday at his home in the village of Thommeak Trai in Kandal Province, Cambodia, about 30 miles from the capital, Phnom Penh. He was 85.The death was announced by the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum. The cause was complications of a stroke he suffered earlier this year.Late in his life, Mr. Bou Meng was one of four living symbols of the Khmer Rouge atrocities that left 1.7 million people dead between 1975 and 1979.Together with another Tuol Sleng survivor who returned to the prison, a mechanic named Chum Mey, he personified the victims. A few miles down the road, the last two surviving leaders of the Khmer Rouge regime were tried. They were convicted of crimes against humanity in 2014 and of genocide in 2018; Nuon Cheadied in 2019, and Khieu Samphan remains in prison.Some 14,000 people were arrested and interrogated at Tuol Sleng, also known as S-21, and almost all were sent to a killing field. As Huy Vannak describes in his 2010 biography, “Bou Meng: A Survivor From Khmer Rouge Prison S-21,” Mr. Bou Meng was spared, after two months of imprisonment and seven days of torture, when a guard called out to a group of shackled prisoners, “Can anyone paint pictures?”Mr. Bou Meng was assigned to paint portraits of the Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, as well as of Marx and Lenin, fearing for his life if he made a mistake. title: U.S. Will Try California Arson Suspect Again After Stunning Mistrial
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTU.S. Will Try California Arson Suspect Again After Stunning MistrialThe man accused of setting the blaze that later turned deadly in the Pacific Palisades is now readying for a new prosecution after a previous effort in June failed.Listen· 3:26 minShare full articleResidents are still displaced more than a year and a half after the fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes in the wealthy Pacific Palisades section.Credit...Philip Cheung for The New York TimesByMaia SpotoAug. 19, 2026,5:02 a.m. ETFederal prosecutors are trying again to convict a 30-year-old man accused of starting one of the most destructive fires in California history, recasting the charges against him after a stunning mistrial.The effort reflects a push for accountability after the deadly 2025 Palisades fire, even after 10 of 12 jurors voted in June to find the man, Jonathan Rinderknecht, not guilty. A federal judgedeclared a mistrial.Prosecutors filed a new indictment on Aug. 13, shaving the number of arson-related felony charges against Mr. Rinderknecht from three to two. One now focuses solely on the Lachman fire, which began on New Year’s and which investigators say smoldered for a week before exploding into the Palisades blaze.Mr. Rinderknecht now faces felony charges of one count of destruction of property using fire — specifically the Lachman fire — and one of arson affecting property used in interstate commerce, which relates to both the Lachman and Palisades fires.An arraignment is scheduled Wednesday in a downtown Los Angeles federal courtroom before Judge Anne Hwang of the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. Mr. Rinderknecht’s retrial is set to begin Oct. 19.At Mr. Rinderknecht’s first trial, the prosecution argued that Mr. Rinderknecht had resented the rich and started the fire with a lighter as “societal revenge.”But Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer argued that New Year’s fireworks had set it off.Prosecutors said that Mr. Rinderknecht had been angry that he hadn’t secured plans for the holiday, and his Uber passengers from that night testified that he ranted about capitalism. Late that night, Mr. Rinderknecht hiked up a Pacific Palisades trail near where the Lachman fire began.As the blaze grew, he called 911 more than a dozen times. Prosecutors said he was trying to cover his tracks. Mr. Rinderknecht’s lawyer, Steven Haney, said it would be “self-destructive and idiotic” for an arsonist to call the authorities rather than leaving immediately.Mr. Haney at the trial said there were gaps in the government’s case. The scene was left unprotected for 12 days, destroying evidence; of 9,000 or so videos compiled in the investigation, none caught the ignition; and no one identified the exact time the fire started, he said.To Dave Ring, a Los Angeles-based civil lawyer who has no interest in the case, the revised charges represent a “distinction without a difference” and prosecutors will still face steep challenges.“I think their case still is going to be incredibly difficult to win,” he said.Regardless of the outcome of Mr. Rinderknecht’s case, the city of Los Angeles and other government agencies could still face civil liability for failures during the fire.Many residents are still displaced more than a year and a half after the fire killed 12 people and destroyed thousands of homes in the wealthy Pacific Palisades section of Los Angeles.Maia Spoto is a reporter covering disability issues for The Times and part of the 2026-27Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.Share full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

title: 5 Things to Know About Mary Peltola, Democratic Senate Candidate in Alaska
content: TakeawaysKey Race ResultsHow Results WorkCompetitive RacesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENT5 Things to Know About the Alaska Senate Candidate Mary PeltolaThe Alaska Native, who grew up along the Kuskokwim River near the Bering Sea and fished for salmon, is the leading Democrat in the nonpartisan primary race.Share full articleMary Peltola won a special election to replace Don Young in Congress in 2022 and was elected to a full term later that year.Credit...Ash Adams for The New York TimesByMichael KruseAug. 18, 2026Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native and moderate former congresswoman running on a platform she describes as “fish, family and freedom,” is the leading Democrat in Alaska’s nonpartisan primary election on Tuesday.The top four finishers regardless of party will advance to the general election in November. To have a shot at taking back control of the Senate, Democrats almost certainly will need Ms. Peltola to beat Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent.Here are five things to know about Ms. Peltola.She is Yup’ik.Ms. Peltola’s father, Ward Sattler, a teacher and bush pilot, moved to Alaska from Nebraska. Her mother, LizAnn Piicigaq Williams, was a member of the Yup’ik group of Indigenous peoples of western Alaska. Ms. Peltola grew up along the Kuskokwim River near the Bering Sea, fishing for salmon, picking berries and eating seal and moose meat. In 1995, she won the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant, a competition in which she wore a squirrel skin parka and a wolf hair headdress.She has been in and around politics for years.Ms. Peltola, 52, grew up going to events for Don Young, the longtime Republican congressman, because her father was friends with him. After attending four different colleges — she never graduated — she ran for the State House in 1996 and lost. She ran again in 1998 and won. Representing Bethel, 400 miles from Anchorage and nearly 1,000 miles from the capital of Juneau, she spent a decade in the state legislature. She was elected to Congress in a special election in 2022 to replace Mr. Young after his death and was elected later that year to a full term. She was the first Democrat to hold the seat in a half-century, the first woman to represent Alaska in the U.S. House and the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress. title: Eric Barlow Wins Wyoming’s Republican Governor Primary Over Trump-Backed Candidate
content: TakeawaysKey Race ResultsHow Results WorkCompetitive RacesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTRancher Beats Trump-Backed Candidate in Primary for Governor of WyomingEric Barlow’s defeat of Megan Degenfelder, the state superintendent of education, again showed the limits of the president’s favor.Listen· 3:21 minShare full articleEric Barlow, a Wyoming state senator, at a campaign stop in Jackson, Wyo.Credit...Charlie Nick/Jackson Hole News & GuideByJack HealyAug. 18, 2026Eric Barlow, a rancher and state senator in Wyoming, won the Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, The Associated Press said, beating a candidate endorsed by President Trump in one of the country’s most staunchly Republican states.Mr. Barlow’s victory means he is all but certain to become the next governor of Wyoming, where Republicans hold every statewide office, and voters gave Mr. Trump his largest margin of victory in the 2024 presidential election.This year, legislative races in Wyoming have turned into a contest between the right and far right as ultraconservative candidatespushed to take controlof the State Senate, where more moderate Republicans have held sway. Mr. Barlow ran a campaign that focused on problem solving and lowering the temperature of Wyoming’s internecine Republican brawls, in contrast to his Trump-endorsed rival, Megan Degenfelder, who promised to stock state agencies with “bulldogs.” He also defeated Brent Bien, a far-right conservative and retired Marine Corps colonel who won the endorsement of the Wyoming Republican Party.Mr. Barlow’s victory suggested that Wyoming’s heavily Republican electorate preferred a lower-key leader similar to the incumbent governor, Mark Gordon, rather than a bomb-throwing conservative or culture warrior. Mr. Gordon, a mainstream Republican, is leaving office after two terms.His win also showed the limits of Mr. Trump’s power to tilt a Republican primary in a sparsely populated rural state where many voters make up their minds by chatting with candidates at barbecues, county fairs and rodeos.Ms. Degenfelder, Wyoming’s state superintendent of public instruction, touted the president’s support, her battles “against the radicals’ agenda” and her advocacy of the state’s ban on transgender athletes in girls’ sports.Mr. Barlow is widely expected to win in November against the Democratic nominee, Ken Casner, a Vietnam veteran who runs a retail shop and cafe.Mr. Barlow, often sporting a white cowboy hat, ran as a “fourth-generation ranch kid” who served in the Marines before rising through the ranks of Wyoming politics, where he spent two years as speaker of the State House.Mr. Barlow emphasized his support for public lands — an issue that unites conservative hunters and liberal environmentalists in the American West — and vowed to change the tone of Wyoming’s increasingly bitter politics.In onememorable videocritical of the negative mailers swamping voters, Mr. Barlow — who is also a veterinarian — pulled on a long plastic glove, reached into a mailbox and retrieved a pile of yak dung.Mr. Barlow and Ms. Degenfelder promised a continuation of the Republican policies that have dominated Wyoming for years. Both oppose abortion, and they vowed to support the mining and energy industries that drive much of the state’s economy while also shoring up its struggling rural health care systems.Jack Healy is based in Colorado and covers the west and southwest for The Times.Share full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

title: Natalie Harp, Trump’s Most Devoted Aide, Is Always by His Side. What Exactly Does She Do?

She works out of the Oval Office and she’s got a regular seat on Marine One. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She stays up late with him drafting social media posts.She rarely speaks on camera and yet she is never not there, ever-present with a wide smile and her eyes fixed on the president.She is Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old West Wing aide who is the utmost gatekeeper to President Trump, a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command. The public’s interest in Ms. Harp exploded after she was revealed last week to be one of the lucky few who joined the president inside an airplane catering container to be whisked out of Turkey under threat of attack by Iran.This week she became the subject of a political attack line delivered by Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia, who said of the president: “He doesn’t want to do the job. White House aides, lawmakers on Capitol Hill, conservative influencers and at least one cabinet member took to the ramparts on X to defend Ms. Harp’s honor. There were accusations of sexism from the right and cries of snowflakery from the left. Mr. Trump deflected when a reporter from CNN asked him about Mr. Ossoff’s comments. But a social media account run by the administration then attacked the reporter in unusually personal terms, invoking her children.The furor intensified the spotlight on this seldom-heard-from and sylphlike woman who has long fascinated and frustrated people around the president. title: California Passes New Rule Regulating Replacement Car Tires
content: AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTCalifornia Becomes First State to Regulate the Squish of Car TiresThe rule to require efficient replacement tires was praised by environmentalists. But manufacturers warned that the change would hurt American companies and increase tire prices.Listen· 5:28 minShare full article67California’s efficiency standards for replacement vehicle tires will take full effect in 2033.Credit...Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesBySoumya KarlamanglaAug. 18, 2026California already has strict rules on how much pollution vehicles can release through exhaust pipes, how many toxic metals that brake pads can shed onto streets and how quickly carmakers must transition to electric fleets.This week, California added another to the list: how much tires can squish as they roll along the road.California this week became the first state in the nation to set energy-efficient standards for replacement car tires, which the state says will both lower fuel consumption and cut greenhouse gas emissions. The move comes as gas prices remain high as the war with Iran continues and as the Republican-led federal government tries toundermine other fuel efficiency effortsin California.At issue is the concept of rolling resistance, a measure of how much a tire deforms from the pressure of hitting the road. The more the tire squishes, the more work it is for the car to keep the wheels turning — and the more fuel the vehicle burns. (For a similar reason, it requires more energy to pedal a bicycle with half-inflated tires than one with fully inflated ones.)Replacement tires typically have more rolling resistance than the tires that cars are sold with, which tends to result in fewer miles per gallon. That’s because auto manufacturers often use more efficient tires on new models in order to meet vehicle emissions standards. But drivers tend to be price conscious when they buy replacement tires and sacrifice efficiency for cost.The new rule, which the California Energy Commission approved on Monday, requires that replacement tires sold in the state have the same rolling resistance on average as the tires sold with new vehicles by 2033. The rule will be phased in, with the first set of changes required by 2029. Currently, only about 30 percent of tires meet the 2033 standards, according to Nancy Skinner, a state energy commissioner.We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. title: 5 Things to Know About Ashley Moody, Republican Senate Candidate in Florida
content: TakeawaysKey Race ResultsHow Results WorkCompetitive RacesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENT5 Things to Know About Senator Ashley Moody of FloridaThe Republican incumbent has President Trump’s support, but has little name recognition to many in her state.Share full articleSenator Ashley Moody, Republican of Florida, won the Republican Senate primary on Tuesday.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York TimesByPatricia MazzeiReporting from MiamiAug. 18, 2026Senator Ashley Moody, who is defending her seat for the first time, won the Republican Senate primary in Florida on Tuesday.Here are five things to know about Ms. Moody, 51, who is serving her second year in the Senate.1. She was appointed to the Senate by Gov. Ron DeSantis.Mr. DeSantis, a Republican,named Ms. Moody, a loyal ally, to replace Marco Rubio in the Senate once Mr. Rubio was about to be confirmed as secretary of state. At the time, Ms. Moody was the state’s attorney general, having been elected in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. Mr. DeSantis praised her “demonstrated record of delivering results.”2. She is running with President Trump’s endorsement — and without major Republican opposition.Mr. Trump endorsed Ms. Moody in July 2025 and reiterated his support for heragain last week, saying that she is “doing a tremendous job.” Ms. Moody’s Senate appointment made her an immediate favorite in the election to finish the remainder of Mr. Rubio’s term, and no well-known Republican candidates challenged her in the primary.3. She remains little-known to many Florida voters.Despite having won two statewide races, Ms. Moody, polls have shown, has relatively low name recognition for an incumbent, a risk for any politician seeking re-election. But Florida Republicans have huge advantages over Democrats in voter registration, fund-raising and field organizing. And Ms. Moody, her supporters point out, has been underestimated in the past — and won.4. She is a quieter candidate in a state of big personalities.Some Republicans have worried that Ms. Moody, whom they consider deliberate and effective,is too cautious a campaigner. Her style is much different from those of the gregarious Mr. Rubio and the indefatigable Senator Rick Scott, a fellow Republican. Since Ms. Moody would be assuming a prominent role on the Republican ticket in a year that the party could face mounting losses in the midterm elections, some Republicans hope to see more of her ahead of the November general election.5. She is a fifth-generation Floridian.Before being elected attorney general, Ms. Moody was a circuit court judge in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, for about a decade. She had earlier worked as a federal prosecutor, and is married to a law enforcement officer.Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.Share full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

title: When to Expect Election Results in Alaska, California, Florida and Wyoming

Polls there will close at 8 p.m. Eastern.Results will likely be in late on Tuesday, officials say, based on how quickly votes were counted and reported in the state’s last primary. Readers can follow along here withThe New York Times’s vote tracker.Results will be certified when the state’s election canvassing commission convenes, on Sept. 1.WyomingIn Wyoming, polls will close at 7 p.m. local time (9 p.m. Eastern), at which point counties will begin tabulating early votes and those that came in on Election Day. Election officials anticipate that most results will be known late on Tuesday night.You can watch the results come in on Tuesday night withThe Times’s vote tracker. The state canvassing board will meet on Sept. 1 to certify the tallies.CaliforniaCalifornia is holding a special general election to fill former Representative Eric Swalwell’s vacated House seat.Polls will close at 8 p.m. local time (11 p.m. Eastern), at which point the state’s election officials will begin tallying the votes they received through early voting and mail ballots.
