content: Top Candidates Advance in Alaska Senate Race as Democratic Socialist Scores Florida UpsetA Democratic former congresswoman will face Alaska’s incumbent Republican senator in November. In Florida, Angie Nixon overcame a huge fund-raising disadvantage to defeat Alex Vindman.PublishedAug. 18, 2026UpdatedAug. 19, 2026,7:55 a.m. ETShare full articleLatestPinnedTim BalkHere’s the latest.A pivotal Senate race in Alaska took shape, a democratic socialist won a stunning upset in a Democratic Senate primary in Florida and President Trump faced endorsement setbacks as a series of primary contests were held across the country Tuesday.In Alaska, Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, and former Representative Mary Peltola, a well-funded Democrat, advanced in the state’s nonpartisan primary. Both parties consider that race critical in the battle for Senate control. In Florida, State Representative Angie Nixon, the democratic socialist, defeated Alex Vindman, who raised 16 times as much money as she did. It was thelatest primary victoryfor the Democratic Party’s ascendant left wing.“This win was for the little guys and girls,” Ms. Nixon told jubilant supporters in Jacksonville.As of early Wednesday, results were still coming in after a day featuring primaries in three states — Alaska, Florida and Wyoming — and a special election in Northern California to fill the seat of former Representative Eric Swalwell, whoresigned in the spring. That race had not been called.Mr. Trump’s endorsement, a powerful force in Republican primaries, was not enough to lift candidates in Florida and Wyoming.Representative Cory Mills of Florida, a Trump-endorsed Republican under investigation by the House Ethics Committee after an assault allegation,was defeatedby Ryan Elijah, who was backed by some House Republicans. (Mr. Mills denies any wrongdoing.)Catalina Lauf, a health care entrepreneur supported by Mr. Trump,fell to the media mogulJim Schwartzel in a primary race to replace Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor.And Mr. Trump’s pick for Wyoming governor, Megan Degenfelder, wasdefeatedby State Senator Eric Barlow. That endorsement defeat came in a state Mr. Trump won by 46 percentage pointsin the 2024, his largest margin of victory in any state.In the race to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, who is term-limited, RepublicansnominatedMr. Donalds, who is backed by Mr. Trump. Democratsput their hopesin former Representative David Jolly, a onetime Republican. Florida has not elected a Democratic governor since the 1990s.If elected, Mr. Donalds would be the state’s first Black governor. Ms. Nixon, who will face a difficult path in the Senate race, would be the state’s first Black senator.House primaries in Florida played out in districts newly gerrymandered by Republicans. Two Democratic representatives running in new districts, Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Jared Moskowitz, fended off progressive challengers.But Ms. Nixon delivered her party’s left wing a surprise victory. Her candidacy will test how far a democratic socialist can go in an increasingly Republican state; Florida has several large Latin American communities that have long been skeptical of socialism.Here’s what we’re watching:The Other Sullivan:Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who Republicans have accused of entering the Alaska Senate race as a spoiler, was leading the lesser-known candidates competing for the remaining two spots on the four-person ballot as of Tuesday night local time.Read more ›Replacement for Swalwell:In San Francisco’s sleepy suburbs, voters were choosing between Aisha Wahab, a progressive state lawmaker, and Melissa Hernandez, a moderate Democrat supported by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’smain super PAC.The race was too close to call early Wednesday.Deceptive ads:In Alaska’s primary, advertisements may not have been as they seemed. An intensifying trend of election meddling appeared to havegone into overdrive in the state.A district divide:Ms. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who is white, wonher primaryin a historically Black congressional district after the Republican gerrymander eliminated her district. Shedefeated four Black Democrats.Show moreAug. 19, 2026, 2:16 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaAt an aviation museum in Anchorage, Senator Dan Sullivan celebrated advancing to the general election and portrayed himself as a grass-roots candidate focused on local issues, while accusing “D.C. Democrats” and “Lower 48 liberals” of funding his opponent, Mary Peltola. Sullivan is also benefiting from significant spending by Republicans outside Alaska. He criticized Peltola’s recent staff shake-up, saying “My campaign’s not melting down like some other campaigns.”Aug. 19, 2026, 1:27 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaPeltola spoke briefly to supporters at a brewery in Anchorage, thanking them for their work and taking aim at Senator Dan Sullivan as she turned toward the general election. She did not take questions from reporters, even as she shook hands with volunteers before leaving the event.ImageCredit...Ash Adams for The New York TimesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 19, 2026, 1:22 a.m. ETChristine ZhangElection Data ReporterThe first batches of results from Alaska included about half of the expected vote inall three statewide races. The results include ballots cast on Election Day and early votes cast through Thursday. Most mail ballots, along with early votes cast after Thursday, will be counted in the coming days.Aug. 19, 2026, 1:15 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaAs expected, Mary Peltola and Senator Dan Sullivan easily advanced. It’s still early, but Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher whom Republicans have accused of entering the race as a spoiler, is leading the lesser-known candidates competing for the remaining two spots on the four-person ballot.Aug. 19, 2026, 1:15 a.m. ETAnna GriffinA scion of Democratic politics makes the runoff for Alaska governor.ImageTom Begich, one of 17 candidates who ran for governor in Alaska’s primary, will be on the ballot in November.Credit...Ruth Fremson/The New York TimesTom Begich, a singer-songwriter and former state lawmaker with a rich family legacy in state politics, has finished in the top four in the 17-person primary for Alaska governor and will make the runoff in November, The Associated Press said.Another Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, also secured one of the four spots in the general election.Campaigning on a promise to make Alaska more affordable and find new ways to fund public education, Mr. Begich capitalized on his family’s name recognition, endorsements from some of the state’s leading progressive groups and a condensed Democratic field.Mr. Begich’s father, Nick Begich Sr., served in the U.S. House as a Democrat. His brother, Mark Begich, was a Democratic U.S. senator. And his Republican nephew, Nick Begich III, is the state’s current member of the U.S. House.“I love my state, I know what it means to serve this state, and I don’t see us on the right path right now,” Mr. Begich, 65, said in an interview last month. “I think I’m the only one in this race who both understands the challenges facing us and has a plan to solve them.”He and the three other top finishers will compete in a November election that will use ranked-choice voting. Alaskans are selecting a successor to Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican who is barred from seeking a third term.Alaskans have backed President Trump in the last three presidential races, but unaffiliated voters outnumber both Republicans and Democrats, and the Legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents.Show moreAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 19, 2026, 1:13 a.m. ETAnna GriffinA progressive Democrat makes the runoff for Alaska governor.ImageJonathan Kreiss-Tomkins at a coffee shop in Fairbanks, Alaska, last month.Credit...Ruth Fremson/The New York TimesJonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who entered politics as a teenager on Howard Dean’s presidential campaign, won the chance to become the youngest governor in Alaska history by securing one of four spots in the November general election, The Associated Press said.Another Democrat, Tom Begich, also secured one of the four spots, according to The A.P.Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old Democrat, pitched himself as the only candidate capable of bringing together Democrats, Republicans and unaffiliated voters to solve Alaska’s fiscal crisis and population loss. As a five-term Democratic state legislator from Sitka, Alaska, he represented a southeastern district that Republican presidential candidates have consistently won.He was among the top fund-raisers in the17-candidate primary, raising much of his money from out-of-state donors linked to the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, but he also campaigned hard in rural Alaska. That included driving a snowmobile to the Arctic Ocean and riding a skiff 450 miles down the Yukon River.“We’re potentially at a moment where the next governor and the next Legislature will be making decisions similar to the start of the pipeline here,” he said in an interview last month, referring to the Trans-Alaska Pipeline, built five decades ago. “It’s going to take a different approach to do this right.”He and the three other top finishers will compete in a November election that will use ranked-choice voting. Alaskans are selecting a successor to Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican barred from seeking a third term.Alaskans have backed President Trump in the last three presidential races, but unaffiliated voters outnumber both Republicans and Democrats, and the Legislature has been governed for nearly a decade by a coalition of Democrats, Republicans and independents.Show moreAug. 19, 2026, 1:09 a.m. ETWilliam P. DavisAlaska has reported only about a quarter of its votes, but it’s already clear that Mary Peltola and Senator Dan Sullivan will advance to the general election. The other two spots in the state’s top-four primary remain up for grabs, with Dan J. Sullivan — the candidate who shares the incumbent’s name — leading a field of more than a dozen others.Aug. 19, 2026, 1:05 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaPeltola and Sullivan advance in crucial Alaska Senate contest.ImageFormer Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, and Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, will advance to the general election for an Alaska Senate seat.Credit...Kerry Tasker/Reuters; Eric Lee for The New York TimesA high-profile Senate race in Alaska is officially set: Mary Peltola, a Democrat and former congresswoman, and Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, advanced from the state’s top-four nonpartisan primary on Tuesday night local time, according to The Associated Press. They will face off in November in a race that could determine control of the Senate.Ms. Peltola was seen as the only Democrat who could pose a formidable challenge to Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent running in a conservative state known for its independent streak. An Alaska Native, Ms. Peltola is a former commercial fisher and a former state legislator. She rose to political stardom with an upset win for the state’s only House seat in 2022, becoming the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in decades.Both candidates have significant resources at their disposal as their parties gear up for a highly competitive sprint to November. Mr. Sullivan, a Marine veteran who is a supporter of President Trump, has forged strong bonds with the state’s various constituencies during his tenure in the Senate, including Native and fishing groups. But he faces headwinds given Alaska’s high cost of living and citizens’ frustrations with the current administration.One wild card still to be determined is whether a different primary candidate also named Dan Sullivan will advance to the four-person general election ballot. This Mr. Sullivan, a retired teacher from the tiny fishing village of Petersburg, drew criticism from Republicans who decried his candidacy as a Democratic trick meant to confuse voters and split votes with the sitting senator. The Republican-run state elections division removed him from the ballot this summer before being overruled by the courts.The lesser-known Mr. Sullivan has insisted that his long-shot bid is legitimate and not a ruse. If he advances to the ballot in November, he could play a spoiler role in a state with just about 600,000 registered voters.Ms. Peltola claimed early momentum this spring after entering the race, but her campaign hit some snags in recent days. Last week, she distanced herself from former Vice President Kamala Harris, who sent out a fund-raising appeal on Ms. Peltola’s behalf that threatened to undermine Ms. Peltola’s image as an independent-minded candidate unaffiliated with national Democrats or politics in the Lower 48.Her campaign alsounderwent a staffing shake-uplast week, as she fired several longtime campaign aides and contractors and swapped out campaign managers.Show moreAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 19, 2026, 12:40 a.m. ETJennifer MedinaReporting on California politicsThe two candidates in California’s special election also faced each other in the June primary, when Aisha Wahab received 43 percent of the vote, compared with 17 percent for Melissa Hernandez. But AIPAC and other outside groups have recently spent millions of dollars supporting Hernandez and attacking Wahab, and the race is now expected to be much closer.Aug. 19, 2026, 12:36 a.m. ETWilliam P. DavisIn the special election in California’s 14th District, Alameda County has reported some ballots returned early but no Election Day votes. The county has historically taken several hours to count and report Election Day votes, which are expected to come in batches. Those votes make up a relatively small share of the outstanding vote. Most of the remaining ballots are mail ballots that will be counted over the next week or so.Aug. 19, 2026, 12:25 a.m. ETChristine ZhangElection Data ReporterThe first results in Alaska areexpectedbetween 12:45 a.m. and 1 a.m. Eastern, according to the state’s Division of Elections. Most of the state is four hours behind Eastern time, while the western Aleutian Islands are five hours behind.#2026PrimaryWe anticipate the first set of unofficial results being published between 8:45pm and 9pm on election night.Updates can be found at:https://t.co/WNcPa2yRt4See lesspic.twitter.com/P8thFmPtwL— Alaska Division of Elections (@ak_elections)August 18, 2026Aug. 19, 2026, 12:02 a.m. ETChristine ZhangElection Data ReporterThe first votes out of Alaska will consist of results from those who cast ballots on Election Day or through Thursday as part of the state’s early voting period. The bulk of the mail-in ballots, as well as early vote ballots cast after Thursday,will be countedin the coming days. Mail-in ballots that are postmarked by Election Day will still be counted as long as they reach the Division of Election within 10 days.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 19, 2026, 12:00 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaAlaska also features competitive races for governor and its sole House seat. A host of Republicans and two prominent Democrats are vying to succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican who is term limited. In the House race, the matchup is likely to be set between Representative Nick Begich, a Republican, and Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and educator running as an independent.Aug. 19, 2026, 12:00 a.m. ETKellen BrowningReporting from AlaskaPolls are now closed in most of Alaska, where Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, are expected to easily advance to the four-person general election race for U.S. Senate. The intrigue revolves around who will claim the third and fourth spots — those candidates could be potential spoilers who split votes with the front-runners in November. One of the lesser-known candidates is also named Dan Sullivan; Republicans fear his presence on the ballot in November could confuse voters and harm the sitting senator’s re-election chances.Aug. 18, 2026, 11:52 p.m. ETCaroline SolerElection Data ReporterSince Alaska has an unusual nonpartisan primary system, in which the top four finishers advance to the general election, public polling there can be scarce. That’s because pollsters rarely survey voters in contests with four or fewer viable candidates.In the state’s at-large House race, where Representative Nick Begich, a Republican, and Bill Hill, an independent, are expected to advance, no polls have been conducted since Matt Schultz, a Democrat, dropped out in mid-July. In the Senate race, where the prominence of Mary Peltola, a Democrat, and Senator Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, has led to only one primary poll, showing Peltola and Sullivan with more than 40 percent support.In the crowded governor’s race, eight polls have been conducted this year, with Tom Begich, a Democrat (and Nick Begich’s uncle), leading each by narrow margins over a crowded field.Aug. 18, 2026, 11:40 p.m. ETMichael KruseHere are 5 things to know about Mary Peltola, a Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska.ImageMary Peltola won a special election to replace Don Young in Congress in 2022 and was elected to a full term later that year.Credit...Ash Adams for The New York TimesMary Peltola, an Alaska Native and moderate former congresswoman running on a platform she describes as “fish, family and freedom,” is the leading Democrat in Alaska’s nonpartisan primary election on Tuesday.The top four finishers regardless of party will advance to the general election in November. To have a shot at taking back control of the Senate, Democrats almost certainly will need Ms. Peltola to beat Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent.Here are five things to know about Ms. Peltola.She is Yup’ik.Ms. Peltola’s father, Ward Sattler, a teacher and bush pilot, moved to Alaska from Nebraska. Her mother, LizAnn Piicigaq Williams, was a member of the Yup’ik group of Indigenous peoples of western Alaska. Ms. Peltola grew up along the Kuskokwim River near the Bering Sea, fishing for salmon, picking berries and eating seal and moose meat. In 1995, she won the Miss National Congress of American Indians pageant, a competition in which she wore a squirrel skin parka and a wolf hair headdress.She has been in and around politics for years.Ms. Peltola, 52, grew up going to events for Don Young, the longtime Republican congressman, because her father was friends with him. After attending four different colleges — she never graduated — she ran for the State House in 1996 and lost. She ran again in 1998 and won. Representing Bethel, 400 miles from Anchorage and nearly 1,000 miles from the capital of Juneau, she spent a decade in the state legislature. She was elected to Congress in a special election in 2022 to replace Mr. Young after his death and was elected later that year to a full term. She was the first Democrat to hold the seat in a half-century, the first woman to represent Alaska in the U.S. House and the first Alaska Native ever elected to Congress. She lost her seat in 2024.She lost her husband in a plane crash.Ms. Peltola, has been married three times. Her third husband, Eugene “Buzzy” Peltola Jr., was killed in 2023 when a small Piper PA 18-150 Super Cub he was piloting crashed in the mountains of southwestern Alaska. The cause, according to the accident report: an overload of moose meat and antlers attached to the side of the plane.She is known as a less partisan bridge builder.When Ms. Peltola was in the Alaska Legislature, she started “Fish Fridays” — weekly get-togethers in her office at which she fed her colleagues salmon. She helped with grass-roots outreach during Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski’s write-in campaign in 2010. And when Ms. Peltola got to Congress, she hired several of Mr. Young’s staffers — Republicans — including his chief of staff. She is friends with Sarah Palin, the former Alaska governor and Republican vice-presidential nominee, who once called Ms. Peltola a “real Alaskan chick.” During her time on Capitol Hill, Ms. Peltola was the co-chair of the Blue Dog Coalition for Policy, the caucus of centrist Democrats. “I certainly wouldn’t call myself a liberal,” she once said.She calls herself “Alaska first.”Ms. Peltola is one of the top recruits of Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, who has called her “the final piece of the puzzle” in the Democrats’ efforts to regain control the chamber — but Ms. Peltola is running against Washington as much as she is any of her opponents.In her campaign pitch, she targeted “the rigged system in D.C. that’s shutting down Alaska while politicians feather their own nest.”“No one from the Lower 48 is coming to save us,” she said.Show moreAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 18, 2026, 11:40 p.m. ETMack LiedermanHere are 5 things to know about Dan Sullivan, the Alaska senator seeking re-election.ImageSenator Dan Sullivan, who is seeking his third Senate term, supports President Trump more than Alaska’s other senator, Lisa Murkowski, does.Credit...Eric Lee/The New York TimesSenator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, is seeking a third term in the Senate in a competitive race that also features a well-known Democratic challenger and a man who shares his name.Here are five things to know about Mr. Sullivan, the junior senator from Alaska, who is competing on Tuesday in a nonpartisan primary in which the top four finishers advance to the November general election.1. Mr. Sullivan lost a court battle to kick another Dan Sullivan off the ballot.He’s Senator Dan S. Sullivan. One of his opponents is Dan J. Sullivan, a retired fifth-grade teacherwithout much of a political backgroundbut with a lot of name recognition. The lesser-known Mr. Sullivanhas saidhis aim is to unseat the incumbent senator, but he has done little campaigning. Republicans fear that voters could confuse the two, and have accused Democrats of planting the second Sullivan to divide votes in what could be a close race. Democrats in the state, including the leading candidate in the race, have denied the accusations. Mr. Sullivan, the senator, brought the battle to court, but he ultimately lost in June, whenthe Alaska Supreme Courtruled that Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, giving voters two Sullivans to choose from.2. The senator faces a strong Democratic challenger.Alaska has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly two decades, but the conservative-leaning state has long inched toward the political center, and most Alaska voters arepolitically unaffiliated. Astate pollhas shown that former Representative Mary Peltola — awell-fundedDemocrat making an appeal to working-class, independent and Native voters — is competitive. National Democrats view Alaska as a must-win if they are to retake the Senate. The Cook Political Reportconsidersthe race a tossup.3. President Trump has endorsed Mr. Sullivan.The senator has been a reliable supporter of Mr. Trump, includingon the Iran warandsweeping tariffs, during the president’s second term. But Mr. Sullivan has occasionally broken ranks, voting with Democratsagainst Mr. Trump’s plansfor a new White House ballroom and an effort to set up an “anti-weaponization” fund. Still, he is far more tethered to the right than Senator Lisa Murkowski, the state’s senior senator, a Republican moderate and a longtime party swing voterwho has criticized Mr. Trump. “Sullivan may have positioned himself a little too far to the right for a lot of Alaskans,” said Glenn Wright, a political scientist at the University of Alaska Southeast. Mr. Sullivan’s ties to Trump could cause re-election troubles in Alaska, Mr. Wright said, given inflation and rising oil prices under the president, particularly in a state with a high cost of living.4. He once worked in the State Department under President George W. Bush.Mr. Sullivan, 61, is a Marine veteran with a long track record in government. He was the assistant secretary of state for economic, energy and business affairs under President Bush from 2006 to 2009. Mr. Sullivan also served as Alaska’s attorney general and as commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources before first winning his Senate seat in 2014. “Alaska has a history of politicians with big personalities,” Mr. Wright said. “Sullivan, by all accounts, is quietly competent.”5. He has emphasized his local endorsements.Mr. Sullivan features a picture with Mr. Trump on his campaign website, but he does not include the president in his list of endorsements. The incumbent has earned the support of the largest commercial fishing organization in the state, labor unions and a group representing Alaska Native corporations. He has been a staunch proponent ofmajor oil and mining projects.Show moreAug. 18, 2026, 11:29 p.m. ETRuth IgielnikElection Data ReporterIn California’s 14th Congressional District, a primary tonight will be the third of four elections held this year in which the same candidates are facing off for the seat formerly held by Eric Swalwell, who resigned after allegations of sexual misconduct.The special primary runoff tonight will decide whether Aisha Wahab, a state senator, or Melissa Hernandez, the president of the Bay Area Rapid Transit board, completes Swalwell’s current term. They also faced each other in a June 16 special primary, and a June 2 primary for the general election, with Wahab winning both of those races by wide margins. Recently, however, Wahab has been the target of outside spending by super PACs over statements she made about Israel and Gaza.Regardless of who wins tonight, both women will face off again in November for a full term in slightly redrawn district.Aug. 18, 2026, 11:17 p.m. ETTheodore SchleiferUnusual ad spending raises the prospect of election meddling in Alaska.Carol Hafner (left) and Richard GraysonJulio Cortez/Associated Press; Caitlin O’Hara for The New York TimesIn Alaska’s primary on Tuesday, not all ads may be as they seem. Don’t assume that all of the commercials boosting Republican candidates are backed by the G.O.P. or that spots promoting Democrats are backed by Democratic money.That’s because the ascendant trend ofelection meddling— in which partisans try to shape the outcome by boosting a fringe candidate, or one seen as less formidable, from the other party in hopes of elevating a likely loser into the general election — appears to have gone into overdrive in the 49th state. And Alaska’s unique primary, in which the top four candidates advance to the general election, has added another dimension to the ad wars.About $800,000 has been spent in the last few weeks by the super PAC Fair Deal Alaska to not only attack the leading Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, but also boost two lesser-known hopefuls, the Green Party candidate Richard Grayson (who lives in Arizona) and Carol Hafner, another Democrat who could pull votes away from Ms. Peltola. That could benefit the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan. Fair Deal Alaska formed just late last month, meaning its donors have not yet been disclosed.Not to be outdone, another $2.2 million has come from a super PAC called Right for Alaska to oppose Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and also boost long-shot candidates, Alaskan Party member Earl Southworth and Republican Jerry Heikes, both of whom could pull votes from Mr. Sullivan.And then over the final two weeks, another $300,000 has been spent by the American Democracy Project, a third super PAC, to support David Leslie, a Democrat.The groups did not respond to requests for comment.Some of the hangers-on have voiced surprise in media interviews that there are apparently well-funded super PACs spending on their behalf.Alaska’s newish primary system, in which the top four candidates advance from Tuesday’s primary into the general election, makes the state especially ripe for subterfuge. Aside from the surge in super PAC spending, there have been accusations that one candidate —a different Dan Sullivan— is a plant meant to siphon support from the incumbent.Alaska also uses ranked-choice voting in the general election as part of its new system.In a close race, as the matchup between Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan (the sitting senator) is expected to be, the partisan leanings of which candidates take the other two general spots could shape whether Republicans or Democrats control the seat — and perhaps the U.S. Senate itself.Show moreAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 18, 2026, 11:11 p.m. ETJennifer MedinaReporting on California politicsThe polls have just closed in the special election for California’s 14th congressional district. The winner of tonight’s race will fill out the rest of term for Eric Swalwell, who resigned amid sexual misconduct allegations earlier this year. The race became far more contentious in the final weeks of the campaign as AIPAC spent more than $2 million in the race.It might be a long time before we know the results in this election. The state is notorious for taking a long time to count and many there believe this could be a close race.Aug. 18, 2026, 11:10 p.m. ETBayliss WagnerRepublican primary voters across the country have overwhelmingly supported President Trump’s picks. But he faced some notable setbacks tonight.In Florida, Representative Cory Mills, whom Trump endorsed in February, lost his primary, while Catalina Lauf, a health care entrepreneur he announced his support for last week, lost an open primary in Florida’s 19th Congressional District. In Wyoming, Representative Harriet Hageman, who was backed by Trump, won the Senate primary, while schools chief Megan Degenfelder, his pick for governor, did not. Other Trump-endorsed candidates have lost in a range of states in recent weeks.While his endorsement remains the most coveted prize in Republican primary politics, in this primary season, it has not always been a ticket to victory.Aug. 18, 2026, 10:58 p.m. ETJack HealyA rancher edges his Trump-backed opponent to win the G.O.P. primary for Wyoming governor.ImageEric Barlow, a Wyoming state senator, at a campaign stop in Jackson, Wyo.Credit...Charlie Nick/Jackson Hole News & GuideEric Barlow, a rancher and state senator in Wyoming, won the Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, The Associated Press said, beating a candidate endorsed by President Trump in one of the country’s most staunchly Republican states.Mr. Barlow’s victory means he is all but certain to become the next governor of Wyoming, where Republicans hold every statewide office, and voters gave Mr. Trump his largest margin of victory in the 2024 presidential election.This year, legislative races in Wyoming have turned into a contest between the right and far right as ultraconservative candidatespushed to take controlof the State Senate, where more moderate Republicans have held sway. Mr. Barlow ran a campaign that focused on problem solving and lowering the temperature of Wyoming’s internecine Republican brawls, in contrast to his Trump-endorsed rival, Megan Degenfelder, who promised to stock state agencies with “bulldogs.” He also defeated Brent Bien, a far-right conservative and retired Marine Corps colonel who won the endorsement of the Wyoming Republican Party.Mr. Barlow’s victory suggested that Wyoming’s heavily Republican electorate preferred a lower-key leader similar to the incumbent governor, Mark Gordon, rather than a bomb-throwing conservative or culture warrior. Mr. Gordon, a mainstream Republican, is leaving office after two terms.His win also showed the limits of Mr. Trump’s power to tilt a Republican primary in a sparsely populated rural state where many voters make up their minds by chatting with candidates at barbecues, county fairs and rodeos.Ms. Degenfelder, Wyoming’s state superintendent of public instruction, touted the president’s support, her battles “against the radicals’ agenda” and her advocacy of the state’s ban on transgender athletes in girls’ sports.Mr. Barlow is widely expected to win in November against the Democratic nominee, Ken Casner, a Vietnam veteran who runs a retail shop and cafe.Mr. Barlow, often sporting a white cowboy hat, ran as a “fourth-generation ranch kid” who served in the Marines before rising through the ranks of Wyoming politics, where he spent two years as speaker of the State House.Mr. Barlow emphasized his support for public lands — an issue that unites conservative hunters and liberal environmentalists in the American West — and vowed to change the tone of Wyoming’s increasingly bitter politics.In onememorable videocritical of the negative mailers swamping voters, Mr. Barlow — who is also a veterinarian — pulled on a long plastic glove, reached into a mailbox and retrieved a pile of yak dung.Mr. Barlow and Ms. Degenfelder promised a continuation of the Republican policies that have dominated Wyoming for years. Both oppose abortion, and they vowed to support the mining and energy industries that drive much of the state’s economy while also shoring up its struggling rural health care systems.Show moreAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAug. 18, 2026, 10:54 p.m. ETTim BalkA Trump-backed candidate wins the G.O.P. Senate primary in Wyoming.ImageRepresentative Harriet Hageman at a hearing in Washington, last year.Credit...Valerie Plesch for The New York TimesRepresentative Harriet Hageman, a close ally of President Trump’s, won the Republican primary race for Senate in Wyoming on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press.Ms. Hageman, whorose to prominencefour years ago by defeating Representative Liz Cheney, will be an overwhelming general-election favorite in Wyoming, one of the most conservative states.Ms. Hageman, 63, is runningto replace Senator Cynthia Lummis, a retiring Republican. Ms. Lummisendorsed Ms. Hageman in January, describing her as a “real workhorse” and a strong champion for Mr. Trump’s agenda.Ms. Hageman, a daughter of a state lawmaker, is campaigning on a pledge to fight what she casts as federal government overreach into water rights and private property rights in Wyoming. She was alsoendorsedby the Wyoming Republican Party and by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the nation’s largest business lobbying group.Mr. Trumpendorsedher by late December, immediately establishing her as an all but prohibitive favorite in Wyoming. He carried the state by 46 percentage points in the2024 presidential election, his largest margin of victory in any state.In 2021, Mr. Trumpsupercharged the House candidacyof Ms. Hageman, a Cheyenne trial lawyer who had only a small political following before Mr. Trump backed her bid to unseat Ms. Cheney, one of his fiercest Republican critics.Before her House run, Ms. Hageman had served as a Republican National Committee official, and also lost in a 2018 run for the Wyoming governorship. She once was an ally of Ms. Cheney’s and a critic of a Mr. Trump’s, evenreferring to him in 2016 as “racist and xenophobic,”but by 2020 had transformed into a fervent supporter.After Mr. Trump lost the 2020 presidential election, she amplified his false claims that the election had been rigged. She has called him the“greatest president”of her lifetime.With Mr. Trump’s support, she thundered past Ms. Cheney in 2022,winning by more than 37 points.Ms. Cheney — whose father, Dick Cheney, was President George W. Bush’s powerfulvice president— had become one of Mr. Trump’s top targets for retribution after she helped lead the House panel investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.Ms. Hageman said Wyoming was “fed up with the Jan. 6 commission” and “fed up with Liz Cheney.”Although Ms. Hageman’s primary race for Senate this year was not competitive, Mr. Trump continued to issue statements of support for her into the final month of the race, in which she faced a group of long-shot challengers.“Harriet has ALWAYS delivered for Wyoming,” he wrote onsocial media in early August, “and will continue to do so in the United States Senate.”Show moreAug. 18, 2026, 10:33 p.m. ETSusan Cooper EastmanReporting from FloridaState Representative Angie Nixon, who begins the general election as a clear underdog to Senator Ashley Moody in the Florida Senate race, said a brief interview with The New York Times tonight that she would defy expectations in November the same way she won the Democratic primary. “By going out and having conversations with people,” she said.Nixon added: “They are going to lie and call me all kinds of names. He also bested two former House members and several candidates who had previously run for Congress and lost — all in other states before moving to Florida.During a wild primary, many of the candidates tried to prove their Florida bona fides as well as their alignment with the president.Mr. Schwartzel is heavily favored to win the November general election in the solidly Republican district, which is based in the Fort Myers area in Southwest Florida. Florida, one of the states holding primaries on Tuesday, was among those where the G.O.P. pushed through changes intended to give them an advantage in November.When the dust settled, Republicans were able to draw more seats that benefited them than Democrats were, handing them a new structural advantage as they headed into a midterm election in which Democrats were favored to make gains.The redrawn districts in Florida alone could eliminate four seats held by Democrats — one in the Tampa area, one in the Orlando area, and two in the Fort Lauderdale area — effectively slashing the number of its blue-leaning districts in half.The rare spate of mid-decade redistricting began last year, as President Trump urged Texas Republicansto take the rare stepof redrawing maps to create more safely Republican seats. title: Judge Allows Limited Testing in Trump Plan to Paint Eisenhower Building White
content: Trump RemakesWashingtonBallroom ConstructionKennedy CenterReflecting PoolThe ‘Triumphal Arch’Eisenhower BuildingHelipadAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTJudge Allows Limited Testing in Trump Plan to Paint Eisenhower Building WhiteA federal judge ruled that initial preparatory steps, including testing out paints on the building’s gray granite exterior, could proceed for now.Listen· 3:00 minShare full articleThe Eisenhower Executive Office Building in May.Credit...Allison Robbert for The New York TimesByZach MontagueReporting from WashingtonAug. 18, 2026A judge ruled on Tuesday that the Trump administration could inch forward on a plan to paint the gray granite exterior of the Eisenhower Executive Building white.In an order from the bench in Federal District Court in Washington, Judge Dabney L. Friedrich said that initial tests to evaluate how the paint would affect the building’s walls and other preparations would not directly harm preservationist groups who sued to stop the effort.But she warned that she would intervene if the administration moved ahead with a full paint job before other legal questions were settled.Judge Friedrich said that the government’s descriptions of its immediate plans on Tuesday were far more preliminary than the full painting of the building President Trump had proposed as part of his larger effort to alter many of Washington’s most recognizable landmarks to suit his taste.The Dwight D. Eisenhower Executive Building, built in the French Second Empire style, was completed in 1888 and planned to absorb the growing staff of the Departments of State, War and the Navy. Its design stood out from the classical revival style of surrounding buildings, with unpainted exterior granite wallsmade from stonequarried in Virginia and Maine.Mr. Trump has said he wishes to paint the whole building. In aninterviewon Fox News in November, Mr. Trump said he was “getting bids right now from painters” to work on the project, calling the building “ugly” and its gray a color “for funerals.”In asworn statementahead of the hearing, Heather Martin, a White House official, said the plan included “minimally invasive” paint tests and an exploration of other measures “that would improve, restore and better preserve” the building’s facade.Historical preservation groups sued in November to block the painting,asking Judge Friedrichto freeze any effort to alter the building before the project underwent several environmental and architectural reviews. After the Trump administration announced its intent to move ahead with an initial study in July, the groups filed an emergency motion to stop it.While Judge Friedrich, a Trump appointee, declined to stop the testing, she ordered that the parties jointly update her on the project every 14 days. She said the larger questions remain about whether the General Services Administration, the agency that has been responsible for the building, could delegate its maintenance to the White House.“We would have preferred that no invasive testing occurs until the administration followed the legally required process, but today’s decision is about limited testing,” said Greg Werkheiser, a lawyer from Cultural Heritage Partners, one of the groups suing.“The much larger questions about whether the president can paint the Eisenhower Building and whether the White House can exempt this project from federal law remain open in this active case,” he said.Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.A version of this article appears in print on, SectionA, Page14of the New York editionwith the headline:Plan to Paint Granite Landmark Gets Approval to Inch Forward.Order Reprints|Today’s Paper|SubscribeShare full articleRelated ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

As a publicist I’ve seen my fair share of difficult personalities, but my new boss blew all of that out of the water. She micromanaged everything, contradicted her own instructions, second-guessed every decision and spoke negatively about employees to clients. Former employees have since reached out to tell me they experienced many of the same things.When I gently raised concerns about her management style, she told me that she would never change and tried to get me to resign. Two weeks later, after having quietly hired a replacement, she terminated my employment.I’m thrilled to be free of her toxicity, but if someone had told me what they experienced before I accepted the job, I would never have left my previous position. (While I was interviewing, I tried to learn what I could but came up short.) Do I have an obligation to warn other people about this workplace? Is there an ethical way to do so? Part of me worries about retaliation even if what I say is accurate.— AnonymousYour main obligation is to be honest with anyone who asks you about jobs at this firm: The workplace was chaotic, the management style was controlling and the boss was insulting. But I’m not sure what — beyond being clear and direct to people seeking your opinion — you might do to productively “warn” other people. Mass email? Ad in the local paper? Sandwich board?I mean, you’re the publicist, so you probably have some better ideas than I do. (Hire a skywriter?) But you also know that attention cuts both ways. It’s not just that your boss might retaliate, but also that anything intended as a warning might read differently when it travels beyond a circle of trusted friends, colleagues and advice seekers.You could, for example, leave a negative post on a workplace-review site like Glassdoor. But a single negative review from an angry former employee is as easily dismissed as heeded. You could raise the stakes and write an excoriating blog post with your name attached. But how confident are you that the strangers reading it would trust your account over your former boss’s version? Enough to wager your professional reputation?This may sound bleak and cynical to some readers, but I’d guess it’s a professionally familiar dilemma to you. Anything beyond privately communicating your toxic experience to people you trust — and who trust you in turn — is just as likely to backfire as it is to accomplish your goals. It’s admirable you want to save your peers from making the same mistake you did, but not at the expense of your career or sanity.The fact is that in addition to the psychological warfare she committed, this woman also did you a favor. She fired you quickly, saving you from many excruciating months or years trying to make an irredeemable situation work. Don’t waste that favor by expending unnecessary emotional energy on her, or on hypothetical other future employees, when you’re not even getting paid. Your time is better spent applying to new jobs, and enjoying days free of difficult personalities.We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. That means that, for the fourth month in a row, Americans’ real wages — how many sandwiches, haircuts and gallons of gas they can buy with an hour’s pay — actually fell.Wages vs. inflationNote: Data is not seasonally adjusted. Inflation data is the year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index. Wages are year-over-year changes in average hourly earnings. October 2025 is missing from the inflation data because of the government shutdown.Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics.The New York TimesSuch declines are unusual. In the years before the coronavirus pandemic, real wage growth sped up and slowed down with the ebbs and flows of the economy. But pay never fell outright for more than a month or two at a time.Then came the pandemic and the ensuing surge in prices, which led to the sharpest decline in inflation-adjusted wages since the 1980s. From February 2021 to June 2022, the buying power of the average American’s paycheck fell more than 4 percent.The latest shock, driven by the jump in energy prices tied to the war with Iran, hasn’t been nearly as severe. But coming on the heels of the earlier decline in pay — and at a time when affordability and the cost of living remain top of mind for many voters — it has sent measures of consumer sentiment tumbling.“The real hourly wage is absolutely the fundamental building block of working Americans’ living standards,” said Jared Bernstein, an economist at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research. “When it’s falling in real terms, that’s a huge problem for folks who are already stressed by affordability concerns.”We are having trouble retrieving the article content.Please enable JavaScript in your browser settings.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. title: July Retail Sales Notch Biggest Drop in Over a Year
content: U.S. EconomyInflation Eats Pay GainsJobs ReportStock RecordRetail Sales DropInterest RatesGas PricesAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSupported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTUnexpected Drop in U.S. Retail Sales as Shoppers Feel the SqueezeThe data for July showed the biggest drop in more than a year, as American households face the economic strains brought on by persistent inflationListen· 2:34 minShare full article92U.S. shoppers spent less in July, as consumers struggled with persistent inflation, higher grocery bills and rising housing costs.Credit...Zack Wittman for The New York TimesByKim BhasinAug. 14, 2026American consumers pulled back on spending in July, a surprise slowdown after stronger sales in the first half of the year.Retail sales last month fell 0.6 percent from June, the biggest drop in more than a year, according to data the Census Bureau released Friday. The unexpected decrease, which is not adjusted for inflation, followed a 0.2 percent rise in sales in June.Gas stations, auto dealers and electronics stores were among the categories where sales declined in July. Shoppers also spent less at e-commerce shops, though economists attributed this to the shift of Amazon Prime Day, a major sales event for the online retailer, to June this year.American households have been struggling to cope with economic strains brought on by persistent inflation, including higher grocery bills and housing costs. That has left lower-income consumers strapped for cash, with many trimming their shopping lists at the supermarket and delaying big-ticket purchases like home renovations.The U.S. economy has been resilient, despite the effects of the war in Iran, trade tariffs and other economic obstacles. But after a surge in job creation earlier this year, employersshed 23,000 jobsin July, and job gains were revised down by more than 100,000 for April and May. Inflationeased slightlylast month, although the cost of living remains elevated.Economists said consumers may be in slightly better shape than the numbers implied. Bernard Yaros, the lead U.S. economist for Oxford Economics, said in a note that the labor market remained balanced and that wealthy households continued to spend.“Though the latest numbers warrant a downgrade to the spending forecast, it’d be premature to write off the consumer,” Mr. Yaros said.But the disappointing retail sales may also be an early sign of a longer-term slowdown, with shoppers no longer enjoying the boost from robust tax refunds this year, elevated energy prices and lingering concerns about income growth, Oliver Allen, a senior U.S. economist for Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a note.“It suggests a sharper slowdown in spending lies ahead,” he said.Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.A version of this article appears in print on, SectionB, Page5of the New York editionwith the headline:Retail Sales Dipped in July As Shoppers Felt Squeezed.Order Reprints|Today’s Paper|SubscribeRead 92 commentsShare full article92Related ContentAdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT

title: Chatbots Are Pushing Us Toward a Post-Human Internet
content: ArtificialIntelligenceA.I. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.Supported bySKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe ContextChatbots Are Pushing Us Toward a Post-Human InternetIn matters of work, school and even romance, we turn to A.I. chatbots. But what happens when the bots begin talking to one another?Listen· 10:24 minShare full article219Credit...Photo illustration by Chantal JahchanByCallie HoltermannAug. 14, 2026Remember job applications? You know, you’d write a résumé and a cover letter. Someone would read them. You’d fish out a tasteful button-down and try to charm your interviewer. Maybe your one-liner or a question about your amateur bowling career would help you score the position. Maybe you’d never hear back.That’s all changing. When Christian Vinson applied for jobs in finance this year, he knew he was really auditioning for artificial intelligence. Many companies now use screening software to sift through piles of applications, so he spent close to 10 hours teaching two A.I. chatbots about his work experience. He filled in details about his education, a banking internship and five years in the Army. He then prompted the bots to tailor his cover letter to hundreds of job listings.A.I. had written his applications, and A.I. was reading them too — a dog chasing its own tail. “This is the new normal,” says Vinson, 30, who landed a job at an investment bank in New York.We live in a world in which A.I. tools have found their way to the center of a staggering number of professional, academic and personal interactions. Lately these chatbots and agents have been doing more than just talking to us. Students arewriting essayswith ChatGPT, and teachers are using A.I. tograde them. Workers are sending lengthyA.I.-generated emailsto colleagues, who are responding with walls of chatbot text of their own.A.I podcast hostsare holding forth with A.I. podcast guests on topics like gas prices,the Iran war— and artificial intelligence. Tech wants to take all this even further: In March, Meta acquired a social network designed for bots totalk to one another.The dead internet theory, a concept popular in tech circles, holds that most digital traffic will eventually be software, leaving humans as a minority voice. We may now have a corollary of that prediction — let’s call it a bot loop — when the humans on both sides of an interaction hand over their role to artificial intelligence. These recursive exchanges can be eerie and error-prone, a single mistake bouncing back and forth uncorrected over and over. Stranger still, they flip our conversational dynamic inside out, turning chatbots into the interlocutors and humans into their enablers.Depending on whom you ask, bot loops might be banal, dystopian or genuinely useful. title: Revealed: FCC chair Brendan Carr’s close ties to White House and rightwing media
content: Brendan Carr was appointed as FCC chair by Donald Trump.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrendan Carr was appointed as FCC chair by Donald Trump.Composite: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty ImagesMediaRevealed: FCC chair Brendan Carr’s close ties to White House and rightwing mediaInternal documents obtained by Guardian show White House meetings, scheduled calls with top Trump officials and communications with Fox News producersJeremy Barrin WashingtonWed 19 Aug 2026 11.00 BSTLast modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.01 BSTShareBrendan Carr was very firm.“As a general rule, we don’t get into any discussions that happen with the White House or don’t happen with the White House,” Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), told Politico’s Dasha Burnsin a recent interview. Burns had pressed Carr to explain how exactly he came to issue a highly unprecedented order forcing ABC to apply early to renew its eight local broadcast licenses just one day after the man who appointed Carr, Donald Trump, and his wife Melania called for ABC to be punished for a joke made by late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.“Did you get a call or talk to the president either before or after you made that announcement?” Burns had asked. Later in the interview, Carr repeated his policy: “As a general matter, I don’t speak publicly about conversations with the White House, or whether they happen or don’t happen.”While Carr may not be keen to detail his relations with the Trump administration, a trove of FCC documents – obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request and lawsuitfiledby the advocacy group Democracy Forward, and provided to the Guardian – shed light on the close working relationship between Carr, his top staffers and members of Trump’s White House team.Between 12 March 2025 and 11 February 2026, Carr attended at least eight meetings at the White House, according to the records, and had at least three scheduled calls with administration officials, including two conversations with chief of staff Susie Wiles. He also spoke by phone with administration officials such as controversial health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.In addition, the files provide insight into Carr’s media strategy, including communications with producers at Fox News, and make public previously undisclosed meetings he has held with media titans such as Fox Corp chief executive Lachlan Murdoch and Sinclair Broadcast Group chair David Smith.View image in fullscreenFree press advocates at a protest in support of first amendment rights in Washington earlier this month.Photograph: Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Free Press“These records show a remarkable breadth of access to FCC leadership for this administration’s political allies, conservative media figures, and powerful industry interests, including companies and organizations with business before the commission,” said Dan McGrath, special counsel, oversight at Democracy Forward. “This raises serious questions about whether the FCC is operating as an independent regulator, or whether political relationships and industry influence have become too intertwined with its decision-making.”The White House meetings, which are memorialized as Microsoft Outlook calendar items, occasionally include details about the topic of discussion. For example, on 29 August 2025, Carr was listed as the organizer of a “White House deputies” meeting focused on “FAA/Spectrum issues,” which also included chief of staff Greg Watson and Arpan Sura, a senior counsel focused on spectrum, space and artificial intelligence.Another White House meeting, in November 2025, was titled “Drones – Principals meeting”, making obvious the focus.But a 2 June 2025 calendar entry shows only that Carr attended a “WH mtg”, giving no further details on the nature of the visit.While it’s not uncommon for FCC chairs appointed by a president of their party to meet and confer with the administration, Carr is known to be unusually well-synched with the priorities of the Trump White House, particularly with its focus on using the levers of government to punish the legacy television networks that Trump has derided as fake news. Countering past precedent,he has deniedthat the agency is “independent” because the president can remove commissioners at any time. ABC cited Carr’s “repeated public statements confirming his allegiance to the president and the president’s agenda”in a lawsuit filed Tuesdaychallenging the FCC’s early license renewal order.Tom Wheeler, who served as chair of the FCC under President Barack Obama, called the meeting logs “very interesting” and “lots of fun”, particularly those memorializing conversations between Carr and Wiles in the winter of 2025. But, he told the Guardian: “I don’t think it’s terribly unusual.”View image in fullscreenIn the summer of 2025, a calendar entry noted that White House office of the deputy chief of staff for strategic implementation Nick Luna would “call BC cell”, referring to Carr’s cellphone.In early February of this year, the calendar shows a scheduled call between Carr and health and human services secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, noting “Secretary Kennedy to call Chairman Carr Directly” for what appears to be a quick 15-minute conversation.View image in fullscreenIn early February of this year, the calendar shows a scheduled call between Carr and RFK Jr, noting “Secretary Kennedy to call Chairman Carr Directly”.double quotation mark*Secretary Kennedy to call Chairman Brendan Carr Directly*A few days later, Carr was in the West Wing of the White House for a meeting with director for domestic policy council Vince Haley,described by the Wall Street Journal last yearas “the Most Influential Trump Adviser You’ve Probably Never Heard Of”.Also in February, Carr traveled to the Department of Justice to meet with Omeed Assefi, who served as acting assistant attorney general for the antitrust division. No reason was given for the meeting, though there is obvious overlap between the regulatory oversight functions provided by the justice department and the FCC over media mergers that involve the transfer of television licenses.Carr’s meetings with media power-brokersThere is nothing unusual or nefarious about the chair of the FCC meeting with the leaders of media companies his agency regulates – though such meetings are kept private unless they are directly related to an agency matter, which would then require a publicly filed “ex parte” acknowledgement of the conversation. Notably, though, most of Carr’s meetings with media executives (and personalities) represent companies that appeal to conservatives.View image in fullscreenMatt Gaetz at a rally in Henderson, Nevada in October 2024.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersIn June 2025, Carr met in his office with Matt Gaetz, the former GOP congressman and one-time attorney general nominee who in December 2024 joined the far-right cable network One America News as a host. Charles Herring, OAN’s president, was listed as an optional attendee.View image in fullscreenIn January 2026, Carr and his aides had a previously unreported meeting with Lachlan Murdoch, Fox’s head of government relations Kristopher Jones, and FCC-focused Fox senior vice-president Joe Di Scipio, who had requested the meeting.View image in fullscreenCarr and his aides had a previously unreported meeting with Lachlan Murdoch, Fox’s head of government relations Kristopher Jones, and senior vice-president Joe Di Scipio, who had requested the meeting.double quotation markI would like to set up a meeting with Chairman Carr and Lachlan Murdoch at the FCC on Friday, January 30.In February 2026, Carr met with David Smith, the powerful chair of the conservative media company Sinclair, which in September 2025 had briefly acceded to Carr’s wishes and pre-empted Jimmy Kimmel Live over comments the late-night host had made about the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk.View image in fullscreenAn expert communicator who rarely deviates from talking points, Carr is a regular presence on conservative media podcasts, radio shows and television programs.In April 2024, Carr reached out to a booker for the Fox News morning show Fox and Friends to see if the show might be interested in having him on to discuss “tech issues”, including legislation involving TikTok, and shared links to videos of his past appearances on the network. “No worries at all if there’s nothing that makes sense,” Carr wrote.
