title: Exclusive: You Can Finally Buy a Fairphone—a Sustainable, Repairable Smartphone—in the US
content: Julian ChokkattuGearAug 18, 2026 6:30 AMYou Can Finally Buy a Fairphone—a Sustainable, Repairable Smartphone—in the USMore than a decade after launching in Europe, the Netherlands company is now selling its repairable phones in the US, starting with the Fairphone (Gen 6+).Photograph: Courtesy of Julian ChokkattuCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyYour iPhone, SamsungGalaxy, andGoogle Pixelhave a 1-year warranty. Unless you cough up extra dough for an extended service plan, you’ll pay a hefty fee if you damage the screen and need a replacement (around $329 for aniPhone 17done directly fromApple).But it doesn’t have to be this way. What if you could order the part from the manufacturer and do therepair yourself? That dream is finally being realized for American consumers, thanks toFairphone. The Dutch company is bringing its repairable and sustainably built Android smartphone—the Fairphone (Gen 6+)—to the US. Each one comes with a screwdriver.A replacement screen from Fairphone costs just $90. A new USB-C port is $20. A fresh battery is $40. In all, there are 12 modular elements you can swap yourself. It remains the only smartphone series with a 10/10 repairability scorefrom iFixit, not to mention an unmatched 5-year warranty andsoftware updatesthrough 2033.The new Fairphone (Gen 6+) is a small upgradeover the Gen 6that the company launched last year. It has a newer Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor and double the RAM at 12 GB, but is otherwise largely the same device (hence the “plus” in the name). It now comes in Cobalt Blue, a nod to the miners who extract the cobalt used to make phone batteries, and the company’s efforts to improve working conditionsin mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo.The new Fairphone is available on Amazon and atFairphone.comfor $650, and it’s officially certified to work on T-Mobile and AT&T’s networks.While this is the first time the company has brought its flagship mobile product into the US, its expansion to the States began last year with itsrepairable earbuds and headphones. (The company is also teasing its next-generation Fairbuds 2 wireless earbuds, launching later this year, which it says set “a new bar for repairability and performance.”)Photograph: Courtesy of Julian ChokkattuFairphone has been selling its ethically built smartphones in Europe for more than a decade. Its devices are easy to repair, and many of the components that make up the product are sourced sustainably. The Gen 6+, for example, is made with more than 50 percent fair-trade or recycled materials. The company supportsliving wages for factory workersin its supply chain, and its devices are assembled with renewable energy and are 100 percent e-waste neutral. The company is also aCertified B Corpwith a platinumEcoVadis rating—two independent certifications that back up its environmental and labor claims.Fairphone CEO Raymond van Eck tells WIRED that he sees his company’s products as a good alternative for consumers who arefeeling the pinchof the current economy. “If you look to the US market, it’s heavily duopolistic with very little real consumer choice,” van Eck says. “Americans are exhausted by planned obsolescence, closed-box ecosystems, and expensive yearly upgrades.”The US is a tough market to crack, with a duopoly held by Apple and Samsung. It’s worse for phone brands not sold through US carriers, which is how most Americans acquire new phones—carriers drive as much as 66 percent of smartphone sales, according to a 2025 report from the International Data Corporation. This situation has forced many companies to pull out: OnePlus recently announced its decision toexit the North American market, following several other phone makers over the last few years, includingHMD Global, Sony, and LG Mobile. To counter that narrative, van Eck says Fairphone is already in discussions with major carriers and mobile virtual network operators (MVNOs) to sell its device through their stores.While Google's Android powers the company’s mobile hardware, there’s a version you can buy powered byMurena’s de-Googled /e/OSfor $699. Fairphone also has a few features of its own. For example, you can flip a physical switch on the Fairphone (Gen 6+) to enableFairphone Moments, a minimal interface designed to reduce digital distractions. Van Eck hopes the minor performance boost in the Gen 6+ will help it support more advanced software features—such as AI-powered capabilities that often require more RAM. Speaking of, he says Fairphone isn’t immune to the challenges of theglobal memory crisis, but its “deep relationships” with suppliers have tremendously helped the company secure components.“We do not view our codependence on US technology as a compromise or a downside, but as a powerful synergy,” van Eck says. “You could say we take the best of US innovation, which drives the industry performance, and we wrap it with European care for the planet and people. This creates, I would say, a stronger product than either side could build in isolation.”The company is finally growing, too, thanks to anewfound marketing strategyof focusing on the quality of the product rather than the company’s ethical mission. It’s seeing growth year over year for the fourth quarter in a row, with phone shipments jumping 74 percent in the first half of 2026 compared to the prior year. Van Eck says 80 percent of people who bought the Fairphone Gen 6 are also new to the brand.“We are really now expanding toward a more mainstream crowd,” he says. “That is helping us tremendously and also giving a lot of confidence that we are really on the right path.”The Gen 6+ arrives only a year after the Gen 6, but van Eck says the company still plans to stick to its cadence of launching new phone generations every two years and is not moving to a yearly device launch like many of its big tech counterparts.Nathan Proctor, who leads the US Public Interest Research Group’sRight to Repaircampaign, is excited for Fairphone’s US entry and whether it will incentivize Big Tech to improve the repairability of their own hardware. He says there’s a market for people who want modular, fixable phones.“It’s proof that it can be done—if companies wanted to make eminently fixable modular products, they could,” Proctor says. “There’s no technological reason why they can’t do it; it really is what they’ve decided to produce. It does raise the question: Why isn’t more of our technology easy to fix? People are going to start thinking about smartphones as longer-term investments, especially as prices have gone up for these phones.”
generated_summary: Fairphone has been selling its ethically built smartphones in Europe for more than a decade. Its devices are easy to repair, and many of the components that make up the product are sourced sustainably. The new Fairphone (Gen 6+) is available on Amazon and atFairphone.

title: Can AI Coexist With Privacy? Proton’s Andy Yen Says It Will Have To
content: Andy GreenbergPrivacyAug 18, 2026 6:30 AMCan AI Coexist With Privacy? Proton’s Andy Yen Says It Will Have ToProton’s CEO is a champion of encryption for everyone. So why is he going all in on un-encryptable AI?Photo-Illustration: WIRED Staff; Alex Wong/Getty ImagesCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyIn the eyesof many privacy advocates, AI is just anothersurveillance technology. It supercharges online tracking and real-world spying tools, sifts through vast troves of everyone’s data to spit out its results, and then encourages users to share their deepest secrets and desires with a cloud-hosted large-language model.Surveillance capitalismmade AI possible, and AI returns the favor by making surveillance more powerful and the businesses that run on it more data-rich and profitable than ever.Andy Yenis among the most influential voices in the tech industry who equates AI with privacy invasion. He’s the founder and CEO of Proton, one of the world’s most popular encryption-focused tech companies. He says the push to integrate AI into every consumer tech product—whether people want it or not—is driving new users in droves to Proton’s products, which are, put simply, the end-to-end encrypted versions of every Google service from Gmail to Google Docs, Sheets, Calendar, and Meet.Yet Yen isnotanti-AI, he says, any more than he is anti-internet. In late June, Proton released the latest version of its very own AI chatbot, Lumo—just one way that Proton is integrating AI ever more deeply into its suite of tools, but seeking to do so in a way that’s more voluntary and preserves users’ privacy far more than the typical tech giant.That willingness to embrace the apparent contradiction between AI and privacy is just one way in which Yen’s views don’t cut cleanly across party lines—from current US politics to the lessons of Edward Snowden’s leaks to the question of the best corporate structure for a tech company that’s not solely designed to maximize profit. You can read our conversation about all of it here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.This interview has been edited for length and clarity.ANDY GREENBERG: I want to start by asking about your background and the origin story of Proton. You’re a trained particle physicist. You worked at CERN, the nuclear research facility, but you were inspired by the leaks of Edward Snowden back in 2013 to create Proton, right?ANDY YEN:I’m not actually a tech person or even an entrepreneur by training, so I really happened into this field a little bit by accident. I used to work at the Large Hadron Collider, which is a particle accelerator. It’s the largest in the world.I’ve heard of it ...Yes. And what you may not know is that every once in a while, the accelerator gets turned off for upgrades, and these upgrades can take quite a bit of time.So Proton was created in one of those upgrade cycles, where the physicists had a little bit more free time because the experiment wasn’t running, and they were upgrading it.So this is just, like, a period when Swiss physicists get to sit around over beers and think about privacy technologies?Yeah, yeah. This was the summer after Snowden had come out about government surveillance. So Snowden really informed the world about mass surveillance at the government scale. But if you imagine what the NSA knows about you and then compare that to, say, what Meta or Google might know, it’s really quite tiny.So the realization we had sitting in that cafeteria was, yeah, government surveillance is a problem, but the much bigger problem is corporate surveillance. I would argue today that if you look at the US government, they don’t even need the NSA. They can just directly subpoena Google, Facebook, and these giant companies, which they do on a very routine basis.So inadvertently, the business model of the internet had brought us into an age where we had the highest amount of surveillance at any time in human history, and that seemed [like it was] really not the way the internet should have gone. And that’s what really motivated us to think, what are ways we can address this problem?Proton is really a response to that. Today, the default business model of the internet is that everything you do is recorded, shared, monetized, and abused for purposes that are beyond your control. And we should really build an internet where privacy isn’t an add-on that you can maybe get if you go through five menus and click ten different buttons; it should be the default.And that was what led to the creation of Proton Mail back in 2014.And if you can bring us up to the present, where is Proton today, for people who may not be familiar with it?In 2014, if I went out on the street and I asked somebody, “How does Google or Facebook make money?”—probably one in 10 people would give me the correct answer. Today, if I go out into the world, it’s not10out of 10, but probably six or seven would actually know the answer. What that really means is the concern that people have for their data online has massively increased in the past decade.So Proton went from having a couple hundred thousand users to now over a hundred million. And email is the core of Google’s business model. You know, the reason Google can track you is that you’re logged in, and the reason you’re logged in is that you have a Gmail. And so if you are able to attack that piece, that’s actually the most effective piece to first dislodge somebody out of the Google ecosystem.So we started with email, did a calendar, file storage, documents, essentially recreating the entire Google Workspace, but in a more privacy-first way, and I would say without the creepy business model that Google employs.So how many people have you actually dislodged from Google? How many minds have you freed?We’ve dislodged a hundred million people so far, and we hope to dislodge a lot more in the decades to come.That’s an impressive number. How many of them are paying customers?Well, it’s a freemium business model, so most of them use it for free, but the typical conversion rates that you see for freemium business models are usually between 1 and 3 percent, and Proton sits in that bucket as well.You mentioned a couple of these landmarks in the history of surveillance capitalism, starting with Snowden. Today, anecdotally, the reason that more people are asking me about Proton than any other is AI. People keep asking me—my own family, my friends—if they should switch to Proton, and they’re asking because they’re sick of having AI pushed on them in Gmail in particular.Are you capitalizing on this AI backlash, this resistance to AI that is making people think about their privacy?We are capitalizing on it, and we’re making it easier than ever now to switch. So for example, now there’s an easy switch tool on Proton where you can basically bring all your emails from Google automatically and get everything put into Proton in just a couple clicks.But my take on this trend is actually a little bit more nuanced. AI is surveillance. The internet is surveillance. And that’s something that we have to come to terms with. The genie’s out of the bottle; we’re not gonna put it back in, and we are not gonna be returning to a pre-AI world. If we accept that as a fact, the key question becomes: Who do we want to have as the future stewards and controllers of this new future that we’re all stepping into today?And the options are: Number one, it can be the gigantic tech companies of the world who have done everything possible in the last two decades to prove that they cannot be trusted with your data; or maybe it can be some other independent tech companies with different business models. So Proton is also building AI features and AI tools, because I think if the privacy companies do not find a way to step in to build privacy-first AI, we are essentially ceding the future to tech companies that don’t have the best interests of users at heart.This is what happened in the late ’90s, early 2000s when we let Google, Meta, Yahoo, and these other companies take over the entire [digital economy]. So our push into AI is really to try to avoid a repeat of that mistake that was made several decades back. We think it’s important to actually be present there.Are you in fact excited about AI?Yeah. If I were to describe Proton’s stance, I would say we were reluctantly pulled in, but we saw the writing on the wall. Once we came to the conclusion that AI was here to stay, it was unavoidable—if we were to fulfill our mission—that we also [had to] enter the space to provide an alternative.I would probably prefer a world where AI didn’t exist, but it’s here.Interesting. Do your users agree?This has shifted quite a bit in just the last two to three years. When we first came out with the AI features in Proton, there was quite a bit of backlash. People were sort of like, “Why are you doing this? It’s a waste of resources. It’s not what Proton stands for. You’re just becoming like another tech company,” you know. But then, after we put out Lumo last year, what we really saw in the weeks and months after was: The exact same person who was flaming us for putting out this feature in July was now flaming us for not making Lumo better.They’re like, “Oh, this is not good enough. You gotta make this a better product.”So I don’t think they’re allergic to AI as a concept. I think they’re allergic to what AI represents in the Big Tech definition of AI. But when Proton does it in a way that actually ensures privacy, security, and ownership of their data and their conversations, then actually they’re OK with it.Well, it’s an interesting framing: Would you rather that Google have access to your chats with an AI, or would you rather trust Proton? But I was kind of surprised, when I dug into how Lumo works, that it is not end-to-end encrypted chatting with an AI.The privacy promise of Lumo is exactly that—a promise from Proton that “we’re not gonna look at these logs. In fact, we’re not gonna log this at all.” It’s not the kind of technical promise of encryption, which is “mathematics has prevented us from reading your email.”Yeah, with Proton Mail, the guarantee is actually mathematical. As a physicist, I like mathematical guarantees, right? The issue with LLMs is that the technology for doing that in a fully end-to-end encrypted way is not there yet. I think it will get there in a couple years.So the choice was either to sit on the sidelines and wait a few years for the tech to get there, or wade in and begin to understand the space and begin to offer a product. Now, a promise is not as good as a mathematical guarantee, but a promise made by the right people is still actually quite substantial.Of course, I hope in the years to come to be able to upgrade to a promise that is mathematically guaranteed. And there’s some interesting research work being done by Nvidia that in probably two years’ time will get us to a point where you can actually do LLMs in a fully, let’s say, end-to-endprotectedway.I’m trying not to get too nerdy here, but are you talking abouthomomorphic encryption?No, it’s basically—do you know about TPMs, trusted platform modules, and how that works a little bit?Yeah. If I could try to summarize it, it’s kind of like: You can’t encrypt the whole chat, but you can use cryptography to create a technical guarantee that part of the computer won’t look at another part of the computer.There’s a kind of secret enclave where these chats can happen, and it cannot be inspected by the rest of the server, essentially. So that creates a kind of technical guarantee of privacy. It’s certainly not end-to-end encryption, but it seems like something, in fact, that you could be doing today.I mean, other people are doing it. So can you explain why Proton is not?This is why I didn’t say end-to-end encryption, I said end-to-end protected. Because it’s not technically end-to-end encryption, it’s as you say: You can run the processing on the GPUs, but in a way that the rest of the pipeline that delivers the tokens to and from the GPU is not able to view it.And through using this secure execution environment, you can have a cryptographic guarantee that nobody else along the pipeline could look at what was sent to the GPU.That’s maybe the best simplified way to explain it. And yeah, it’s possible to do some of this already today, but there are certain, let’s say, performance issues. It’s still a little bit clunky. It doesn’t have proper support across the entire stack. So I wouldn’t say it’s impossible, but it’s gonna get easier to do in the years to come.Got it. Well, it is interesting, though, that people are already doing this today. Other products do use these trusted execution environments; they don’t just promise not to look at your conversations. But you don’t feel like it’s up to snuff yet? It doesn’t have certain features? What’s lacking? Why is Proton not using this now?Well, first, you have to re-architect essentially your entire platform in a way to do that. So it’s quite a bit of work. Also, when we put out Lumo last year, a year ago, the technology for AI was a lot more immature, right? Then there’s also the interfaces with the GPUs themselves.So, you know, Proton is not running on a cloud. We run our own infrastructure. And so then you’re pipelining it, and the libraries that Nvidia provides to do that have to be good, have to be stable, they have to be completely working, they have to be fleshed out, they have to be, you know, making sure there’s no security issues.So the technology for me, like I said, it’s, it’s almost mature, but we’re probably in a better position to fully deploy it in, let’s say, the next year or two.OK.So it’s pretty close. Some people are already doing it, but we have a bigger deployment environment.We have tens of millions of people using Lumo. We cannot move fast and break things as Mark Zuckerberg would say. We have to do things in a more careful and considered way because we have all the security requirements that we also have to keep in mind as well.Yeah. I mean, to be fair, I think people do trust Proton, and that’s why people switch to Proton.But the people who use Proton also have trust issues. They don’t want to trust anybody! I mean, for anybody who uses cryptography—you don’t want to believe a promise, you want to believe the math. So I don’t know if you’re committing to it here that you will switch …Yeah, we are committing to it. And actually, if you look at Lumo’s security model, which is published, you’ll see that we’ve already built the infrastructure to kinda do this. We’re just missing the last piece, at the interface to the GPUs. Look, I don’t wanna give too much away, but some might infer from this that perhaps some work has already been done on this in Lumo already.OK, very interesting.Now, setting AI aside, the other most common reason I get asked about Proton these days is, of course, this fear of creeping fascism in the US and around the world. This is an extremely fraught political moment, and people are afraid of surveillance—in some ways more than ever before—from governments.Is that also pushing people towards Proton? Are you seeing a Trump bump?We definitely saw a Trump bump, but we also saw a Biden bump. I think privacy is one of those few issues that is not really partisan. It’s something that is appreciated by both the left and right. So when Biden came into power, the people who supported Trump said, “Well, I’m not comfortable with these crazy leftists having control of my data and spying on me.”And then when Trump got into power, people on the left said, “Well, I’m not comfortable with these crazy fascists having access to my data.” So it’s a concern for both sides.You probably know, in privacy, the famous “nothing to hide” argument, right? You know, “I don’t need privacy, because I have nothing to hide, and I’m not doing anything illegal.”Even if that is true, the problem is that what is considered illegal changes over time.So you have nothing to hide as long as you agree with the current definition of what is, quote-unquote, “illegal.” It doesn’t really matter your political leaning, whether you’re on the left, on the right, or in the center. Privacy is something you should care about because it’s the only guarantee you have that, no matter how the next election goes, your data is secure.Yeah, I mean, I would love to get on board with this bipartisan push for privacy.But I feel like we have to acknowledge that this current administration has vowed to use the Department of Justice to prosecute its political adversaries; that it has vowed to deport millions of people living in America; that it’s given billions of dollars to ICE to carry out that mission. I mean, I don’t mean to be the first one to take a political side here, but it does feel like we’re in a certain moment.Yes. And the moment is especially relevant because I can give you maybe the European context to this. You could pretty accurately say that politics in the US really lurched to the right in the past 10 years or so, and the same thing’s happening in Europe as well.In the UK, if the election were to be held now, it’s quite possible that the far-right Reform party could win. If you look at France and you look at the polling for the next presidential election, Le Pen, even with her ankle bracelets, has a decent chance of winning. In France or in Spain or even in the US, if you were to put in place more surveillance, more regulations, more controls over the free internet because you think that might prevent the far right from coming into power—well, if they come into power, they’re going to take the new regulations, the new surveillance ordinances, the new surveillance powers that you have put into the legislation, and they’re gonna use that against you.So the powers that Trump is using today to suppress dissent and go after people that don’t agree with him: Actually, he didn’t pass any new legislation on this at all over the course of his most recent term. In fact, he was using powers that were already in place when Obama was around, when Biden was around, and maybe even from further before, right?Absolutely.So probably these powers should not have been there in the first place. They were probably tolerated for a long time because people thought, “Oh, well, I trust the current people in power.” But this can change very quickly in a democracy. And this is the cautionary tale. Age verification, [requiring] ID to use the internet, data retention laws, all the stuff that is being pushed out: When the far right gets into power, you’ve just given them, like, all the tools they need to really mess up democracy.So we need to have a more balanced approach. This is why I look at a lot of these legislative efforts that are being pushed across Europe these days, and I think people are not thinking through what can actually happen if they succeed today in passing these new regulations.Going back to Snowden, this is exactly what he called turnkey tyranny.He was warning not just that the Obama administration would use these surveillance powers, but that they were building a machine that any tyrant could turn the key on and create a panopticon.I guess the question is, do you feel like that is happening now in the US in particular?Well, it’s already happened in the US.Like I said, Trump didn’t pass any legislation. He just took the powers that were already present there, that any president could have deployed, and he deployed them in the way that he saw fit, which was in ways that people didn’t anticipate. But this is why you have to have foresight when you pass legislation.You need to be careful in legislation because you cannot always assume that your preferred party is still gonna be in power in the future, and you need to consider, “Would I be happy to have this law on the books if it was somebody else in power?“ And if the answer is no, then you probably should not pass that law.I have to press you on this just a little bit, though, because there was some controversy over your statements about partisan politics in the US a couple of years ago. Around the time that Trump was elected, you tweeted, “Ten years ago, Republicans were the party of big business and Dems stood for the little guys, but today the tables have completely turned.”I think people got mad about that, and then Proton put out a statement that actually kind of backed it up, that included this line, “Until corporate Dems are thrown out, the reality is that Republicans remain more likely to tackle big tech abuses.“ Do you stand by that a couple of years into this Trump administration? Where did that come from? Was it a kind of subtle endorsement of the left, actually, in opposition to centrist Democrats, or can you explain this?Well, actually, the context around this was talking about the antitrust pick that Trump put in place. And, you know, to be completely fair, when Biden made his antitrust pick, I liked that pick as well, so I also praised that one, right?And I actually thought Trump picked the right person for antitrust. I thought that was a good candidate. The pick that I liked was eventually fired by Trump, and probably the prospects of antitrust at the DOJ level are not gonna be the same now as they were when Gail Slater was still in place.What I think is interesting, though, is if you look at what’s happening on Capitol Hill, senators Grassley and Klobuchar have reintroduced the American Innovation and Choice Online Act, right? So that’s back. I don’t know if it’s going to pass this time around. It didn’t make it under Biden, but the fact that the bill got reintroduced and is being discussed does show that antitrust is not dead in the US.And this is, in my opinion, very important because the European Commission is not gonna be able to effectively regulate American tech companies. It just does not have the power and the capability to do that. The only government that can really regulate US tech is actually the US. So the cutting edge of antitrust enforcement, the place that will make the biggest impact, is still the US.And I think we need to do our best to support antitrust efforts, because this is the one thing that is going to make a difference. Capitalism is not gonna solve this problem for us. In fact, we know very well that capitalism is the creation and the cause of this problem. My suggestion for Democrats—as they prepare for the midterm elections and maybe taking back the White House—[is that] I think Bernie was correct in his assessment of why they lost the last election: You need to be able to offer something different if you want to actually be competitive. And today, if I look at tech policy, views on antitrust, and willingness to challenge the big corporations that in my view have way too much power, there is not much of a difference between the two parties in the US.And that is something that we’ve seen over and over again, where every single administration is unable to get antitrust passed.So essentially, it sounds like you are just an anti-corporatist above all. Like, you were kind of voicing your support, maybe your optimism, that the Trump administration would take an antitrust approach to Big Tech. It doesn’t seem like that happened. In fact, I would say that Big Tech has completely lined up behind Trump. I worried reading your statement that maybe Proton was lining up behind Trump as well. It doesn’t sound like that’s the case. If anything, it sounds like you are ready to join the Democratic Socialists of America. Is that correct?Well, look, I don’t really discuss politics, but I did give away most of Proton to a nonprofit foundation. And Bernie would probably approve, let’s put it that way.I’d like to come back to Proton’s interesting organizational structure later.Yeah.But the EU has also shown signs of wanting to undermine encryption, and now we see the advent of “Chat Control,” which I think will voluntarily ask big tech companies not to put backdoors into end-to-end encryption—as privacy advocates have always feared—but rather to scan content on the endpoints, which is arguably a different way of undermining people’s privacy.What do you think of this push for surveillance in some form in Europe? What is it like to be a privacy-preserving anti-surveillance company in Europe today?The thing that I found disappointing is that the push for Chat Control actually came from the political left. It was actually the socialist minister from Denmark when Denmark had the presidency of the EU.Now, in the end, I think the EU did the right thing because it split Chat Control into sort of two versions. There’s the version where you’re allowed to voluntarily do scanning—so this is what we call 1.0—and there’s a version 2.0, which is that you’ll be forced to do scanning. It was not voluntary anymore.Right. And we should say what this scanning is: The idea is that because information might be encrypted in transit, you scan people’s computers at the endpoints. You scan their phones.You scan the phone. So before you write a message, it’s gonna check with Big Brother if the message is OK. If it’s not OK, it sends it to the police, and the police come arrest you. This is basically what 2.0 would have done.And that sounds crazy, right? Itiscrazy. So I think there was enough opposition in Europe that people woke up to the dangers of that.These things, like zombies, have a way of coming alive again and reappearing. But my take is that actually 2.0 is dead. And 1.0, the voluntary scanning, probably shouldn’t have passed. But that, for me, is not so objectionable, because it doesn’t break end-to-end encryption. It doesn’t force scanning. It just allows you to do it on a voluntary basis if you decide that you want to do that.Meaning the company, though, not the user.Yeah, yeah, yeah, the company decides. So essentially Google and all these companies, now they’re gonna go scan all your shit, and they’re gonna do it happily, now that they have legal cover to do it. Proton is not gonna do it.With this kind of voluntary scanning model, maybe it creates more pressure for people to move from Google to Proton. But it also seems like it will create an environment where the government can say, essentially, “Look, all these other companies opted in, but Proton, you’re protecting all of these evildoers. What’s your problem?” And that creates pressure on you. Perhaps it’s a foot in the door to create a more mandatory kind of scanning.Yeah, once you open the door a little bit, it becomes easier to push the door open wider, and this is something that we have to be very careful about.I would say, though, Europe has this problem. The European economy today is not competitive. There are massive economic problems that are impacting the entire continent. And what I think is important is that there has to be a tech sector that can be successful in Europe, because tech is the driver of most economic growth for the past couple of decades.And Europe today doesn’t have a tech sector. Effectively, it doesn’t. And if you want to build a tech sector in Europe, what is going to be the competitive advantage for your industry? You are not gonna have more money or a bigger market than the US. Not gonna compete there. You’re also not going to work longer hours than the Chinese. I’m from Taiwan, so I can tell you it’s not gonna happen, right?I have lived in Europe for 15 years. And it’s also not gonna have the efficiency of China, where democracy is kind of an afterthought. So if you don’t have the money and the talent of the US, and you don’t have the speed and the scale of China and the work ethic of China, what do you have left to actually compete with effectively?I think the only thing that Europe has left is actually the values. What Europe stands for is democracy, freedom, privacy, and security. And the four things that I mentioned are predicated on the concept of trust. So trust is actually Europe’s only competitive advantage in the digital era. And if you pass legislation like Chat Control, which undermines that trust, what you’re basically doing is destroying the foundation for your future economic success.This is the message that I’ve been trying to push in Brussels and other capitals across Europe, because once you realize that, you understand how ridiculous and how counterproductive something like Chat Control is.As we were saying, Chat Control might actually push more people to Proton in the short term. That brings me to this question we were talking about earlier: What is Proton’s incentive? Is Proton a for-profit company? I know you’re part of a Swiss foundation. Can you explain? What is Proton seeking as a corporation?Well, our structure is quite unique. Maybe the best way to answer your question is to look at Google. Google’s slogan used to be “Don’t be evil," right?Of course, yeah. Circa 2006-07.What happened? How did Google go from “Don’t be evil” to, well, basically evil?I think two things happened. One, there was a misaligned interest between Google and its users. Because today, if you’re a user of Google, actually you’re not Google’s customer, right? You’re the product that they’re selling to the real customers, which are the advertisers. So there was a fundamental conflict of interest that was inherent in Google’s business model.The number two thing was: A corporation is kind of a very imperfect vehicle because it is legally compelled to act in the best interest of shareholders. And the best interest of shareholders is the maximization of profit, even at the expense of users and customers of that business.And that, if you think about it, is another misalignment of interests that exists in the corporate role. So going back to the question of my politics, you could say that I’m an anti-corporatist, right? I don’t believe in the corporation as the correct structure to meet the needs of society as a whole.So Proton’s structure is, let’s say, a way to try to resolve that paradox.Well, could I ask: What is the structure?The structure today is that the largest shareholder, the controlling shareholder, is a nonprofit foundation. And the sole asset that this foundation holds is actually shares of a for-profit, Proton AG.The reason I suspect this is going to work is twofold. Proton the corporation is accountable to its shareholders. But the biggest shareholder is a nonprofit foundation whose mission is democracy, privacy, security, and freedom around the world. That means the company will never be pressured to take actions that undermine that, because it is inconsistent with the mission of its primary shareholder.On the other hand, the company does make a profit. It is self-sustaining. It doesn’t have VC investors. Its employees actually have stock options, so they retain a profit incentive, and will have to compete in a capitalistic market in an efficient and effective way to survive in the dog-eat-dog world of capitalism as a corporation.This is also a protection for the foundation, because a foundation actually is controlled by its funders. If you’re a foundation and all of your funding comes from one or two entities, guess what? Actually, you’re controlled by those one or two entities.But Proton Foundation gets all its money from a profitable company which it controls, so it is not subject to pressure from external stakeholders either. And this is why the combination of the corporate with the foundation, in my opinion, is a self-reinforcing structure that actually protects both the company and the foundation.We’ll see in 10 years if I’m right or wrong.I don’t know. I’ve never heard of a tech company that works quite like this before.It’s about checks and balances. The fact that the nonprofit owns a profitable business means that it’s not begging around every single year for donations. That means it’s sustainable, it’s secure for the long term. But the company being controlled by the nonprofit means that the company needs to embody and adhere to certain values.It has never been done. It is completely an experiment. It very well may fail in the next couple years. We’re gonna see how this goes. But I think it sort of avoids the pitfalls of both of the examples that I gave, and so this is the answer that I arrived at as a pragmatic anti-corporatist.Well, let’s check in in 2036. Before I let you go, there is one other question I wanted to ask you. This is perhaps just my personal obsession. Proton has successfully end-to-end encrypted so much of its users’ lives, and especially their work lives, but there’s still Slack, this massive repository of sensitive workplace communications.Yeah, none of it is encrypted. Same goes for Discord, Microsoft Teams, whatever flavor of this you use in your organization. It all feels like this huge vulnerability. This giant repository of searchable, unencrypted communication about everything we’re talking about in our workplaces can be breached or obtained by law enforcement, just subpoenas.So when is Proton going to release Proton Slack, Proton Discord?I can’t answer the when, because that assumes I’m doing it. Can’t confirm or deny. I’m gonna keep it like that. But I agree with you. I think that’s a problem, and it’s something that we think a lot about.You know, we recently released Proton Meet, which is the end-to-end encrypted Microsoft Teams or end-to-end encrypted Zoom. And that starts to put us closer to the chat space as well, because actually you can chat when you’re having a video call on the side. And the chats are actually end-to-end encrypted. We’ve already figured that out. So I think we have the pieces to do it. And stay tuned. I hope to be able to solve this problem for people someday in the future.All right. Thank you, Andy. I really appreciate you doing this. Great to talk.Great. Thanks a lot for having me on.Update: 8/18/2026, 10:56 AM EDT: WIRED has corrected a section where the speaker was wrongly indicated as Andy Yen, when it was actually Andy Greenberg.How to ListenYou can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tapthis link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re onSpotifytoo.

title: The Cop Who Took On Flock
content: Dhruv MehrotraThe Big StoryAug 18, 2026 6:00 AMThe Cop Who Took On FlockAfter Noel Pichardo called out his city's embrace of Flock surveillance cameras, he was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in less than two years.Photograph: Tony LuongCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyCommentLoaderSave StorySave this storyOn an earlyfall afternoon in 2023, midway through a shift in Pawtucket’s District Five, Rhode Island police officer Noel Pichardo noticed a strange camera perched on a utility pole over West Avenue.Pichardo was 28, five years into the job, and alone in his cruiser during one of the brief lulls between responding to the typical churn of radio calls for domestic disputes, petty disturbances, and welfare checks. The camera was compact and solar-powered, angled down toward passing traffic. Pichardo made a U-turn and drove beneath it again, more slowly this time, to get a better look.He then began searching for the cameras on roads near highway ramps, at major intersections, along the routes into and out of the city. He found them again and again. By the time Pichardo finished circling the district, he knew exactly where he had seen them before.Two years earlier, officers had gathered on the second floor of a small police substation in Pawtucket for a presentation abouta surveillance systemmade byFlock Safety.A high-ranking police official stood in front of a PowerPoint and explained that the company’s automatic license plate readers could identify passing vehicles not only by their license plates but by bumper stickers, roof racks, and other distinguishing features. Investigators could search for a particular car across jurisdictions and, camera by camera, reconstruct where it had been.The system was presented as another tool of routine police work, a way to recover stolen cars, locate suspects, and find missing people. But as Pichardo listened, he found himself thinking less about the vehicles police wanted than about all the others. In a medium-size city like Pawtucket, where a handful of roads carried people nearly everywhere they needed to go, a record of a car’s movements amounted to a record of a person’s life—the places they visited, the people they saw, the routines they followed.As Pichardo understood it,the Flockproposal had gone nowhere because the city could not afford a permanent installation. So he let it slip from his mind.But now, on that afternoon on West Avenue, the cameras were all over his district.Pawtucket’s cameras are one small piece of a sprawling vehicle-surveillance system that touches nearly every state in the country. Flock markets its platform as the nation’s largest fixed license-plate-reader network, processing billions of sightings each month. Because departments can open their records to agencies elsewhere, a camera installed by one municipality can become searchable by investigators hundreds or thousands of miles away.Close-up of a Flock Safety camera.Photograph: Tony LuongIn 2021, around the time of Pichardo’s training, Flock offered Pawtucket police a free 60-day pilot. Seventeen cameras went up around the city as part of a regional test that also included Cranston and Woonsocket, according to records reviewed by WIRED. The rollout quickly drew criticism. The ACLU of Rhode Island accused the department of installing the cameras surreptitiously, after the pilot began without prior public input or notice to the city council. Pawtucket chief of police Tina Goncalves later apologized, saying that the department would “work better in the future” to communicate with the city council.The pilot ended later that year, and in May 2023 the local TV news reported that Pawtucket was not moving forward with the installation. Pichardo believed the idea was a dead letter.It was not. In September 2023, records show, Pawtucket moved forward with a two-year deployment worth $128,000. Records show that the city planned to install 20 cameras along many of its busiest roads, including Newport Avenue, Main Street, Broadway, Smithfield Avenue, and West Avenue—where Pichardo first noticed one hanging over the road.“Wait a minute,” Pichardo recalled thinking. “When did we make this decision to put these up?”Within months, Pichardo’s questions would set off a chain of events that, he says, ended his career in law enforcement. They would also eventually place him, somewhat improbably, at the center of a backlash against Flock that unites large factions of the American left and right.For a policeman,Pichardo contains more than his share of contradictions. He speaks with a thick Rhode Island accent that sounds like something lifted from a cop movie, but he peppers his conversation with occasional references to Nietzsche or obscure films. He describes himself as private by temperament but seems driven to stand out.Having spent some of his childhood in a poor neighborhood where drugs and gangs were part of the landscape, Pichardo says he learned that it was safest to keep his opinions to himself and stay out of other people’s business. When he was 12 or 13, he learned that his father, who had returned to the Dominican Republic several years earlier, had done so because he had a criminal record and was told it would be best if he left the country. Becoming a police officer offered a way of drawing a line between his father’s path and his own. After studying in the criminal justice program at Salve Regina University in Newport, Pichardo entered the police academy and joined the Pawtucket department in 2018. To hear him describe it, he’s always been something of an outlier on the force. “I’m possibly the only cop who would voluntarily go to musicals,” he once told me.In the weeks following that fall shift when he first noticed Flock cameras all over town, Pichardo kept picking at the question of how the cameras had returned. Detectives, he says he learned after asking around the department, were already using the system, though many patrol officers like himself appeared to know little about it.Pichardo contacted his work district’s local city council rep and asked how the cameras had been approved—his first time speaking to a politician, he says—but didn’t emerge with a clear answer. (Records show that the department had notified the purchasing board that it planned to move forward, but there was no public vote before the cameras were installed. The question of approval surfaced only afterward, when a council member asked whether the deployment should have come before the council. Officials said no. Installing the cameras was, they explained, an “administrative prerogative.”)Police officers swear oaths to uphold the law and report wrongdoing. Inside the department, Pichardo said, the unwritten rule was simpler: Don’t rat. He understood that speaking publicly could end his career. But he says he was inspired by whistleblowers like Frank Serpico and Edward Snowden, men of conviction who broke with powerful institutions and spent years living with the consequences. Pichardo has a pronounced sense of right and wrong and a tendency to treat compromise as betrayal. “You should never sell your integrity,” he says.License plate readers are a routine investigative tool, useful for locating stolen cars or identifying suspect vehicles without stopping large numbers of motorists. Experts broadly agree that reducing unnecessary police encounters and high-speed pursuits is a good thing. But to Pichardo, that usefulness was beside the larger point. Pawtucket had created a new form of surveillance over public movement with no debate, helping to build a world in which the government could quietly record where ordinary people went. It was not a world he found acceptable. If the officers who understood the system would not raise that question, he wondered, who would?Pichardo was still wrestling with whether to speak out about Flock when he brought it up with his wife, Emily. “Do what you believe is right,” she said; they would deal with whatever followed. After that, without notifying anyone in the department, Pichardo called a reporter at Pawtucket’s local newspaper.The article inthe Valley Breeze was published on October 11, 2023. Its headline was blunt: “Pawtucket Officer Has a Big Problem With New Cameras.”In the article, Pichardo called Flock a “grave threat” to privacy and warned that the system was ripe for abuse. He said he had learned of the full deployment from the newspaper itself, not from his own department. If a patrol officer knew so little about the cameras going up around the city, he asked, how much could the public possibly know? The whole thing gave him, he said, “1984vibes.”This was not whistleblowing in the conventional sense. Pichardo did not reveal a secret program, leak internal documents, or expose a specific abuse. In some respects, the newspaper knew more about the deployment than he did. What he offered instead was the rare perspective of an active-duty police officer breaking ranks to publicly argue that his own department had adopted a powerful surveillance system without enough scrutiny.Photograph: Tony LuongWhen the article appeared, the first text Pichardo received came from another officer.“I want to congratulate you on your testicular fortitude,” it read. The officer added that he was proud of Pichardo for doing what he believed was right. Then he warned him: The brass was furious.Pichardo says many officers supported what he had said to the Valley Breeze. Others, mostly older officers, viewed him as a traitor. One officer asked how he still had a job. Around the station, he was told that officers were calling him “Valley Breeze” behind his back. One sergeant, he says, told him he should quit.Within weeks, the warnings began to look prescient.Police internal investigationsare not criminal cases. Their purpose is generally narrower—to determine whether an officer has violated a policy, code of conduct, or general order. Investigators interview witnesses, review body-camera or surveillance footage, collect reports and emails, and question the officer at the center of the complaint. The interview is typically recorded, and the officer is often accompanied by a union representative.The process generates paper. A complaint. A notice of investigation. Lists of possible policy violations. Interview recordings and investigators’ notes. Findings, disciplinary recommendations, and notices of punishment.Before the Valley Breeze article appeared, Pichardo’s disciplinary record appears to have consisted of a single incident: In 2021, while working a police detail at a production of the musicalAnnie, he refused a vendor’s request that he wear a face mask, and he received a written reprimand and a two-week suspension. After Pichardo spoke out against Flock, he received notice of an internal investigation into his conduct on October 25, 2023. It would be the first of many.The department’s complaint, which originated from Chief Tina Goncalves, stated flatly that Pichardo had spoken to a newspaper without prior authorization, had undermined the authority of the police department and its chief, and had suggested that information collected by Flock cameras could be used improperly. His comments, the notice said, were “liable to cause harm to the reputation of the department and affect the impact on the community.”The potential violations included the department’s mission statement, code of ethics, media-relations policy, and a rule labeled “Criticism & Malicious Gossip.”Pichardo was ordered to appear at the Office of Professional Standards, a basement-level room in the Pawtucket police headquarters. Across from him, he says, were a lieutenant and a sergeant. A union representative sat beside him but said little.The interview lasted somewhere between 30 and 45 minutes, Pichardo recalls. The questions were straightforward at first. Had he spoken to the reporter? He had. Had he done so without authorization from the department? He had. Why?Pichardo gave much the same answer he had given the newspaper: The cameras were tracking people across the city, and the public had a right to know how they were being used. Pichardo says the lieutenant disagreed. Not every police tactic, he told Pichardo, was the public’s business. Departments did not disclose every method they used or every form of surveillance available to them.The investigators accused Pichardo of violating the public’s trust by speaking to the press.“I thinkthis departmentviolated the public trust,” he says he retorted. Then they asked who, in his view, should be held responsible. “The chief,” Pichardo said.WIRED could not review the underlying investigative file, including the recording that might confirm or contradict Pichardo’s account. The city declined to provide the file even when Pichardo requested records concerning his own case. Pawtucket officials did not respond to WIRED’s questions about the denial.A disciplinary agreement signed in early 2024 does, however, state that Pichardo made “critical statements to the media” about Flock and the department’s leadership. Pichardo maintained that his comments were constitutionally protected speech. The department expressly denied that position in the agreement.After consulting an attorney, the Pawtucket police union came to the conclusion that Pichardo’s comments were constitutionally protected and sent the city a letter warning that if it disciplined him, it would likely violate his rights. According to union lodge president Michael Cioe, the department initially sought a six-month suspension but reduced the proposed punishment after the union threatened litigation.Rather than fight the case through disciplinary hearings and possible state or federal litigation, the two sides reached an agreement. Pichardo would serve a 30-day unpaid suspension for speaking to the paper.Pichardo said he accepted the deal because he didn’t want his coworkers to see him as their enemy. “I wanted the war to end,” he says.By then, the department had already opened another investigation into his conduct.A month afterinvestigators questioned Pichardo about speaking to the Valley Breeze, another internal investigation notice arrived. In December, the department opened an inquiry over Pichardo’s failure to appear for a municipal court hearing about a traffic citation, which resulted in an additional two-day suspension. Chief Goncalves was again listed as the complainant.Then, in March, about a week after he returned to work from the suspension, yet another notice landed—this one concerning an encounter that had allegedly taken place nearly 15 months earlier.The incident involved a man who was being taken to a hospital for a mental health evaluation. The complaint alleged that Pichardo grabbed the man’s arm, refused to let him retrieve a jacket, and would not allow him to feed his cat. When the man pointed out that the cat could not open a can of food on its own, Pichardo allegedly replied that “cats can take care of themselves” and laughed.During his interview, Pichardo says he told investigators that the cat already had food and that other officers and mental health clinicians present could confirm that he had handled the encounter appropriately. Pichardo says the inquiry didn’t sustain the allegations, and he received no discipline.By the spring, Pichardo felt sure that the department was trying to send a message with these three investigations. Inside the department, Pichardo says, there was an unspoken expectation that his disciplinary agreement with his superiors would end his public criticism. Nevertheless, in April he accepted an invitation to testify at a public hearing before the Rhode Island House Judiciary Committee, where lawmakers were considering legislation regulating automated license plate readers.The hearing was carried live on the legislature’s Capitol Television network. Pichardo spoke off the cuff. He told lawmakers that the proposed legislation did not go far enough. Flock, he argued, was tracking people’s movements, and although he was “not a lawyer,” he believed the system raised serious Fourth Amendment concerns. He said the cameras had captured his own plate five times in a single day, cited an out-of-state officer who used Flock to track his ex-wife, and questioned whether police should possess technology with that kind of cross-jurisdictional reach.At times, Pichardo’s confidence outran his precision. He asserted that officers’ use of Flock could not be monitored, although the system does in fact maintain user logs and performs regular audits. In interviews with WIRED, he acknowledged the distinction but argued that logs were only as meaningful as the people responsible for reviewing them. He pointed to cases in other jurisdictions where officers had used Flock to track romantic partners or conduct improper searches, sometimes without the misuse being caught until much later. His broader point, he said, was that “anybody’s capable of anything” when given a powerful tool without sufficient guardrails.About a week later, in response to his testimony, the Rhode Island Police Chiefs’ Association sent a letter to the committee singling Pichardo out by name. It called his testimony “inaccurate at best” and, at worst, “inflammatory and patently false.” The association accused him of misunderstanding Flock’s capabilities, disputed his description of the system’s auditing, and suggested that he either lacked familiarity with the technology or had “an agenda where, in his mind, the truth is irrelevant.”Back at work, Pichardo says, his union representatives were annoyed that he’d spoken up again. (The union disputes this characterization.) Other officers, even those who largely agreed with him about Flock, or at least respected what he was doing, started to express concerns. One sat Pichardo down and said that if he wasn’t careful, he might lose his job and never work as a police officer in Rhode Island again. “You’ve got to think about your family, dude,” Pichardo recalls him saying.A Flock Safety camera in Pichardo’s area.Photograph: Tony LuongOn May 10,2024, a new incident set yet another internal investigation of Pichardo in motion: A delivery driver came to Pawtucket police headquarters to report that someone had thrown a bottle of soda at her vehicle during what she described as a road-rage encounter. Pichardo spoke with her, concluded that no crime had occurred, and declined to prepare a report.The woman later spoke with a sergeant, asking for the incident to be documented, and Pichardo was directed to write a report. According to the department's records, the delivery driver was not initially asking to file a formal complaint against Pichardo, but she did return to the station later that day, recording portions of her exchanges with Pichardo on her cell phone.Pichardo told her that Pawtucket is an urban environment where people argue and throw things, accused her of acting like a child and having a tantrum, and complained that she had “won” by persuading a supervisor to overrule him.Several days later, the woman filed a formal complaint with the Office of Professional Standards.Investigators reviewed the recordings and interviewed another officer on duty. The videos, investigators later wrote, showed the woman remaining largely calm as Pichardo became increasingly dismissive. They sustained more than a dozen allegations, including neglect of duty, insubordination, incivility, and conduct unbecoming.Pichardo acknowledged to WIRED that his conduct was indefensible. “I should still be the bigger person,” he said.What he disputed was the punishment: a 40-day unpaid suspension and removal from the detective eligibility list. He also says the union told him he was barred from taking the sergeant’s exam for two years. He was notified of the suspension on the day his second son was born, just as he was about to start paternity leave, meaning that his first 40 days at home with his baby were unpaid—a coincidence he alleges was deliberate.By early 2025,Pichardo had come to believe the department was finished with him. He no longer trusted that, if a traffic stop, arrest, or routine encounter generated another complaint, anyone in command would give him the benefit of the doubt. He more or less began to avoid active patrolling, he says. Between calls, he often waited at the Fraternal Order of Police building, which he helped maintain, or remained inside his patrol car rather than looking for the next stop. “I was trying to stay off the radar,” he later recalled telling investigators.Then two more investigations arrived.The first grew out of a dispute over a snowbound Volkswagen. On February 10, Pichardo responded to what appeared to be an unregistered vehicle stranded in the snow, concluded it was already disabled and had been ticketed, and gave the owner until the following day to move it. A supervisor ordered him to return and have the car towed instead. Pichardo questioned the instruction over the radio before complying. The department concluded that he had essentially been insubordinate.The second began less than two weeks later. Pichardo responded to a mother who wanted police to document her 13-year-old son as a wayward child after she suspected he had been burning paper inside their home. Pichardo declined to take a report, concluding that she lacked evidence and appeared more interested in having the state remove the boy than documenting a crime. Before leaving, he told her to go inside and “be a mother.”The department combined the investigations. Rather than focus only on the underlying incidents, investigators reconstructed nearly an entire workday of Pichardo’s life in excruciating detail. Using dispatch records, time sheets, cruiser GPS, and location data transmitted by Pichardo's body camera, they mapped his movements throughout the day of the family call. (They didn’t use Flock data; they didn’t need to.) Their reconstruction concluded that he had spent approximately four hours and 57 minutes at police facilities or the Fraternal Order of Police building rather than on patrol.Pichardo did not dispute where he had been. He explained that he helped maintain the union office and that officers routinely waited there between calls. From the department's perspective, the location data showed an officer spending much of his shift inside police or union buildings instead of policing the city. The department was recommending termination. The resulting complaint explaining the decision ran 25 pages. It contained 32 administrative charges—10 stemming from the tow dispute and 22 from the family call—and assembled nearly every disciplinary matter from Pichardo's career.On the morning of July 16, 2025, after roll call, a major asked Pichardo to stay behind.He knew what was coming.Chief Goncalves had signed a complaint the day before recommending his termination. The major handed it to him and explained that he was being suspended with pay while he decided whether to request a hearing in accordance with Rhode Island's Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. He had five days.Pichardo took the complaint home. But the more he thought about it, the less sense it made to fight. Even if he won, he believed, he would return to a department whose leadership had already decided it no longer wanted him.Two days later, after seven years as a Pawtucket police officer, Pichardo resigned.His letter was brief. Policing, he wrote, had meant a great deal to him and his family, but over the previous three years the department had made clear that he was no longer welcome because of his “philosophical convictions.” Remaining, he wrote, would only bring more grief to him and his family.He did not apologize for speaking out."My only regret," he wrote, "is that I was not articulate and/or diplomatic enough in my attempts to explain my position." On the 18th, he walked the letter to the Office of Professional Standards, shook hands with his coworkers, turned in his badge, firearm, radio, and keys, and left police headquarters for the last time.Pichardo alleges that the investigations and escalating discipline he was faced with were retaliation for speaking out about Flock. The reality may be more complicated. His union, which had backed him when the department sought to punish him for his comments to the Valley Breeze, says it saw no evidence that the later investigations were retaliatory. They believed another Pawtucket officer who engaged in comparable conduct would have faced similar discipline.Whether that is true is difficult to establish. Pichardo does not deny that he broke department rules in several of the incidents. His argument is that the rules were enforced differently against him—that conduct that might have earned another officer a warning became an internal inquiry, and misconduct that might otherwise have brought lesser discipline resulted in lengthy unpaid suspensions. He claims he had seen other officers do worse and face less. There is no way to know what would have happened to the version of Pichardo who never called the Valley Breeze.After resigning, Pichardospent months trying to remain in law enforcement. He applied to other police departments, private-security jobs, and campus police positions, including one at his alma mater, Salve Regina University. Some never responded. Others interviewed him before deciding not to move forward. An acquaintance who works in campus security at a local college eventually asked around and offered an explanation: "You're blackballed."He found work instead as a caregiver for a person with intellectual and developmental disabilities.Pichardo tried to tell himself that he had done enough. But he couldn’t shake the feeling that he had left something unfinished. “My conscience was still haunting me,” he told me. “I just wanted to be able to say I tried.”So he sat down with a friend who started a YouTube account for Pichardo, and they recorded a video.Another Flock camera.Photograph: Tony LuongSince I started speaking with Pichardo in April, the debate over Flock has spread far beyond Pawtucket. Across the country, cities have fought over whether to keep the cameras, some jurisdictions have canceled contracts or imposed new restrictions, and lawmakers in both Republican- and Democratic-led states have pushed for new limits on how the systems can be used. For Pichardo, there is something distinctly American about the backlash. The country has long attached dreams of freedom and self-determination to the car, a mythology reflected in advertising and even in the names of the vehicles themselves: Explorer, Expedition, Escape, Maverick, Liberty. Americans who agreed on little else could still recognize the promise of the open road—that, for a little while, a person might simply leave and be left alone. To Pichardo, Flock threatened that promise.“That’s freedom,” Pichardo told me. “The ability to drive somewhere and no one knows where you’re going.”The video opens with Pichardo sitting alone in a plain room, dressed in a crisp cream-colored shirt, daylight spilling through a nearby window. Looking directly into the camera, he tells viewers that speaking publicly is "one of the strangest things" he has ever done. But, he says, he feels obligated to warn them about a technology that has quietly spread into communities across the country."To put it bluntly," he says, "if you own a car, you are now being tracked."He expected a few hundred people to watch. Hundreds of thousands did.Within weeks, an email arrived from one of Tucker Carlson's bookers. Pichardo assumed it was a prank; he had never really sought a political audience. He had deleted his social media accounts years ago and had little interest in becoming a pundit. But in mid-July, there he was, spending nearly 20 minutes discussing license plate readers, surveillance, and the meaning of privacy with the former Fox News host. He was explaining Flock to one of the largest audiences in American media, in a video bombastically titled “Whistleblower Reveals the Largest Mass Surveillance Operation in History and the Coming Slave State.”Podcasters started reaching out, followed by local reporters and The Washington Post. Strangers urged him to run for office. Others told him to build up his YouTube channel, lean into the moment, and turn the audience into a career.The prospect was not without appeal. Pichardo was still rebuilding his life after losing his job; a large audience might offer money, security, even a new profession. But something about it felt dishonest. “The only reason people know who I am,” he told me, “is because I criticized something.”He had watched enough people online to recognize what he thought of as a trap. You begin with sincere convictions about serving the public, then you begin tracking an audience, and in time, he says, “you become a parody of what you were before.”His mind returned, he says, to a passage from the Gospel of Matthew. “What profit is it to a man,” the verse goes, “if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?”What Say You?Let us know what you think about this article in the comments below.
