Read ourPrivacy noticeAndy Burnhamhas been accused of being “prolier-than-thou” by using his working class roots to win votes.Political novelistRobert Harris, a lifelong Labour supporter, has toldThe Independenthe deplores attempts by the prime minister to appear more “proletarian” than he is.Harris called it a “prolier-than-thou” attitude – political slang based on the phrase “holier-than-thou” – a hypocrite who claims they are more authentically working class than others.Since entering No 10,Burnhamhas talked often of hisbackground as a working class Catholic Northernerand feeling “an imposter” at Cambridge University as a result.Harris, brought up in a council house and who also studied at Cambridge, said he “hated” it when politicians like Burnham “turn on the system that created them” and claimed to have had an “awful” background.Labour statesmen of the past like 1960s home secretary Roy Jenkins had far more genuinely poor origins but never used it to boost their popularity, said Harris.He also argued Burnham’s “desire to be liked” risked making him look “facile and glib” and forecast public “disillusion” with him could set in soon.In an in-depth interview withThe Independenteditor-in-chief Geordie Greig forIndependent TV, Harris spoke for the first time of his “painful” rift with Britain’s former ambassador to the USPeter Mandelsonafter he was forced to resign over the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.Watch Geordie Greig’s full interview with author Robert Harris belowHe reveals that he and Lord Mandelson, godfather to one of Harris’s children, had had no contact of any kind since shocking details of Mandelson’s links to paedophile Epstein emerged earlier this year.The fact that neither had reached out to the other “speaks volumes”, says Harris.He discloses a hilariousFawlty Towers-style “don’t mention the war” incident at dinner withTony Blairand wife Cherie at No 10 whenHarris fell out with Blair over the 2003 Iraq war.Harris tips home secretaryShabana Mahmoodto become Labour’s first female prime minister, and suggestsBurnham’s surprise choice of “malleable” John Healey as chancellormay have been because “formidable” Mahmood intimidates him.Harris, author ofFatherlandandConclave, was speaking in the run-up to the publication later this month of his latest novel,Agrippa, about the right-hand man to Roman emperor Augustus.Explaining why he objects to the way he says Burnham and Starmer have played up their working class beginnings, Harris says: “Andy Burnham (has) talked about… (he was) very prolier-than-thou about his Labour roots – likeKeir Starmergoing on about his toolmaker father and all of this rather desperate stuff.”British statesman Roy Jenkins, former Labour minister who served as president of the European Commission, was born to a miner father who was jailed for his political views – but Jenkins never tried to capitalise on it, states Harris.open image in galleryPolitical novelist Robert Harris in conversation with Geordie Greig(The Independent)He adds: “I went to Cambridge from a comprehensive school. The system worked for me as it did for Burnham. I hate Labour politicians turning on the very system that's created them.Harris fears Burnham’s administration will “soon run into problems”.“He is a deft politician. I think he’ll ride the waves very skilfully. Whether he will be able to tackle the fundamental problems in the country, I don’t know.“As so often, his weaknesses and strengths are often just the same trait. He has a desire to be liked, knows how to make people like him and knows how to communicate with people.“At the same time this can make him look rather glib, facile, and willing to bend… he’ll say something to get out of trouble in a tight spot, and then won’t be able to follow through. So there will be a process of disillusion – it seems hard to think that there wouldn’t be.”Burnham’s rates cut for pubswas an attempt to woo Labour voters who had defected to Reform, led by beer-drinking Nigel Farage, argues Harris, but it was “old-fashioned” to see pubs as working class.“One of the great things about Blair was I thought he had taken class out of politics. I mean, he was a public schoolboy leading (the Labour Party).”Harris hesitates, clearly troubled, when asked if he has been in touch with Mandelson.“It’s a very painful subject, personal subject,” he says.“I haven’t spoken to him. He hasn’t called me or got in touch since he was sacked as ambassador. So that’s where we stand. I haven’t got in touch with him. He hasn’t got in touch with me. I can’t say any more than that. I think that merely that speaks volumes.”Pressed further, he says: “I don’t want to add to his troubles. People watching or reading this can guess the state of play.”open image in galleryRobert Harris was reluctant to discuss his friendship with Peter Mandelson(The Independent)It sounds as though the friendship is broken for ever.Reflecting on the wider aspect of the Mandelson-Epstein scandal, Harris says he hates seeing politicians “hunted down by the mob” – just as they were in the time of Agrippa in Rome.But it also illustrates what motivated him as an author: “It shows you why it’s so interesting to write about power… this combination of morality, law, power, personal weakness, personal strength, the drama of it.”Harris says Starmer’s downfall was caused by his weakness and because he lacked “the ferocity of convictions” that a leader like Margaret Thatcher had, or the ability “to see something through once he’d settled on it”.“He buckled again and again. The problem for Starmer was purely personality; I don't think he could get on terms with a lot of his cabinet.”Harris sees parallels between the Roman empire, the frequent subject of his novels, and modern politics.So-called strong-man leaders such as Trump and Putin were like Emperor Augustus, “essentially dictators” who used power to make themselves rich.In a more benign fashion, Harris says there was “definitely something of the Agrippa-Augustus relationship” to the alliance between Blair and his chancellor, and later successor as PM, Gordon Brown.Brown was “blunt, direct, brooding” – like Agrippa: Blair was “the charming, younger, slighter, front man” – like Augustus.Harris concedes he had such a “close liaison” with Blair when Labour came to power in 1997, he was effectively part of “Team Blair” – for a while.He and wife Gill Hornby, also a novelist, were early guests at Chequers, the prime minister’s official country residence in Buckinghamshire, and he and Blair “got on well”.But he and Blair became “too close”, says Harris, recalling how their friendship ended in acrimony over the Iraq war, which Harris strongly opposed.After early foreign policy successes, Blair foolishly “thought he could walk on water”, says Harris. After Harris made his views clear, Blair tried to patch things up, inviting Harris and his wife to another private dinner with him and Cherie, this time at No 10. Blair appealed to him: “Come on, we, we should get together.”But the dinner backfired. Harris says: “It was clear that this gamble (the Iraq war) was failing badly.”open image in galleryHarris said he became ‘too close’ to Tony and Cherie Blair(Andrew Parsons/PA)To his surprise, the war was raised not by Blair but by Cherie, who announced France’s president Jacques Chirac “had behaved appallingly because he’d opposed the war”.Blair tried to stop her. “Tony said, ‘Now, don’t let’s get onto the war’. You know, it was like – don’t...”I completed the sentence for Harris: “… don’t mention the war?” – as in the famousFawlty TowersTV series where hotel owner Basil Fawlty (John Cleese) tries, and fails, not to mention the war to a German guest.”Harris laughs: “Yes, it was a touch ofFawlty Towers.”It led Harris to reassess Cherie Blair’s political leanings: “She’d always been painted as the leftier of the two, (but she) actually had called round Labour MPs to urge them to support the war.”The “froideur” with Blair continued, but the episode had the benefit of inspiring one of Harris’s most successful novels,The Ghost– more than loosely based on Blair and the Iraq war – and a movie version starring Pierce Brosnan and Ewan McGregor.It is about a British ex-prime minister mired in scandal over a controversial foreign policy collaboration with America. Blair himself was far from pleased.“He said to my publisher, ‘The next time Robert writes a book, tell him to make it up, find his own character’.”By contrast, Cherie was amused.“It was quite funny because… her role, the ex-prime minister’s wife, was played by Olivia Williams. She saw Olivia at some reception and said, ‘Oh, I've seen you playing me in the film’.“Olivia said, ‘I hope it wasn’t too upsetting’. She said, ‘No, I got to sleep with Pierce Brosnan and Ewan McGregor!’”While he is lukewarm about Burnham, Harris glows with admiration for home secretary Shabana Mahmood, whom he has met.“She is blunt, plain speaking, clever, charismatic, talked like a human being, very much what Tony was like at the beginning.“And she’s got a lot of courage, as Tony had. I wouldn’t be surprised if she doesn’t end up as Labour’s first female leader.”Mahmood is “head and shoulders above” most of the rest of the cabinet.Harris, who remains well connected in Labour circles, observes mischievously: “I heard that Burnham backed off making her chancellor because she’s too formidable; she wouldn’t be pushed around. He’s got a more malleable figure (as chancellor) in John Healey.”An intriguing theory.Harris is proud of the fact that he has never once voted Conservative and claimsthe party could be out of power for decades because of Boris Johnson.“He could have ruined it (the Tory party) for a generation. Once you start throwing away the rules and adopt a Trumpian approach to morality and lying, then something goes out of politics.”One of the themes inAgrippais how the huge power of Roman leaders could turn them into monsters.open image in galleryHarris’s latest novel, Agrippa(PA)“If you want to look at power, really you can do little better than to go to the Roman world because it’s all stripped down and simple.”The personal consequences of winning and losing power in modern British politics are less violent, but not so different in essence, according to Harris.“You have to take decisions quite ruthlessly. You have to often drop old colleagues, old friends. Look at the bloodletting that’s in the cabinet just lately with Burnham coming in.“A lot of people will feel that Burnham is a monster, just as a lot of people thought that Starmer was when he fired so many.“It is a very difficult thing to become a successful politician and not turn into a monster. Harold Wilson (Labour prime minister in the 1960s and 1970s) said the trick was to learn to take criticism, harden yourself, absorb it or ignore it, but not to become a monster.“That is a fine line.”More aboutAndy BurnhamRobert HarrisTony BlairShabana MahmoodKeir StarmerPeter MandelsonJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
generated_summary: Robert Harris accuses Burnham of ‘desperate’ attempt to play up working class roots by novelist. Labour prime minister’s 'desire to be liked' risks making him look ‘facile and glib’

title: Bristol osteopath struck off after telling patient that ‘having sex with children is OK’
content: NewsUKHome NewsBristol osteopath struck off after telling patient that ‘having sex with children is OK’Jeremy Marquette also said that he does not ‘believe in rape’Alex BousfieldWednesday 19 August 2026 12:04 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryJeremy Marquette has been struck off for a series of ‘inappropriate’ comments to patients(Linkedin)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeAn osteopath who told a patient “it’s OK to have sex with children as long as they have hit puberty” has been struck off.Jeremy Marquette, who worked at Toward Health Clinic in Bristol, started a sexualrelationshipwith one of hispatientswhile continuing to treat her, atribunalfound.Mr Marquette knew that the woman had a history of mental illness and previous sexual trauma, it found.He also made a series of “wholly inappropriate” comments to patients related to sex, including that he “raped the brains” of two patients.He also told a patient that he does not “believe in rape” and “there are always two sides to the story and the man should always be believed”, the tribunal heard.The General Osteopathic Council (GOC) has now struck him off the register.open image in galleryJeremy Marquette was an osteopath at Toward Health Clinic, pictured(Google Maps)Mr Marquette became an osteopath in 2016.The allegations were made by three different patients whom he treated between 2021 and 2023.None of the patients can be named for legal reasons but are referred to in the tribunal’s decision as Patient C, Patient D and Patient E.It was found that Mr Marquette had started a “wholly inappropriate personal and sexual relationship” with Patient C. She would stay over at his house, where they would hug and kiss and she would sleep topless in his bed, the tribunal heard.She was a “vulnerable” person at the time and had experienced extensive amounts of childhood trauma.Mr Marquette denied that they ever had a sexual relationship because there had been no “kissing or contact of a sexual nature” and he had not said anything in a romantic way.But Sue Ware, the chair of the committee, said that the committee found the patient’s evidence “persuasive”."She gave a clear account of the relationship that had developed between her and [Mr Marquette],” Ms Ware said.“[He] was also aware that Patient C had had problems with her mental health in the past and had been the victim of more than one sexual assault, as he had recorded in her notes: 'Mental health quite bad after sexual assault 2 years ago July 2, was already in counselling for younger assault suicide.'”Mr Arquette was found to have made “inappropriate” comments to Patient C, including saying that she was a “cripple” and that “it’s OK to have sex with children as long as they have hit puberty”.He also said he would write a screenplay about her trauma and sell it to Hollywood.Patient E alleged that she started dating Mr Marquette 15 months after being a patient. Mr Marquette denied the allegation and said it was 'malicious and untrue.'He made further comments that she was a “cripple” and would have died by suicide if it was not for him. He also got her to pay for his MOT and never paid her back.Simon Butler, representing Mr Marquette, said that Patient C's allegations had been “retaliatory” because of Patient E's friendship with Mr Marquette.“Mr Butler suggested that Patient C had been motivated by a deep sense of abandonment and profound betrayal,” the tribunal heard.Mr Arquette also made inappropriate comments to Patient D, in which he said “I do not believe in rape” and “there are always two sides to the story and the man should always be believed”, the tribunal heard.The GOC panel found that Mr Marquette was guilty of unacceptable professional conduct.The panel said: "The Committee considered that the facts found proved collectively demonstrated a serious departure from the standards required of an osteopath."The Committee’s findings demonstrated that, in summary, [he] had transgressed appropriate professional and sexual boundaries with more than one patient."One of those patients, Patient C, was vulnerable and as the Committee had found, [he] had been sexually motivated in some of his actions towards her."Despite the fact that the relatively brief relationship between [Mr Marquette] and Patient C’s had only involved touching, kissing and sharing the same bed (they had not had sexual intercourse), she was (as he had identified) vulnerable as a result of previous mental health difficulties and a previous history of sexual assault."The Committee therefore had no doubt that [his] conduct as regards Patient C alone had to be regarded as serious and would certainly have the effect of undermining public trust in the profession of osteopathy."If you are a child and you need help because something has happened to you, you can call Childline free of charge on 0800 1111. You can also call the NSPCC if you are an adult and you are worried about a child, on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adults on 0808 801 0331.If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit theSamaritanswebsite to find details of your nearest branch.If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit988lifeline.orgto access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go towww.befrienders.orgto find a helpline near you.More abouttribunalrelationshipPatientsBristolMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: BBC’s Emma Barnett reveals she’s had hysterectomy ‘I never wanted to have’
content: NewsUKHome NewsBBC’s Emma Barnett reveals she’s had hysterectomy ‘I never wanted to have’The presenter had the procedure just two days before her documentaryFighting EndometriosisairedHarriette BoucherWednesday 19 August 2026 11:21 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryEmma Barnett has revealed she had to undergo a hysterectomy(BBC/Raw Media Productions)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeBBCpresenterEmma Barnetthas revealed that she had to undergo ahysterectomythat she “didn’t want to have” as a result of her cripplingendometriosis.The 41-year-oldTodayprogramme host said her symptoms became “a lot worse” in her final weeks of filmingdocumentaryFighting Endometriosis, in which she discusses her life-long struggle with thecondition.Just two days before the documentary aired in June, Ms Barnett had to undergo a sudden and extensive endometriosis surgery, ahysterectomyto remove her womb and a gallbladder removal.She wrote on Substack: “I felt blind-sided and robbed. Even though my care had been superb and doctors, utterly brilliant.“But this was not the road I had envisioned for myself. I had the hysterectomy I never wanted to have.”open image in galleryMs Barnett first revealed her diagnosis in 2024(BBC/Raw Media Productions)Ms Barnett has frequently spoken out about the debilitating pain she experiences from endometriosis, a condition where tissue grows outside the uterus and causes swelling, bleeding, and severe pain during a period.She said she did not want or plan to have her recent surgery, but said the situation became “urgent and non-negotiable”.“I didn’t want this procedure because it’s major surgery. It’s frightening and a hardrecovery- something I am living now. I didn’t want it because I wanted there to have been medicine or treatment to help my endometriosis. It felt and feels too extreme.“Is such major surgery what anyone would ‘choose’? Yes, I officially and legally consented to the procedures - in so much as you can know what you are letting yourself in for.”Ms Barnett said she did not “buy into the idea that the womb is sacred and at the heart of being a woman. I am still very much a woman and me.“I am grateful to it because somehow it managed to help me have two children. Having your womb removed without having children if you wanted them is a totally different situation - one I must acknowledge.”open image in galleryEndometriosis costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year(Alamy/PA)Earlier this year, Ms Barnett spoke out about a“horrific” experiencewith endometriosis where she couldn’t “remember a single thing” about a radio broadcast after being hit with intense pain.The presenter previously had a laparoscopy, a surgical procedure to surgically remove endometriosis, which she said was difficult to recover from, and provided no pain relief.She returned to air on Wednesday morning after an 11-week recovery, which she described as “one of the most humbling experiences of my life.”The cause of endometriosis is unknown and affects around one in 10 women, according to Endometriosis UK.Some 1.5 million women in Britain suffer from the condition, which costs the UK economy £8.2bn a year in treatment, loss of work and healthcare costs.More aboutEmma BarnettEndometriosisHysterectomyBBCRecoverydocumentaryJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Camilla reveals she almost let slip King Charles’ cancer diagnosis before official announcement
content: NewsUKHome NewsCamilla reveals she almost let slip King Charles’ cancer diagnosis before official announcementThe Queen spoke on the emotional strain of keeping Charles’ diagnosis a secret and admitted to ‘longing to let it out’Laura ElstonWednesday 19 August 2026 11:08 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverCamilla hears personal stories of overcoming homelessness in NorfolkGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeThe Queenhas reflected publicly for the first time on the emotional strain of keeping the King’s cancer diagnosis private prior to the official announcement.Attending a public engagement at a Maggie’s cancer support facility in 2024, Camilla carried out her duties in full knowledge ofCharles’s condition, just days before the news was released to the world.Her thoughts on managing the troubling diagnosis behind closed doors were shared in a short film produced jointly by Buckingham Palace and Maggie’s to mark the charity’s 30th anniversary.Describing the experience two years ago as "quite difficult", the Queen admitted to "longing to let it out", before adding: "obviously I couldn’t".She acknowledged that she "almost said something", yet determined that the timing was not right.open image in galleryCamilla admitted she wanted to tell people about the diagnosis(@RoyalFamily/Buckingham Palace)Camilla also reflected on supporting her "poor husband", observing how the King chose to focus on his work following his diagnosis as his personal method of dealing with the situation."Nothing stopped him. He just said ‘This is my way. I’m going to cope with it’," she said.Maggie’s chief executive Dame Laura Lee, who engaged in conversation with Camilla at Clarence House for the video, commended the Queen for her fortitude during that 2024 visit.Serving as president of Maggie’s, Camilla officially launched the charity's new centre at London's Royal Free Hospital on January 31 2024, at a time when the King was recovering after undergoing treatment for an enlarged prostate.As revealed in the video, Charles had already been diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer by the time of the event, ahead of the formal palace statement issued five days later on February 5.The health of the 77-year-old monarch, who is still receiving cancer treatment, is reported to be continuing in a very positive direction. Towards the end of last year, Charles noted it was a "personal blessing" that his schedule of treatment was being reduced.Reflecting on the visit, the Queen stated: "I remember coming to see a Maggie’s just after the King being diagnosed. Nobody could say anything at the time. That was quite difficult. I almost said something but, you know, I felt that it wasn’t the time to say."(I) looked at everybody who was suffering and all the relations and I think it made me realise even more how important these places were."open image in galleryDame Laura Lee (right) commended Camilla for the strength she showed during the difficult period in 2024(Getty)During the recorded discussion, Dame Laura remarked to the Queen: "It was just a week before it became public and the courage that must have taken for you…"Camilla responded: "Well it wasn’t… I was just longing to let it out but obviously I couldn’t."Speaking about her interactions with visitors during the engagement, she said: "I was almost questioning them. I didn’t want to pry too deeply."But normally when I went in, I was just talking to them, but I don’t know, I felt it was much more deep."Dame Laura highlighted the growing number of visitors seeking support at their centres following the King’s willingness to speak openly while maintaining a productive schedule, noting a 12% increase in male visitors to Maggie’s locations.Charles returned to public-facing duties in April 2024, under three months after his treatment commenced.Known as a committed workaholic, the King had previously been described by the Queen as someone who "won’t slow down and won’t do what he’s told", even after receiving his diagnosis.In Wednesday’s video, which was made available on YouTube, she said: "Look at my husband. Nothing stopped him. He just said ‘This is my way. I’m going to cope with it’."She added: "It made me realise even more how important these places were.open image in galleryCharles returned to public-facing duties under three months after his treatment commenced(PA)"It had never really come back to roost at home, and suddenly your husband is diagnosed, and you think ‘Goodness I’ve been talking to all these people and now I’m the one with some relation who’s got to help to look after my poor husband and try and understand it all."The seven-minute film was recorded by the Queen to highlight the vital assistance Maggie’s offers cancer patients, alongside promoting resources available for relatives and encouraging men who might feel reluctant to seek help.She further called for every hospital to feature a Maggie’s centre.Dame Laura praised Camilla, who has served as president of the charity since 2008, for speaking "powerfully of her own emotions" and displaying a "natural response" as a wife, while also praising the King for his openness.She said: "To hear her speak so powerfully of her own emotions when visiting our Royal Free centre, while knowing about His Majesty’s diagnosis, is a huge honour."The King’s openness about his diagnosis has undoubtedly helped others to be more open themselves and to now hear the Queen’s completely understandable and natural response as a wife shines a light on why it is so important that family and friends also get the support they need."Operating 27 facilities across the UK built within the grounds of major NHS cancer hospitals, Maggie’s provides support to hundreds of thousands of individuals annually.The organisation delivers comprehensive care for those affected by cancer, offering free psychological, emotional and practical support through drop-in sessions that require no appointments.More aboutKing Charles IIICamillaCharlesdiagnosisCancerJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: UK gas prices hit three-year high – here’s what it means for your bills
content: NewsBusinessUK gas prices hit three-year high – here’s what it means for your billsThe prices are up but still less than a quarter of the level seen during Russia’s invasion of UkraineKarl MatchettBusiness and Money EditorWednesday 19 August 2026 11:00 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverRealted video: US vice-president JD Vance says keeping gas prices low is 'goal number one' of Iran warSign up to our free money newsletter for investment analysis and expert advice to help you build wealthSign up to our free money email for help building your wealthSign up to our free money email for help building your wealthEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeUK naturalgas priceshave hit a three-year high, raising concerns that households will face an extended period of higherenergy billsthrough winter and beyond.Prices reached above 158p per therm on Wednesday, according to Trading Economics – the highest level since January 2023.The price, likeoiland other commodities, have been significantly impacted by the Iran war, first rising in March before pulling back across April to June when a ceasefire appeared possible.As well as the Middle East conflict, supply and demand constraints have impacted on the price, with the extreme hot weather pushing up electricity usage andstorage levels across Europe lowerat this time of year than usual, ahead of normal higher needs in winter.However, the price remains far lower than in 2022, when it surged far above 600p.How will the rise of UK gas prices affect your bills?Wholesale gas prices make up a significant part of the total cost of energy bills but there is a lag between when prices change and when they impact on the figures seen on bills.Ofgem sets the price cap every three months, with the next announcement due around 26 August to set the cap for October to December.Rising prices now will not impact that price cap; Ofgem tracks price averages across a rolling period of time, so current gas prices will contribute towards the period for January to March, announced in November.Jess Ralston, head of energy at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU), said: “To many households this will feel like a horrible reminder of the first gas crisis after Russia invaded Ukraine. Even more worrying is that wholesale gas prices have reached a near four-year high which is likely to cause more increases to future bills.Get a free fractional share worth up to £100.Capital at risk.Terms and conditions apply.Go to websiteADVERTISEMENTGet a free fractional share worth up to £100.Capital at risk.Terms and conditions apply.Go to websiteADVERTISEMENT“ This is a result of the UK's continued exposure to high gas prices caused by the war in the Middle East – our reliance on gas for home heating is a particular concern as although electric heat pump sales are on the up, we still lag behind European neighbours going further and faster to reduce gas dependence.“More gas from the North Sea won't lower prices – as this and previous governments have admitted – so the new prime minister will have to look elsewhere for long term relief. Renewables are already squeezing gas off the system, reducing the times it sets the price for our electricity and so lowering wholesale power prices by a third last year.“But the UK doesn’t control the price of gas, so unless that shift continues we're putting the prices we pay to heat and power our homes in the hands of geopolitics and actors like Putin and Trump.”Meanwhile, Thomas Pugh, the chief UK economist at consultancy firm RSM, suggested that one knock-on effect of rising energy prices would be no change to interest rates from the Bank of England this year.“Interest rates are likely to remain on hold this year, and renewed rises in oil and natural gas prices will keep the MPC alert to another inflation surge. That points to no rate cuts until 2027,” he said.More aboutgas pricesEnergy Billsnatural gasOilJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: What is endometriosis and what are the symptoms?
content: NewsUKHome NewsWhat is endometriosis and what are the symptoms?The painful condition causes cells similar to those in the lining of the womb to grow in other parts of the bodyRebecca Whittaker&Anna DruetWednesday 19 August 2026 10:48 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverEmma Barnett CLIP Endometriosis-male Pattern BaldnessGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeRadio presenterEmma Barnettrevealed she has had a hysterectomy after battling withendometriosis for decades.The Today Programme presenter shared the news on Wednesday morning, revealing she had undergone surgery after being taken to hospital forendometriosis.In June, Ms Barnett, 41, made a documentary,Fighting Endometriosis, looking at the system-wide inflammatory disease which affects about 1.5 millionwomen in the UK, causing symptoms such as chronic pain, fatigue and infertility.Writing on her SubstackTrying with Emma Barnettshe said:“I didn’t want this procedure because it’s major surgery. It’s frightening and a hard recovery - something I am living now. I didn’t want it because I wanted there to have been medicine or treatment to help my endometriosis. It felt and feels too extreme.”The painful condition causes cells similar to those in the lining of the womb to grow in other parts of the body. But, despite endometriosis affecting around one in 10womenin the UK, it takes an average of eight years to get a diagnosis.open image in galleryEmma Barnett revealed she has had a hysterectomy as she returned to BBC’s Today Programme(BBC/Raw Media Productions)Here’s everything you need to know about endometriosis:What is endometriosis?Endometriosis causes tissue similar to that which grows inside of the uterus (the endometrium) grows in other parts of the body.In most cases, this growth happens on and around organs in the pelvic cavity, and the tissue in endometriosis acts just like it would inside the uterus: it grows, thickens and tries to shed with every menstrual cycle.But in rare cases endometriosis tissue can grow in the lungs or deep inside the chest cavity, according to The Endometriosis Foundation.The tissue that grows outside of the uterus, whether thats in the pelvis area or outside, has no way of leaving the body and it can cause a lot of pain and lead to other complications, including infertility.It can take almost a decade to get a diagnosis, leaving women to struggle with debilitating pain with no treatment for years.Endometriosis can begin around the same time as the first period which may lead a person to think a high level of pain is “normal” for them, when it could actually be caused by endometriosis or by another medical condition.Another reason a person might not recognise the symptoms of endometriosis as anything other than those commonly prevalent around menstruation, is that they are often cyclical, meaning they occur at the same time as the period.open image in galleryEndometriosis affects about one in 10 women in the UK(Getty/iStock)What are the symptoms and when do they usually start?Symptoms of endometriosis generally develop before the age of 30 and can include any of the following: heavy periods, painful menstrual cramps, pain during or after sex, painful bowel movements and urination, pain in the abdomen or lower back that can last throughout the cycle, and difficulty getting pregnant.Should you experience any of these, it is always important to speak to a doctor.What causes it?It is still unclear exactly why endometriosis occurs; but oestrogen production, genes, and the immune system are all thought to play a role in the development of this condition.There is evidence that endometriosis can be passed down through the genes, meaning a person may be more likely to have it if someone in their biological family does.Additionally, someone may also be more likely to develop endometriosis if they reproduce later in life, or not at all.Many people with endometriosis are informally diagnosed and treated based on their symptoms, but in more severe cases, an official diagnosis of endometriosis can be confirmed with a laparoscopic surgery.Does it cause any complications?Infertility is a common complication of endometriosis, and can cause distress to many, but it can often be avoided if the condition is treated early.Other long lasting symptoms such as pain, can affect daily life, work and relationships.Symptoms of endometriosis usually stop after the menopause – although it's possible to have symptoms after menopause, according to the NHS.What surgery is offered for endometriosis?Surgery is offered when other treatments are not working or if a patient has lots of endometriosis.Some patients are given surgery to remove areas of endometriosis or fluid-filled sacs (ovarian cysts) caused by the condition, others have their womb removed (hysterectomy) or ovaries (oophorectomy), according to the NHS.In some instances part of the bladder or bowel is removed if endometriosis is growing in these areas.Anna Druet is a research scientistat period and ovulation tracking appClue.More aboutEndometriosisWomen's Healthlifestyle newsEmma BarnettJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost Read ourPrivacy noticeAndy Burnham has been urged to take the UK into theEU’s Migration and Asylum Pact to help tacklesmall boat arrivals.The move would allow the UK to legally return migrants to the first EU country they entered and grant Britain access to the bloc’s biometric database, the Liberal Democrats say.Lib Dem leader SirEd Daveyalso hit out atBrexit, which he said had made it more difficult to carry out checks on those crossing the Channel, because the Home Office no longer has access to EU-wide data sets containing criminal history and other information on those whoseasylum applicationshave been denied elsewhere.Sir Ed said: “Farage and the Conservatives should hang their heads in shame for breaking our borders with their bad Brexit deal.“But instead of apologising to the British public, they are now exploiting the mess they created for their own gain.open image in galleryThe Lib Dems said their plan could ‘end the small boats crisis’(PA)“We have a plan that would finally end the small boats crisis: a pact with every EU country that will allow us to return people who come over the Channel, taking away the major pull factor that Farage and co created and destroying the business model of the criminal gangs.”We are campaigning to rebuild Britain's relationship with Europe. Join ushereThe party’s home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson also said Reform would “sooner send in the Navy at taxpayers’ expense and strip British people of hard-won rights by leaving the ECHR than admit they’re responsible.”The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which has been in place since June 12, aims to make the system more efficient and stable, in part by preventing refugees moving from the country they first arrive in.It includes a new duty on asylum seekers to apply for asylum in the first country they enter.Other measures include new screening and registration rules, an expanded system for tracking biometric data and fast-track procedures for those from countries with a low likelihood of being granted asylum.open image in gallerySir Ed Davey (Jordan Pettitt/PA) hit out at Brexit(PA)Joe Meighan, policy adviser at campaign group European Movement, said: “People were told that leaving the EU would mean greater control over illegal migration; instead, we have seen precisely the opposite. This is not simply about Britain’s borders; it is about the security of our entire continent. They never will.“We need to work with our European partners, sharing information, tackling criminal gangs and making borders across our continent safer and more secure. title: Should you book your flu vaccine now? Expert advice as NHS opens appointments
content: NewsUKHome NewsShould you book your flu vaccine now? Expert advice as NHS opens appointmentsNHS flu jabs start from 1 September for children and pregnant womenRebecca WhittakerWednesday 19 August 2026 10:16 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverWhat causes the winter flu and how does it differ from other types of flu and colds? | DecomplicatedGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeTheNHSis urging millions of people to book theirflujabs early ahead ofthe winter rush.Flu season may seem like months away, but the health service is starting preparations earlier byopening its booking systemto eligible people, including pregnant people and children.The NHS has had to treat record numbers of patients this summer amid five back-to-back heatwaves.It now wants to do everything it can to ease winter demands.In 2025, nearly 19 million people received theirflu jabin England, and around 104,000 hospitalisations are estimated to have been avoided as a result.Here are all the details on who is eligible for a free flu vaccine and the optimal time to get it.open image in galleryThose over the age of 65, pregnant people, and those with certain health conditions are all eligible for a free flu jab (file photo)(PA Wire)How to get a flu jabCertain eligible groups can get a free NHSflu vaccine. These are people who:are aged 65 or overhave certain long-term health conditionsare pregnantlive in a care homeare the main carer for an older or disabled person, or receive a carer's allowancelive with someone who has a weakened immune systemAnyone eligible who wants to book a flu jab can: contact their GP surgery to book an appointment; book at a pharmacy online or in the NHS App; or find a pharmacy that offers free NHS fluvaccination.Those who are not eligible for a free NHS jab but still want to receive a vaccination can pay for a private service. This is offered at pharmacies like Boots and Superdrug, usually for around £20.When do flu vaccinations start?Vaccinations start on 1 September and run through to March.Flu season usually peaks in December and January, so the NHS is starting vaccinations in autumn, to ensure those at risk are protected and fewer people are hospitalised.Local NHS services will begin sending invites to the first cohort of people eligible – children and pregnant women – next month via their GP practice, NHS app or letter.Other cohorts will begin receiving the jab from 1 October. These include those aged 65 years and over, all adults in a clinical risk group, and adults in care homes, carers and people in close contact with the immunocompromised and frontline healthcare workers.This year’s cohort includes adults aged 75 years and over, residents in a care home for older adults, and individuals aged 6 months and over who are immunosuppressed.open image in galleryFlu vaccination will start from September for pregnant women and children(Getty/iStock)How long does it take for the flu vaccine to take effect?The flu vaccine takes about two weeks to reach peak effectiveness.That’s because the immune system needs time to produce the protective antibodies against the influenza viruses in the vaccine.But the vaccine offers protection for about three months.Ideally, patients should get the vaccine at the start of winter so they are protected before getting exposed to the winter flu.Why you should get the flu vaccineAlthough getting a flu jab doesn’t stop a flu infection, it does reduce the chance of severe illness. It also reduces the chance of passing the flu on to someone else who is vulnerable.Chief nursing officer for England Duncan Burton said: “The NHS is kicking off its preparations for winter earlier than ever, with millions of flu jab appointments for pregnant women and children available to book from today ahead of vaccinations starting next month.“The flu jab is one of our best defences against winter illness. It takes just a few minutes, but it can protect you for months, helping to prevent serious illness, avoid hospital admissions and keep the most vulnerable people.”More aboutNHSflu jabflu vaccineVaccinationFluJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Smart motorway drivers face criminal convictions and huge fines for ignoring red X signs
content: TravelNews & AdviceSmart motorway drivers face criminal convictions and huge fines for ignoring red X signsCameras dotted across the Smart motorway network catch the offendersTristan KirkWednesday 19 August 2026 09:55 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverSmart motorways pose ‘ongoing’ risk of deaths, coroner saysGet the Travel Insider newsletter for tips, deals, and inspiration from our global travel editorGet inspired with our free Travel Insider newsletterGet inspired with our free Travel Insider newsletterEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeSmart motorway drivershave been hit with criminal convictions and more than £100,000 in fines, court costs and victim surcharges this year for ignoring “red X” lane closure signs, research has found.Dozens of errant motorists are hauled before the magistrates’courtsof England and Wales every month after beingcaught driving in a motorway lanethat has been temporarily shut down.The red X signs can be triggered automatically or by National Highways, to close a lane when there has been a crash, a vehicle is stranded, or workers are in the carriageway.Cameras dotted across the Smart motorway network catch the offenders, and many thousands are issued with £100 fixed penalty fines.But Press Association research has shown that somedriversface a full criminal prosecution for breaking the lane-closure rules.Since the start of this year, court records show 378 drivers have been convicted of ignoring the red X signs after being caught out by the automatic cameras, leading to fines totalling £48,409, costs of £33,255, and £20,183 in victim surcharges.Most guilty motorists are also issued with three penalty points, some ending up with a driving ban if they already have points on their licences.open image in gallerySmart motorway drivers have been hit with criminal convictions and more than £100,000 in fines, court costs and victim surcharges this year for ignoring "red X" lane closure signs, research has found(PA)The RAC said it was “concerning” that drivers were continuing to flout the red X rules, which were first introduced with the advent of Smartmotorwaysmore than a decade ago.“The signs play an absolutely fundamental role in keeping people safe,” said RAC road safety spokesman Rod Dennis.“This is especially the case on those where the hard shoulder has been removed permanently, as the safety of a driver who has broken down in a live lane will depend entirely on other people reacting to the red X by moving to another lane.“We implore drivers to take heed of these signs whenever and wherever they see them – not doing so might very well be putting people’s lives in danger.”Last week, 12 motorists were convicted of ignoring the signs, in private court hearings dealt with under the fast-track single justice procedure.School governor Paul Hollowell, 56, from Warrington, Cheshire, wrote to the magistrate to admit the offence, and said he tried to avoid a full criminal prosecution by agreeing to pay a fine and signing up to a driver safety awareness course.open image in gallerySince the start of this year, court records show 378 drivers have been convicted of ignoring the red X signs after being caught out by the automatic cameras, leading to fines totalling £48,409, costs of £33,255, and £20,183 in victim surcharges(PA Wire)But he ended up in court anyway after his laptop ran out of battery before the online course had finished, so he failed to meet the requirements of an out-of-court settlement.“I chose the driver awareness course so I can learn from the mistake and avoid such driving error in the future,” he wrote.Mr Hollowell was fined £384 by Manchester Magistrates’ Court, he received three penalty points on his licence, and he must also pay £120 costs and a £154 victim surcharge.Miles Luckett, 33, from Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, said he saw the red X sign was showing because of a broken-down van as he joined the M1 at junction 15a in Northampton at about 1.30pm on February 20.“Due to traffic conditions in the adjacent live lane at the moment of joining, I made a split-second judgment call that an immediate sharp lane change posed a safety risk,” he wrote.“While I was attempting to react safely, I fully accept that a red X is a mandatory instruction and deeply regret my misjudgment in not slowing down sooner to merge.”The data from the Smart motorway cameras show the red X had been showing on the inside lane for more than four and a half minutes when Mr Luckett’s BMW, and other vehicles, passed by.He was issued with a £72 fine by Boston Magistrates’ Court, three penalty points, and a £29 victim surcharge.open image in galleryThe RAC said it was ‘concerning’ that drivers were continuing to flout the red X rules, which were first introduced with the advent of Smart motorways more than a decade ago(PA Wire)Vauxhall driver Christopher Harvey, 60, from Rickmansworth in Hertfordshire, and van driver Andreas Charalambous, 65, from Southgate, north London, were both caught out within 30 minutes of each other as they used the M25 near junction 18 on February 9.Harvey told Stevenage Magistrates’ Court that there was “no obstruction in front of me” and he could not understand how he could have avoided the offence.He was fined £177 after entering a guilty plea, given three penalty points, and ordered to pay £120 costs and a £71 victim surcharge.Charalambous said the lane to his right was “very busy” when he saw the lane closure sign, and it “took a while before there was a sufficient and safe clear distance to be able to move lanes”.At Stevenage Magistrates’ Court he was given a £40 fine, three penalty points, £120 costs, and a £16 victim surcharge.More aboutdriversmotorwaysCourtsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Soaring energy prices see inflation rise to highest level since March
content: NewsUKHome NewsUK inflation rises to 2.9% in blow for BurnhamThe rise in energy bills has driven a sharp increase in inflation, moving further away from the Bank of England’s targetKarl Matchett&Dan HaygarthWednesday 19 August 2026 07:41 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryEnergy bill hike have driven inflation(AFP/Getty)Sign up to our free money newsletter for investment analysis and expert advice to help you build wealthSign up to our free money email for help building your wealthSign up to our free money email for help building your wealthEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeInflationrose to 2.9% in July amid higherenergy pricesand fears the summer’s heatwave could start putting pressure on food costs.In figures announced today, Consumer Prices Index (CPI) inflation has risen to 2.9% per cent in July,up from a 15-month low of 2.6 per cent in June.The rise in inflationfollows the 13 per cent hike in Ofgem’s energy price cap last month, which saw the average gas and electricity bill increase by £221 to £1,862 a year.That hike in energy bills has contributed significantly to the rise, as shown by core inflation - which strips out energy and food costs - remaining locked at 2.6 per cent, unchanged from June. But with no end in sight to Donald Trump’s war on Iran, households can expect to continue to feel the squeeze.The government’s Great British Summer Savings Scheme, which cuts prices on family attractions and children’s meals thanks to a VAT reduction until September, may have helped mediate rising inflation – but not enough to prevent it moving further away from the Bank of England’s 2 per cent target.There are also concerns over food inflation, with producers warning earlier this week thatsoaring temperatures and droughts across the UK and Europeare set to drive prices higher.CPIH figures, which include household costs and is the ONS’ preferred metric, rose from 2.8 per cent to 3.1 per cent, with housing and household services, as well as furniture, made the largest upward contributions.ONS deputy director for prices Mike Hardie said: “Inflation rose in July, driven by a sharp increase in gas prices following this month’s change to theenergy price cap. This was the largest rise in gas prices for almost four years.“Other upward pressures included furniture prices falling by less than usual for this time of year, and also a smaller fall for clothing prices due to reduced discounting.“The prices of raw materials and goods leaving factories slowed again, driven by a drop in the prices of crude oil and refined petroleum respectively.”open image in galleryRising energy bills contributed to higher inflation(AFP/Getty)Despite expectations of rises in future, in response to the July figures The Food and Drink Federation said: “It’s good news for consumers as food inflation continued to fall for another month in July. This isn’t what we’d historically expect to see following a supply chain shock like the war in Iran. This is partly due to the time it takes for these shocks to pass through to consumer prices and partly due to the fact that food manufacturers have learnt from the previous energy shock brought on by the war in Ukraine, adapting contracts and diversifying suppliers to keep costs down.”However, the FDF’s chief economist, Dr Liliana Danila, warned that supply chain disruption and “extreme weather” will make it “very challenging for manufacturers to swallow any higher costs.”Food and drink annual inflation fell from 1.7 per cent in June to 1.3 per cent in July, with fish (13.6 per cent) and fruit (8.1 per cent) rising fastest and pizza (-8.5 per cent) and butter (-5.3 per cent) falling quickest.Kevin Brown, savings expert at Scottish Friendly, cautioned households that the months ahead could see more concerning numbers when it comes to their grocery shopping.“Energy may only be exerting part of the pinch this autumn. Expensive fuel and fertiliser are adding pressure to food production and supply chains, while an exceptionally hot summer raises another threat to harvests,” he said. “As a result, families may continue to feel the inflationary fallout from this at the till as well as through their utility bills.”Jonathan Raymond, investment manager at Quilter Cheviot, similarly noted the expectation remains that wider inflation figures remain elevated across the board until this year.“A renewed spike in inflation has been expected as the war in the Middle East continues to navigate a clunky ceasefire,” he said. “Things remain far from normal in the Strait of Hormuz and look unlikely to be resolved any time soon, meaning pressure is likely to remain on prices for the remainder of the year at least.“That said, inflation is expected to moderate in the coming months as government activities begin to take effect on the headline number. Cuts to VAT on energy bills and discounted leisure and hospitality offerings will begin to feed through in official numbers.”However, despite inflation remaining well above the Bank of England’s two per cent target, few analysts currently expect this level of inflation to strong-arm the BoE’s Monetary Policy Committee into raising interest rates.With unemployment still close to 5 per cent andjob vacancies at five-year low levels, the UK is “better placed than most developed economies to avoid second-round inflation effects,” said David Rees, head of global economics at Schroders.Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG, said that inflation was likely to continue an upward curve to reach a peak of about 3.5 per cent by year’s end, though with the caveat that “the outlook remains highly dependent on how the conflict in Iran evolves and its impact on global energy prices.”Meanwhile, business leaders urged Andy Burnham’s government to do more to support firms in the lead-up to the Budget.“Just as it adds to the cost of living, rising inflation pushes up the cost of doing business. Ministers should act now to bolster business confidence as the fallout from the Iran war, a spike in energy prices and higher costs of employment are holding back firms across the capital and beyond,” said Matthew Fell of BusinessLDN.“Making good on a manifesto commitment to overhaul business rates, postponing the introduction of a new levy that will make housebuilding more expensive, and ensuring the proceeds of any new overnight visitor levy for London are used to support growth would all help to put the economy on a surer footing.”The British Chambers of Commerce added: “The government must use the Budget as an opportunity to back business, cut costs and deliver growth. The Chancellor needs to give firms the breathing space they desperately need by outlining ambitious measures to drive forward trade, investment and productivity.”More aboutenergy pricesEnergy price capInflationUK EconomyJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Andy Burnham to lead UK growth from No 10 North in major power shift
content: NewsUKUK PoliticsAndy Burnham to lead UK growth from No 10 North in major power shiftThe Prime Minister is expected to work at No 10 North once each week during his premiershipMike TaylorWednesday 19 August 2026 09:06 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverOverjoyed PM Burnham calls opening of new No 10 North base as 'best day of his life'Stay on top of the latest political news with our View from Westminster newsletterGet the latest political headlines with our free emailGet the latest political headlines with our free emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeAndy Burnhamhas outlined plans for thenew No 10 Northto assume control over economic growth from the Treasury,framing the shift as a move to divest power from Whitehall.According to the Prime minister, the Treasury will maintain its focus on overseeing public finances,whereas the regional 10 Downing Street office in Manchester will lead economic expansion.Speaking in an interview withThe Times, he stated that chancellorJohn Healeycompletely backs the decision, characterising it as part of a "huge transfer of power".“There’s a job to be done around control of public finances. It’s just the dual job of growth and control of public finances (that) sometimes clouds the growth mission,” he said.“And particularly having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the wider Whitehall system.”TheManchesterbranch ofDowning Street in Heron Houseis already up and running and officials have said it will cost taxpayers no extra money.Andy Burnham suggested the Treasury would focus on controlling the public finances while his outpost of10 Downing Street based in Manchester would lead the charge on boosting the economy(PA Media)The prime minister is expected to work at the outpost once each week during his premiership, as part of his move to push power out of Westminster.Reflecting on his time in office so far, Mr Burnham conceded the controversy over the early release of prisoners had led to a “bumpy” introduction to his premiership.But he said justice secretary Alex Norris would present a “much better solution” on 1 September after the government faced pressure to block two of Pc Andrew Harper’s killers from being freed in January under previous plans.He said the biggest adjustment to life in No 10 was “the relentlessness of it and the scale of it”, adding that his initial policy offerings had not been “earth-shattering” but that the public “just want something to make life a little bit better” and had been waiting for a “sense of action” from Downing Street.Asked if he was prepared to be disliked, the prime minister criticised some politicians who he said made a “fetish” out of being “tough” and “masochistic”.“Isn’t the job to be popular by making people’s lives better?” he said.“Isn’t that what you should be doing? content: NewsUKHome NewsMapped: Where thunderstorms and heavy rain will hit the UK this weekThe Met Office has forecast an ‘intense downpour’ across parts of England and Wales after the driest July on recordHarriette Boucher&Bryony GoochWednesday 19 August 2026 09:06 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverEngland and Wales suffer driest July on record in summer of extreme weatherGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. title: Shaun the Storm? Sheep could lend his name to weather event as Met Office opens vote
content: NewsUKHome NewsShaun the Storm? Sheep could lend his name to weather event as Met Office opens voteThe public is being asked to choose between Shaun and his cousin Timmy the lambAnna LorenWednesday 19 August 2026 08:57 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverShaun the Sheep makes appearance in Barbour's 2023 Christmas advertGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeThe public is being asked to think woolly hard about the name for a future storm.TheMet Officeis inviting people to choose between two characters from the beloved animated TV seriesShaun the Sheep– the titular character Shaun or his cousin Timmy the lamb.Whichever name is chosen will join the weather service’s official storm names list for the 2026/27 season.The vote is a collaboration withthe Oscar-winning animation studio Aardman, which producedShaun the Sheepalong with other beloved titles likeWallace & GromitandChicken Run.The winning name will be announced on 1 September.However, there may not be a storm Shaun or Timmy as they are named alphabetically each storm season, and the furthest the Met Office has ever made it through the alphabet is to L, withStorm Lilian in August 2024.open image in galleryShaun the sheep, right, with his cousin Timmy the lamb(PA)“Namingstormshelps our weather warnings reach more people and encourages the public to take notice when severe weather is approaching,” said the Met Office’s head of warnings and guidance Holly Clements.“This collaboration with Aardman gives us a fantastic opportunity to engage new audiences and explain why storm naming matters, helping people understand the risks severe weather can bring and the actions they can take to stay safe.”Last year, more than 50,000 storm name suggestions were submitted for the 2025/2026 season.Stormy McStormFace, Dame Judi Drench and David Blowy were among some of the names which did not make the cut.Only 21 were chosen – all public suggestions, including tributes to loved ones and pets such as Amy, Dave, Stevie and Violet.open image in galleryNick Park, the creator of Shaun the Sheep, with a statue of the titular character(PA Archive)The Met Office began naming storms in 2015. It works with Ireland’s meteorological service Met Éireann and KNMI, the Dutch national weather service, to develop the annual storm names list each year.“It’s brilliant to be teaming up with the Met Office to give fans the chance to help choose a future storm name,” Amy Pearson, director of brand marketing and PR at Aardman, said.“Rain or shine, weather is a familiar part of life on Mossy Bottom Farm, making this a fun and meaningful way to connect Shaun and Timmy’s world with an important public message.“Whoever you’re backing, we hope the vote sparks some fun conversations about severe weather and how it can affect all of us.”Aardman, which was founded by Peter Lord and David Sproxton, had its 50th anniversary this year.The filmShaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom, the third feature-length film about the characters, will be released on 18 September.More aboutAardmanMet OfficestormsJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
