title: Burnham unveils £442m plan to end homelessness and get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas
content: NewsUKUK PoliticsBurnham unveils £442m plan to end homelessness and get rough sleepers off streets by ChristmasThis week, the government has committed to ‘offer everyone a route off the streets this Christmas’Athena StavrouWednesday 19 August 2026 08:47 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverCamilla hears personal stories of overcoming homelessness in NorfolkStay on top of the latest political news with our View from Westminster newsletterGet the latest political headlines with our free emailGet the latest political headlines with our free emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeAndy Burnhamhas promised to work to "get everyone in forChristmas" as part of his ongoing pledge to eradicaterough sleeping.The prime ministeris seeking to recreate measures introduced during thecoronavirus pandemic, when the Everyone In scheme brought thousands of street sleepers intoshelteracross England.According to the latest annual national statistics released by theGovernmentin February, an estimated 4,793 people were sleeping rough on a single night in autumn 2025 in England.The total marked an all-time record high, alongside a fourth consecutive annual rise.During that period, 43 per cent of the overall rough sleeping population was concentrated in London and the South East.Newer data for London published last month showed a 10 per cent year-on-year drop in the number of rough sleepers in the capital, prompting a charity boss to insist ending rough sleeping in London and beyond is “within reach”.Some 3,959 people slept rough in the capital between April and June this year, research from the CombinedHomelessnessand Information Network (Chain) showed, down from 4,392 in the same period in 2025.open image in gallery‘No-one should have to bed down in a doorway or outside a station,’ Burnham said(James Manning/PA)This week, the government has committed to “offer everyone a route off the streets this Christmas”, although there is no defined duration as to how long local authorities might be expected to take people in for, and it is understood to be accepted that not every rough sleeper might take up the offer.Mr Burnham has also said he will host what is being described as a first-of-its-kind national summit this autumn to “bring together leaders from across society – from business, finance, charities, health, faith communities and more – to ask what role each of them can play in ending rough sleeping”.The prime minister, who pledged as his “first instruction” on day one in No 10 “to end rough sleeping in our country”, suggested people living on the streets has begun to become accepted over the years.He said: “No-one should have to bed down in a doorway or outside a station. But we’ve seen it for so long that it feels like Westminster has started to accept it.“I won’t accept it. That’s why my first instruction as Prime Minister was to end rough sleeping. And it’s why today we’re getting started with a national drive to get everyone in for Christmas.“We did it in the pandemic, we can do it again. But it needs all of us.“Government will put the money in, but I’m asking leaders in communities and sectors across society to play their part locally too.“Let’s get people out the cold. And let’s bring back hope.”Mr Burnham has announced an additional £102 million, from uncommitted budgets within the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), to go towards immediate routes for people off the street this winter, including an £8.4 million boost to the Ending Homelessness in Communities Fund, in recognition of the work of charities, faith groups and community organisations in this area.open image in galleryHousing Secretary Angela Rayner said new funding would ‘help thousands of people leave the streets behind’(Joe Giddens/PA)The £102 million will go alongside the £340 million announced last month in funding for new support to get long-term rough sleepers into settled accommodation.MHCLG said areas facing the greatest pressures with regard to homelessness will get the largest share of support and that mayors will be expected to work alongside councils to “play a leading role in driving local action to end rough sleeping” including deciding what help is needed and where.Housing secretary Angela Rayner said: “When the Prime Minister pledged to end rough sleeping, we said we’d move urgently from words to action. Today we’re delivering on that promise.“This funding will help thousands of people leave the streets behind, move into secure homes and get the support they need to rebuild their lives.“Working alongside councils, mayors and charities, we’re backing local areas to tackle rough sleeping at its roots, giving people the security, dignity and opportunity they deserve, and restoring hope to those who have been let down for far too long.”Ms Rayner has previously declined to put a target deadline on the government’s pledge to end rough sleeping, when asked about Mr Burnham’s commitment that his government would work to “finally end long-term rough sleeping across the UK at the earliest opportunity”.Homelessness charities welcomed the announcement as a “strong start” that puts the country on a path to end rough sleeping, while opposition critics said it lacked detail and substance.Shelter chief executive Sarah Elliott said: “The Prime Minister’s pledge to get everyone sleeping rough off the streets by Christmas is a game-changing move and exactly the kind of bold leadership needed to end the housing emergency.”She added: “Tackling the most visible form of homelessness is a strong start, but the almost 178,000 children hidden away in grim temporary accommodation also need somewhere to call home.“The Prime Minister must apply the same unwavering ambition to delivering the council housing revolution he promised.”Lord John Bird, the crossbench peer and co-founder of the Big Issue, said: “Covid proved that when we decide rough sleeping is unacceptable, we can act and get people in off the streets. This Christmas commitment is a welcome return to that spirit.open image in galleryBig Issue founder Lord John Bird has backed the pledge(PA)“But it’s important that people are not just brought in from the cold for a few weeks, only to be sent back out again.“To that end, I’m encouraged to see the Prime Minister is allocating millions in tried-and-tested localised solutions that offer wraparound support for long-term rough sleepers.”He added: “Where access to a home isn’t possible straight away, providing good quality accommodation with a clear plan to support people into settled housing is a vital first step.”Shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said: “Andy Burnham promised to end rough sleeping in Manchester, and failed because he didn’t do the hard work necessary.“Now he is pledging to end it nationally without any plan for delivery. And as with many of his other commitments, there is very little detail on how this one will be paid for.”Sir James added: “Labour must come clean on what other programmes they are cutting to pay for this project.“Otherwise, struggling families will fear that yet more Labour tax rises are on the horizon.”More aboutAndy BurnhamHomelessnessShelterPrime MinisterJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
generated_summary: Burnham unveils £442m plan to end homelessness and get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas. This week, the government has committed to ‘offer everyone a route off the streets this Christmas’

title: Premium dog food recalled as dozens of pets develop serious eye issues
content: NewsUKHome NewsPremium dog food recalled as dozens of pets develop serious eye issuesA ‘potential link’ has been found between a key ingredient, buckwheat, and an eye conditionRosie SheadWednesday 19 August 2026 07:15 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverRelated video: Pug crowned World’s Ugliest Dog in hilarious 50th anniversary contestGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeA high-end pet food brand has initiated arecallfollowing dozens of reports regarding suspected eye problems in dogs.Years, asubscription serviceoffering freshdog food"tailored" to an animal’s needs, emailed customers on Monday night to say that it had identified a "potential link" between its buckwheat ingredient and a dry eye condition.The business, which boasts that its fresh meals are prepared by chefs, urged owners to stop feeding Years’ products to theirpetsor any other animal.Years said that by Sunday, it had received reports of 57 suspected cases of dry eye.The company said on its website: “This follows a small number of reports of dogs having a potential adverse eye reaction to buckwheat, a common and approved ingredient, which we include in our meals.“As of 16 August, this has affected 0.1% of our customers.”open image in galleryCookie (pictured) has received multiple treatment for eye issues, her owner said(David Felton/PA)Yearsadvertises gourmet dog meals including pork shoulder and apple stew, turkey thigh and cranberry fricassee and a steak and kidney hotpot.David Felton, from Edgware, north London, said his dog Cookie had developed eye issues in April after eating the food for two-and-a-half years. He estimated he had spent around £1,500 so far on treatment andvetbills.The PR consultant said his spaniel cross had been in “a lot of pain” and had received several different treatments after he and his wife had noticed her eyes were “getting really gunky”.He took Cookie to a vet, who initially diagnosed her with a corneal abrasion – a scratch on the eye which could be caused by an irritant getting stuck.After two weeks of treatment, the six-year-old dog was showing no signs of recovery so was referred to a specialist who diagnosed bilateral dry eye disease, he said.Cookie’s eyes are being treated twice a day with a steroid paste as well as over-the-counter drops and a gel to ease her discomfort.Mr Felton stopped using the Years food immediately after receiving the company’s email on Monday.Asked how he felt about Cookie’s illness, he said: “Extremely worried because this sort of came out of nowhere and it’s been so unexplained as to the causes of it, and obviously with your pet you don’t want to see them suffering and in a way they’re like a member of family.“You love them to bits just like you would your own child so anything that causes them pain and discomfort is quite upsetting for everyone involved.”open image in galleryMr Felton said Cookie had been in ‘a lot of pain’(David Felton/PA)He added: “Never did it occur to us that it could be a link to the food because the crazy thing is people buy Years because they want to feed their dog like high quality foods.“If I just wanted to buy a cheap, readily available dog food, I would have just like gone to the supermarket and just got a kind of a cheap kibble.“It’s just incredibly disheartening because obviously people that buy fresh food like Years buy it because they’ve kind of bought into the idea that feeding their dog a fresh, healthy food made out of fresh, healthy ingredients is going to do them well.”The 39-year-old said the situation was “mind-blowing”, adding: “I think everyone, all of the customers right now, are just reeling from this news.”On its website, Years said it began receiving “multiple reports” of dogs experiencing sudden dry eye in both eyes in late July and launched an investigation on 1 August.Years said symptoms could include redness, cloudiness or dullness in the eyes, excessive blinking or squinting, pawing at the eyes and thick discharge as well as general discomfort around dogs’ eyes.The company urged its 40,000 customers to contact their vet “promptly” and to mention the Years product recall if they spotted any of the symptoms.Years told customers that their subscription will be paused for an initial period of six weeks while the company makes fresh meals using quinoa in place of buckwheat and apologised for the “worry and disruption” caused.The firm said it will publish the investigation’s results.More aboutdog foodrecallPetssubscription servicevetJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
generated_summary: Premium dog food recalled as dozens of pets develop serious eye issues. ‘potential link’ has been found between a key ingredient, buckwheat, and an eye condition.

title: Detectives face investigation over alleged failings which led to Simon Levy murders
content: NewsUKCrimeDetectives face investigation over alleged failings which led to Simon Levy murdersTwo BTP detectives are being investigated over ‘alleged failures to progress or supervise an investigation’ into sexual assaults by Levy on the London Underground in October 2024Emily DaviesWednesday 19 August 2026 00:54 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryLevy, 40, was jailed for life earlier this month(British Transport Police)For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeThepolice watchdoghas launched an investigation into two British Transport Police (BTP)detectivesafter a serialsex offenderwas left free to murder two women and rape a third.Simon Levy’s crime spree spanned from 2018 to 2025 and includedmyriad sex attacks on women in public spacesand twomurders, as theMetropolitan Police, BTP and the courts failed to stop him.Levy was on bail as his attacks on women escalated to double murder.The Met, BTP andCrown Prosecution Servicehave all admitted failings in how they dealt with him.A probe has now been launched into the conduct of two BTP detectives over “alleged failures to progress or supervise an investigation” into two reported sexual assaults by Levy on the London Underground in October 2024, theIndependent Office for Police Conduct(IOPC) said on Tuesday.It comes after the IOPC previously said an investigation into alleged failures of two Metropolitan Police officers in their management of Levy following his prison release on licence in February 2023 was “ongoing”.open image in gallerySimon Levy’s crime spree spanned from 2018 to 2025 and included myriad sex attacks on women in public spaces and two murders(Metropolitan Police)A spokesperson for the watchdog said of the investigation into the BTP officers: “Levy was arrested in November 2024 regarding these incidents but was bailed to return to custody in January, with his bail further extended twice until May 2025 to allow for the investigation to be completed.“During this period, Levy committed multiple further sexual assaults on trains, and other serious offences including murder and rape.“We received a voluntary conduct referral from BTP on August 12 and decided an independent investigation was required.”“The families of murder victims Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo and Sheryl Wilkins, and the woman who survived the rape attack, have been notified of our investigation,” the spokesperson added.The BTP said: “It’s in the public interest for independent and objective scrutiny to be applied, and we will fully co-operate with the IOPC’s independent investigation.”Levy, 40, was jailed for the rest of his life earlier this month after being convicted of killing grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and mother-of-four Sheryl Wilkins, 39, in August that year.He suffocated both women in sexually motivated attacks, with Ms Valencia-Trujillo found in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London, and Ms Wilkins behind a car park wall near Tottenham High Road, north London.open image in galleryLevy was convicted of killing grandmother Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo mother-of-four Sheryl Wilkins(Metropolitan Police)When he turned killer, Levy had already subjected a third woman to a brutal rape in January 2025 in the same car park where Ms Wilkins’s body was later found.The surviving victim had told police where her attacker lived.Levy committed the murders after having been jailed in 2021 for groping two women in the summer of 2018, one at Notting Hill Carnival and the other at a party in Camden.He sexually assaulted a prison guard while behind bars in 2022 but was still released the following year, going on to sexually assault a woman on the Tube in October 2023 and allegedly rape another in May 2024, for which he was recalled to prison and released again in August that year.Levy was arrested by BTP in November 2024 for sexual assaults on the Tube, but delays in organising an identification parade until the following April left him free to carry out the rape and first murder.Following Ms Valencia-Trujillo’s death, Levy was released on bail at two magistrates’ court hearings in May and June 2025.The Crown Prosecution Service admitted it had not opposed bail at the first hearing, and the prosecutor had not given the court all the relevant information for consideration at the second hearing.There were another three crown court hearings that he failed to attend for various reasons, yet no arrest warrant was requested.Less than two weeks after a hearing on August 11, he murdered Ms Wilkins.The murders of Ms Valencia-Trujillo and Ms Wilkins over eight months in 2025 were interspersed with sexual assaults on six women on the Tube and Overground.More aboutBTPCrown Prosecution ServiceMetropolitan PoliceIndependent Office for Police Conductmurderspolice watchdogMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Anti-Muslim hate in London rising at ‘alarming rate’, charity says
content: NewsUKHome NewsAnti-Muslim hate in London rising at ‘alarming rate’, charity saysA monitoring group has found that there were more incidents of anti-Muslim prejudice and hate in the first six months of this year than in the whole of 2023Aine FoxWednesday 19 August 2026 00:01 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryA Tommy Robinson-organised rally has been criticised over alleged instances of Islamophobia at the event(PA)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeIncidents ofanti-Muslim prejudice and hatein London during the first six months of this year have already exceeded the total figure recorded for the whole of 2023, according to a monitoring group.Describing the collated statistics as "alarming", the monitoring organisation Tell Mama highlighted datarevealing a sixfold surgein annual London cases from 2021 to 2025.The organisation stated that the figures reflect a "sustained escalation of anti-Muslim hate", adding that behind every report is "a Londoner who was made to feel unsafe simply because of their faith".Figures stood at 313 in 2021, before more than doubling to 818 in 2022, and rising each year since to a record of 1,909 last year.From January to the end of June this year, Tell Mama logged 1,031 reports, surpassing the 1,028 total reports gathered throughout 2023.A Unite the Kingdom rally, organised by activist Tommy Robinson in central London in May, faced sharp criticism from one of the capital’s deputy mayors over instances of Islamophobia she said occurred at the event.open image in galleryTommy Robinson organised the United the Kingdom rally in May(PA)Outside Parliament, some protesters called for the "removal of Islam", while Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, shared a video of himself saying that, were he to become prime minister, he would "stop Islam", adding: "It’s time for many Muslims to leave this country."Iman Atta, director at Tell Mama, said: "What is most alarming is the trajectory: from just over 300 reports in 2021 to nearly 1,100 in the first half of this year alone."A worrying rise in repeat victimisation and heightened levels of targeted anger are leaving victims with a fractured sense of personal safety, highlighting the urgent need for robust counter-extremism strategies rather than political platitudes."This is not a temporary blip, it is a sustained escalation of anti-Muslim hate, and it demands a sustained and uncompromising no-nonsense response from our public institutions."A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said: "We will not tolerate attacks on the Muslim community. Hate crime in all its forms – including ongoing efforts to tackle racism, anti-Muslim hate crime, and other forms of hatred in the capital – remains a core policing priority."Our focus on tackling these hateful offenders is starting to work, and in the last 12 months the Met has increased positive outcomes – including arrests and charges – for anti-Muslim hate crime by 57%."open image in galleryA spokesperson for the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said ‘anti-Muslim hate has absolutely no place in London(PA)In July, another organisation recording anti-Muslim hatred said it had recorded 70 attacks at Muslim places of worship across the UK in the 12 months to July, including vandalism and intimidation.The British Muslim Trust was appointed last year to receive investment from the Government’s Combatting Hate Against Muslims Fund.Bringing together the Aziz Foundation and Randeree Charitable Trust, the trust analyses data to help identify the drivers behind a rise in anti-Muslim hatred.A spokesperson for the mayor of London said: "Anti-Muslim hate has absolutely no place in London. The rise in attacks on Muslims in London and across the country is vile and the police have the mayor’s full support in taking a zero-tolerance approach."They said the mayor had provided "a record £16 million – more than any other mayor – to support grassroots community groups to stand up to hate and intolerance and fund services for victims of hate crime".More aboutAnti-MuslimIslamLondonTommy Robinsontell mamaJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Children’s helpline says number of calls about child domestic abuse cases has risen 80% in five years
content: NewsUKHome NewsChildren’s helpline says number of calls about child domestic abuse cases has risen 80% in five yearsThe charity received 8,488 reports in the last year compared to 4,599 in 2021-2022Holly EvansWednesday 19 August 2026 00:01 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryConcerns for children experiencing or witnessing domestic abuse has increased in the last five years(NSPCC)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeAchildren’s charity has seen an 80 per cent increase in reports of concern for a child experiencingdomestic abuse in the last five years.TheNSPCCreceived 4,599 contacts with the primary concern being domestic abuse in 2021-2022, with this rising to 8,448 in 2025-2026.Almost a third of these cases resulted in a referral to local agencies such as police forces and children’s social services.One person who called the NSPCC Helpline said: “My sister recently left an abusive situation with her six-month-old baby, but her ex-partner is still in control of their finances and emotionally abusing her.“Her ex has drained their accounts so she can’t buy what she needs for my niece.“The ex is bombarding her with threats online and via text, even saying they will kill themselves if she doesn’t go back or let them see the baby. Where can we get support and protection for my sister and niece?”Domestic abuse can include coercive control as well as emotional, verbal, physical and financial abuse.Witnessing abuse can have a lasting impact on a child’s mental health, with signs including aggression, bed-wetting, attention seeking, tantrums, anti-social behaviour, withdrawal and problems in school.open image in galleryAlmost a third of child welfare contacts end in a referral to local agencies including police or social services(NSPCC)Margaret* suffered years of abuse at the hands of her ex-husband. She said: “I had always known Tony* was controlling, but after our wedding he became emotionally and psychologically abusive, threatening me and belittling me all the time. Then he started being physically abusive.“We had two children and he became abusive towards them too, shouting and beating them with belts and shoes when I wasn’t there. I could see that they were really affected. They were subdued, sullen and didn’t really behave like children at all.“One day, I finally snapped and called the police. They helped get us to a safe house.“I was really worried about whether my children would be able to get over the abuse they had witnessed and endured. They took part in the NSPCC’s domestic abuse programme, and the light has come back into their eyes. They changed from quiet and subdued children to boisterous and playful – like they’ve released whatever they’d been holding on to.“If there are any parents reading this and going through something like us, or you know someone who is, help is out there. I know my children will be OK, but without help, they may not have been.”Paddi Vint, NSPCC Helpline Service Head, says: “It’s alarming that we are seeing record levels of adults contacting our Helpline about a child experiencing domestic abuse."Domestic abuse is often hidden, with stigma and shame making it harder to ask for help. Children and young people might also feel frightened and confused, keeping the abuse to themselves.“If you’re worried about a child, you can speak to our free NSPCC Helpline in complete confidence. Reaching out can be the first step to help families begin to move forward.”If you are a child and you need help because something has happened to you, you can call Childline free of charge on 0800 1111. You can also call the NSPCC if you are an adult and you are worried about a child, on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adults on 0808 801 0331*Names have been changed to protect identitiesMore aboutNSPCCChildrenMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Boy, 5, who fell to death from 15th-floor flat ‘could have been trying to reach biscuits’
content: NewsUKHome NewsBoy, 5, who fell to death from 15th-floor flat ‘could have been trying to reach biscuits’Aalim Ahmed died after falling from a kitchen window at the residential block in Plaistow, east London in 2024Helen WilliamTuesday 18 August 2026 23:27 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryThe inquest took place at Walthamstow Coroners’ Court on Tuesday(Google Maps)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeA young boy who fell to his death from a 15th-floor window had lived in a "clearly loving environment", aninquesthas been told.Aalim Ahmed died after falling from the kitchen window of a residential tower in Plaistow, eastLondon.The five-year-old died instantly, with his "distraught" father Makail Ahmed running down from the top-floor temporary socialhousingflat to find his son's body shortly before 6am on 16 May 2024.Mr Ahmed and the child's mother, Sahra Osman, have blamedNewham Counciland described his death as "preventable", following reports that Ms Osman had repeatedly raised safety concerns about the property.Aalim’s parents stepped out of the proceedings at Walthamstow Coroners’ Court when audio capturing his final moments was played.The couple left the room on Tuesday while grainy CCTV audio recorded outside the building was played to those present.A young child’s voice is twice heard counting down “3, 2, 1” and “a loud clang” follows some seconds later, according to a statement read on behalf of Detective Constance Joe Linton who carried out a review of CCTV footage outside Jacobs House.He added that after the commotion, “you can hear another young child shouting ‘Aalim'”, who would appear to be the boy’s brother who was then three years old.Mr Ahmed was “topless and clearly distressed in the footage” as he found his son, DC Linton told the court.DC Linton said “it is most likely from the footage available” that Aalim had “jumped out” of the flat at Jacobs House in New City Road “of his own accord without the presence of a third party”.A post-mortem examination found Aalim died from “multiply injuries due to or as a consequence of trauma” from a “fall from height.”Detective Inspector Jamie Humm, who investigated the incident, said there was “no evidence or suspicion he (Aalim) had been forced.”“The flat was well furnished and it was clearly a loving environment for a child,” he noted.He added the soon after arriving at the scene he was satisfied “there was no evidence of a crime not that I thought there would be,.”Ms Osman has told the court she was “scared” and “horrified” when Newham Council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, stating that Aalim was autistic, had “no sense of danger” and the place was not suitable for her young family, which also included a newborn baby girl.open image in galleryAalim Ahmed’s parents described their son’s death as “preventable” and blamed Newham Council, after claims Ms Osman reported safety concerns about the flat on multiple occasions(Google Maps)Despite engineers having been to look at the repairs, she felt the flat was still not safe and there were “open windows”, according to Ms Osman.All the windows were closed before the family went to bed, the inquest heard.Aalim could have been climbing to get a biscuit from a cupboard but the windows had “faulty” restrictors and her ongoing complaints to get them fixed led only to a series of workmen who did not sort the problem, she said.Biscuits were found on the kitchen table but it is still not known how the child would have got to the window, the court heard.Assistant coroner Ian Wade, who described the audio recording as “poignant”, said: “Aalim at his tender age and with hisautismcould not have known what could have happened.“It seems to me that he would not have meant to have deliberately taken the stance to have harmed himself.”Robert O’Sullivan, of the London Ambulance Service, recalled that “a number of colleagues were visibly shocked” after finding the boy and as a cordon was placed around the building.In his statement, he recalled: “There was an adult male shouting ‘I have told them about the window’.”He was not sure if this meant it had been reported to the council.The right-hand kitchen window was open and the room was cordoned off.Sergeant Christopher Diment, who was among the officers who attended the scene, said Mr Ahmed was “clearly distraught, pacing around and shouting”, and was “overcome with grief”.When they went into the flat Mr Ahmed was saying something about the state of the windows, he told the court.Ms Osman has denied any suggestion she may have “forced” the window open to cope in hot weather.Successful smoke and fire alarm tests were carried out in April 2024 and the council engineer also noted there was mould in the bedroom and kitchen, an extractor needed repair and a living room window latch needing fixing.Ms Osman told the inquest she used this opportunity to tell him that the kitchen window also needed to be fixed, but the engineer says the living room latch was the only a problem mentioned.Aalim’s family had worked with an occupational therapist to help support his needs.His teacher Esme Johns said the boy had to be reminded not to do or touch something because he “lacked danger awareness”.She added “he would say sorry, but found it difficult to understand”.The hearing continues.More title: Man used AI chatbot and flew to Somalia in bid to become ‘martyr’ for Islamic State
content: NewsUKCrimeMan used AI chatbot and flew to Somalia in bid to become ‘martyr’ for Islamic StateMohamed Mohamoud was found guilty of preparing acts of terrorismBen MitchellTuesday 18 August 2026 23:25 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryThe trial took place at Winchester Crown Court(Alamy/PA)For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeA man who travelled toSomaliain a failed bid to join the so-calledIslamic State(IS) has been found guilty of preparing acts of terrorism.Somali-born Mohamed Mohamoud, 22, who moved toBristolto live with his mother and brother, was convicted of the offence following a trial at Winchester Crown Court.Mohamoud had denied the single charge but admitted attempting to join Islamic State.The jury convicted the Somali-born defendant after hearing that he flew to the east African country in a bid to join the terrorist organisation.Naomi Parsons, prosecuting, told the court that Mohamoud travelled to Somalia in January 2025 in a bid to be a “martyr” for Isis.But he returned to the UK on March 3 after failing to reach the group because of ongoing counter-terrorism operations.She said: “At some stage whilst living in the UK, he became radicalised. He embraced the ideology of Islamic State.“And with this came a strong desire return to Somalia and join Isis, to join the ‘Mujahideen’, it literally means one who struggles or a fighter, who operate in the mountainous areas near a city called Bosaso, in the north of the Puntland region.”“Indeed, not only was it a strong desire, but Mr Mohamoud viewed it as his duty.”open image in galleryThe jury convicted the Somali-born defendant after hearing that he flew to the east African country in a bid to join the terrorist organisation(Chris Ison/PA)Ms Parsons said the defendant made attempts to find a contact to help him join the terrorist group but having failed to do so, he booked a return flight to Somalia anyway and flew on January 30 2025.His attempts to join Isis included interacting with an AI chatbot used by Isis recruiters to filter potential new members, the court heard.She said that despite having a return ticket for March 3, Mahamoud had not planned to return to the UK.The prosecutor said: “As messages show, Mr Mohamoud had no intention of returning to the UK. Indeed, he aspired not simply to join Isis, but he aspired to martyrdom.”Ms Parsons said that after failing to join up with Isis because of counter-terrorism operations in the country, he returned to the UK where he continued to keep in contact with the Isis recruiters and told them: “Any time, you say the word, I will return.”Giving evidence, Mohamoud denied preparing acts of terrorism but admitted attempting to join Isis.He told the court that he was born in Somalia but his parents separated when he was three years old and he was taken with his younger brother to live with his stepmother in the UAE.He then lived between Somalia and the UAE until he moved in 2020, at the age of 16 or 17, to live with his mother in Bristol whom he had seen only once since his parents had split up but he said that he did not get on with her.The defendant said that he went to college where he studied English, maths and cooking but said he was not religious until he started watching YouTube videos by a channel called BlackBeardGuy.He said he became interested in religion and joining IS after watching “extreme” videos on YouTube and TikTok.More aboutSomaliaIslamic StateBristolMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

Read ourPrivacy noticeAround 100firefightersand 15 fire engines are battling a waste fire in southeastLondon.London Fire Brigade(LFB) said theblazeon Landmann Way, inDeptford, involves about 50 tonnes of household waste stored at a waste facility.The brigade was alerted shortly before 8pm, with crews responding from Deptford, East Greenwich, Old Kent Road and neighbouring fire stations.Smoke and flames from the blaze in Deptford, as seen from Millwall(PA)A video posted online shows significant flames and thick smoke rising into the air above surrounding buildings.It is understood firefighters tackled a blaze at the same facility in June when a van and a car were destroyed and one man was treated on scene by London Ambulance Service.Station commander Duncan Rees said: “Approximately 100 firefighters are tackling a large fire at a recycling centre on an industrial estate on the border of Bermondsey and North Lewisham.“First calls were received at 1958 and 15 fire appliances are now in attendance.“Fire crews along with colleagues from partner blue light services are working hard in difficult conditions to bring the fire under control.“One of the brigade’s 32-metre turntable ladders title: Mapped: Worst regions hit by deadly UK salmonella outbreak as cases rise
content: NewsUKHome NewsMapped: Worst regions hit by deadly UK salmonella outbreak as cases riseThere have been more than 200 cases of salmonella in the past yearRebecca WhittakerTuesday 18 August 2026 18:13 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverEggs recalled after multistate outbreak of salmonella infectionsGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeOne person has died and hundreds have fallen ill withsalmonellafood poisoning.The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has launched aninvestigationinto the cause of more than 200 cases ofsalmonella in the past yearas cases spike in recent weeks.While salmonella usually causes diarrhoea and stomach cramps, more than a third of the cases in thiscurrent outbreakhave needed hospital care.Salmonella symptoms include being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, high temperature(Getty/iStock)Salmonella can happen at any time from eating or handling contaminated food, but this outbreak has been linked to a specific strain.How many cases have been recorded?Between 11 August last year and 1 August this year, 207 cases were identified: 199 in England, six in Scotland, one in Wales, and one in Northern Ireland. London registered the highest total among English regions with 47 confirmed cases, while Yorkshire and the Humber recorded 38.People affected include babies and people as old as 90, according to the UKHSA.What is causing the salmonella outbreak?The latest wave of salmonellainfectionsare thought to be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.Hannah Charles, lead epidemiologist for gastrointestinal infections at UKHSA, said: “We’re working with Food Standards Agency and other public health agencies to investigate a salmonella outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK.“Salmonellosis is often caused by eating or handling contaminated food and can be spread rarely from person-to-person.“Salmonella generally causes a mild illness, although vulnerable groups with weakened immune systems may experience more severe illness.”What is Salmonella and what are the symptoms?Salmonella is a type of bacteria which is commonly spread by eating food contaminated with it.Symptomsinclude being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, high temperature and feeling unwell and can usually start within a few hours or a few days of eating food that caused the infection.Most people with a salmonella infection do not need hospital treatment and can recover at home within four to seven days by drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.However, in this outbreak 38 per cent of people infected required hospital admission, and two individuals suffered potentially life-threatening infections in their bloodstream.“Symptoms of a salmonella infection include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. Anyone who is concerned about symptoms should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance,” Dr Charles said.“There are simple steps to prevent the spread of salmonella: wash your hands thoroughly after using the bathroom and before preparing and handling food, cook food thoroughly, and if you have any symptoms, avoid handling food for others where possible,” she added.More aboutsalmonellainvestigationSymptomsInfectionsJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Boris Johnson’s Covid U-turns were like a ‘slow-moving car crash’, former aide says
content: NewsUKUK PoliticsBoris Johnson’s Covid U-turns were like a ‘slow-moving car crash’, former aide saysLee Cain said the government was making the same mistake ‘over and over again’Kate DevlinPolitical Reporter&Athena StavrouTuesday 18 August 2026 17:01 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverIn The Room: Lee Cain on the 'slow-moving car crash' of Covid commsStay on top of the latest political news with our View from Westminster newsletterGet the latest political headlines with our free emailGet the latest political headlines with our free emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeA series of Covid U-turnsmade byBoris Johnson’s government were like a “slow-moving car crash” that saw it make the same mistake “over and over again”, his former director of communications has said.Lee Cain, who served inDowning Streetfrom July 2019until the end of 2020, toldThe Independent’sIn the Room podcastthat “avoidable” mistakes in No 10 woulddrive the communications team “bonkers”.“It was just a slow-moving car crash, and that did happen quite particularly at the start ofCovid,” he said. “It happened quite a few times. Luckily, I think, even in politics, once people make the same mistake over and over again, they did start listening.”open image in galleryLee Cain (right) was Boris Johnson’s director of communications(AFP/Getty)Mr Johnsonwas forced to make a number of significant U-turns during thepandemic, with several key policy decisions scrapped.He repeatedly ruled out a second national lockdown both in and outside of the House of Commons – claiming in mid-October that Sir Keir Starmer’s support for a short term shutdown of the country was “the height of absurdity”. The second lockdown began on 5 November.The then PM also famously encouraged all parents to send their children to school on the first day of term in January 2021, only to announce he was closing every school in England again that evening.The previous August, amid intense and growing pressure, the government was forced into a humiliating U-turn when it announced it was dumping plans to base A-level results on a controversial algorithm, with ministers publicly apologising for the distress the fiasco had caused pupils and parents.Mr Cain said there had been a discussion within No 10 at the start of the pandemic, about keeping pubs and bars open – but asking people not to visit them. That particular idea, he said, he thought had come from Mr Johnson himself.open image in galleryThe Covid pandemic erupted just months into Boris Johnson’s term as prime minister(PA)“I remember saying, as my sort of role as a sort of political Cassandra at the time, that perhaps this wasn’t the best of all worlds… And I remember saying ‘This won’t last 24 hours. We will not hold this position because people will simply ask, ‘If people shouldn’t go, which you’re suggesting, why don’t we close the pubs and clubs?’”He predicted that, had the plan gone ahead, “we would U-turn because that’s what happened quite frequently at that point. So we’d U-turn very quickly. Boris would lament the whole thing and say, ‘Well, how did we get in this idea? I never thought of – I didn’t want to do this. How did we end up in this position?’”The situation was “bonkers because it was so avoidable,” he said, “...it was just a slow-moving car crash, and that did happen, particularly at the start of Covid it happened quite a few times. Luckily, I think... even in politics, once people make the same mistake over and over again, they did start listening.”Listen to the full episode ofIn The RoomonApple PodcastsandSpotify, or watch onYouTubeMore aboutlee cainBoris JohnsonpandemicDowning StreetCovidIn The RoomJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Former Farage ally suspended from Reform after hitting out at Zia Yusuf
content: NewsUKUK PoliticsFormer Farage ally suspended from Reform after hitting out at Zia YusufTim Montgomerie suggested in a podcast that ‘Nigel has fallen out of love with Zia’Athena StavrouPolitical ReporterTuesday 18 August 2026 16:57 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverReform’s Robert Jenrick and Zia Yusuf in public spat over party’s immigration policyStay on top of the latest political news with our View from Westminster newsletterGet the latest political headlines with our free emailGet the latest political headlines with our free emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeReform UKhas suspended a high-profile supporter and one-time Farage ally after he criticised the party’s home affairs spokespersonZia Yusuffor not being a “team player”.Tim Montgomerie, a commentator and senior party figure, has beenopenly critical of Mr Yusufin recent weeks and suggested in a podcast that “Nigel has fallen out of love with Zia”.Nigel Farage hit out at Mr Yusuf for calling a former Tory defence secretary a “traitor” and suggesting that Ben Wallace should be prosecuted for his role in Afghans coming to Britain after the UK’s withdrawal.Reform UKhas now confirmed Mr Montgomerie has been suspended from the party.Speaking onTheSpectator’s Coffee House Shots podcast, Mr Montgomerie said: “It was unprecedented for Farage to criticise him last week, but did he take down the tweet that Nigel criticised? No. He wouldn’t. He’s loyal to Nigel as he has to be if he wants to succeed him, but in terms of being able to really play as a team player...“He has consistently freelanced on Twitter, on, for example, accepting Conservative candidates, Suella Braverman and Robert Jenrick, even though he knew they were being wooed. But it was his way of trying to undermine that policy.”It is understood he was notified of his suspension before the podcast was broadcast, after having publicly criticised the party on many occasions.open image in galleryReform UK has now confirmed Tim Montgomerie has been suspended from the party(BBC)Responding to his suspension, Mr Montgomerie claimed Nigel Farage did not know about his suspension, as he accused someone within the party of leaking the news.Saying he would appeal the suspension, he said in a video posted to X: “ Over the last two years, I have given my everything really to support Reform, and if they want to kick me out, they're going to have to kick me out after an argument.”He added: “I take some comfort from the fact that Nigel Farage did not know about my suspension, and he more than anyone knows all the stuff I've done behind the scenes to help Reform.”He also revealed on the podcast that Mr Yusuf “did not talk to me” for three months after the home affairs spokesperson found out he had helped Robert Jenrick defect to Reform, and accused him of behaving “like a child”.“A lot of people are on not-speaking terms with Zia, and it’s nearly always Zia who initiates it,” he said.“It needs to end. You cannot behave like a child in politics.”A senior Reform source said: “The General Secretary and Chairman have had months of complaints regarding Tim’s behaviour and conduct. They saw fit to take action and protect the party.“Reform will never engage the Tory briefing wars and toxicity that goes with them - the correct course of action has been taken. Disagreements should happen behind closed doors, not in the eye of the national media.”Last week, Mr Montgomerie criticised Mr Yusuf for his attack on Ben Wallace, a former soldier who served in Northern Ireland.He said on X, formerly Twitter: “This isn’t acceptable from Zia... Zia’s language and attitude towards any opponent is inappropriate and counter-productive. Opponents are opponents... they aren’t enemies... or “morons”.”He added that “one of the biggest question marks over Nigel Farage’s leadership is whether he brings Zia under control. ZY is a man of huge talents, but too much of his social media output is intemperate and reinforces Reform’s number one problem: our negative tactical voting challenge.”open image in galleryLast week, Montgomerie criticised Yusuf for his attack on Ben Wallace, a former soldier who served in Northern Ireland(Reuters)Nigel Farage later said his home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf had gone “over the top”, tellingThe Sun: “That’s too strong a word. I shall give him a ticking off.”Last month, Mr Montgomerie admitted the Reform UK leader “cannot hide away” from growing questions over the £5m donation from Christopher Harborne, made weeks before Mr Farage stood in the 2024 general election.After Mr Farage insisted “no one cares” about the money, and when asked by BBC Breakfast how much of the gift he had spent, said: “It’s none of your business,” Mr Montgomerie said: “Well, that wasn’t Nigel Farage’s best interview performance, let’s put it that way. He cannot hide away from this issue.“People do not normally get a £5m gift. We get a box of chocolates, we get a bottle of champagne.”More aboutTim MontgomerieZia YusufReform UKJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: Tranquil cluster of islands revealed as England’s friendliest place - but this London borough is the least friendly
content: NewsUKHome NewsTranquil cluster of islands revealed as England’s friendliest place - but this London borough is the least friendlyTwo areas of Devon and a London neighbourhood ranked in the top fiveHolly EvansTuesday 18 August 2026 15:39 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryA view of Great Bay in the Isles of Scilly(Getty Images/iStockphoto)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeEngland’s friendliest place has been revealed - and it is a three-hour ferry away from the mainland, but only home to around 2,300 people.TheIsles of Scilly, which are located 28 miles off the coast ofCornwall, have ranked the highest in new analysis of government data looking at social division across all 296 local authorities in England.The National Conversation survey, which has been designed by the University of Oxford, asks participants to rate questions such as how lonely they feel, how many of their neighbours can be trusted and how proud they are of their local area.Across the five inhabited islands, only three per cent said they felt lonely, 94.5 per cent said different backgrounds get on well and 88.8 per cent said they belonged to the neighbourhood and spoke to their neighbours at least monthly.open image in galleryRichmond upon Thames in south-west London was also ranked as one of the friendliest places in England(Getty/iStock)Other areas to make the top rankings for England include South Hams, West Devon, Derbyshire Dales and Richmond upon Thames.Each of them had scored high figures among their residents for community cohesion and civic life.Meanwhile, Barking and Dagenham ranked as the least friendliest place in England, with only 42.8 per cent expressing pride in their local area and 10.1 per cent saying they felt lonely.The overall average across England for loneliness fell at 6.6 per cent.Other areas that scored low on the index included Ipswich and Stoke-on-Trent as well as Mansfield.The National Conversation survey is set to collect thousands of views that will inform a report later this year by the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion, which is co-chaired by former Tory home secretary SirSajid Javidand former Labour policy co-ordinator Jon Cruddas.Upon launching the project Sir Sajid said: Our country is in real peril. Unless we can regain a shared sense of what unites us – of what we have in common – we risk being torn apart by our differences.“That vision won’t come from politicians – it can only come from the public.”The study noted that it had been introduced at a “critical moment for Britain’s social fabric”, noting recent violent riots, attacks targeting migrant communities and declining trust in institutions.Professor Melinda Mills, director of the Leverhulme Centre for Demographic Science at Oxford Population Health, and lead investigator on the project, said: “There is an urgent need to understand how people across the UK are experiencing social change, trust, belonging, and community life.“Much of the current debate relies on assumptions, fragmented polling, or political rhetoric. The National Conversation aims to provide a rigorous, evidence-based picture of what people are actually experiencing and feeling in their everyday lives.”More aboutIsles of ScillyBritainCornwallSajid JavidJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

title: The drones that the UK supplies Ukraine following Russia’s threat
content: NewsUKHome NewsThe drones that the UK supplies Ukraine following Russia’s threatUkrainian forces used unmanned aircraft manufactured by two UK companiesRebecca WhittakerTuesday 18 August 2026 15:26 BSTBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverZelensky urges G7 to stop critical supplies reaching RussiaGet the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeRussiahas warned of “consequences” following reports thatBritish-built droneswere deployed to hit targets on itsmainland for the first time.Ukrainian army sources toldThe Timesthatdronesmade by two British companies have been used in thepast six monthsto attack targets including oil refineries in Volgograd and near Moscow and logistics hubs.Russia’s embassy to the UK said in a statement on Monday that the reports “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of theUkrainecrisis” and accused Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy”.The UK has provided money to Ukraine to procure military equipment, such as drones and missiles(AP)“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it added.“The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”What drones does the UK supply to Ukraine?One drone was developed by BAE Systems subsidiary Callen-Lenz and tested by the Royal Navy.The Nyran drone, which was built in Wiltshire, was used to strike Belgorod near the Russian border, the report published inThe Timessaid.According to the defence company the drone can fly more than 150 miles.“We deliver a range of capabilities into the UK MoD as part of the UK’s support to the defence of Ukraine,” the company confirmed toThe Times.“The Nyan uncrewed air system provides a rapidly developed platform proven in meeting emerging threats within highly contested environments.”There is a second drone made in British factories and used by the Ukrainian military, but the name of this company has not been revealed for security reasons.It’s launched using a catapult system and has a range of more than 600 miles.What else does the UK supply?The UK has provided Ukraine with Storm Shadow missiles, but the supply is finite, and their range is only around 155 miles.Former chancellor Rachel Reeves also confirmed a £752m payment to Ukraine earlier this year as part of a larger £3.36bn loan.In April, the UK announced the biggest ever drone package for Ukraine, delivering at least 120,000 drones for Ukraine this year.The package included thousands of long-range strike drones, intelligence and reconnaissance drones, logistics drones and maritime capabilities, which are all battle-proven on Ukraine’s frontline.According to the Ministry of Defence the majority of this investment was set to be spent with UK-based companies, including Tekever, Windracers and Malloy Aeronautics.However, British parts have also been found in Russian drones. Volodymyr Zelensky said microcomputers for flight control, manufactured in the UK, were discovered in drones involved in a deadly assault. Parts from other allied countries, including the US were also found.He called for more stringent sanctions against British companies implicated in supplying components for Russian drones.More aboutdronesRussiaJoin our commenting forumJoin thought-provoking conversations, follow other Independent readers and see their repliesCommentsMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
generated_summary: Ukrainian forces used unmanned aircraft manufactured by two UK companies. Russia’s embassy to the UK said the reports ‘confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of theUkrainecrisis’

title: Architect struck off after threatening to kill client’s five-year-old daughter
content: NewsUKHome NewsArchitect struck off after threatening to kill client’s five-year-old daughter‘I will kill them all. It’s what I will do,’ Joan Beltri told officials after being fired from a projectAlex BousfieldTuesday 18 August 2026 15:19 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryCarolina Sampietro and her husband James Escoda-Francoli hired Joan Beltri to work on a new beauty clinic, Winchester Medical Aesthetics(Ollie Thompson/Solent News)Get the free Morning Headlines email for news from our reporters across the worldSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailSign up to our free Morning Headlines emailEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeAnarchitecthas been struck off after subjecting his former clients to a months-long campaign of “harassment,abuseand threats” over construction blunders at a new clinic project.Joan Beltri even said that he was “so angry” with Dr James Escoda-Francoli and Carolina Sampietro that he would kill them and their five-year-old daughter.The married couple hired Mr Beltri to work on their beauty clinic in the cathedral city ofWinchester.However, the architect, who first registered in the UK in 2010, failed to gain council permission for work on the Grade II-listed building, a tribunal has heard.He also severed a gas pipe while doing work that he was unqualified to do.The Spanish national then threatened to "kill them all" and insulted Dr Escoda-Francoli, claiming that his wife was sleeping with other men.He said: "If I saw you in the street, I would spit in your face."open image in galleryThe clinic, which will open in October, is in a Grade II-listed building(Carolina Sampietro/Solent News)Mr Beltri has now been struck off by the Architects Registration Board (ARB).Dr Escoda-Francoli is a top oral surgeon working in Hampshire, who was previously an associate professor at the University of Barcelona, and Ms Sampietro is a registered aesthetics nurse.The couple moved to the UK from northern Spain in 2016.Mr Beltri started working for Ms Sampietro and Dr Escoda-Francoli in August 2024 after they bought the Winchester building, which they planned to turn into an aesthetics clinic which will open in October.There were disputes between Mr Beltri and his clients, often centred around which work should be subcontracted and which work he should do himself, the tribunal heard.When he was working on the project, he failed to make a written agreement about the works, failed to ensure the build was in accordance with building control, and did not get planning permission to start work on a Grade II listed property.Mr Beltri also carried out work that he was not qualified to do, such as cutting a gas pipe because there was a leak after the boiler was changed.open image in galleryJoan Beltri accused Carolina Sampietro, pictured, of being unfaithful and threatened to kill her and her five-year-old daughter(Carolina Sampietro/Solent News)The couple ended Mr Beltri’s contract in November 2024 and reported him to the ARB.In the following months, he became increasingly abusive, leaving voicemails saying "I have never come across such a son of a b**** as you" and "you’re a bunch of motherf******".He referred to Dr Escoda-Francoli as a "homosexual" and alleged that Ms Samprieto was unfaithful.It was also heard that Mr Beltri threatened the couple’s daughter while speaking to ARB officials.Mr Beltri said "he was so angry he would kill them and their child", the tribunal heard.The architect told an ARB official: "I will kill them all. It’s what I will do. Their parents, their family, and their children."Mr Beltri told the ARB tribunal: "I do not apologise for the communications because I maintain that I did not use abusive or threatening language. I do not accept the characterisation of my conduct as harassment, abuse or threats."In its decision, the panel said: "The Committee accepted the evidence of all the witnesses that they had found the communications from [Mr Beltri] deeply distressing."The Committee is satisfied that it is appropriate to describe [Mr Beltri]’s actions as a campaign of harassment, abuse and threats from April until August 2025, when the ARB instructed solicitors to write to [Mr Beltri]."open image in galleryMs Samprieto says Mr Beltri’s abuse has had a long-lasting effect on her(Carolina Sampietro/Solent News)Speaking after the tribunal concluded, Ms Sampietro said that her experience with Mr Beltri had been a "nightmare".She said that friends recommended Mr Beltri to her, as they were both from the north of Spain.However, the last straw was when he cut the gas pipe in the building, which had residents upstairs, and left it open for several hours, she said.She claimed that Mr Beltri sent her "hundreds of emails every day" and that her Facebook account was blocked because there were so many fraudulent attempts to log in."He is obsessed with all of this, but with me particularly. He doesn’t go after my husband usually. He is more abusive with me."I reported him to the police and at the moment he is living in Spain so that is better."Mrs Sampietro said that she now takes more safety precautions, including making sure the windows and doors are shut and locked, due to Mr Beltri’s threats against her family, including her young daughter."It reassures me that he won’t come back to the UK if he can’t work as an architect here," she said."It is not done yet, but it is a little bit better because at least he can’t work in that space and he can’t do that to any other people."It is peace of mind because I wouldn’t want this to happen to anyone ... it was a nightmare."More aboutArchitectWinchestertribunalabuseharassmentMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next
generated_summary: Architect struck off after threatening to kill client’s five-year-old daughter. Joan Beltri told officials after being fired from a project. He failed to gain council permission for work on a Grade II-listed building.

content: NewsUKCrimeTwo serving officers arrested in major Police Federation fraud investigationOfficers arrested Mukund Krishna, the former chief executive of the federation, and two other men, in MarchEllie CrabbeTuesday 18 August 2026 15:09 BSTBookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoveropen image in galleryThe City of London Police, as the lead force for fraud investigations, confirmed the arrests of two men and two women(PA Archive)For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsSign up to our free breaking news emailsEmail*SIGN UPI would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read ourPrivacy noticeFour more people, including two serving police officers, have been detained in connection with an inquiry into alleged bribery and fraudlinked to the Police Federation of England and Wales.The City of London Police, as the lead force for fraud investigations, confirmed the arrests of two men and two women at an address in Leatherhead, Surrey, on Tuesday.Both women are in their 50s; one was held on suspicion of bribery, fraud by abuse of position of trust, and fraud by failing to disclose, while the other was arrested on suspicion of fraud by abuse of position of trust.A man aged in his 50s was detained on suspicion of bribery, fraud by failing to disclose, and fraud by abuse of position of trust. A man in his 40s was arrested on suspicion of fraud by abuse of position of trust.All four were brought to a police station for questioning.open image in galleryCity of London Police, the lead force for fraud investigations, said it arrested two women and two men at an address in Leatherhead, Surrey, on TuesdayDetective Superintendent Jim Halkett, of the City of London Police’s domestic corruption unit, said:“Our investigation continues to make significant progress, with officers working through a number of lines of inquiry to establish the full facts and circumstances surrounding this case.“We would like to thank everyone who has already come forward with information. This has been valuable and continues to play an important role in helping us move our inquiries forward.“This remains a complex and high-profile investigation, and we recognise the public and media interest in it.“With criminal proceedings now active, we ask that media take care with their reporting and avoid speculation that could impact future court proceedings.”It comes after officers arrested Mukund Krishna, the former chief executive of the federation, and two other men, a 51-year-old man from Wales and a 55-year-old man from Bristol, in March as part of the probe.Mr Krishna was suspended from his role in March and he and two other men were later bailed until September.More aboutPolice officersPolice FederationbriberyMost popularPopular videosBulletinRead next

will see the“first meaningful rain for a long time”following weeks ofheatwavesand dryweather, which has left many parts of the country facing water shortages and has seen several restrictions introduced.The Met Office said that a rainy front will begin to sweep down from Northern Ireland and Scotland towards the south ofEnglandand Wales early this week, kicking off a wetter week with cooler conditions that are much closer to average for the time of year.Meanwhile, heavy showers are expected to hit theUKon Thursday, missing some areas but bringing the chance of surface flooding in places where rainfall is particularly intense, it added.Additionally, the BBC reports that temperatures will fall below average across the country in the coming days.It says that places could see the mercury fall to single figures, while sheltered valleys in the Brecon Beacons could see lows of 3C or 4C on Friday morning, with lows of 5C or 6C in parts of the Cotswolds.The BBC forecast adds: “This drop in temperature might come as a bit of a shock for some after being accustomed to the hotter-than-average weather we’ve seen for weeks.”The change comes after the UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer, which saw the hottest day of the year recorded in Kew Gardens, London, on Thursday when temperatures reached 38.1C.The forecast rain may bring some welcome relief to parched land and firefighters tackling wildfires.But it is unlikely to bring an end to widespread drought conditions that have put severe pressure on wildlife, farmers, transport, emergency services infrastructure and water resources.Liz Stephens, professor in climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading, said the southeast of England will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.She said: “Here in the South East, we’re still a month’s worth of rain below what we would normally expect by this point in the year, despite the heavy rainfall in January and February.“As a result, while any rain which falls this week may help reduce the immediate wildfire risk, it will take many weeks of sustained rainfall for vegetation to recover and our rivers and reservoirs to return to normal.“This means that we should expect hosepipe bans to be in place for some time.“Floods can still occur during drought conditions and surface water flooding can even become more likely as baked soils are unable to soak up rainwater as quickly.”open image in galleryDrought, hosepipe bans and wildfires have been a feature of the UK summer(PA)More than 27 million people across Englandhave now had hosepipe use restricted in their area.Wessex Wateron Monday became the latest utility firm to announce ahosepipe ban, citing increased demand during the dry weather but also longer-term weather forecasts that mean resources must be protected for customers and the environment.It is the first time it has put restrictions in place in 50 years –since the summer of 1976.The firm said the temporary use ban would come into effect on Tuesday for all 1.4 million customers that it supplies with water across areas in Bath, Somerset, Dorset and Wiltshire.Mike Silverstone, the Met Office’s deputy chief forecaster, said: “Many areas in England and Wales are desperate for rain; this week some of these areas will see the first meaningful rain for a long time.”Through Tuesday, showers are expected to continue in the north of the country, particularly in the North West, and another area of rain will move into the South West by the evening.This will then likely spread east across the South, bringing the first spell of widespread rain to areas in need the most, he added.“Thursday will be a day of heavy showers across much of the UK, while some of these will be heavy, some areas will miss them altogether,” Mr Silverstone said.“As some of these showers could be intense, there is a chance of some surface water flooding as the rain falls on very dry and hard ground.”open image in galleryA drone view of hay bales on parched land as drought conditions continue in many parts of Britain(Reuters)By Friday, the conditions are expected to turn drier once again through the weekend, and next week is forecast to have more rain.About the Wessex Water ban, Ruth Jefferson, the firm’s chief executive, said the company was contacting larger business customers who are high water users to encourage them to avoid non-essential use and encouraging households to make small and simple changes such as taking shorter showers and letting the lawn go brown.“After 50 years without a hosepipe ban in the Wessex Water region, the first since the famous drought of 1976, this isn’t a decision we’ve made lightly, and we’re sorry for the inconvenience it will cause,” she said.“But the prolonged and extreme dry weather has meant demand across our region has consistently remained at more than 400 million litres per day, 30 per cent above average for this time of year and the equivalent of almost half a million hosepipes running for a full hour every day.”Elsewhere, wildfires have ravaged parts of the UK, including in the West Midlands, where a blaze in Stourbridge destroyed 19 homes.Several fire services have asked people to only call 999 to report a genuine emergency.In an update on Monday, the National Fire Chiefs Council said 1,132 wildfires have now been recorded across England and Wales in 2026 so far – a record high for the number between January and this time of year.More aboutUKMet OfficeWeatherWessex
