title: How soon will the drought be over?
content: How soon will the drought be over?Image source,Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesImage caption,Rain has returned to parts of the UK this week but after months of dry weather will it be enough to end the drought?ByKate Stephens,Senior science journalistandHelen Briggs,Environment correspondentPublished18 August 2026It is the question many people are asking: when will the drought be over, and how much rain will it take for things to return to normal?Contrary to public perception, a drought does not end with a few days of rain.Water must flow back into rivers, reservoirs, and the stores beneath our feet in the tiny spaces between soil, sand, and rock. This can take months.According to scientists, the key question is not "Has it rained?" but "have water resources recovered?"More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected?Published1 day agoHow bad is the drought?Dr Katie Facer-Childs from the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology says there is not a straightforward answer to when this drought might end, because it has not been caused simply by a lack of rainfall, but also higher than average temperatures."This year we've gone through meteorological, soil moisture, and river flow drought," says Facer-Childs.Meteorological drought is when rainfall is below normal.Next comes soil moisture drought, which begins to affect agriculture. Soil is like a type of reservoir - those stores are depleted by thirsty trees and plants, and evaporation during hot temperatures.Then comes river flow drought, where river levels fall, and, finally, if dry conditions persist for long enough, groundwater and reservoir levels decline, leading to the most serious impacts."However, we have not yet reached severe groundwater and reservoir drought, so that means there's hope," says Dr Katie Facer-Childs.The British Geological Survey,externalsays no groundwater sites around the UK are currently reporting record lows - with nearly half at normal levels.When will we know the drought is over?The first clear indication usually comes in late autumn and winter, when we typically see more rainfall and experts can assess whether that water is moving through rock layers into underground stores, known as aquifers.Dr Kevin Collins, senior lecturer in environment and systems at The Open University, says even when autumn rains arrive, people often assume the drought is over.But sustained rainfall is needed over months rather than a few heavy rainfalls.Hydrologists should know by February or March whether aquifers and human-made reservoirs have been replenished. But recovery from the environmental impacts can take years.A dry winter will make the current drought worse and heighten government concerns.Prof Tim Palmer of Oxford University says it will be "catastrophic" for the UK next year if the rains do not come.There is some hope. Over Europe, there are signals for a wetter-than-average autumn, potentially influenced by global ocean changes, including the developing El Niño weather phenomenon. However, there remains considerable uncertainty.What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures?"The government needs to start planning for a worst-case scenario where the rains don't return in sufficient amounts this winter, and next summer is similar to the last two," Prof Palmer says.Heavy rain after drought brings new challengesParts of the UK have experienced a flash drought - a type of drought that develops very rapidly, driven by extreme heat, very low rainfall and exceptionally high water demand.The problem is that once conditions become extremely dry, subsequent heavy rainfall can trigger flash flooding because the land is unable to absorb the water effectively.This creates a cycle of rapid swings between drought and flooding, which is what people mean by weather whiplash.Heavy showers and thunderstorms bring risk of flash flooding to UKPublished1 day agoAs the climate warms, scientists say rapid swings between wet and dry conditions are increasing and areexpected to get worse,external.A recent study,externalfound the UK is likely to experience faster transitions between droughts and floods, especially in south-east England and parts of the north-west of the country.Researchers warn this growing "volatility" could make water supplies, agriculture and infrastructure harder to manage as conditions switch rapidly between extremes.Image source,Leon Neal/Getty ImagesImage caption,Following the August 2022 heatwaves London experienced flash floods as parched soils were unable to cope with heavy rainIs this the 'new normal' and can we adapt?Neil Entwistle, from Rebalance Earth – and a former professor at the University of Salford says: "We're in the new normal. And that new normal is we'll get a lot of heavy rain and short amounts of rain."He argues that floods and droughts are "two sides of the same coin".For centuries, the UK has modified landscapes to move water off the land as quickly as possible by draining uplands and peatlands, straightening rivers and disconnecting rivers from floodplains.As a result, when rain falls it moves rapidly and can cause flooding."This is a wake-up call that we do need to see a fundamental shift in how we think about water," he says.Related topicsDroughtClimateEnvironmentMore on this story200-year-old bridge hidden for a century seen again after droughtPublished1 day agoSummer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met OfficePublished11 August

title: More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected?
content: More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected?Image source,Matt Cardy/Getty ImagesByMark Poynting,Climate reporter,Jess Carr,Data designerandPhil Leake,Data journalistPublished2 July 2025Updated 17 August 2026Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales are under drought conditions, with repeated heatwaves leaving water supplies under strain.Both England and Wales provisionally recorded their driest July on record. This lack of rainfall - on top of hot, dry weather in spring and early summer - has begun to take its toll on rivers, crops and nature.Wessex Water has become the latest water provider to announce a hosepipe ban - the company's first for 50 years - taking the total number of people under such a measure to nearly 30 million.So how is your area doing and are you in a drought?There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle.If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies.Environmental bodies in each UK nation decide whether to declare drought or water scarcity by assessing current water resources alongside weather forecasts.Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans, if they are not already in place.While drought is driven by prolonged dry weather, water scarcity occurs when demand for water outstrips the available supply. This summer, restrictions have been introduced in some areas to help manage high demand.But while recent months have seen temperatures regularly exceed 35C, winter was much wetter than usual.It has raised questions about how effectively water resources are being managed, and whether the UK is prepared for the drier summers expected with climate change.Most of England and all of Wales in droughtSo far, ten UK water companies have announced hosepipe bans. This means hosepipes cannot be used for watering gardens, washing vehicles and windows, and filling pools.Nine companies are spread across central, southern and eastern parts of England, and one is in Wales.In England, nearly three-quarters of the country is now in drought, according to the Environment Agency (EA). Northern parts of England are in "prolonged dry weather" - the category below drought.Elsewhere, the whole of Wales is in drought, with Natural Resources Wales saying sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".There are no official droughts currently in Northern Ireland.Scotland does not declare droughts but monitors "water scarcity".While conditions have improved in some parts of Scotland following recent rainfall, some eastern areas remain in the two most extreme categories of "moderate" or "significant" scarcity, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.Rivers, reservoirs and groundwater - how are supplies?Our three main sources of water are rivers, reservoirs and from deep underground.Almost all river flows in England and Wales were classed as "below normal", "notably low" or "exceptionally low" in July, according to the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology (UKCEH)."This is the third time in the last five years that drought conditions have intensified rapidly following exceptional spring and summer dryness," said Steve Turner, a hydrologist at the UKCEH.He added that low river flows are likely to persist well into the autumn.England's reservoirs are some way below average levels for the time of year. Wales' reservoirs are also declining, but Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water has said its water resource position is "relatively strong".Reservoir levels in Northern Ireland and Scotland are close to average, according to the latest available data.South-east England relies more heavily on groundwater than reservoirs.Groundwater originates as rainfall and is naturally stored beneath the surface in the pore spaces and fractures in rocks.Groundwater levels are generally declining following the prolonged dry weather, but almost half of monitored groundwater sites recorded levels considered "normal" or higher in July.Water can flow more slowly through some rock types than others, sometimes taking years to fully respond to current conditions.These groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.It is why groundwater droughts in the south of England generally take a longer time to develop but can be longer-lasting if they do occur.Is climate change to blame?Droughts are complex phenomena, driven by a mix of natural and human causes.The Met Office expects the UK to experience drier summers on average in future as the world warms, though there has been no clear trend so far.But rising temperatures can play a more direct role by drawing extra moisture from the soil via evaporation."A warmer atmosphere is thirstier for moisture and this can mean water in the soil, rivers and reservoirs are depleted more effectively, leading to more rapidly onsetting droughts, heatwaves and wildfires," said Richard Allan, professor of climate science at the University of Reading.But there are other factors that determine whether dry conditions lead to water shortages, including how we use water.Ina landmark reviewinto the water sector of England and Wales, water companies were criticised for historic underinvestment in water infrastructure.As part of plans to address water shortages, the government and water companies are planningnine new reservoirs for England by 2050, in addition to one under construction at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.But the EA has warned that measures to tackle water leaks and control water demand - potentially including hosepipe bans -may be needed in England too.Water companies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland - which are all public bodies or non-profit - also said they were taking steps to secure future supplies.Get in touchTell us how you're affected by the hosepipe ban.Contact formContact formA really simple guide to climate changePublished14 JanuaryHow climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floodsPublished5 November 2025'Hotter and hotter and hotter' - Europe's new climate in seven chartsPublished4 JulySatellite images show impact of heatwaves and drought on UK landscapePublished31 JulySign up for our Future Earth newsletterto keep up with the latest climate and environment stories with the BBC's Justin Rowlatt. Outside the UK?Sign up to our international newsletter here.Related topicsClimateDrought

title: Consultation ending on controversial Rosebank oil field
content: Consultation ending on controversial Rosebank oil fieldImage source,PA MediaImage caption,The decision will ultimately be taken by Energy Security Secretary Miatta FahnbullehByKevin KeaneScotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspondentPublished17 August 2026Supporters and opponents of the controversial Rosebank oil field have been making their cases as a consultation on the plans draws to a close.The industry regulator is consideringrevised applications for the £8.7bn project off Shetland and the Jackdaw gas fieldafter a court ruled that they had been unlawfully approved.Environmental campaign group Uplift, which was behind the successful legal challenge, argues that recent extreme heatwaves and wildfires are evidence that more drilling will "wreck the planet"But the boss of oil company Adura, CEO Neil McCulloch, says fossil fuels will be needed for years to come and that producing them domestically will generate billions in tax revenues.He told BBC Radio Scotland the Rosebank field was of "low significance" compared with total production globally - but would be "very, very significant" in terms of the jobs it would provide in the north east of Scotland.McCulloch said he was confident there was a "balance of advantages" in approving Rosebank and added: "The ball is back now in the government's court."Image source,AduraImage caption,The Petroljarl Rosebank production vessel has been floated into position ready for productionIsobel Reid from Uplift has called on the government to reject the applications, insisting that more drilling will "wreck our planet" and result in more extreme weather."The prime minister must take urgent steps to deal with the root of the problem - burning fossil fuels is what feeds climate change," she said.The Rosebank oil field andthe Jackdaw gas field, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, had been approved under the previous Conservative government and construction is well under way.A legal challenge was brought at the Court of Session in Edinburgh in 2024 which argued that consent was given without fully considering the impact of burning the fossil fuels which will be produced.The previous decisions wereruled unlawfuland sent back to the regulator Opred to be taken again.The judge ruled that the operators could continue preparatory work at the sites but must stop short of producing oil and gas until a final decision had been taken.Rosebank is estimated to contain the equivalent of up to 300 million barrels of oil and at its peak will produce approximately 69,000 barrels a day.Most of that is oil which will be shipped to Europe for refining before being sold on the open market.A fresh environmental impact assessment (EIA) concluded that the oil and gas it produces will generate about 250 million tonnes of planet warming greenhouse gases over its lifetime.That figure is equivalent to about two thirds of the UK's total emissions for 2024.The industry argues that will simply displace imported oil rather than generate new emissions and the EIA - which was produced by Adura - concluded that the emissions were "not significant".Image source,PA MediaImage caption,The Prime Minister visited victims of a wildfire in Stourbridge which has destroyed homesPrime Minister Andy Burnham is coming under pressure over the decisions about both Rosebank and Jackdaw.Visiting victims of the West Midlands wildfire on Friday, he told BBC Five Live that there needs to be a focus on adapting to the changing climate, including considering aerial firefighting resources.But he said there needs to be a "pragmatic approach" towards domestic oil and gas.He added: "We won't be able to stop using oil and gas for some time. That's just a fact."The question is whether we can accelerate use of it so that we pay for the transition."The consultation on Jackdawclosed last weekand the Rosebank consultation ends later on Monday.Ultimately the decision is a quasi-legal one which will be taken by the regulator Opred and approved by the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.Although no timetable has been set for the final decision, the operator says a relatively quick decision could see the Jackdaw field producing gas by the winter.Related topicsNorth Sea oil and gasOil & Gas industryClimateEffects of global warmingShetlandMore on this storyWhat is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields?Published2 days agoPM faces pressure as Jackdaw licence consultation closesPublished10 AugustJackdaw boss warns of winter fuel shortage risk if gas field not approvedPublished9 July
generated_summary: Consultation ending on controversial Rosebank oil field. The decision will ultimately be taken by Energy Security Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

title: Muir resignation demand is 'not personal' says UFU
content: Muir resignation demand is 'not personal' says UFUImage caption,Ulster Farmers' Union president John McLenaghan rejected a claim that the UFU was trying to dictate government policyByEimear FlanaganBBC News NIPublished17 August 2026The president of Ulster Farmers' Union (UFU) has said his organisation's demand for the resignation of Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir is "not personal".The UFU called on the Alliance politician to quit on Friday over his department's handling ofa controversial cull of 51 cattle in Fivemiletownin County Tyrone.Alliance has claimed the UFU's call was not motivated by animal welfare concerns, but by its opposition to Muir because he stands up to its "vested interest" in agriculture.UFU President John McLenaghan insisted the dispute was "not about personalities" adding that Muir's decision to appoint a single person to conduct a review into the cattle cull was the "straw that broke the camel's back".The UFU wanted an independent panel of experts to examine the circumstances of the cull which took place on a Fivemiletown farm on 29 and 30 June.The cattle's owner had been disqualified from keeping animals for life after being found guilty of a number of animal welfare offences in May.When a court order to rid him of ownership of the cattle was not compiled with, the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) stepped in.The animals were shot and killed by Daera's humane slaughter team, but some of the shootings took placewithin earshot of members of the public, causing distress.The UFU expressed shock over the cullasking "whether every possible alternative was properly considered",externalbefore the cattle were killed.Muir has previously insisted that Daera had "no choice" but to cull the animals.On Friday, the minister hit back at those calling for him to quit, saying "the days of the Ulster Farmers' Union dictating government policy are over".He added that he was "arguably the first minister in the history of this state that is not beholden to one vested interest".Muiralso said,externalthe operation was not "authorised nor directed by me" but he as "the responsible minister... ordered an external independent review because the public deserves clear answers".Image caption,Andrew Muir previously insisted that Daera had "no choice" but to cull the cattleUFU says dictating claim is 'unfair'The UFU president rejected the claimed that the union was trying to dictate Daera policies."This organisation has 120 years of history", McLenaghan told theBBC's Good Morning Ulster programme."It has worked with every government there has been, every competent authority there has been - whether it's Westminster or Stormont."Any political party that has held the ministry, we've worked with them to help them, to help our farmers, to help our industry."To describe that as dictating is not only unfair on the Ulster Farmers' Union, it's also actually somewhat disingenuous."McLenaghan pointed out that the UFU is often invited to work with Daera on "co-design" projects because of staffing and resources issues within the department.The UFU president insisted that the call for Muir to quit was made after details of the review into the Fivemiletown cull were confirmed.The process is to be led by Dr Martin Blake, a former Chief Veterinary Officer for Ireland, and he is expected to report by early autumn."We were always clear that in order for this review to be thorough, to get the answers that we need, it needed to be more than just purely an analysis of 'did the vets follow procedure?'," McLenaghan said."It needed to look into the legalities of the process and also take consideration of both animal and farmer welfare... that we didn't get."'Motivations behind this'Warning: This article contains an image of dead animals that some may find distressingSpeaking on the same programme, Alliance deputy leader Eóin Tennyson claimed the cull was being used as an excuse to target Muir's job."The fact that the UFU have called for a resignation before that review has even concluded, I think speaks very plainly to the motivations behind this," he said."They are not concerned about the case at Fivemiletown or animal welfare issues, as they profess."They are concerned about the fact that for the first time in the history of the Northern Ireland Executive we have a minister who is not beholden to vested interest."Tennyson argued the review needed to be carried out quickly and if Muir was to appoint a larger panel of experts that would delay the outcome of the process.But McLenaghan said if there were three people on the panel, like the UFU had requested, they could "share the workload" and it could be completed faster.What happened in Fivemiletown?Image source,OtherImage caption,The cattle were shot dead in a field in County Tyrone in JuneAnimal welfare inspections on the farm dating back to 2022 identified serious concerns, including the presence of emaciated animals, feed contaminated with urine and faeces and 33 animal carcassesThe farmer was found guilty of a number of animal welfare offences in May including:Thirteen charges of failure to dispose of an animal carcassOne charge of failure to comply with an Animal By-Products noticeSix charges of causing unnecessary suffering to an animalOne charge of failure to produce medicine recordsThe court issued a deprivation order on 8 June, meaning that the farmer had to have the animals removed from his ownership.As is practice, he was given two weeks to appeal the sentence, or to transfer, sell or give away his stock.He was then given an extra week.On 29 June, when the extended grace period had lapsed, the departmental humane slaughter team arrived at the farm to begin destruction of the remaining 51 animals by shooting them.The operation was completed on 30 June.Some members of the public witnessed the operation in one of the three areas across the farm that the animals were in.Questions about how the operation was conducted were first raised by a local councillor, then concerns were expressed by politicians and farming leaders.Related topicsNorthern IrelandAgricultureCattleAnimal welfareFivemiletownNI agricultureMore on this storyCattle cull witness says shootings were something no-one should ever seePublished10 AugustExternal review ordered into 'wild west' style shooting of 51 cattlePublished2 AugustQuestions over 'wild west' style shooting of 50 cattle, as review carried outPublished31 July
generated_summary: Muir resignation demand is 'not personal' says UFU. UFU wanted an independent panel of experts to examine the circumstances of the cull. The cattle's owner had been disqualified from keeping animals for life after being found guilty of animal welfare offences.

title: About 100 homes swept away after Hurricane Lala lashes Hawaii
content: About 100 homes swept away after Hurricane Lala lashes HawaiiImage source,Getty ImagesByHafsa Khalil,Brandon DrenonandBen Rich,lead weather presenterPublished15 August 2026Updated 17 August 2026Hawaii has been hit by flash floods and mudslides that have swept away homes after category one Hurricane Lala skirted Big Island, leaving one person dead in a car accident.More than 100 properties were uprooted from their foundations on Big Island, but Governor Josh Green said there "amazingly" did not seem to have been any wider loss of life.Despite not even making landfall, the storm still dumped up to 32in (81cm) of rain in places, sending torrents raging down mountainsides. More than 200,000 households were without power.Although Lala has since weakened to a tropical storm and was tracking westward, south of Hawaii, the danger is not over, say officials.The storm's eyewall howled within 30 miles (48km) of Big Island's South Point overnight, but it was close enough to bring flash flooding, Hawaii County said on Sunday.After gaining hurricane strength on Saturday afternoon, packing wind speeds of 91mph, Lala's winds have now decreased to near 65mph, said the National Hurricane Center (NHC) in its latest advisory at 20:00 EDT (00:00 GMT) on Sunday.To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be playedFigure caption,"It's actually hard for us to see... I've got a lot of water in my eyes," says a local reporter during a live TV broadcast on the Hawaii County coastBut tropical storm warnings remain in effect for all eight of Hawaii's major islands on Sunday.Governor Green told a press conference: "It appears that the properties that were washed away did not, at least as of this moment, to my knowledge, have any fatalities associated with them."There were a lot of people that went to hospital for minor accidents."To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be playedFigure caption,Watch: Strong winds and downpours in Maui and Honolulu as storm Lala approachesAbout 180 Hawaii National Guard members were deployed to help with the emergency response.Some 219,000 customers had lost electricity on Hawaii as of Sunday afternoon local time, according to tracker PowerOutage.Three hospitals also lost power, but they had backup generators.Big Island's two main airports, Hilo International and Ellison Onizuka Kona, were temporarily closed, but have since reopened.According to the governor, 190 flights have been postponed.In Maui, some residents were left without water supply on Saturday.Image source,Getty ImagesIniki, a powerful category four storm, was the last hurricane to hit Hawaii back in 1992.It caused six deaths and $3bn in damage after making landfall on the southern coast of Kauai.Hurricane season in the US has been relatively quiet the last few years - the last major storm was category three Hurricane Milton, which hit Florida in October 2024.This year has seen a strong El Niño - a periodically occurring area of unusually warm surface water - develop in the Pacific, driven in part by climate change.As hurricanes and typhoons feed off warm sea waters, this spike in ocean temperatures could facilitate a higher number of storms that grow to have a greater intensity.Related topicsUnited StatesSevere weatherHawaiiHurricanesMore on this storyWorld's oceans hit record-high July temperaturesPublished10 August
generated_summary: About 100 homes swept away after Hurricane Lala lashes Hawaii. One person dead in a car accident. More than 200,000 households without power.

title: Belgian wildfire doubles in size on third day tearing through nature reserve
content: Belgian wildfire doubles in size on third day tearing through nature reserveTo play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be playedFigure caption,Watch: Firefighters rush to contain wildfire in Belgian nature reserveByDearbail Jordan & Emma RossiterPublished15 August 2026Updated 16 August 2026A wildfire described as the largest in Belgium's recent history has more than doubled in size in 24 hours, local officials said on Sunday.Hundreds of firefighters are spending a third day beating back flames tearing through Hautes Fagnes - the country's largest nature reserve - prompting the evacuation of two nearby villages.Local farmers hauled water tankers towards the park near Belgium's eastern border with Germany, backed by water-bombing aircraft and helicopters sent from Sweden and the Netherlands.The blaze is one of several wildfires reported across Europe this weekend, with at least two killed in forest fires on a Greek island off the coast of Athens on Sunday.Belgian officials have warned that high heat and the park's terrain - which consists of bog-like territory, moorland and forests - have hampered efforts to extinguish the fire.It spread from 80 hectares (200 acres) on Friday to 850 hectares on Saturday morning - before consuming 3,000 hectares by early Sunday, AFP news agency reported citing local officials.Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin said two of its fronts - heading towards Jalhay and Monschau - had been brought under control.But the blaze continued to advance on Sunday, with its active front reported to be a kilometre long.Authorities earlier said the conditions remained challenging and that they were relying heavily on aerial assistance to tame the flames, though no homes have been affected.Image source,ReutersImage caption,Local farmers joined fighters from both sides of the border to tackle the blaze on SundayTwo water-bombing aircraft arrived from Sweden on Sunday afternoon to back up four helicopters - two Belgian and two Dutch - already on site.Nicolas Yernaux, spokesman for the regional authorities in Wallonia, had said on Saturday that the fire was the country's "largest in recent history".Firefighters had "allowed parts of the heathland to burn because the area is very difficult to access", he added.Rescue teams have been unable to access the area where fire broke out, meaning its cause remains unknown.Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,The aftermath of the fire in a scorched area of the nature park, pictured on SaturdayForest fires have also been reported in Croatia, Spain and Serbia since Friday, after a summer of extreme heat that has seen swathes of land across Europe eithergoing up in flames or being scorched brown.Local officials in Landes, south-western France said a wildfire had triggered the evacuation of 650 residents on Saturday.The fire began on Thursday and, according to authorities, reignited on Saturday - with more than 500 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze.The EU's climate monitoring service, Copernicus, has confirmed that western Europe experienced its hottest June-to-July period on record.Related topicsEuropeBelgiumWildfiresFranceSevere weatherMore on this storyEurope's scorched landscapes seen from space after summer heatwavesPublished4 days agoDozens injured and thousands evacuated in Croatia wildfirePublished4 days ago
generated_summary: Belgian wildfire doubles in size on third day tearing through nature reserve. At least two killed in forest fires on a Greek island off the coast of Athens on Sunday.

title: 'Days of the farmers' union dictating policy are over' - Muir
content: 'Days of the farmers' union dictating policy are over' - MuirImage caption,There have been calls for the Agriculture Minister, Andrew Muir, to resignByLouise Cullen,Agriculture and environment correspondentandFinn Purdy,BBC News NIPublished14 August 2026The Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir has said "the days of the Ulster Farmers' Union (UFU) dictating government policy are over".It comes after the UFU extended a vote of no confidence in the department to include the minister, the permanent secretary and the chief vet, over how acull of 51 cattle was carried outin County Tyrone.The cows were shot in June, leading to complaints about the manner of the cull which was carried out within earshot of members of the public.The UFU President John McLenaghan had said there were concerns about the independence of a Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) review into the incident.'Extremely challenging'Muir said he would continue to engage with the UFU and had spoken with its president on Friday morning.He added that the situation he had inherited in the department was "extremely challenging", with issues building up "due to wrong government policy previously".He said he was "arguably the first minister in the history of this state that is not beholden to one vested interest".Muir described some of the speeches at a protest outside Stormont on Monday as "pure electioneering" and called on his fellow politicians to "calm it down".Death threatsEarlier this week, Muir said adeath threat had been made against him. He alsoreceived one in June.On Friday, he said "the police will be coming looking" for those who threatened or abused anyone in public life.In a statement to BBC News NI, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it does "not discuss the security of individuals and no inference should be drawn from this"."However, we will continue to do all we can to ensure that all of our politicians are supported and that they can undertake their role free from fear and intimidation," Insp Roberts said.Reaction from civil servants' unionThe UFU also called for Daera's Permanent Secretary Katrina Godfrey and the Chief Veterinary Officer Brian Dooher to resign.In response, the senior civil servants' union the FDA said it was "entirely inappropriate" to call for the resignation of officials who were "duty-bound to serve ministers" and "could not defend themselves publicly".The minister has previously saidthere was no reasonable alternative to the cattle being euthanised on siteand has insisted it was a last resort as officials had to act on a court order.Anexternal review of the cattle cull was announced by Daera earlier this month, but the UFU's Executive Committee met on Thursday night.Image caption,Ulster Farmers' Union president John McLenaghan said the UFU "no longer have confidence that the Department can deliver"In a statement on Friday the UFU said it "does not have the confidence in the independence of the review as presently constituted, including the scope of the Terms of Reference and appointment of a single person to conduct it."The UFU has consistently maintained that an investigation into an incident of this seriousness must be demonstrably independent, robust and capable of commanding the confidence of farm families and the wider public."John McLenaghan said calling for resignations was not a decision his union had taken "lightly".However he added that confidence had been "severely damaged".He said the most recent event is "just one of many instances where farmers feel that the Department has lost touch with farmers"."We no longer have confidence that the department can deliver."A Daera spokesperson said they and the minister were aware of the decision."An external independent review is already underway to review the action taken by Department officials in response to the Deprivation Order in Fivemiletown," they continued."There are many strategic issues and challenges for agriculture."It is vital we face up to those challenges together to restore our environment and ensure a sustainable future for agriculture".Responding to the vote against the two named senior officials, the FDA union's Robert Murtagh said: "This kind of performative stunt, naming and targeting officials, does not aid understanding and undermines the need for constructive dialogue."The UFU's action appears also to be seeking to pre-empt and to influence the independent review already now in train."It should be awaiting its findings and recommendations before jumping to respond to voices who do not care about public service or indeed public servants."What happened in Fivemiletown?Warning: This article contains an image of dead animals that some may find distressingAnimal welfare inspections on the farm dating back to 2022 identified serious concerns, including 33 animal carcasses, feed contaminated with urine and faeces, and emaciated animals.The farmer was found guilty of a number of animal welfare offences in May and disqualified from keeping animals for life.The offences included:Thirteen charges of failure to dispose of an animal carcassOne charge of failure to comply with an Animal By-Products noticeSix charges of causing unnecessary suffering to an animalOne charge of failure to produce medicine recordsThe court issued a deprivation order on 8 June - that the farmer must have the animals removed from his ownership.As is practice, he was given two weeks to appeal the sentence, or to transfer, sell or give away his stock.He was then given an extra week.On 29 June, when the extended grace period had lapsed, the departmental humane slaughter team arrived at the farm to begin destruction of the remaining 51 animals by shooting them.The operation was completed on 30 June.Some members of the public witnessed the operation in one of the three areas across the farm that the animals were in.Questions about how the operation was conducted were first raised by a local councillor, then concerns were expressed by politicians and farming leaders.The AERA committee was recalled to discuss the incident, and quiz the minister and veterinary officials.What was the Stormont committee told?The committee heard that officials had been working with the farmer after "numerous" inspections, beginning in 2022.The agriculture minister Andrew Muir said those had revealed a "grotesque" situation and "a large number of animals were caused unnecessary suffering", leading to the deprivation order."That order legally required the department to deprive the individual of any livestock."The department had no choice."And so my officials took the necessary steps to fulfil this legal obligation."It emerged that a total of 21 animals had been removed during the grace period, but 51 remained on the farm.Image source,OtherImage caption,The cattle were shot dead in a field in County Tyrone in JuneOfficials said animals in two of the areas on the farm were disposed of by 13:30 on 29 June.The slaughter operation in the final area was stopped when a local farmer offered to buy some of the remaining cattle.But the animals could not be rounded up, and escaped onto the road.They were eventually herded back and a vet recommended they be shot.One remaining animal was disposed of on 30 June.The carcasses were removed later that day.Questions have been asked about the weapons used, the amount of ammunition, and why slaughter in situ was chosen as the method of disposal.Deputy Chief Veterinary Officer Gemma Daly described the cattle as "semi-feral" and said staff had expressed concerns over the years about how to handle the animals without causing them stress, or risking injury to themselves.Senior Principal Veterinary Officer Elsie McGarvey said the department was "technically" potentially in breach of the court order by extending the grace period.She added that approximately half of the animals were not suitable for the food chain and others were too young.And she said officials were "always prepared" that the farmer would be disqualified and they "knew" removing the animals would present "significant issues".How will the review be carried out?Before the committee met, the minister announced thatan independent external review,externalwould be conducted.It will be led by Dr Martin Blake, a former Chief Veterinary Officer for Ireland.His work will include looking at the decision-making, risk assessments and communication around the operation.He will make recommendations, based on his examination of the records and any interviews he carries out.Muir said Dr Blake's review would be "thorough but not prolonged", and told the committee it would be complete "by early autumn".The UFU has called for the review to be conducted by a panel of experts, rather than an individual.An uneasy relationship - analysisAgriculture and environment are uncomfortable but inseparable bedfellows under the department.And the relationship between Daera and the UFU has been fractious in the past.The UFU's Executive passed a vote of no confidence in the department - not the minister - in October last year.That came after an outcry over the initial consultation document for the Nutrients Action Programme.It has since been revised by a stakeholder group of farmers, agri-food representatives, conservationists and environmental groups.But the size of the protest on Monday about this incident shows farmers are not happy.The findings of Dr Blake's review will be closely scrutinised.The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has tabled a motion of no confidence in Andrew Muir which requires 30 signatures to make it to the floor of the Assembly.But any change at the top of the department would have to come from the minister's party - or the minister himself.And there are just seven months left for this minister to get a substantial number of significant policies past the Executive.What is a deprivation order?A deprivation order may be issued by a court when a person is convicted of animal welfare charges.It requires that person to be deprived of ownership of the animal - to have it taken away - and for the animal to be disposed of.The court may specify how that disposal will happen, or it may delegate that decision to a person appointed to carry out the order.Thelegislation,externalstates that "disposal" includes destroying an animal.Related topicsNorthern IrelandAgricultureCattleAnimal title: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteries
content: Indian solar mission's new findings throw light on enduring Sun mysteriesImage source,MATIAS BASUALDO/EPA/ShutterstockImage caption,Scientists say the temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physicsByGeeta PandeyBBC Correspondent,Reporting fromDelhiPublished14 August 2026One of the most enduring mysteries that has been puzzling scientists forever is how the Sun's outer atmosphere - the corona - is millions of degrees hotter than its surface. And how does the corona continue to remain so hot despite frequent eruptions during which it loses huge amounts of energy?Astrophysicists in India now say the latest findings fromAditya-L1, the country's first solar observation mission in space, have provided them some vital clues to unlocking those mysteries. Their findings are revealed in a recent paper published in the prestigious Astrophysical Journal Letters.The temperature variations in different regions of the Sun defy the laws of physics, says leading Indian solar astrophysicist Prof R Ramesh of the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) who led the study.If you cut through the Sun's layers, deep inside is the core where the temperature is 15 million Celsius. Travel outwards to the surface or the photosphere - the part that we see from the Earth - it's about 5,500C. Far away from the core is the Sun's outermost layer or corona where the temperature is about 2 million C - it can sometimes go up to 40 million C.Prof Ramesh says the corona is where extreme weather events - such as solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) - originate, during which large amounts of energy is released by the Sun into space. The CMEs cause beautiful auroras, and they can also affect life on Earth by causing geomagnetic storms that can knock down power grids and affect weather and communication satellites.In normal or low-activity times, the Sun launches two to three CMEs a day. During the maximum solar activity cycle that comes every 11 years, there can be 10 or more in a single day."Now if the Sun is losing such huge amounts of energy with each CME and it's not replenished, the star at the centre of our solar system would lose all its energy and Earth would plunge into an irreversible deep freeze," Prof Ramesh says.But since that's not happening, it means there's a "mechanism" by which the corona is able to maintain its inexplicably high temperature, he says.Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,An illustration that shows the structure of the Sun - from the centre to the periphery are the core, the radiation and convection zones, the photosphere, the chromosphere and the coronaScientists put it down to two factors - one, the bubbling boiling motions on the Sun's surface that constantly generate waves which, as they travel outwards, carry energy to the corona - a bit like sea waves carrying foam and froth to the shore.The second is the "tangled magnetic field lines" in the Sun's atmosphere that constantly snap and then reconnect. Prof Ramesh says a CME occurs when these twisting, looping lines - which resemble braided hair - rupture, throwing out massive clouds of magnetised plasma and gas in space. They often originate near sunspots, which are darker, cooler spots on the Sun where magnetic fields are particularly strong."But then these lines reconnect and the Sun replenishes the lost energy back within hours," he adds.Why 2026 will be a year like no other for India's Sun missionHow important are India's Moon mission findings?Why it costs India so little to reach the Moon and MarsIn their paper, Prof Ramesh says they have been able to quantify how much energy each of the two systems supply to the corona – which explains both why it's so many times hotter to begin with and how it retains that temperature after consistently losing energy.Their study, he says, clearly shows that it's the second system that supplies most of the energy."Though the waves generated as a result of the bubbling, boiling motions on the Sun's surface generate and transport energy, their contribution is very little - they supply only 7% of the energy requirement."The remaining 93% comes because the Sun reconfigures itself and replenishes the lost energy."Image source,Getty ImagesImage caption,The Sun's corona is only visible with the naked eye from Earth during a total solar eclipseTo arrive at that calculation, Prof Ramesh says they studied a "very energetic" CME that took place on 5 August 2024. Emissions were recorded by Aditya-L1's coronagraph called Velc (Visible Emission Line Coronagraph)."We saw that in 10 hours after the CME, the tangled field lines were able to go back to their original place, they reconnected and corona's energy was reconfigured," he said.Aditya-L1: India's Sun mission reaches final destinationChandrayaan-3: India makes historic landing near Moon's south pole"We do recognise that energy generated by bubbly motions plays a major role in it, but we have evidence that it is not sufficient. Our study shows that the magnetic field lines snapping and reconnecting everywhere on the Sun are the primary source for supplying most of the energy."These data, Prof Ramesh says, "provide an important benchmark" for future studies into the potential energy generation mechanisms in the Sun's atmosphere."I think they would help answer the fundamental questions of physics that defy logic," he says.Follow BBC News India onInstagram,external,YouTube,external,Twitter,externalandFacebook,external.Related topicsThe SunSpaceSpace explorationIndiaScience & EnvironmentAstronomy

title: Romania shuts only nuclear plant as heat causes huge drop in Danube River level
content: Romania shuts only nuclear plant as heat causes huge drop in Danube River levelImage source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,The second of the two 706-megawatt nuclear reactors at Cernavodă was disconnected just before midday on ThursdayByJaroslav LukivPublished13 August 2026Romania has shut down its only nuclear power station because of extremely low water levels in the Danube river caused by prolonged hot weather affecting much of Europe.The Cernavodă plant, where two reactors produce about 20% of Romania's electricity, is not expected to be restarted within the next 10 days.Earlier this week, authorities tried to increase the water flow to the plant - which uses the Danube for cooling - by sinking barges loaded with rocks in the river.Neighbouring Hungary has so far avoided a shutdown of its only nuclear plant in Paks, which also uses the Danube. The waters in Europe's second-longest river have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries.The second of the two 706-megawatt reactors at Cernavodă was disconnected from the Romanian electricity grid just before midday on Thursday."We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," plant director Romeo Urjan told the AFP news agency.The first reactor had already been shut down in July.Until now, Cernavodă had only been shut down once before in 2003.The shortfall in power is usually covered by solar and wind during the hot, windy daytimes - but traditional coal- and gas-powered generation will have to be supplemented by imports during the evenings.Romania also has huge hydropower capacity, although that has been heavily cut by the same low river levels that caused the nuclear shutdown.In Hungary, Prime Minister Péter Magyar warned last month that the Soviet-era Paks, which has four nuclear reactors, could be forced to shut down entirely for the first time.Plant officials said that levels in the Danube were so low that the suction nozzles used to take in water could not reach it.To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be playedFigure caption,Sunken WW2 ships emerge from Danube after drop in water levelsClimate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe.It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service.This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires.The Rhine - another of Europe's key waterway - is also suffering low water levels, which is severely limiting traffic.The continent's agricultural sector has also taken a noticeable hit.Italy's largest agricultural trade association, Coldiretti, said climate-related damage - such as hail, drought and wildfires could exceed €3bn (£2.6bn; $3.5bn).France's Environment Minister Monique Barbut warned that data from the country's national statistics agency suggested the recent heatwaves could rack up €10bn to €15bn in direct and indirect costs.The Dutch bank Triodos said the extreme heat and its consequences could wipe out much of the projected economic growth for the EU.The European Commission had forecast growth of 1.1%, while the IMF expected the euro area to grow by around 0.9%.Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,Greek firefighters have been deployed to stop a wildfire from spreading further into the residential areas of the popular Siviri resortIn Greece, more than 200 people - mostly tourists - were evacuated on Friday from the popular resorts of Siviri and Fourka in the northern Halkidiki peninsular because of a raging wildfire.Meanwhile, as many as 80 departments across France are now on a heatwave alert, as temperatures are expected to exceed in some places 40C (104F) on Friday.The country has already been devastated by fires in recent weeks, with the blazes causing more damage this year than at any time since World War Two.Spain - which is also still recovering after recent deadly wildfires - on Thursday recorded temperatures as high as 37C in central areas.Image source,ReutersImage caption,The UK on Thursday saw its hottest day of the year so far, with the Met Office reporting a provisional recording of 38.1C in LondonThe UK on Thursday saw its hottest day of the year so far, with the Met Office reporting a provisional recording of 38.1C in London's Kew Gardens.Multiple fires were burning across the West Midlands, with several people reported injured and four homes destroyed.Rain is expected to arrive in more places of the UK over the weekend, but the BBC climate and science team says it will take more than showers to bring the UK's widespread drought to an end.Related topicsRomaniaNuclear powerHungaryHeatwavesClimateEuropeMore on this storyDanube river's low water levels reveal remains of WWII soldiers and motorcyclePublished7 days agoRhine falls to record low levels as drought strains Europe's riversPublished3 August
generated_summary: Romania shuts only nuclear plant as heat causes huge drop in Danube River level. Second of the two 706-megawatt nuclear reactors at Cernavodă was disconnected just before midday on Thursday.

title: Temperatures soar to 38C as amber extreme heat warning in effect
content: Temperatures soar to 38C as amber extreme heat warning in effectImage source,Getty ImagesByHelen WillettsLead Weather Presenter,Reporting fromBBC Weather CentrePublished13 August 2026The UK has experienced its hottest day of the year so far on Thursday with a provisional temperature of 38.1C (100F) in Kew Gardens.It is the second time the UK has reached 38C this year – the first was at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.The only time a temperature this high has been recorded twice in a calendar year was in 2022.It comes as a rare amber weather warning for extreme heat is in effect across a large swathe of the UK, as the peak of the UK's fifth heatwave hits.Image caption,Amber extreme heat warning from the Met OfficeThe extreme heat warning will be in force until 23:59 BST across Eastern England, London and the south-east, the Midlands, north-west England, south-west England and parts of Yorkshire and Humber.It will run alongside amber heat health alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency across the entirety of England.In effect until 21:00 BST on 14 August, these warn of significant impacts across health and social care services, including a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions.Adding to the risks associated with the heatwave, a tropical night - where temperatures fail to drop below 20C - is also on the cards in places as increasingly humid air spreads into western areas.The cumulative effect of persistent heat by day and night can place additional stress on the body.Temperatures will begin to fall away by the weekend, although at their lowest they will still be average or a little above average for mid-August.Image caption,Forecast temperatures for the peak of the heat on ThursdayMore temperature records fallTemperatures exceeded 37C in a number of locations on Thursday afternoon.This provisionally sets a new record for the number of days in a calendar year with temperatures of 37C or above.It has only happened nine times since records began - and three of those occasions have been in 2026.Thursday is the 38th day this year when temperatures somewhere in the UK have exceeded 30C - the previous record was 34 days.It adds to a long list of other records set this year.Wednesday became the first day in August to reach 35C or more, making it the 4th consecutive month to reach this temperature.Lingwood, Norfolk, recorded 38C on 26 June - a new UK temperature record for the month of June, and the highest reading so far this year.Currently the hottest August day on record stands at 38.5C, recorded in 2003.As long as August temperatures remain average or above for the month as a whole, this summer will replace 2025 asthe warmest on record.More on this storySummer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met OfficePublished11 AugustHow much rain will end the drought?Published6 AugustIs there a hosepipe ban in my area? title: Cloudy skies lead to mixed fortunes for Scotland's eclipse hunters
content: Cloudy skies lead to mixed fortunes for Scotland's eclipse huntersImage source,BBC Weather Watchers/Mrs BrownImage caption,The view of the eclipse from Orkney was - like for much of Scotland - obscured at least partially by cloudsPublished12 August 2026Updated 13 August 2026Across Scotland, lucky skygazers have caught glimpses of the eclipse - despite cloud covering much of the view.The Sun disappeared almost entirely behind the Moon, in what was the most dramatic solar eclipse visible from the UK since August 1999.The spectacle started just after 18:00 on Wednesday evening, and lasted about two hours, with the Sun setting about 21:00.At the beginning of the eclipse, heavy cloud cover across much of Scotland left visibility poor. But as the phenomenon progressed, cloud in some areas cleared at least partially, offering glimpses of the rare celestial event.To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.This video can not be playedFigure caption,Clouds cover partial solar eclipse in GlasgowParts of Spain and Portugal witnessed the phenomenon of a total eclipse, but in Scotland the eclipse shadow meant that up to 95% of the sun was obscured by the Moon.At its peak, only an arc of the Sun was visible in Scotland. In areas where the clouds obscured the view, some viewers reported that it temporarily got a little darker than it otherwise would have been, as the Moon blocked the light from the Sun.While there will be smaller solar eclipses over the next few years, the next total eclipse will not take place until 23 September 2090.The view from the westExperts had suggested that west was best for those hoping to see the eclipse.They had advised eclipse watchers to find a spot in an elevated location with unobstructed views west.Image caption,Crowds at Whitelee Wind Farm hoped to see the eclipse, but clouds mostly obscured the viewWhitelee Windfarm at Eaglesham in East Renfrewshire hosted one of the biggest eclipse events in Scotland.BBC Scotland's Selena Jackson said 50-60 people had gathered there to watch the spectacle.She said that cloud cover scuppered the view for most of the time, but about 19:00 the clouds parted and a sliver of the sun was visible from behind the moon.Some of the crowd gasped as the sight came into view.Image caption,Excited eclipse hunters waited patiently on Ayr Beach - but there was not much to see for them due to cloud coverImage caption,Those at Ayr Beach were disappointed with their view of the eclipseAt Ayr Beach, the BBC's Ben Philip said it temporarily felt darker, cooler and eerily quiet during the eclipse.But he felt the dozens who had gathered to witness the eclipse left disappointed not to have got a better view.On a few occasions, the odd break in the cloud gave a glimpse of the Sun and the Moon for a few seconds.One member of he public who came to the beach to see the eclipse said: "The cloud just wasn't on our side."Calton Hill 'busier than Hogmanay'Image caption,Large crowds gathered on Calton HillEdinburgh saw some of the biggest crowds as the east of the country started to look more promising for the skygazers.One member of the public who had travelled up the capital's Calton Hill told the BBC that the view point was busier than it usually was on Hogmanay.Hundreds of people had gathered there for the eclipse.Neil Martin, president of the Astronomical Society of Edinburgh, described the vista as "pretty incredible", saying: "You never get bored of this view."BBC News's Lorna Gordon said the Moon came across from the right, eating into the Sun, and left a crescent at the top.A large cloud momentarily covered the sun entirely, but when it cleared ahead of the maximum eclipse a cheer erupted from the crowd.At the point the light became muted and subdued, and the noise from the crowd softened as they took in the spectacle.Image caption,Sandy and Nick Burgoyne delayed their flight so they could catch the eclipseSandy and Nick Burgoyne were meant to be heading home to the USA on Wednesday morning but decided to delay their flight so they could catch the eclipse.They had been in Edinburgh for a week to see some shows.From their vantage point on Calton Hill the eclipse took place right above the Edinburgh skyline.It was, they both said, much better than the one they saw in New York in April 2024 - and well worth delaying their journey home for.Image source,BBC WeatherWatchers/SkyWatcherImage caption,The eclipse viewed from Haddington in East LothianMembers of the public sent in their pictures from around the country - here's a selection of some of the best shots.Some of the most striking pictures of the eclipse came from the north, where cloud cover was lower and therefore allowed for better viewing.Image source,BBC WeatherWatchers/KnottSamImage caption,The view from Stonehaven in AberdeenshireImage source,BBC Weather Watchers/Anne's WorldImage caption,It was cloudy in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire, but it was still possible to get a good view of the eclipseImage source,BBC WeatherWatchers/20vtmacdImage caption,From Aberdeen's Bieldside, the spectacle was clear - despite the cloud coverImage source,BBC WeatherWatchers/Wellies Full of WaterImage caption,Dundee got a good view of the eclipseImage source,BBC Weather Watchers/Jack MarchImage caption,The early stages of the eclipse were clear in Dornoch in the Highlands, despite the cloud coverRelated topicsAstronomyThe SunEclipsesScotlandEdinburghMore on this story'Phenomenal' sight as millions wowed by once-in-a-generation solar eclipse

title: Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trend
content: Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'Vulture King' is fighting to reverse the trendImage source,Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption,Some see them as sinister but these birds play a vital role in nature's cycleByMakuochi OkaforBBC Africa,Reporting fromAwka-Etiti, NigeriaPublished13 August 2026"People fear the environment where the shrine is. No evil will ever happen here. So, nobody fights vultures that perch here," a man they call the Vulture King tells the BBC.Mostly associated with death and decay, perhaps it is not surprising that when vultures disappeared from the skies across many West African cities, they were not missed.Yet across the continent, their disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, as conservationists warn that hunting linked to traditional beliefs and spiritual practices continues to threaten several vulture species to the point of near extinction.Without vultures, ecosystems would lose a natural defence against the spread of disease.Thankfully in one part of south-eastern Nigeria, residents are bucking the trend.Awka-Etiti is home to a sacred forest surrounding a shrine dedicated to a deity known as Nguma.At first glance, the site is an unremarkable cluster of tall trees wrapped in thick greenery. But at its heart stands an ancient tree that locals say has watched over the community for hundreds of years, and remains the spiritual home of the shrine.This is a largely Christian community but some residents continue to observe traditional practices, in which vultures play a key role.Local resident Chukwuemeka Igwe, who has earned the nickname King of Vulture, thanks to his tireless volunteer work with Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), says "the indigenous don't hunt vultures".Instead, locals sometimes offer fresh animal sacrifices at the shrine which attract the birds, he explains."And there is an adage we use here that says: 'When you put down a sacrifice and you do not see vulture[s], know that something happened in the spirit world'."It means that vultures are a good omen when a sacrifice has been made because their presence suggests that the deity has accepted the sacrifice and heard the residents' appeal to its power.Image source,Ifiokabasi Ettang / BBCImage caption,Chukwuemeka Igwe is proud of the nickname given to himNow in his 50s, Igwe says the birds have been a feature of daily life in this town for as long as he can remember, walking around among humans and scavenging for food.Yet for many who venture into the wild elsewhere on the continent, vultures are not the first birds to capture their attention. Rarely do we stop to admire vultures through binoculars or photograph in awe.In the eyes of many people, vultures are downright ugly. But scientists say they provide one of nature's most important cleaning services.Vultures consume dead animals within hours, helping prevent carcasses from becoming breeding grounds for dangerous bacteria and diseases.Their disappearance can have serious consequences, says NCF conservation biologist Stella Egbe: "In places where the total collapse of vultures has happened, there has been impact of rising zoonotic diseases."Vultures' powerful stomach acids allow them to safely consume infected animals, helping stop diseases such as anthrax and rabies from spreading.Without vultures, experts warn ecosystems lose a natural defence system.Rapid urban growth across Africa has also played its part, transforming landscapes, and destroying many of the tall trees that the birds nest in.Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,Cape Vultures are one seven types facing extinctionHabitat loss is far from the only factor.Poisoning is the cause of death for an estimated 60% of vultures in Africa,according to BirdLife International,external.These issues will be high on the agenda when researchers from across the region meet in Abuja later this year to review the West African Vulture Conservation Action Plan, which was drafted in 2022.Experts say the use of vultures and their body parts in traditional medicine and Vodun (also known as Voodoo) has emerged as one of the most significant drivers of their decline, especially in West and southern Africa.Dead adult vultures in Nigeria used to sell for around 25,000 to 30,000 naira ($18 to $22; £13 to £16) each - but can now fetch up to 200,000 naira ($145; £107) per bird, says Egbe.Vulture eggs and nests are increasingly targeted too, which for such a slow-breeding species is a catastrophic and "shocking" development, says Egbe.Adult vultures usually reach sexual maturity between the ages of five and seven, and produce only one chick every year or two. Plus many young vultures do not survive their first year."And so you imagine what will happen if a nest is removed and eggs are removed. That means a pair of vultures will not have a next generation for that year. So in addition to hunting, you're removing their habitat, you're removing their homes," she adds.Seven species of vultures in Africa are now classified as globally Endangered or Critically Endangered by BirdLife International, the authority for birds on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.A recent BirdLife report says African vulture populations have fallen by between 80% and 97% over a period of 50 years.The group also says that in January 2020 more than 2,000 hooded vultures were found dead in Guinea-Bissau, many with their heads removed - a sign of belief-based practices rather than natural causes, researchers say.As vulture populations continue to fall across the region, conservationists have been searching for communities where these birds are not hunted, feared or exploited.They found one such example in Awka-Etiti.Yet in recent years, Igwe says he and other residents became worried when they noticed outsiders arriving to hunt the birds and vulture numbers dwindled.In his quest to save the birds he visits markets, buses and public spaces to spread the word: "I tell them that vulture is helpful to human life".He says he "cannot run away" from his unusual nickname of Ezeudene, or the King of Vulture."I'm fighting to make nature exist the way it's supposed to be."Working with the NCF for the past six years, Igwe has mobilised community leaders, local groups and security teams to protect the birds from outside hunters, with local bylaws now helping to formalise their protection.Local volunteers monitoring the birds say they have now recorded more than 160 vultures, up from about 20 recorded in 2017.Gift Ufuoma / BBCWe've heard shocking news that people are not just going for vultures anymore, they're going for the nests and even the eggs."Dr Stella EgbeBiologist, Nigeria Conservation FoundationNigeria has become a major hub for the illegal trade of vultures, conservationists say, partly because of its biodiversity and porous borders."We are doing everything possible to make sure that the smuggling of items, including vultures, including donkeys, and other species outside the country is suppressed to the barest minimum," insists Abdullahi Maiwada, a spokesman for the Nigerian Customs Service.He says customs officials have carried out seizures of protected wildlife and supported prosecutions linked to illegal trafficking.It is an example of how Nigeria is trying to live up its commitments as a member of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites) - under which endangered species are not allowed to be traded across borders.But Maiwada admits to the BBC that enforcement alone is not enough - education will be crucial too."We may not be able to do it without the cooperation or understanding of members of the community," he continues. "If people understand why these species should be preserved, then our enforcement will only be complementary to those who decide to be recalcitrant."That message has been at the heart of conservation work in Awka-Etiti and across parts of Nigeria.Although reliable population data remains limited, conservationists say there are encouraging signs in Awka-Etiti, with local engagement helping residents become vigilant against outside hunters."The missing vultures are almost back. If you go to the marketplace now, you see vultures. At one time they disappeared, but now they are coming back," Igwe confirms.Egbe believes that this small, south-eastern town demonstrates what is possible when communities lead conservation efforts."What we've done in Awka-Etiti is one very good example of a success story where people have taken charge of what's going on in their environment. That makes us happy."For Igwe, every returning bird represents hope.But with populations still collapsing across Africa, he knows protecting them will require much more than one community.Additional reporting by Abayomi Adisa, Ifiokabasi Ettang and Natasha BootyYou may also be interested in:Congolese scientists find new monkey with orange lips 'hiding' in forestPublished16 JulySaving South Africa's threatened albatross from lethal fishing linesPublished31 December 2025Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticidesPublished5 AugustGo toBBCAfrica.com,externalfor more news from the African continent.Follow us on Twitter@BBCAfrica,external, on Facebook atBBC Africa,externalor on Instagram atbbcafrica,externalRelated topicsAfricaNigeriaWildlifeReligionConservationBBC Africa podcastsFocus on AfricaThis Is Africa

title: Rare cows part of estate's rewilding project
content: Rare cows part of estate's rewilding projectImage source,Nick HowardImage caption,A herd of White Park cows is being introduced at Castle Howard EstateBySeb CheerYorkshirePublished6 hours agoA rare breed of cattle has been introduced to the grounds of a historic house in North Yorkshire as part of a 30-year conservation project.The arrival of the White Park cows, thought to be one of the most ancient species of its kind, is the latest phase of the Bog Hall rewilding scheme on the Castle Howard Estate, near Malton.Their grazing in the newly-sown meadows would "help create a more varied habitat structure", the estate said.Head of natural environment, Guy Thallon, said reintroducing animals had been "inspiring for the whole Castle Howard team and beyond", with further plans to release beavers in the autumn.Approximately three miles (5km) of fencing has been installed ahead of their release, with badger tunnels and otter passes built to maintain safe routes for wildlife."The conservation volunteers have been preparing the site by creating ponds and planting willow," Thallon said."We can't wait to see the positive impact of nature's engineers in the coming years."Image source,David ScottImage caption,The rewilding project covers 440 acres within the Howardian Hills National LandscapeMeanwhile, the cows have taken up residence in the project area, where they will live outside all year round.The herd was chosen because it is suited to "outdoor conservation grazing, including in wetter grassland habitats", the estate added.It is priority-listed by the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, which describes it as "likely the most ancient native cattle in the British Isles".'Rare opportunity'The Bog Hall Habitat Bank project hopes to restore and rewild 440 acres of agricultural land into a "thriving space for nature", the estate said.Part of the area, which sits within the Howardian Hills National Landscape, is designated as a Site of Importance for Nature Conservation.The project is being delivered in partnership with nature restoration company Environment Bank.Image source,Emma RayeImage caption,Guy Thallon says it was "exciting" to see the cattle exploring their new homeThe scheme began in 2024 and volunteers have so far restored meadows and created scrub banks to protect saplings.Ponds and leaky dams have also been installed to hold more water across the site.Thallon said children from nearby primary schools had designed signage for the fencing around the area, featuring "animals they would like to see in the Bog Hall Habitat Bank project in the future".Fraser Rutherford, head of marketing at Environment Bank, said for pupils, it was a "rare opportunity to follow nature restoration throughout their school years and see firsthand how native wildlife returns to a landscape".Get in touchYour VoiceContact formContact formListen to highlights fromNorth Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latestepisode of Look North.Related topicsMaltonCastle HowardConservationRewildingMore on this storyRewilding project could see beavers return to estatePublished17 November 2024Tamworth pigs introduced to rewild nature reservePublished17 June'Squashed poo' a sign of water voles' successPublished5 days agoRelated internet linksBog Hall Habitat Bank

title: Work on £1.5m nature reserve to start next month
content: Work on £1.5m nature reserve to start next monthImage source,Town and Manor of HungerfordImage caption,The project has been supported by the local community, the charity saidPublished18 August 2026A £1.5m project to build a new nature reserve for a town on poor quality, unmanaged meadows will start next month.The Kennet Valley Wetland Reserve will be constructed on about 16 hectares (40 acres) of land at Undy's Meadow, on the northern edge of Hungerford and close to the River Kennet.The Town and Manor of Hungerford, the charity thatorganises its Tutti Day celebrations, is behind the plan.Kate Edwards, from the charity, said the nature reserve will be a "very special thing"."It's going to be a proper nature reserve; it will be somewhere you can go and sit quietly," she said."The focus is the wildlife and we're going to be privileged enough hopefully to sit on the benches, walk the paths and see and hear the willow warblers and the grasshopper warblers. Hopefully lots of wetland birds will come in and use the area."She said the community has given the plan the "most incredible support" and that construction work must be carried out between September and December.It must not be done before September because of nesting birds but cannot be done after December because the ground would be too wet.The first stage of work, including a landscape, paths and boardwalks, is expected to be in place by next summer.Get in touchYour VoiceContact formContact formRelated topicsBerkshireHungerfordWildlife conservationWildlifeConservationWetlandsEnvironmentNatureRelated internet linksTown and Mayor of Hungerford

title: Solar panel critic now 'supporter of plan'
content: Solar panel critic now 'supporter of plan'Image caption,Chris Chadwick (left) is now in favour of Len Shephard's (right) solar panel site proposalByJon LockhartGuernseyPublished18 August 2026A critic of a proposed solar panel site in Guernsey says he is now a "complete supporter of the plan" after going through the details with the applicant.Applicant Len Shephard said his proposals for 72 panels on a site behind his house in St Sampson could power five Guernsey households and save 505 trees a year.Theapplication initially received a complaintfrom Chris Chadwick, due to the site being defined as a greenfield area. However, Shephard and Chadwick have since met to go through the applications details, and Chadwick said he had been won over.Planning officials are still considering the application.Image caption,Chadwick said that the plan has had "a lot of thought put into it"Shepard said Chadwick became a supporter after he was "able to show him all of the information"."He was good enough to just say: 'Well, it's nothing like I thought in the first place.'"The information is available to a degree on the planning website but there was no substitute for sitting down like this."He added the panels would be "fully demountable" and in the future "someone can just take it apart and you'd never know it was there".Shephard said the site was "used for greenhousing" and had sat for "45 years doing nothing" due to buried greenhouse materials beneath the field.He said: "It's designated as greenfield because there's no choice for the planning. It's either horticulture or agriculture."So we're kind of stuck with that... you're not going to be able to do any farming on it."He added that proposals to build on greenfield sites should "be looked at on a case-by-case basis".More news stories for GuernseyListen to the latest news for GuernseyChadwick explained his initial complaint was due to "little detail" being available online about the application.He said: "It just said 72 panels and my initial reaction was that's going to cover all of the area."I saw the planning application right at the end of its period of notification so, by the time I looked at the website, the data wasn't there."After learning more, Chadwick said Shephard "has put a lot of thought into making this work as best as possible."Chadwick said he is now a "complete supporter of the of the plan" because Shephard had "considered all of the things that I asked questions about".He said that "the panels are being stood up off the ground" so that grass and wildlife has access to the sun.Chadwick added: "He probably won't see financial return from it his lifetime, so it's not a commercial decision: it's an altruistic decision to actually do the right thing."The application has just seen a site assessment undertaken, according to theStates' planning website,external.Follow BBC Guernsey onX,externalandFacebook,externalandInstagram,external.
