title: South Korea’s Nuclear Dilemma
content: The structure of global security has been changing in profound ways. In Europe there is a major conventional war, and the potential for armed conflict seems to be increasing in other parts of the world including East Asia. The United States is no longer seen as a reliable security guarantor by its allies. One of the puzzling aspects of the global security architecture is that nuclear powers no longer seem to possess a coherent understanding of what their arsenals are for. Strategic capabilities are increasingly developed with conventional weapons, while nuclear deterrence fails to deter major conflict, a phenomenon that Rose Goettemoeller has referred to as “The Strange Defeat of Nuclear Deterrence.” This has the paradoxical consequence that regional powers feel the increasing need to acquire nuclear weapons. South Korea faces this dilemma very acutely. North Korea is increasing its nuclear arsenal and has developed a significant alliance with Russia even as Pyongyang has renounced unification and designated South Korea as its enemy. At the same time, the preparedness of the United States to defend its allies in the region hascome into question. This is exacerbated by the fact that the continental United States is now within reach of North Korean ballistic missiles. The result has been an intense debate in South Korea about whether the country should acquire nuclear weapons. On July 27, retired Lieutenant General Chun In-bum publishedan article in the Korea Timesthat elaborated on a sophisticated proposal for South Korea to acquire a nuclear weapons arsenal, which Seoul would own but which would be imbedded in an integrated network of deterrence with the United States. This would resemble some of the deployments of nuclear weapons in Europe in the early Cold War, with a dual-key system that would require the consent of the host country and the United States for weapons to be launched. Chun admitted that this would raise significant issues with regard to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), verification, and decision-making. Public surveys in South Korea have shown up to80 percent supportfor South Korea acquiring a nuclear weapons capability. Among South Korean policy elites, there is less enthusiasm due to the potential consequences for the alliance with the United States, South Korea’s adherence to the NPT, and the economic implications. Policymakers tend to prefer a “threshold capacity” whereby South Korea would have the capability to quickly develop nuclear weapons but would not actually do so while the alliance with the U.S. remains in place. Strengthening nuclear deterrence on the Korean Peninsula can take several forms. One possibility would be to redeploy U.S. nuclear weapons in South Korea with the purpose of signalling to North Korea, China, and Russia that extended deterrence is serious. In Europe, the deployment of U.S. nuclear weapons was accompanied by the development of independent nuclear deterrents by Britain and France. But these nuclear arsenals were developed in a different environment when the strategic conflict with the Soviet Union was at the core of global security. The United States was unable to prevent the development of these independent arsenals and therefore chose to integrate them into its posture on European security. All of the proposed variants face the dilemma of “entrapment or abandonment.” Countries hosting U.S. nuclear weapons do not want a nuclear conflict to start without their consent, but they want extended deterrence to be effective. Likewise, the United States does not want to be embroiled in a nuclear conflict initiated by an ally. The fundamental dilemma is how to make nuclear deterrence credible to the adversary while balancing the risks in a manner acceptable to all parties. The problem with Chun’s proposed scheme is that it does not resolve this fundamental dilemma. If the United States maintains escalation control, this amounts to a veto in a different form. If South Korea had independent launch authority, then the United States could find itself in a nuclear conflict against its will. It is really unclear therefore whether the implementation of Chun’s proposal or anything similar would solve the underlying problem. South Korea’s negotiations with the United States over the transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) over ROK forces – a process that hasdragged on for two decades– illustrate the practical difficulties of such arrangements. OPCON transition requires highly coordinated intelligence and communication systems, interoperability, training, and finely tuned relations between South Korean and American commanders. Nuclear decision-making would be more complex and would have to include the U.S. president, but given the geography of the battlefield, decision times could be extraordinarily short. It would require substantial reassurance that there would be no unauthorized launch but the threat of retaliation would have to be credible to the adversary. A South Korean nuclear arsenal, even if embedded in an alliance command structure, could complicate the regional security environment. It could encourage Russia to enhance its support of North Korea and its sharing of technology with respect to nuclear delivery and control systems. Beijing would be likely to consider such a capability as a threat to its own security. The decision to deploy the ballistic missile defense system THAAD in South Korea in 2016 provoked a major reaction from China with the imposition of political and economic costs. Then-South Korean President Moon Jae-in managed to partly assuage China by promising no further deployments of THAAD batteries and no integration into a region-wide U.S. led missile defense network. A South Korean nuclear arsenal is likely to provoke an even more serious reaction, including economic sanctions, increasing military deployments and potentially the deployment or retargeting of Chinese nuclear forces against South Korea. It could also rekindle the nuclear debate in Japan and lead to further nuclear proliferation. It is hard to predict how North Korea would react to a South Korean nuclear arsenal. It is true that deterrence of a North Korean nuclear attack would be enhanced. At the same time, it could provoke even more acceleration of North Korea’s efforts to develop a secure nuclear capability that could also strike the United States. It would not necessarily inhibit low-level attacks below the threshold of direct armed conflict. It would also change the narrative of a democratic South Korea acting in conformity with international law versus a rogue North Korean state if South Korea were to abandon its commitments to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Leaving the NPT is not just a reputational or technical issue. While South Korea would no longer be obliged to forego the manufacture or possession of nuclear weapons, the United States would be constrained under Article I of the NPT not to transfer possession or control over nuclear weapons to South Korea or provide any nuclear assistance. The civil nuclear technology cooperation between the United States and South Korea – the “123 Agreement” of 2015 – would be in jeopardy. There is little immediate prospect that Chun’s ideas can become policy. But that does not mean that there are no paths forward. The integration of U.S. nuclear weapons and conventional forces into operational planning, nuclear consultation, integration of early warning, intelligence, missile defense, and various signals regarding the commitment to extended deterrence and no tolerance of North Korea aggression could strengthen stability. If South Korea feels it can no longer rely on the United States, then it could develop its own nuclear deterrent. But it would have to face the consequences, which may include international isolation, severe strains on (or even the collapse of) the South Korea-U.S. alliance, and a more hostile international security environment. title: Kyrgyzstan Liquidates More Companies Over Sanctions Risks
content: 19 more companies have been ordered to close down, and more than 140 have been cut off by their state-owned banking partners. Another 19 Kyrgyz companies arebeing ordered to close downas Bishkek strives to assuage Western concerns about the evasion of Russia sanctions. Kyrgyzstan’s top leaders, including President Sadyr Japarov, have long denied that the country was aiding in the circumvention of sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine. InAugust 2025, Japarov told state media outlet Kabar, “On our part, not a single case has been reported of circumvention of sanctioned goods going to Russia.” That same month, he denouncedsanctions against Kyrgyz banksas “politicized.” Then, during hisU.N. General Assembly speech in September 2025, Japarov railed once again against sanctions targeting Kyrgyz banks, claiming, “The sanctions imposed on Kyrgyzstan are based on false information spread by certain non-governmental organizations and dishonest people.” A year later, Japarov may not have changed his tune but the Kyrgyz government has changed its tactics from outright denial to action.The proximate trigger appears to have been pressure from the European Union. In February, the EU’s sanctions envoy, David O’Sullivan, paid a visit to Kyrgyzstan. O’Sullivan told reporters that trade flows suggest that some goods “are being imported into Kyrgyzstan with the sole purpose of being re-exported to Russia, in breach of our sanctions.”He went on: “We are not asking Kyrgyzstan not to have trading relations with Russia. We only ask that that trading relationship does not involve the deliberate circumvention of our sanctions by the transmission through Kyrgyzstan of sanctioned EU goods to Russia.” Two months later, in April, the EU used its “anti-circumvention tool” for the first time, and the target was Kyrgyzstan. This paved the way for the EU to “restrict the sale, supply, transfer or export of specified sanctioned goods and technology to certain third countries” considered to be at high risk of providing pathways for the circumvention of sanctions. These goods included machining centers – used in the production of high-precision metal components for missiles and drones – and communications technologies. The EU’s decision was based on trade data, which is difficult to explain in any way that isn’t sanctions evasion.According to the EU, available trade data for the first 10 months of 2025 revealed an 800 percent increase in Kyrgyzstan’s imports of goods that appear on the EU’s Common High Priority (CHP) list – that is, the list of prohibited dual-use goods and advanced technology items used in Russia’s war effort. In the same period, trade data revealed a 1,200 percent increase in the export of CHP items from Kyrgyzstan to Russia. After the EU’s decision, Kyrgyzstan began to shift its approach from outright denial to at least the appearance of compliance. In May,Kyrgyzstan’sMinistry of Justiceannounced that it had ordered 50 companies “involved in operations ​with high sanctions risk” to close down. The Kyrgyz government did not name the companies or the sectors affected. Then inearly June, Kyrgyzstan’s Minister of Economy and Commerce Bakyt Sydykov was appointed special representative for sanctions policy and minimization of sanctions risks. Later that month, two state-owned Kyrgyz banks – Eldik Bank and ABank – ended partnerships with more than 130 companies due to alleged sanctions risks. Again, the companies were not named, complicating any effort to verify the government’s claims. Following an August 18 meeting chaired by Sydykov, the government offered an update. Of 40 companies “whose activities could be associated with increased sanctions risks” that were identified in June, 19 will be ordered to liquidate. From July to August, a press release following the meeting noted, Eldik Bank had ended business relations with 109 companies, with 20 more in the process of being shut out. ABank, the release stated, had ended relations with 35 companies and had 40 more “undergoing due diligence. title: Exercise Rotor Clap III and Mission Sudarshan Chakra: Options for Pakistan
content: India is trying to establish a defensive shield against airborne objects, from drones to missiles. An Indian Air Force helicopter takes part in Exercise Rotor Clap III at the Pokhran firing range in Rajasthan, Aug. 1, 2026. The Indian Air Force (IAF) concluded a week-long helicopter drill, Exercise Rotor Clap III,on August 2at the Pokhran firing range in Rajasthan. The exercise was conducted to validate a key operational concept of shooting down unwarranted low-flying loitering munitions and drones. The exercise is part of an attempt by the IAF to plug the loopholes exposed during Operation Sindoor, especially pertaining to theincursionof Pakistani drones deep into Indian territory. This carries serious consequences for Pakistan, as it is linked to India’s attempt to establish a defensive shield against airborne objects, as evidenced by New Delhi’s pledge to operationalizeMission Sudarshan Chakra. As its name suggests, this was thethirditeration of Rotor Clap, a drill conducted by the IAF to take out drones using its rotary assets. Rotor Clap was inaugurated in 2019; however, Rotor Clap II and III gains special significance because they followed India’s launch of Operation Sindoor in May 2025. For the IAF, the Rotor Clap exercises are an attempt to test and validate new warfighting tactics, techniques, and procedures, with a central focus on shooting down slow-moving airborne targets. The latest exercise involved rotary-wing platforms from the IAF fleet,includingApache, Prachand, Mi-25/35P, Rudra, and Mi-17V-5 helicopters. Rotor Clap III was held under the aegis of the IAF South Western Air Command, which saw the activation of its units at forward operational bases in Rajasthan, bordering Pakistan. The air rotary maneuvers were conducted there because both Prachand and Apache helicopters are deployed in different air stations and aviation bases in Rajasthan. Prachands of the IAF have been deployed at the IAF Jodhpur air station since 2022, while Apaches are with the 451 Army Aviation Squadron based inJodhpur.The field activity suggests these helicopters could be a broader part ofMission Sudharshan Chakraand serve as its airborne leg to intercept and neutralize aerial objects. Rotary platforms have demonstrated in recent conflicts that they are as effective as other defense systems at shooting down intruding aerial objects. For instance, an Israeli Air Force Apache helicopter shot downsix dronesin a couple of minutes during the 202512-dayIran-Israel war. As India has closestrategic cooperationwith Israel, there is a strong possibility that the IAF may have approached the Israeli Air Force for assistance on counter-drone operations. A key question arises as to whether India has sufficient numbers of helicopters to carry out the task of tracking and shooting down airborne drones and loitering munitions. The backbone of the Indian helicopter fleet would be the indigenously developed Prachand, designed and manufactured by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). The IAF and Indian Army Aviation Corps currently have10 and fivePrachand helicopters in service, respectively. In the future,156additional units will be inducted into the fleets of both services: 66 to the IAF and 90 to the Indian Army. These 156 helicopters will be delivered by2032. The order could becompleted earlieras well, as HAL has partnered with Adani Defense Systems and Technologies Limited and Bharat Earth Movers Limited (BEML) to boost its annual production. Likewise, theRudraattack helicopter, also made by HAL, will also be used for drone interdiction missions, as it has already been inducted in large numbers by both the IAF and the Indian Army. The IAF has one operational squadron and is expected to inductthreemore, whereas the army has around 75 Rudras across five operational aviation wings. In addition, both services have28advanced Apache helicopters in service: 22 with the IAF and six with the Indian Army. The number will likely increase in the future, as India has already retained the capability to produce parts of the Apache, including its key component,the fuselage. Rotor Clap III indicates that Mission Sudharshan Chakra’s scope has expanded beyond a ground-based air defense shield. It now also entails using helicopters to interdict drones and loitering munitions. It is not as cost-effective a means to interdict low-cost drones as using ground-based air defense guns or jammers; however, it is far less expensive than firing costly missile interceptors. The exercise also envisages that rotary platforms capable of flying low to evade even low-level radars can perform these missions in proximity to the border with Pakistan. All this points to New Delhi seeking to increase its options and expand its horizons to intercept a wide range of airborne threats as part of a wider air defense doctrinal recalibration in response tolimitationsencountered during Operation Sindoor. Amid rapidly changing regional and global dynamics, India’s Pakistan-specific military maneuvers, to the extent of using new tactics earlier employed by Israel against Iran, are a sign of concern for Islamabad. India has astrategic partnershipwith Israel, so the possibility cannot be ruled out that the IAF may have received assistance from the Israeli Air Force in the preparation and execution phase of Rotor Clap III. Israel has a history of supporting the IAF to enhance its warfighting tactics, as evidenced by its timely support during theKargil War. Likewise, India has also been aiding Israel’s war effort against Iran, according to a newly released report byAmnesty International. Pakistan needs to adopt new strategies and tactics to counter the IAF’s evolving tactics. First, Pakistan should induct high-speed loitering munitions, with speed exceeding Mach 0.5, as at this velocity it will be difficult for helicopter-based interdiction by the IAF. Second, to engage Indian rotary platforms that might come close to the border, Pakistan can close the low-level radar detection gap that India seeks to exploit by deploying advanced long-range electro-optical sensors that do not rely solely on line-of-sight radar horizons, along with additional low-level radar deployment. Last but not least, the Pakistan Army and Air Force should conduct joint exercises to develop a joint strategy to counter the IAF’s evolving tactics, thereby enabling them to uphold conventional deterrence at the tactical level. title: China’s Male Matchmakers and the End of ‘Marrying Up’
content: A new wave of matchmaking influencers explicitly treats marriage as a business transaction – and they brutally judge clients’ prospects accordingly. In early 2024, a grandmotherly figure known as“Wang Po”（王婆）became a national sensation in China for her folksy matchmaking performances in Kaifeng. Less than two years later, the country’s online matchmaking scene has undergone an unexpected gender reversal. A new generation of male matchmaking influencers, includingAoye（鳌烨）, Wukong（悟空）, Dachao（大超）, and Tianshu（天书）, has taken over the spotlight. These men have little in common with the traditional image of the matchmaker. Often dressed in business attire and speaking in the language of markets, they assess participants’ appearance, education, family background, income, and assets before telling them what kind of partner they can realistically expect. The male matchmakers’ appeal may partly come from the authority they claim through a language of competition, income, and hierarchy that has traditionally been coded as masculine. But their rise reveals something deeper than a new social media trend: a growing anxiety about marriage itself. For years, China’s most prominent relationship gurus were predominantly women. Figures such asAyawawataught female audiences how to make themselves more desirable, manage relationships, and potentially “marry up.” The underlying message was aspirational: improve yourself, learn the rules, and you might move upward in the marriage market. The new male matchmakers offer a colder perspective. Their signature question is simple: What do you actually have to offer? Scoring systems have become a staple of their livestreams. Participants may be rated from one to 10 based on their appearance and overall qualifications. The terms A8, A9, and A10 are used as shorthand to refer to increasing levels of wealth, with A8 generally indicating tens of millions of yuan ($1.4-1.5 million or more) in assets, A9 hundreds of millions, and A10 billions. Even celebrities can become benchmarks. Ordinary participants who expect to “marry up” may receive a rating of four or five, followed by a blunt explanation of why their expectations are unrealistic.Chinese coverage of the trendhas documented some of these exchanges in detail. The spectacle works because humiliation and reassurance coexist: viewers are shown how harsh the marriage market can be, while being promised that someone can still explain its rules. These influencers have turned private insecurity into a public spectacle of quantification. Marriage is discussed through the language of exchange: What do you bring to the relationship? What does the other person bring? What can you realistically expect in return? This rhetoric resonates in a society where upward mobility increasingly feels uncertain. China had roughly 240 million single people aged 15 and above in 2023,according to government data cited by the Associated Press. At the same time, young people face intense competition over employment, housing, income, and social status. In such an environment, marriage can become another arena for calculating risk. The appeal of male matchmakers therefore lies partly in their willingness to offer “disillusionment,” or 幻灭, as a form of advice. Their message is that there is no secret strategy for transforming an ordinary person into an elite partner. Sometimes, the answer is simply to adjust one’s expectations. This marks a striking shift in the tone of Chinese relationship advice. Earlier theories encouraged people to imagine how they might improve their position in the marriage market. The new wave of male influencers focuses on understanding the position one already occupies. That may explain why these harsh livestreams are so compelling. They turn the uncertainty of modern dating into something that appears measurable, even when the measurements themselves are crude. For viewers anxious about their place in an increasingly competitive society, being told their “market value” can be painful – but strangely reassuring at the same time. The rise of China’s male matchmakers thus points to a changing social mood. In a period when upward mobility feels harder to achieve, people may be losing faith in the promise of “marrying up.” What they increasingly want from a matchmaker is something more uncomfortable: an honest estimate of where they stand. There is, however, a deeper tension in this new form of matchmaking. Once marriage is framed through market value, everyone becomes both buyer and product. And the more relentlessly young Chinese are taught to calculate the price of intimacy, the harder it may become to believe that marriage is supposed to be about anything other than the price. title: Al-Qaida’s Renewed Confidence in Bangladesh
content: Its network is growing, albeit slowly. But this is unlikely to manifest in mass casualty attacks. On August 10, the United Nations Security Council released a report that raised “concern about AQIS [al-Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent] trying to exploitBangladesh to establish cells there.” Although the U.N. report mentioned Bangladesh in only one sentence, it triggered enormous and somewhat surprising media coverage in Bangladesh, with several news publicationsdrawing attentionto Muslim radicalism in the country. Police also swung into action. They instructed field-level police to“remain on high alert.” In recent months, Bangladesh Police have pointed to an upsurge in militant activities in the country. In June 2026, they issueda terror alert, warning of an attack on the Police headquarters. Media reports from last year drew attention to Bangladeshi nationals joining theTehreek‑e‑Taliban Pakistan (TTP). On August 12, police found a handmadepressure‑cooker bombin Dhaka’s Savar area. Bangladesh’s response to militancy has swung between extremes. The Sheikh Hasina regime securitized dissent itself, most visibly when it banned the opposition-alignedJamaat-e-Islami as a terrorist organizationjust days before Hasina’s ouster. It used the “Islamist terrorism threat” to marginalize the opposition and crack down on dissent. This served to secure external legitimacy and approval for its dictatorial rule — a dynamic I find paradoxical. In over a decade of experience tracking Muslim radicalization in Bangladesh, I have seen how militancy was manipulated rather than confronted. In the two years since the ouster of the Hasina regime in August 2024, Bangladesh’s response to militancy has been confused, oscillating between denial — Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed publicly insisted that militancy“no longer exists in the country”— and exaggerated responses, such as the April 2026 police alertwarning of an imminent attackon their own headquarters, an attack that never materialized. Broadly, Bangladesh’s terrorist landscape has comprisedthree streams: the Taliban inspired Jamaat-ul-Mujahideen Bangladesh (JMB), the Islamic State-affiliated Neo-JMB, and al-Qaida-linked Ansar Al Islam (AAI). While JMB recruits are largely Qwami madrasa students, Neo-JMB and AAI have drawn their recruits largely from urban educated youths. There are operational differences as well. While JMB and AAI target secular bloggers and Sufi shrines, Neo-JMB has attacked foreigners, mainly Westerners, describing them as crusaders or Christians. JMB lost much of itsoperational capacityafter the government executed several of its leaders, including Bangla Bhai and Abdur Rahman, in 2007. However, it remains active, though it continues to be decentralized. Triggers such as a political or religious flashpoint could be used by JMB to justify escalating from recruitment and fundraising alone to actual violence. Neo‑JMB, meanwhile, lost momentum following the collapse of Islamic State’s caliphate and the killing of Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi by U.S. forces. ISIS’s pitch to young Bangladeshis was explicitly global: a restored caliphate, anapocalyptic showdown with the “Dajjal”(the Islamic equivalent of the anti-Christ), and a single Qurashiimam(a person who leads prayers in a mosque) commanding the loyalty of the entireummah(global community of Muslims). When Baghdadi’s caliphate collapsed territorially and he was killed in 2019, that pitch lost its anchor. The promise of a caliphate had been rendered false and it had visibly failed, thereby undermining ISIS’s ideological foundation and contributing to its decline. It had ripple effects; it weakened the Neo-JMB’s appeal. As for the AQIS-linked AAI, it gained ground with the decline of the Neo‑JMB. However, its growth has been slow and steady. AAI received a boost when its leader, Mahmudul Hasan Gunobi, who had been jailed in 2021 over an alleged plot targeting Bangladesh’s parliament, was acquitted in 2024. Gunobi has since rebuilt his public following; he now has over 168,000 followers on Facebook, delivers sermons that invoke“global jihad and the caliphate,”and has openly endorsed “Talibani rule” for Bangladesh. Such developments point to AQIS’s ongoing efforts at recruitment, albeit in a restrained and gradual manner. The clearest articulation of AQIS’s post-2024 strategy came from Ustadh Usama Mahmood, in a statement issued through As-Sahab Media addressed to Bangladesh’s “religious community” after Hasina’s ouster in August 2024. He laid out what amounts to a four-part doctrine: embraceda’wah(mass preaching) as the primary vehicle; build “capability for resistance and revolution”; use that capability to pressure the state into reform from outside; and, pointedly, avoid entering government altogether. The document frames electoral or bureaucratic participation as a trap that has historically neutered Islamist movements from Cairo to Islamabad, and argues instead for a long, patient movement-building strategy, deepening roots in the population rather than contesting power directly. This is where AQIS diverges from its old rivals, Neo-JMB and JMB.AQIS’s Bangladeshi messaginghas always been layered onto grievances that don’t expire with a battlefield defeat: the plight of Rohingya refugees, the war in Kashmir, the treatment of Muslims under India’s Bharatiya Janata Party, and a steady drumbeat of domestic complaints about “moral degradation,” secular education policy, and what its Bengali-language magazine Al Balagh and English-language Azan and Resurgence have long portrayed as the marginalization of Muslim identity within Bangladesh’s own state institutions. Because these grievances are renewable, AQIS’s narrative infrastructure survives organizational setbacks in a way that ISIS’s did not. The big question is whether AQIS is on the brink of engaging in violent operations in Bangladesh. At least for now, the answer leans toward a “no.” AQIS has shown patience, and that patience is exactly why a large‑scale campaign of violence is unlikely in the near future, whatever the U.N.’s warning about cell formation might suggest. Al‑Qaida’s global network still feeds off crises in Gaza, Iran, Yemen, and the Sahel. But none of these has yet produced a militant formation with a clear, actionable mandate for South Asia.Ghazwa‑e‑Hindremains more of a theological promise than an operational plan. Inside Bangladesh, the militant scene is fractured into AAI, JMB, and Neo-JMB, but none has shown the coordination needed for a serious offensive. Where the danger feels more immediate is in the case of individual dissent. title: Cambodia: From Scam Empire to Security State
content: War with Thailand pushed Cambodia to enact a sweeping scam crackdown. Now the ruling elite is leveraging the same crackdown to consolidate its political control. The remains of Me Teuk Bridge, previously the primary route into Thmor Da, in Cambodia’s Pursat province, as seen on Aug. 6, 2026. The bridge was destroyed by a Thai F-16 airstrike on Dec. 13, 2025. It was two days after Christmas, just before 7 a.m., when Paul heard the first explosion. The 50-year-old Nigerian national had struggled to make a living as an English teacher in Vietnam and applied for a well-paid admin job in Cambodia, only to find he’d been sold to a criminal group running online scams. Beaten and tortured into compliance, he had been transported from site to site as bosses raced to evade a wave of raids on the country’sbrutalscam compounds – by this point estimated to holdhundreds of thousandsof people who, like Paul (we have changed his name for his safety), had been trafficked into forced criminal labor in the scam and illegal gambling industry. By December, he was in Choam, a tiny jungle outpost where Khmer Rouge dictator Pol Pot is buried, confined to a scam compound complex centered around a casino that once served Thai gamblers hopping across the land border. That border had been closed since June, just before fighting broke out between Cambodia and Thailand. Now, after months of fragile peace, the conflict had erupted again. Bosses told workers not to panic; Choam was not a target. Plus, Paul had never seen any sign of Cambodian soldiers or military vehicles from the windows of his guarded office-dormitory, and by the morning of December 27, the two sides had already negotiated aceasefire. But hours before it came into effect, Thailandattacked. “The next thing we start hearing, seeing drones. Blasting. Bombing upon bombing,” said Paul, his voice shaking. He says he survived by sheltering in a concrete drain, while scam bosses frantically hung Chinese flags from windows to show Thai surveillance the buildings were not Cambodian-controlled, but the main hotel-casino was hit again and again. “A lot of people died there. And on the road, strings of bullets tearing the body of people’s cars,” he said. “If a bullet can tear a car [like that], what about a human being?” The border dispute that sparked the conflict goes back decades, but targeting and capturing scam industry infrastructure under the guise of combatting crime has been weaponized as a tactic by both sides since mid-2025, when the Thai military beganbombing scam hubson Cambodian soil. The Thai military framed this as an effort to contain a global security threat that generates huge illicit revenues while fueling corruption and instability, and declared the conflict to be, in part, a “war against scammers.” Cambodia initiallyaccusedThailand of exaggerating the scale of the problem as a pretext for illegal incursions into its territory, but faced with a far stronger and better-equipped army, and under pressure from countries it relies on for military aid, the government swiftly changed direction, launching a comprehensivecrackdownon domestic scam compounds. At first, it looked like Cambodia’s political elites were cornered. To repair frayed relationships with the United States andChina, they not only had to admit the scale of forced online criminality compounds operating with impunity across the country but potentially sacrifice an industryworthhalf the country’s GDP and pivotal incementingcomplicit elites’ grip on power. But instead of losing their hold over the country, Cambodia’s ruling families have turned the scam crackdown to their advantage, leveraging this diplomatic rehabilitation project to boost Cambodia’s military might, commandeer billions of dollars’ worth of real estate built and funded by criminal investors, and consolidate authoritarian control. FBI Director Kash Patel meets with Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet to discuss the Cambodian government’s anti-scam crackdown in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, July 22, 2026. Photo credit: Facebook/Samdech Thipadei Hun Manet, Prime Minister of Cambodia Having spent years denying the existence of a large-scale, entrenched online scam industry, and even punishing those who attempted to expose it, Cambodian officials nowclaimtheir crackdown drove 300,000 scammers out of the country and saw over 250 compounds closed. While some of these compounds may be a single building, others are huge, interconnected real estate projects with their own supporting infrastructure, collectively constituting entire towns that had beenpurpose-builtby criminal investors to the tune of billions of dollars. In June, Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who chairs Cambodia’s Commission for Combating Online Scams,toldChannel News Asia that all these locations “have been converted into state property.” This represents a staggering transfer of private assets into the hands of an increasingly autocratic governmentdominatedby a clique of political dynasties whose own family members and company co-directors are linked to the scam compounds that have now been seized. That includes#8 ParkandGolden Fortune Science & Technology Park, two“vile”forced online criminality compounds that had been designated for sanctions by the United Kingdom, U.S., and European Union as part of the Prince Holding Group. Prince Group is a Cambodia-headquartered conglomeratedescribedby the U.S. Treasury Department as a “global criminal enterprise built on scam compounds, fraud and money laundering.” Its founder, Chen Zhi, wasappointeda personal adviser (with rank equivalent to a government minister) to Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet; his father, former Prime Minister Hun Sen; former Interior Minister Sar Kheng; and to his son, the current Interior Minister Sar Sokha, who at one stage isreported to have co-ownedJinbei Casino, another entity targeted in the scam crackdown, alongside Chen himself. Sokha denies the reports. In late May, Sar Sokha used an American lobbying firm tofilea petition to remove his name from adraft U.S. billlisting key international cyberscam targets. Ten days later, the General Department of Prisons – overseen by Sar Sokha’s Interior Ministry – postedphotosof the recently emptied #8 Park site, describing this as a new construction site that could be used as a prison facility. Another prison-like scam compound has also been transformed by the Interior Ministry into a literal prison: the former“Mango 2 Park”compound, now an immigration detention center. Some trafficking survivors who managed to escape amid the chaos of conflict and crackdowns now find themselves here, in a building previously owned by one of the same types of criminal group that initially enslaved them. Videos shared with The Diplomat of open sewage running through chronically overcrowded dormitories-turned-cells in stifling tropical heat suggest living conditions under the new management may be even worse. This appears to be part of a broader strategy by Cambodia toexpandprison capacity. New facilities are being built all over the country to ease critical overcrowding. Cambodia’s prison population hastripledover the past decade, pushing the system to more than 400 percent of its capacity. Somethree-quartersof the population in some prisons are languishing at the pre-trial stage or awaiting final verdict, which can takeyears. The spike in the prison population has been driven largely by sweeping arrests for minor drug offenses, but the past few years have seendraconian censorship lawsincreasingly target political opponents, environmental activists, protesters, and even social media users for simply resharing posts critical of government policy or its handling of the war with Thailand. In February, two Cambodian journalists weresentencedto 14 years in prison for “supplying a foreign state with information prejudicial to national defense,” after taking a photo with soldiers at the border that inadvertently appeared to show unplanted landmines in the background. The ruins of a casino now occupied by Thai troops in Thmor Da, Pursat province, Cambodia, Aug. 6, 2026. Photo by Nathan Paul Southern. There are concerns that this growing prison population is providing a literally captive workforce for a renewed war effort. Since May, the government begantransferringnearly 800 juvenile offenders to prisons along the Thai border as part of a “vocational” program to assist military operations. Backtracking on an earlier proposal to use juveniles to build trenches and defensive infrastructure, Prime Minister Hun Manetsaidthat participants will not serve in combat roles, but are deployed in engineering and construction supporting the military in parts of Pursat province close to the occupied scam town of Thmor Da, and in Oddar Meanchey province, home to scam compound-heavy flashpoints like Choam and the border town of O’Smach. When we visited O’Smach in April, the Thai military was still occupying bombed-out compounds, and even givingmedia toursto journalists who appeared to ask no questions about the numbers of casualties or legal justifications for treating trafficking compounds as military targets. Most local residents had fled, but some of those remaining told us that regular Thai surveillance drones and occasional fighter jets still flew into Cambodian air space, and that small arms fire at the border was common. When we tried to get a closer look at onenotoriouscasino-compound on Cambodian soil,warning shotsrang out from Thai military positions. Less than 12 hours later, Thai soldiers again opened fire during a visit to the border checkpoint by an international delegation of diplomats and military attachés, sparkingconcernsby the British Embassy in Phnom Penh. (A Thai Ministry of Information spokesperson said that all allegations of encroachment into Cambodian territory were “unfounded.”) Thailand’s strategy of centering scam compounds in the conflict may have backfired militarily. Despiteconcernsraised by the rights groupAmnesty Internationaland international media over the sincerity of Cambodia’s scam crackdown and the humanitarian fallout, the country’s political and military leaders are already reaping the rewards from countries whose economies have been hit hardest by the online scam and illegal gambling industry. In January, aU.S. vesseldocked at Ream Naval Base for the first time, following years ofconcernsby Washington that the base, which was recently refurbished with Chinese support, would become a Chinese military asset. In March, senior officers from the Royal Cambodian Army and the U.S. Army Pacific heldplanning discussionsfor the revival of theAngkor Sentinel exercises, which had been suspended since 2017. In April, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited both Thailand and Cambodia, he called for Bangkok torespectthe ceasefire and offered to help broker a peaceful resolution to the conflict, butdescribedChina’s relationship with Cambodia as an “unbreakable bond” and pledged to collaborate ondefense and national security– while urging Phnom Penh to keep working to eradicate scams In June,39 Chinese Type-59Dtanks arrived in Phnom Penh. This year’sGolden Dragonexercises were the largest joint military drills ever conducted between the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces and the People’s Liberation Army, incorporating land, sea, and air operations. China also made good on a2024 commitment to deliver twoType-056C corvetteswarships in April and June. India hasofferedCambodia surveillance drones, demining kits, and military technology to help modernize its armed forces, and in July, Japan officiallysignedan agreement with Cambodia to provide defense equipment under its Official Security Assistance framework. Cambodia is also courting Russia as a potential partner. In April,two Russian naval vesselsmade a three-day visit to Sihanoukville port. Defense Minister Tea Seiha subsequently called forexpanded military cooperationwith Moscow, including increased training and joint exercises, and Hun Manet had a one-on-onemeetingwith Russian President Vladimir Putin in June. Since then, the Russian ambassador to Cambodia has hailed anew eraof Cambodia and Russia relations and said Russia is ready tostrengthenCambodia’s defense sector. Meanwhile, Cambodia’s domesticdefense spendingcontinues to expand. The country’s national budget for 2026 hit a new record of more than$10 billion, including increased allocations for defense and security, with projected growth in military expenditure in coming years. In May, a newconscription lawcame into effect that requires all Cambodian men aged 18 to 25 to serve two years in the military. Seun Sam, a policy analyst at the Royal Academy of Cambodia, says he is “very concerned” that a third round of fighting is on the horizon, especially if the Thai government seeks to appeal to hardline nationalists at home, or the Thai military begins creating “facts on the ground,” building new infrastructure in occupied territory. He believes Cambodia has now sourced sufficient military equipment from around the world to defend itself, but conflict would bring destruction, economic losses, and human suffering to both nations, while providing no meaningful long-term solution. “Even if Cambodia were unable to achieve a complete military victory, it would still have the capability to inflict significant damage on parts of Thailand if all available military resources were employed,” Seun Sam said. “The fundamental question, however, is: what would be the benefit of creating a war?” A Thai soldier mans a barrier made of shipping containers along the border between Thailand and Cambodia in Thmor Da commune, Pursat province, Aug. 6, 2026. Photo by Nathan Paul Southern. It seems only a matter of time. Eight months after the ceasefire, Thai soldiers continue to occupy the ruins of former scam zones andother territories along the border in Pursat, Oddar Meanchey, Banteay Meanchey, and Preah Vihear provinces, and tensions threaten to boil over. On August 6, on the way into Thmor Da – a casino and scam enclave perched atop a mountain, surrounded by forest – UXO warning signs peppered a blown-up bridge that was once the main route in and out. Road signs and roadblocks set up by the Thai military were spray-painted with the word “thieves” in English and Khmer. The town itself was cut in half by a wall of shipping containers, forming makeshift barracks for the Thai soldiers stationed there, beyond which loomed the skeleton of a former casino where the Thai army reportedseizinga cache of weapons in December (Cambodiadeniesthis). Meters from the barricade, Cambodian soldiers, now the town’s only residents, hung around old compounds. These were packed when we last came here in November, and a Rwandan trafficking survivor said he was still trapped inside one when it was rocked by Thai artillery fire at the height of the war. Neither side has shown much interest in seeking justice for victims or dismantling the multi-billion-dollar scam industry. Analysis of Telegram channels used by scam bosses suggests many simply relocated, while the raids and bombings left tens of thousands of exploited foreign nationals re-trafficked, stranded, and destitute, or placed in immigration detention. Of the dozens of survivors we interviewed, not one had been screened for trafficking nor asked to give witness statements to police, despite many having crucial evidence they were willing to share with a criminal investigation. In December, when we arrived at the Cambodian border town of O’Smach in the immediateaftermathof an aerial bombing, several active scam compound complexes, designed to hold tens of thousands of trafficking victims, were engulfed in flames, with a handful of taxis shuttling back and forth to collect some of those who had escaped. One child trafficking survivor sold to a scam group here later described how, as Thai attacks closed in, captors made them choose between relocation to another scamming site or staying behind to risk joining the mounting death toll. A spokesperson for the Thai Ministry of Information did not respond to specific questions about civilian casualties at occupied scam compounds, but claimed all operations were “directed strictly at military targets.” The spokesperson claimed that Cambodian armed forces turned scam workers into human shields by using compounds as military bases and arms depots, launching attacks on Thailand from inside these sites, and that Thailand only discovered that industrial-scale online scams were operating after threats were neutralized and inspections conducted. However, on multiple visits to O’Smach and Thmor Da since July 2025 we documented Thai surveillance drones closely monitoring areas with buildings densely populated by people who were clearly unable to leave. We could find no evidence that occupied compounds targeted by Thailand were being used by the Cambodian military, and no survivors interviewed said they witnessed this. “I never saw any [Cambodian] soldier,” said Paul. “Nobody was firing back. Just the attack from Thailand.” Meanwhile, the ruling Hun family are doing little to dispel the sense that the rumbling conflict emboldens its increasingly iron-fisted rule. In July, a Thai analystpublishedan article warning that engaging in a forever war with Cambodia could help entrench the autocratic regime of Hun Sen, who handed the prime minister role to his son in 2023, but remains head of the Senate and is widely seen as the country’s true political driver. In April, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited both Thailand and Cambodia, he called for Bangkok torespectthe ceasefire and offered to help broker a peaceful resolution to the conflict, butdescribedChina’s relationship with Cambodia as an “unbreakable bond” and pledged to collaborate ondefense and national security– while urging Phnom Penh to keep working to eradicate scams In June,39 Chinese Type-59Dtanks arrived in Phnom Penh. This year’sGolden Dragonexercises were the largest joint military drills ever conducted between the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces and the People’s Liberation Army, incorporating land, sea, and air operations. China also made good on a2024 commitment to deliver twoType-056C corvetteswarships in April and June. India hasofferedCambodia surveillance drones, demining kits, and military technology to help modernize its armed forces, and in July, Japan officiallysignedan agreement with Cambodia to provide defense equipment under its Official Security Assistance framework. Cambodia is also courting Russia as a potential partner. In April,two Russian naval vesselsmade a three-day visit to Sihanoukville port. Defense Minister Tea Seiha subsequently called forexpanded military cooperationwith Moscow, including increased training and joint exercises, and Hun Manet had a one-on-onemeetingwith Russian President Vladimir Putin in June. Since then, the Russian ambassador to Cambodia has hailed anew eraof Cambodia and Russia relations and said Russia is ready tostrengthenCambodia’s defense sector. Meanwhile, Cambodia’s domesticdefense spendingcontinues to expand. The country’s national budget for 2026 hit a new record of more than$10 billion, including increased allocations for defense and security, with projected growth in military expenditure in coming years. In May, a newconscription lawcame into effect that requires all Cambodian men aged 18 to 25 to serve two years in the military. Seun Sam, a policy analyst at the Royal Academy of Cambodia, says he is “very concerned” that a third round of fighting is on the horizon, especially if the Thai government seeks to appeal to hardline nationalists at home, or the Thai military begins creating “facts on the ground,” building new infrastructure in occupied territory. He believes Cambodia has now sourced sufficient military equipment from around the world to defend itself, but conflict would bring destruction, economic losses, and human suffering to both nations, while providing no meaningful long-term solution. “Even if Cambodia were unable to achieve a complete military victory, it would still have the capability to inflict significant damage on parts of Thailand if all available military resources were employed,” Seun Sam said. “The fundamental question, however, is: what would be the benefit of creating a war?” A Thai soldier mans a barrier made of shipping containers along the border between Thailand and Cambodia in Thmor Da commune, Pursat province, Aug. 6, 2026. Photo by Nathan Paul Southern. It seems only a matter of time. Eight months after the ceasefire, Thai soldiers continue to occupy the ruins of former scam zones andother territories along the border in Pursat, Oddar Meanchey, Banteay Meanchey, and Preah Vihear provinces, and tensions threaten to boil over. On August 6, on the way into Thmor Da – a casino and scam enclave perched atop a mountain, surrounded by forest – UXO warning signs peppered a blown-up bridge that was once the main route in and out. Road signs and roadblocks set up by the Thai military were spray-painted with the word “thieves” in English and Khmer. The town itself was cut in half by a wall of shipping containers, forming makeshift barracks for the Thai soldiers stationed there, beyond which loomed the skeleton of a former casino where the Thai army reportedseizinga cache of weapons in December (Cambodiadeniesthis). Meters from the barricade, Cambodian soldiers, now the town’s only residents, hung around old compounds. Just the attack from Thailand.” Meanwhile, the ruling Hun family are doing little to dispel the sense that the rumbling conflict emboldens its increasingly iron-fisted rule. Her work primarily explores trafficking, human rights violations, and environmental crime. Nathan Paul Southern is an investigative reporter and non-traditional security specialist with a focus on transnational organized crime, security, trafficking and the intersection between criminality and governance.

title: Daughter of Former Cambodian Opposition Leader Appointed ‘Special Envoy’ to PM
content: Kem Monovithya’s appointment comes three months after her father Kem Sokha received a royal pardon quashing a 27-year sentence for treason. Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet meets with Kem Monovithya, the daughter of former opposition leader Kem Sokha, in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Aug. 14, 2026. The ⁠daughter of a prominent Cambodian opposition figure has been ​appointed as special envoy to Prime ‌Minister Hun Manet, after a string of high-level meetings late last week. The appointment of Kem Monovithya, which was formalized by aroyal decreeyesterday, was granted at the request of Hun Manet and conferred on her a ‌rank equivalent to minister. The appointment was made after Monovithya held several meetings late last week, including one with Hun Manet and what CambojaNewsdescribedas a three-hour meeting with Manet’s father and predecessor Hun Sen, which also included her father Kem Sokha. On Friday, Hun Manetposted on Facebooka photo of himself standing with Monovithya, describing her as his “sister.” He wrote, “As a new generation of politicians alike, there are some things we ⁠can collaborate on for the betterment of our country, especially ​on the international stage.” The decree comes not long after Kem Sokha, the former leader of the now-banned Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP), received a royal pardon that quashed a 27-year prison sentence for treason. Sokha had been in custody since his midnight arrest in 2017, after which hewas chargedwith “conspiracy with a foreign power” under Article 443 of Cambodia’s criminal code. At the time of his arrest, Sokha was the acting president of the CNRP, which had performed well at national elections in 2013 and local polls earlier in 2017, eating into the majority of Hun Sen’s Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) and raising hopes of a genuine political opening. Hun Manet’s remark about the “international stage,” and the fact that Monovithya is being appointed as a “special envoy,” would suggest that her role will be geared toward the international arena. This would make sense. The Cambodian government has recently come under close foreign scrutiny for the giant online scamming centers that have metastasized over the past five years, some of which have been linked to prominent CPP-aligned tycoons and political figures. While the government is currently in the midst of what it describes as afar-reaching crackdownon scam centers, this has done little to reverse the serious impacts that this has had on the tourism sector and the investment climate more generally. Then there is the ongoing border dispute with Thailand, which erupted into fighting on two occasions last year and remains far from any kind of resolution. A ceasefire in late December has kept the peace, but the situation at the border remains tense due to the Thai military’s occupation of territories at various points along the land border. While the Cambodian government periodically issues statements protesting the Thai occupation of Cambodian territory, the issue has failed to gain much regional or global traction. In this context, it is plausible that Monovithya, who was publicly supportive of the government’s stance during last year’s clashes, will help rally international support for Phnom Penh’s position on the border. As with Sokha’s pardon, however, one should not overinterpret what this means for the domestic political context. While ReutersdescribedMonovithya’s appointment as “a rare concession to the political opposition,” there is little in the recent past to suggest that this presages a genuine political opening. Indeed, the use of royal pardons to quash politically motivated court rulings was a regular feature of Hun Sen’s more than 38 years in power, as a means of managing domestic political opposition and external opinion. This has continued under since his son took over the leadership in 2023. “Without concrete legal action and reopening of democratic space,” the Cambodian analyst Seng Vanlytold CambojaNews, “these encounters remain high-profile political gestures rather than the groundwork for a broad political settlement.” The CPP maintains an “open door” policy to most of its current and former opponents. However, the criteria for entry are that these opponents accept the reigning political dispensation, and divest themselves of independent political ambitions. The logical conclusion is that this apparent reconciliation marks not the beginning of a political thaw but an end to the Kem family as a source of meaningful political opposition in Cambodia. Sokha, 73, said just before receiving his pardon that henow wished“to leave politics behind and spend the rest of his life with his family.” In some ways this is no surprise. Many are the opponents of the CPP who have decided that they would rather try to achieve their goals from within the system than be frozen out permanently, as is the case with Sokha’s former CNRP ally (one longtime rival) Sam Rainsy, who has spent the last decade in exile. Politics remains an unpredictable business in Cambodia, as elsewhere, but one iron law pertains: namely, that any political liberalization will be enacted solely on the CPP’s terms, and in support of the party’s own political goals. title: Is Vietnam’s Energy Transition Entering a New Phase?
content: The country has so far outpaced most of its regional peers when it comes to the production of renewable energy. The Bac Lieu Offshore Wind Farm in Bac Lieu, southern Vietnam. In Southeast Asia, Vietnam has been the undisputed leader when it comes to building renewable energy. In 2017, the government enacted a regulation that offered solar power developers a generous rate if they could build power plants that were operational by 2019. This was followed by a similar incentive for wind. The government did not place a cap on eligible capacity, so there was a huge influx of investment activity as developers and investors raced to get their projectsbuilt before the deadline. As a result, electricity generated from renewables like solar and wind has soared. In 2018, solar and wind accounted for around .4 percent of all electricity produced in Vietnam. Following the 2019 deadline, solar and wind rose sharply as a share of generation. According to thelatest annual reportfrom state-owned electric utility EVN, solar and wind accounted for around 13 percent of electricity generated in 2024. Vietnam has outpaced pretty much all of its regional peers when it comes to the production of clean energy and done it in a very short period of time. But this achievement came at a considerable cost, one that has been borne mainly by EVN. As investors rushed into the market, it created billions of dollars in new liabilities and operating costs because the utility was now obligated to buy electricity from these power plants at a fairly high rate. In a well-regulated energy market, a utility might be expected to raise prices on consumers in order to recover such increased costs. But in Vietnam, as in many emerging markets, electricity prices paid by consumers are tightly controlled by the state. And with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the government was extremely reluctant to pass any cost increases onto Vietnamese consumers. This placedintense financial strainon EVN, with the utility recording a $790 million loss in 2022 and a $1 billion loss in 2023 (calculated using consolidated financial statements at current exchange rates). With cash reserves dwindling and mounting payments to new renewable suppliers, the government finally passed aseries of price hikesonto consumers. By 2025, EVN found itself on much sounder financial footing. Thanks to the price increases revenue rose 11 percent from 2024 to 2025, and the utility posted a net profit of nearly $2 billion. Cash from operations is way up, and the financial peril has faded. But investment in new renewable projects has also slowed way down. EVN has been able to preserve its financial stability not only by increasing revenue, but also because new renewable projects have slowed. Last year, the utility even tried toback-track on some existing projectsclaiming there were questions about regulatory compliance. EVN’s annual report shows that after rising sharply in response to the incentive scheme, the share of wind and solar generation has remained steady at around 13 to 14 percent from 2022 to 2024. This means a lot less new renewable energy has been built in recent years, pivoting away from the previous model whereby EVN acted as the main buyer of renewable power from private developers in order to induce more investment. Does that mean Vietnam’s clean energy ambitions have reached an impasse? Not necessarily. But the road forward may start looking less like the traditional model of centralized state control under EVN, and more like a decentralized system with the gradual introduction of market-oriented mechanisms. A key step in this process is the expanded use of Direct Power Purchase Agreements for clean energy. This allows eligible customers with high energy needs to enter into direct purchase agreements with suppliers of renewable energy, rather than having to go through EVN. A LEGO factory operating out of the Vietnam-Singapore Industrial Park is one of the firstlarge-scale deals of this nature. Samsung also recently agreed to buy electricity from the privately operatedDuc Hue 2 Solar Power Plantthrough the EVN-operated grid. Data centers are also now eligible for direct purchase agreements, an important development given the energy-intensive nature of such operations. The government likewise plans to have a retail electricity market up and runningby next year, which will complement the wholesale electricity market launched in 2019. The long-term impact of these reforms remains to be seen, but the overall policy direction seems clear. Vietnam’s energy sector has traditionally been dominated by state-owned entities like EVN. It has been a centralized model designed to keep the production of energy firmly under the purview of the state, and to insulate Vietnamese consumers from price volatility. But this model has its limits, especially as investment needs increase in response to rapid economic growth. Now the government is pushing reforms that will, it is hoped, introduce more efficient mechanisms that provide a greater degree of flexibility when it comes to producing and consuming electricity. It will also lessen the financial burden on EVN as it pushes the energy sector away from its traditional state-controlled roots, and toward a more decentralized orientation. Will it work, and to what extent can the state truly relinquish control over a vital economic input like energy, especially when it comes to the price paid by Vietnamese consumers? We don’t know. But at the very least, these developments suggest the sector is on the cusp of a new phase and it will be interesting to see where it leads. title: How Southeast Asia and the Gulf Can Shape the Future of AI
content: Neither region can compete directly with China and the United States, but together they have the potential to show how middle powers can shape the AI economy. Full-stack artificial intelligence (AI) capacity is now overwhelmingly concentrated inthe United States and China. Together, the two countries produced80 notable AI models last year. The United States alone operates5,427 data centers, more than 10 times as many as any other country. Of the 33 countries that host any public-cloud AI capacity,only the U.S. and Chinarun it on their own chips, with their own providers. With no global consensus on AI likely to emerge soon, technological development will be governed through an increasingly fragmented landscape of national and regional AI rules. The U.S. takes alaissez-faireapproach, while the European Union focuses onregulationand China onstate direction. The rest of the world largely participates as a “rule-taker.” However, the Gulf and Southeast Asia, neither of which builds the chips or trains the frontier models their AI ambitions require, are attempting to convert that role into leverage. AI cooperation between countries in the two regions is deepening, mutually beneficial, and reaching multibillion-dollar scale. Southeast Asia and the Gulf are building a new kind of AI partnership, one that turns their different strengths into a shared advantage rather than chasing self-sufficiency at the frontier. The two regions share similar dependencies but boast complementary strengths, including the resources to manage them. The Gulf has abundant capital, inexpensive energy, and the capacity to build infrastructure at speed and scale. Saudi Arabia alone is investing $100 billion in AI start-ups and data centers through itsProject Transcendence. Southeast Asia has strong demand. Its digital economy is projected to exceed$300 billion in gross merchandise valueby 2025. Moreover, its data-center market is forecast to more than double by 2030,from $13.7 billion to $30.5 billion. Within the Gulf, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has committed$148 billionto AI infrastructure over the past two years.Stargate UAE, a 1-gigawatt computing cluster that G42, Abu Dhabi’s state-backed AI group, is building with OpenAI, Oracle, NVIDIA, SoftBank, and Cisco, is expected to cost around$30 billion. G42’sJais 2 model, trained on 600 billion Arabic tokens, is developing a homegrown Arabic-language AI ecosystem. The UAE’s advantage is the scale of wealth and the speed of its build-out. Beyond its capital and infrastructure, the UAE also boasts substantial ties with Southeast Asia, particularly with Singapore, Malaysia, and Vietnam. In February of this year,G42 signed a framework agreement with a Vietnamese consortiumworth up to $1 billion to build national AI and cloud infrastructure spanning government systems, industrial applications and academia, in addition to workforce upskilling programs. Vietnam is well positioned to absorb such investment. Itsstandalone AI Lawis already in force, and its national strategy aims to establish the country as a regional AI hub. Vietnam also hostsmore than a quarterof Southeast Asia’s generative-AI start-ups. Malaysia, which attracted$23 billion in data-center investmentin 2024, has formal agreements with the UAE on AI and the digital economy. Masdar, Abu Dhabi’s state-owned clean energy company, signed a$15 billion agreementin January 2025 to develop renewables in the Philippines.Project mBridge, a cross-border digital-currency initiative, links the UAE, Thailand, and Saudi Arabia. TheJoint Declaration on Economic Cooperation between ASEAN and the GCCexplicitly endorsed cooperation in AI and the digital economy, giving the trend political backing. Gulf investors are establishing long-term positions in high-growth digital markets, while Southeast Asia is gaining infrastructure, energy investment, and human capital. The relationship’s strength is its deal-by-deal structure, which matches a specific capability to a specific need and lets cooperation move without requiring region-wide consensus. The recent Iran-U.S.-Israel conflict illustrates how quickly geopolitical events can reshape technology investment and supply chains. While the Gulf has demonstrated considerable resilience, the conflict has reinforced the importance of diversifying its economic partnerships and reducing its excessive dependence on any single market or geopolitical relationship. Against this backdrop, Southeast Asia’s rapidly growing digital economy and the Gulf’s expanding role as a global investor in AI infrastructure are becoming increasingly complementary. A deeper Southeast Asia-Gulf AI partnership is therefore both an economic opportunity and a prudent strategy for enhancing resilience in an era of growing geopolitical uncertainty. Recent research from the AI Asia Pacific Institute identifies the same pattern across theUAE-Singapore memoranda on digital government, UAE-Malaysia cooperation under theMADANI AI initiative, and the UAE-Vietnam framework. A promising next step would be sectoral pilots, each region testing AI in the domain best suited to its own endowments, and learning from the other’s results. Southeast Asia, with its large underbanked populations and fast-growing fintech, is a natural testbed for financial inclusion and small-business credit. The Gulf, with its growing state capacity and legal digitization, is well placed to pilot AI in courts and public administration. These pilots could generate practical lessons for both sides and operate through the bilateral agreements already in place. The same approach could extend well beyond finance and the courts to health, logistics, energy, and language models built for Arabic and Southeast Asian languages. Full-stack and frontier AI capabilities remain beyond the reach of any single middle power, and both the Gulf and Southeast Asia are likely to remain dependent on foreign technology imports for the foreseeable future. But they have an opportunity to show, through cooperation, that middle powers can shape the AI economy with investment, trusted partnerships, and responsible deployment. The U.S. and China may define what AI can do, but Southeast Asia and the Gulf can help identify where AI delivers the greatest economic and social value. While the Gulf has demonstrated considerable resilience, the conflict has reinforced the importance of diversifying its economic partnerships and reducing its excessive dependence on any single market or geopolitical relationship. title: Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing Set For Possible State Visit to Cambodia
content: The trip would be the former general’s sixth, and third to an ASEAN member state, since his appointment as president in April. Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing addresses a joint session of parliament in Naypyidaw, Myanmar, July 31, 2026. Myanmar’s military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing is set to continue his diplomatic charm offensive, with reports of a possible trip to Cambodia surfacing as he departed on a state visit to Russia. The possible Cambodia visit was referenced yesterday in aposton the Facebook page of the country’s Senate, later surfaced by alocal journalist, which showed officials including Senate Secretary General Lay Samkol inspecting the Senate building in preparation for a visit by Min Aung Hlaing “in the future.” The trip has not yet been officially confirmed, and the post did not mention any dates. If it eventuates, the visit to Cambodia would be Min Aung Hlaing’s third to an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member state since taking office as president in April, after visitsto Laos in early JulyandThailand earlier this month. In that time, Min Aung Hlaing has led a push for a normalization of Myanmar’s relationship with ASEAN, which has excluded it from its summits over its failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict. The new government has taken anincreasingly defiant line, dismissing the Consensus as an unwarranted “interference” in its internal affairs and demanding its full readmission to the 11-nation bloc. At the same time, it has sought to engage directly with willing ASEAN member states. Thailand in particular has been a close partner, brokering ameetingbetween Myanmar Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and hits ASEAN counterparts in Bangkok on July 12. During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Bangkok, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul “reaffirmed” Thailand’s commitment “to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.” Since taking office, Min Aung Hlaing has also sought stronger ties with other important external partners, undertaking state visits toIndiaandChinain June. The report of a possible Cambodia visit also came on the same day that Min Aung Hlaingdepartedon a state visit to Russia. During the visit, the former general will hold talks with President Vladimir Putin, Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, and State Duma Chairman Vyacheslav Volodin, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement. He will also attend a Myanmar-Russia Economic Forum, where he will try to drum up investment. According to areportin Myanmar state media, Min Aung Hlaing and Putin “will cordially discuss matters related to the further consolidation of existing friendly relations and strategic cooperation across all areas of mutual interest, including economic, security and social spheres.” The Irrawaddyreported yesterdaythat Min Aung Hlaing would travel to Russia with a large entourage, which “includes cabinet ministers as well as business leaders who are close to his family and military regime.” While the trip is Min Aung Hlaing’s first as president, he visited Russia on five other occasions after leading the military coup of February 2021, reflecting the growing importance of Russia in Myanmar’s foreign relations. During the post-coup period, under the pressure of their mutual isolation from the West, relations between Naypyidaw and Moscow broadened out from their previous focus on defense cooperation and arms sales to encompass trade and investment, nuclear energy, and even space cooperation.
