title: I Know a Way to Help My Relative Who Is Having Money Troubles. But It Could Backfire.
content: Pay DirtI Know a Way to Help My Relative Who Is Having Money Troubles. But It Could Backfire.Advice byKristin WongAug 19, 20266:00 AMPhoto illustration by Slate. Photo by Andrii Iemelyanenko/iStock/Getty Images Plus.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Pay Dirt is Slate’s money advice column.Have a question?Send it to Kristin and Ilyce here. (It’s anonymous!)Dear Pay Dirt,My aunt died seven years ago. I am the executor for her trust. Her will was pretty straight forward: She wanted most of her assets to be split evenly among five relatives (including me), and we are definitely fortunate. One of the accounts I continue to manage is an inherited Roth IRA. So far, I have left it alone and just split the annual required minimum distribution (RMD) equally each year among the five relatives. It’s been a great safety net. But now one of my co-beneficiaries is experiencing significant financial hardship, and her share of the inheritance could help her navigate her way to a better situation.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementI am trying to figure out how to release her share of the funds to her in the most equitable way to all of us. The simplest way I can think of is to release one-fifth of the assets to her, and the remaining four of us will continue to split the RMD moving forward. Does this make sense for all of us? What are the consequences?Part two of this question is: How do I help my relative spend this money wisely? Could I put the funds into an account I control and dole it out over time? She has gone through some tough times in recent years, but she has never been good with money, and I worry that she will blow through this inheritance and have nothing left.I’d greatly appreciate any recommendations, and tips about how to avoid bad outcomes.—What Would Auntie Do?Dear What Would Auntie Do,With so much at stake, you definitely want to consult with a financial planner or an estate attorney—someone who knows the ins and outs of inherited Roth IRA rules and the tax implications that go along with them.Popular inAdviceThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyI Read My Son’s Texts From His Ex-Girlfriend. Uh-Oh.My Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life HellIf you release a chunk of those assets now, I’d worry it might break or trigger certain distribution rules that you can’t undo, and this could have unintentional consequences for how the trust is handled. Or it might affect how the rest of the beneficiaries receive their payouts down the road. Plus, I would imagine you also have to check to see whether the trust even allows you to make an unequal early distribution. The rules have alsochanged over the years.But again, you’ll want to consult a specialist about all of this—someone who is professionally qualified to help you navigate it.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAs for the second part of your question, about how to help your relative with money: I understand you want to be there for a family member, but controlling her finances doesn’t give her the chance to learn from experience—plus, it creates extra work for you. Also, if the money legally belongs to her, putting it into an account you own might even trigger a whole other mess of tax and record-keeping questions.If anything, you could offer to sit down with her, take a look at her finances and give her some input on how to handle her money down the road. Or better yet, talk to a professional who can look at her numbers and help her come up with a customized financial plan. You can offer gentle guidance without becoming her financial planner.—KristinGet advice—submit a question!Please keep questions short (<150 words), and don‘t submit the same question to multiple columns. Photos by Getty Images Plus.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Sign up for the Slatestto get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.Dear Prudence is Slate’s advice column.Submit questions here.Dear Prudence,Earlier this summer, I got married to a wonderful man. The process of wedding planning was stressful, to say the least, but I am so glad to have celebrated with so many loved ones.I have a friend from college with whom I have remained close since we both moved to New York City. We’ve stayed connected through birthday parties, craft nights, walks, and were even roommates for a time. I have considered her a close friend for many years.Last summer, I suddenly stopped getting replies from this friend. To my knowledge, there was no event that caused her to stop replying. Months went by, and not only did she not reply to a simple check-in text, but she also ignored our mailed save-the-dates for the wedding and eventually the actual wedding invitation. I even invited her to my bachelorette party (just dinner and drinks out in the city), but still no reply. I felt really hurt by being ignored, as the wedding was already bringing up a lot of anxiety around friendships and connections from throughout my life. When I tried to call her, I was sent to voicemail, so I stopped. She ultimately did not even RSVP to the wedding.Two weeks after the wedding, she texted me that she was sorry and that she had been overwhelmed by her job and graduate school, but would like to reconnect if I was open to it. This is after 12 months of being ghosted. I miss her friendship, but feel extremely hurt and confused. What do I do?—Ghosted By a FriendDear Ghosted By a Friend,I feel pretty sure that “overwhelmed” is standing in for something more serious in your friend’s account of her graduate school experience. Like “deeply depressed,” “completely isolated,” or “miserable and totally shut down.” If the scenario I’m imagining is accurate, I really feel for her.Still, I hesitate to tell you to jump into fully reconnecting. This is because 1) she hasn’t given an explanation that really justifies the intensity of her ghosting, which makes me concerned that she’s not far enough removed from whatever she’s going through to be in a position to rebuild trust with you, or even to stay in your life long term, and (related) 2) you’re in —or just coming out of—an era of feeling a little uncertain and hurt about your relationships. So it doesn’t seem like a good time for you to set yourself up to participate in her experiment of trying to engage in the basic requirements of friendship again. You struggled a little around your wedding, and now that it’s over, it’s time for you to enjoy being married and deepen your relationships with the people who have demonstrated that they can show up for you, not to make yourself vulnerable to someone with a history of being unsteady.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementPopular inAdviceThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyI Read My Son’s Texts From His Ex-Girlfriend. Uh-Oh.My Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life HellThat said, don’t ignore your friend or cut her off completely (again, I think she was probably having a really hard time and what she did wasn’t personal), and definitely leave the door open for a new version of your friendship, if you really do miss it. Instead of making plans to hang out and expecting your relationship to be the way it was before she cut off communication, try saying something like this:“Hey, it’s really great to hear from you, and I’m sorry last year was so tough. I’m happy you’re on the other side of it. I missed you so much, and I have to say I’m still really hurt and confused by being completely ghosted, especially around my wedding. I wish you could have at least sent a quick text to let me know what was going on with you. And I’m honestly a little nervous that if we did reconnect, you would disappear again. I know I don’t have the full picture of what you were dealing with or how things have changed on your end, but if you’re comfortable talking about it and could help me understand a little bit more about what’s been going on, that would help me a lot and would be a good place tostart.”AdvertisementAdvertisementClassic PrudieMy best friend recently got engaged to a woman I think is awful. In the year and a few weeks they’ve been together, I’ve never seen her treat him compassionately or tenderly. I frequently marvel at the cruel things she says about him in public, even though he laughs these incidents off and swears she behaves differently when they’re alone together. Our other friends have similar concerns. Despite him being in his early 30s, this is his first relationship,and he seems to be rushing things with someone who’s terrible for him out of fear that he’ll never have another chance at love or having a family…Never miss new Slate Advice columnsGet the latest from Prudie and our columnists in your inbox each weekday, plus special bonus letters on Saturdays.Thanks for signing up! title: What Will We Learn From Our Summer of Complicated Mothers?
content: LifeOur Summer of Complicated MothersFrom Lindsay Clancy to Hayden Panettiere, we are seeing the horrific ways that motherhood can go awry.ByShannon PalusFollow ShannonSigned Up For Email AlertsError Signing Up For Email AlertsCloseEnter your email to receive alerts for this author.Thanks for signing up! Photos by Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images and Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Sign up for the Slatestto get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.We have a vision of how motherhood is supposed to be: difficult, but rewarding. Full of sacrifice, but worth it. There are hardships, surely, but they are offset by the moments of pure joy. Something evolutionary and primal kicks in that makes it all possible, the story goes. You become a mom, leaving behind your old self for someone better, stronger, and more loving.Moms rise to the challenge. This is what society tells us, of our mothers, of ourselves when we become mothers. Except, this summer, we are all in a front-row seat witnessing what happens when the much-lauded natural instinct isn’t enough—and when something else kicks in instead.“I grieve that I’m not the mother I thought I’d be and definitely not the mother I want to be,” Hayden Panettiere wrote in the prologue ofThis Is Me,hermemoirpublished in May. Later in the book, she describes going through labor, a cesarean section, and then three hours of surgery to repair her uterus after the birth. Of finally getting to see her daughter, she writes: “I’d always heard that mothers feel an instant rush of love the moment they lay their eyes on their baby, but I felt nothing.”Panettiere died on Sunday, in her home. (The cause of death is still being determined, but foul play isnot suspected.) Though she struggled with substance abuse for a long time—as a teen actress, she wasprovided with “happy pills” by her management team—alcohol addiction in particular reared its head in her months postpartum. She found early motherhood to be a “total blackout of emotion, like my soul was dead.” While she didn’t find euphoria in caring for a newborn, she did find it in wine, vodka, and the 3-ounce bottles of Fireball that you can buy at a gas station. Her daughter is now a preteen, and from when the child was 3 until Panettiere’s death on Sunday at 36, she mostly parented over FaceTime, as she had ceded custody to the father, who lives in Europe.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementHer admission that being a mother simply did not work out how she planned is incredibly sad, and even sadder now. It’s also remarkable. Panettiere offered something we almost never see: a mom who was not a classic “good mom” or even a “bad mom.” It’s clear in the way she writes about her daughter, how she talked about her in interviews this spring, that she loved her. She was just a human being who fell short.Related From SlateMeghan CliffelLindsay Clancy Is on Trial for Killing Her Three Children. That Could Have Been Me.Read MoreThat motherhood can fail to be transformative—or worse, can be transformative in the wrong direction—is not totally undiscussed. Rachel Yoder’sNightbitch,a novel published in the summer of 2021, in which the mother of a young child becomes a feral dog, comes to mind. But it’s also a conversation that tends to be capped with a happy ending, a string of fridge-magnet platitudes.Nightbitchis a story, not real life, and even so, the film version ended up, as one reviewer put it, “defanged.” Amy Adams, who plays the protagonist, delivers those fridge-magnet lines well. (“Do you ever feel like the big secret is that we are gods?” she says. “We are so powerful.”) In the end, all of her ferality can be packaged up into a pleasant take-home message.AdvertisementAdvertisementBut with the Lindsay Clancy trial underway, it’s been hard to escape the fact that a mother’s suffering and sacrifice do not always end with a tidy, happy lesson. In 2023, Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands before jumping out of a second-story window. Now a wheelchair user, Clancy claims that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a rare but extremely serious condition; her state at the time of the killings is being hashed out in court. She has not denied killing her children, but has asked tonot be held criminally responsibledue to what she suggests is her postpartum-induced insanity. It seems clear that this is a loving person whose plan for motherhood ended up in the worst reality imaginable.AdvertisementPopular inLifeWhy Did Trump Lose It Over Natalie Harp—and Who Is She, Anyway? Unfortunately, I’ve Learned Too Much.What has been particularly remarkable to witness about this trial is that it seems like many women are on her side. There has been an outpouring of support for Clancy. These mothers point to evidence that she was a good mom, a mom who searched for a special unicorn activity for her daughter and lamented the pain of sleep-training her son, until she snapped. Women who have had postpartum psychosis themselvesidentify with her, in a “There but for the grace of God go I” way. The simple fact that she was not offered the help she needed postpartum is broadly relatable. I keep thinking about how CNN’s Pamela Brown chimed inas she intervieweda postpartum psychosis survivor about the Clancy case: “I felt like chopped liver after I had my baby. I had my own struggles.” This is a CNN anchor admitting this on live television. We are, I hope, entering into a different paradigm.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementThere is something deeply good about watching women rally behind a complicated, monstrous figure. There is something deeply healing about women sharing their own complicated stories about being postpartum, and broadcasting them to the broader public. The thing I keep getting stuck on, though, is that as novel as this all feels, even this is not enough. In fact, it is maybe not a solution at all. Sharing didn’t save Clancy, who shared that she was having a hard time in Facebook groups. It didn’t save Panettiere, who publicized her experience even before writing about it in her memoir because when she was a star onNashville, the writerswrote it into the show.Sharing is a start, not an end point. And for both Hayden and Lindsay, I grieve that they didn’t have what they needed for their stories to end another way. At the very least, I hope that they will now be a starting point in a broader understanding of what becoming a mother canmean.Get the best of news and politicsSign up for Slate's evening newsletter.Thanks for signing up! title: GLP-1s Have Brought Back One Toxic Habit. Why Can’t We Quit It?
content: Illustration by Slate. Photos by Getty Images Plus.LifeThe Age of Thinvestigation Is Upon UsOzempic, changing beauty standards, and endless reams of digital footprints have us all going down rabbit holes to assess people’s bodies. What is it doing to us?ByPaola de VaronaAug 19, 20265:40 AMCopy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.I recently attended the concert of a pop artist I adore (notthe one in the news). As my friends and I left the venue, we raved about her elaborate performance, her costumes and sets, and her vulnerability on stage. Then, after a beat, one of us cut the silence with an obligatory grimace: “But did you notice she’s gotten so skinny now?”I’d noticed her thinness like I might vaguely recognize white noise playing in the background. Because I’d never considered her to be anything but thin, it took me aback to consider my friend’s question. Our conversation was largely a dead end; we chalked it up to the physical exertion required from touring artists and took our respective trains home. But when I was finally alone that night, within the confines of my own phone screen, I began my research.I started with her most recent Instagram posts. I zoomed in on photos of her in strappy tank tops and bralettes. I considered her defined abs, bare legs, and the outline of her ribs in a bikini. I noted her clavicle, which seemed particularly sharp. And then I scrolled back, and back, and back. I ended upfive yearsback. And then I saw it: Her face was fuller. Was her current look the result of the sad reality that our faces hollow outas we age? No, her legs once seemed more muscular too. I tapped on photos of her in gowns on red carpets, in swimsuits on a yacht, and in bodysuits on sets, the pictures flashing across my screen. She’d always been thin, I concluded, but yes, she was thinner now. She’d gone from being an attainable skinny to the kind of skinny reserved for a rare echelon of women.AdvertisementThus concluded another instance of what I have come to think of as thinvestigation. No, I had not managed to determine how she’d done it, whether it was what she ate, physical exercise, a semaglutide, a depressive episode, an undiagnosed eating disorder, the passage of time, or a mix. But I’d figured out this one piece of it, the part that was available to me: She was thinner now. To be clear, I didn’t feel better for doing it. What was there to do now with all this utterly useless information? Mostly I just felt the shame of ending up years deep in a stranger’s Instagram page. But such is the nature of thinvestigation.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementUntil the last year, my friends and I had never before casually talked about someone else’s body like we do regularly now—not even a pop star. So the fact that it keeps coming up for us is, for me, a warning siren. There were a few years, at the height of the body positivity movement, when we allowed ourselves to dream that the all-consuming diet-culture talk we had been raised on was behind us. Now that seems like an impossibility. Our social media profiles allow us to compare and contrast versions of ourselves and each other with ease. And in this moment of rapid change for weight loss, when being bigger is suddenly more stigmatized, because, the argument goes, ifyou really wanted to, you could get on a GLP-1 and change your life, it’s easier than ever to dissect someone else’s figure.AdvertisementMaybe that’s the reason thinvestigation seems so acceptable these days. Since the rise (and democratization) of Ozempic, weight loss feels like a much easier choice—and to choose to be as thin as possible is a hard one to ignore. Maybe I dug back through five years of photo evidence because it didn’t feel as judgmental as it once would have. But lately, I’ve started to worry over what the opening of these floodgates has done to us, the thinvestigators. After all, once I’ve discovered that someone does indeed look just a little bit skinnier, I go to sleep, and I wake up, still in this body of mine. I look in the mirror at my belly that is still hanging there over the band of my underwear, and I get dressed for another day.A few weeks ago, internet personality and writer Caroline Callowaywrote about strapping20 pounds’ worth of ankle weights to her legs and disguising them under sweatpants so she could qualify for an online Ozempic prescription. She went to the trouble of such a maneuver in order to get from an explicitly referenced 130 pounds down to 115, a feat that, in her words, could only be achieved through “a loss of appetite.” For as long as the internet attention span allows these days, people fumed over her essay. It seemed to drip self-loathing, critics said, and plentypointed outthat it isn’t particularly radical, as Calloway seems to think it is, to tell people that “being skinny will make your life better in every possible way.”AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementWhat can be appreciated about her admission is the unflattering close inspection it gives into the disconcerting trend of using GLP-1s for reasons not considered medically necessary—a means to lose those “stubborn” 15 pounds that exist as the final shred of proof that you live a life of occasional pleasure. Most of those partaking in this are not being as candid; influencers are not setting up their tripods to divulge how they scammed their way into thedrug that is increasingly making its way into medicine cabinets across America. And yet, as the celebrities embark on theirred-carpet appearances,world tours, andfashion runways, there are the signs that are increasingly impossible to ignore. Thegaunt, hollow cheeks, dubbed “Ozempic face”; biceps and quads that are suddenly equal in size; the shrinking clothing sizes on theirShop My Closet pages. Now that weight loss can be the recognizable therapeutic effect of an accessible medication, rather than the product of an opaque combination of diet, exercise, and/or surgery, the impulse to ask “How did they do it?” is even harder to resist.AdvertisementThinvestigation is not new. People are always trying to deduce what is happening to public, famous bodies: For years, an entire ecosystem has flourished ofsocial media accounts dedicatedto figuring out the breast augmentations, rhinoplasty, and fillers celebrities are using to transform their bodies and faces. It’s accepted that a plastic surgeon, in their downtime between face-lifts, might make a vertical one-minute clip speculating about the work someone influential had gotten done. But now that so many on our feeds and screens are rapidly shrinking, and they all have a trove of archival footage of their former selves online, no expertise is really needed. Anyone can thinvestigate on their phone: Is their jaw sharper? Have they shrunk in the past six months in ways the naked eye can just see?AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementEvery red-carpet event—or slight shift in a public figure’s appearance—now seems to inspire a wave of speculation, warranted or not. Recent thinvestigations that have occurred or are ongoing have includedCharlize Theron,Olivia Wilde,Kai Gerber,Kelly Osbourne,Ryan Seacrest, NFLinfluencer Annie Agar,Jenna Ortega, and even influencers with no more than 250,000 followers. At first, much of the discourse around Ariana Grande began in a similar fashion, with people pointing out her weight loss as early as 2023. Her response to these observations was tomake a video defending herselfagainst criticism, which noted that perhaps we should all stop commenting on people’s bodies in any direction, but also stated that it was her previous body that was in fact the unhealthy one. This might have quieted things, but her thinness has only become more pronounced since, fueling conversations during bothWickedmovies and now her world tour. Finally, we have arrived at our current moment: a point where wecan see something is very wrong, and no one has a clear idea of what to do or say about it. Perhaps what we should take away from this is that even seemingly light-hearted observations about thinness are just a few degrees removed from not being as harmless as they might seem. There has to be a way to acknowledge the alarming shrinking currently happening to some of the most visible women among us, to realize that no, GLP-1s don’t make this kind of thinness OK, and to express concern over it. We need to figure out how to do this without being lured back into a conversation so many of us once chose to opt out of.AdvertisementBecause we did opt out, for a while. In certain circles, thanks to the work of fat activists and thebody positivity movement, we’d gotten the closest we’dever beento eradicating weight loss and gain as an acceptable subject for idle chatter over our dinner tables and in our group chats. That this ground we gained is now gone is a loss we have not yet realized the magnitude of. But I’m starting to realize it. Once I finish dissecting whether a public figure is skinnier—possibly at the hands of a GLP-1, let’s zoom in on her eyes to check—I can feel the talk about bodies radiating around me, making me hyperaware of my own and everyone else’s. Examining and investigating the root of thinness, after we’re all already forced to see it on our screens 24/7, has a way of reinforcing our collective obsession with striving for it, attaining it, wondering what it might feel like.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementThere are circles where this kind of talk is endemic, where there never even was that mid-2010s pause in dissecting ourselves. I happen to straddle them both: the world where talking about a dramatic change to someone’s body is impolite and insensitive, and the world where it is the only subject people want to discuss when they first see you.I know the latter so well because in the past year and a half, I myself have undergone dramatically visible weight loss: I’ve lost over 40 pounds and counting, or three pant sizes. Every time I fly back to Miami, where my family lives, the gaggle of comments begins from the older Latino contingent: You’ve lost so much weight! You look so pretty now! You’re so skinny, but you have even more room to lose! Ever since you moved across the country, the weight came right off—you were just in a bad place! How did you do it?AdvertisementThe answers are mostly boring: Yes, I’ve lost weight, and I did it consciously. It starts back here: I had gained weight very quickly during the pandemic and the years that followed. I have a long family history of diabetes, and one day after exiting the shower, I noticed a dark fold of skin by my neck in the bathroom mirror. I took photos of it to get a closer look, and I self-diagnosed it asskin thickeningthat can be an early sign of insulin resistance. I was terrified; it coincided with a life-changing move, and so I suddenly had a catalyst to do something with my fear. Now I walk a lot, I eat mostly whole foods, I read the sugar contents of what I buy at the grocery store. I have not considered a GLP-1 because I don’t want to have to be on a medication for the rest of my life. Even so, I have loose skin in places no twentysomething woman wishes to, and none of my old clothes look as good as they once did. But buying entire new wardrobes is expensive, and tailors are worse, so I’m a baggy-jeans enthusiast.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementI don’t tell them this, because I know these are not the answers they’re looking for, and I don’t want to give fuel to a conversation I find suffocating. Usually, my response to their statements and questions is to smile and say, “Yes, I have. I’m trying!” I grew up watching weight be a lifelong project for the women in my community. I know that their comments are said out of love, and filled with pride and admiration over my having achieved something they themselves have pined for. So, I don’t tell them what it feels like to know they’re paying such close attention to my body. That’s just the world they exist in, and one that I’m a part of too, every once in a while.At the same time, no friend or contemporary pointed out the obvious to me before I was ready to talk about it—even as we talked about the celebrities shrinking around us. I know there’s a line between someone famous and someone we actually know, but at times, I wondered if any of them noticed. I even thinvestigatedmyself: scrolling through old photos and questioning whether I actually looked different. But I know no one will be scrolling deep into my Instagram archives because, as a still-not-skinny person, I know that losing weight is what I “should” be doing.AdvertisementCelebrities are being thinvestigated right now because they’re rewriting the standards of thinness—and the new rules they invent often trickle down to the rest of us. But figuring out whether someone’s body has changed doesn’t actually give us any insight into how it happened. We can suspect misuse of GLP-1s, but we often have no proof. (And what would be different about them if we did? What kind of crime is this, and what would the consequences be? Would we stop watching their movies, listening to their music?) There are many reasons why someone might lose weight: an eating disorder, cancer, a new hobby or workout routine, new medications, getting off medications, a breakup, depression, or, in my case, newfound happiness and also fear. You can’t always tell the difference between when someone is doing it for all the “right” or “wrong” reasons, or is one of those for whom it simply just happened. As much as I wanted to believe my own thinvestigations were born out of righteous criticism of a changing beauty standard, I knew deep down that caring this much felt like diet culture repackaged for a new era—and it feels like as much of a trap as the first time.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementRecently inLifeThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyWhat Will We Learn From Our Summer of Complicated Mothers?This Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyGLP-1s Have Brought Back One Toxic Habit. Why Can’t We Quit It?This Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyThere Is No Male Loneliness Crisis. What’s Actually Happening Is So Much Darker.This Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyThe Obsession With Botox and Filler Has Reached a Dangerous New LevelWhen I did start talking to my friends about what, over the past few years, had been happening to my body, I realized something. These conversations aren’t about the number on a scale or even what I look like now. I focus, rather, on the ways my life is different. I tell them about my walks at the park, or my frustrations with my once carefully curated closet, and the clothes rental service I’m using to figure out a new way to dress. I complain to them during trips to my hometown about my family’s litany of body-related comments. We commiserate over the endless ride we are on when it comes to how societal expectations around this stuff seep into our intimate relationships. My friends are curious, and share their own struggles about their own never-ending pursuits of health, like how hard it is to balance on a reformer Pilates machine and whether we should be figuring out how tofibermaxx. These conversations soothe me. Because wanting to be thin—or to act on our various criticisms of and insecurities about our varied bodies—is not how we are tethered to each other.No, we bond over the actual realities of living.Still, what I have realized is that even with all these positive, humane conversations, something else happens in our heads when we are alone. I can set aside the pop star after the concert, only to find myself dug in when it’s just me and my phone. I can smile and deflect to my family, only to find myself thinking about a comment days later, on a plane ride home. I know that the way we scrutinize and investigate other women eventually makes it back to ourselves, even if we insist that it doesn’t. Maybe I should commit to stopping my own thinvestigations. Or maybe it is simply enough to know that we exist in a world that encourages us all, and especially women, to be as thin as possible—and to decide to try to live differently. I’d like to nod at the madness happening out there and choose to stay inside this warm room a little longer, where I’m laughing and gossiping with the women in my life about everything—or really, anythingbut “how she didit.”Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.CelebritiesHealthInternet CulturePrescription DrugsSocial MediaWomenAriana Grande

title: Donald Trump’s Trickle-Down Misogyny
content: The SlatestDonald Trump’s Trickle-Down MisogynyThis outburst says a lot about how the president’s long history of misogyny is infecting the rest of his party.ByIan Prasad PhilbrickAug 18, 20266:33 PMPhoto illustration by Slate. Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Sign up for the Slatestto get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.It’s perhaps not surprising that Donald Trump, a man who has many criticisms of the press and a long history of demeaning his female critics, reserves special rage for reporters who happen to be women. The latest example happened in the Oval Office yesterday, when Trump called CNN’s Kristen Holmes “a loud, boisterous person” and told her to “be quiet.” The president has attacked female journalists before, but it’s what happened next that really sets this outburst apart—and says a lot about how Trump’s misogyny is infecting the rest of his party.What exactly led to Trump’s outburst?Holmes, who has covered Trump for years, asked the president to respond to comments that Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat,made over the weekendaccusing Trump of neglecting his presidential duties by prioritizing his proposed White House ballroom and traveling with an aide named Natalie Harp (more on that later). Trump responded relatively civilly, calling Ossoff a “Pee-wee Herman look-alike” before going on a tear about the ballroom’s virtues. But later, when Holmes piggybacked on a colleague’s question about Trump wanting to scale back U.S. military drills with South Korea, the president erupted. “Quiet, quiet, quiet,” he said, pointing at Holmes and asking where she worked. “Fake news,” Trump snapped after she said CNN, raising his voice as she tried to repeat her question. “You’re a loud—you’re a loud, boisterous person. You’re fake news. Be quiet. Be quiet. Be quiet!”Not great. But is this really different from how Trump has berated other reporters in the past?Unfortunately, there’s more. After the Oval Office scrum, an X account run by the White House, called Rapid Response 47,twice posted about Holmes’ questionabout Ossoff. The first post called Holmes “a disgraceful, humiliating embarrassment to her alleged profession.” The second got more personal: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question,” it read. “They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”That’s pretty ugly. Has there been pushback?CNNreleased a statementpraising Holmes for asking “a tough, relevant, and newsworthy question on behalf of the American people” and calling personal insults “beneath the office.” Other media figures also spoke up. “Just disgusting behavior by an anonymous account,” Chuck Todd, a formerMeet the Pressmoderator, wrote of the post that mentioned Holmes’ children. “This is so cowardly & pathetic,” posted Stephanie Grisham, a former Trump press secretary turned critic. “Doesn’t an attack against a family undermine the GOP’s family-values messaging?” Holmes’ CNN colleagueBrian Stelter wondered.Why was Trump so sensitive about Holmes’ question?We can’t know for sure, but he may have been mad about her earlier reference to Ossoff—and Ossoff’s to Harp. Harp, 35, is a particularly obsequious Trump aide and one of the few White House staffers who secretly boarded a military plane with the presidentvia an airport catering truckafter Iran threatened to attackAir Force Onelast month. Her proximity and devotion to Trump—she wrote him notes professing “You are all that matters to me” and “I want to bring you joy”—have sparked rumors of an affair, which may explain the White House’s heated response.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementStrange. But this kind of anti-reporter outburst isn’t exactly out of character for Trump, is it?Trump has a contentious relationship with CNN, regularly accusing the network of bias and singling out its reporters for verbal abuse. But the list of female journalists he’s gone after in anger reads like a who’s who of the Washington press corps writ large. It includes NBC’s Yamiche Alcindor (“second-rate”) and Julie Tsirkin (“fake news”), ABC’s Mary Bruce (“a terrible person”) and Rachel Scott (“a horror show”), the New York Times’ Katie Rogers (“ugly, both inside and out”) and Maggie Haberman (“Maggot is a loser!”), Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey (“quiet, piggy”), and CBS’s Nancy Cordes (“a stupid person”). Not even Fox News is safe; on Sunday, Trump criticized network host Shannon Bream and called her show “beyond redemption.” Trump has also gotten mad at male reporters, of course. But the opprobrium he reserves for women who ask him questions he doesn’t like is a notable pattern. That White House staffers apparently felt comfortable anonymously attacking Holmes in personal terms suggests that the impulse has trickled down too.AdvertisementThat kind of trickle-down misogyny isn’t totally new either, though, right?AdvertisementNo. Back when I was a lowly Slate intern helping cover the 2016 presidential election, I wrote about a preteen boy at a Trump rally in Virginia who repeatedly screamed “Take the bitch down!” every time the future president mentioned Hillary Clinton. More than a decade later, the GOP is suffused with Trumpian misogyny. The party remains nearly in lockstep behind a man who bragged about grabbing women’s genitals, wasfound liablefor sexually abusing a woman, and denigrated his female political rivals in sexist terms. It confirmed a Supreme Court justice facing sexual misconduct allegations. And it’s currently standing by a Republican congressmanaccused of abusing his wife and child. Some of the ways our civil fabric has frayed in the Trump era might have happened regardless. But the mainstreaming of sexism into one of America’s two major political parties seems fair to lay at Trump’s feet.Surely there’s something the press corps could do about this?Maybe. But none of the other journalists in the Oval Office with Holmes spoke up as the president berated her. Today I asked the White House Correspondents’ Association whether it has guidance for what reporters should do if the president starts yelling at a colleague. Should they tell Trump off? Should they complain to the White House press secretary? Should they leave the scrum in protest? I got no answer. Butspeaking to New York magazine yesterday, Correspondents’ Association president Jacqui Heinrich—a Fox reporter whom Trump has called “absolutely terrible”—suggested that insults from the leader of the free world may be just one more workplace hazard. “Any number of us have had him push back or snap at a question that we’ve asked, or made a comment,” she said.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementIn fairness, it’s journalists’ job to record how the president answers questions, no matter how lie-filled or abusive the answers. But where once these kinds of outbursts would have made waves, they now seem to ripple at best. Fewer Americans than ever trust the news media,polls show, a credibility problem that Trump has both worsened and exploited; so far, these incidents have yielded no real consequences for a president who, despite his criticisms of the media, feeds on its attention. The result is a no-win situation for all reporters who find themselves face-to-face with Trump, but particularly female ones. If they object to the president’s behavior, it fuels a narrative that the press is out to get him. If they turn the other cheek, it invites accusations that the media is affording Trump a level of grace it would never give another president. The real solution, of course, would be for voters to not elect presidents who can’t handle tough questions—and who regularly fly off the handle when women ask them. But given how Trump’s other impulses have transformed his party, we shouldn’t assume he’ll be the last.AdvertisementTolga AkdoğanAdvertisementPopular inNews & PoliticsThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyDonald Trump’s Trickle-Down MisogynyAll right, you’re caught up on one of the most important stories of the day! title: Why Did Trump Lose It Over Natalie Harp—and Who Is She, Anyway? Unfortunately, I’ve Learned Too Much.

Jon Ossoff said something that seems to have truly pissed off Trumpworld: He gave a speech in which he dared to mention a woman in the Trump orbit named Natalie—just Natalie, no last name given.Speaking at a campaign event—he is up for reelection in November—Ossoff said the following about Trump to a crowd: “While thesailors on theLincolnfight his war, while he fruitlessly drains our munitions and oil reserves, the president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks.” He went on: “He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”Who is this Natalie that Trump wants to—pause for a full-body shudder—travelwith? It’s not anything so obvious as an affair, if that’s what you’re thinking. It’s somehow worse. Natalie is Natalie Harp, but she’s better known as Trump’s so-called “human printer.” As an executive assistant in the White House, she follows him around with a wireless printer, supplying him with a steady flow of articles and memes about him for him to take in. If you’re wondering why such a position is necessary in the age of the smartphone and tablet, recall that our president, ever the boomer, prefers things in hard copy. (Who says he’s not creating jobs?) Harp also sometimes posts for Trump on social media; people on his team have in fact blamed her for some of his very worst, most racist posts. She makesa salary of $150,000doing this, by the way.Related From SlateJessica PishkoIf You Want to Know How Trump 2.0 Is Really Going, I Suggest a Visit to the Dying Trump “Superstore”Read MoreHarp has been part of Trump’s staff, and been reported on in media outlets like the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, for a while now. After a stint as an anchor at One America News Network, she joined Trump’s team in 2022, when she first earned the “human printer” nickname. As that epithet might imply, she is not exactly beloved among the rest of Trump’s staff. It has been reported that those employees have tried and failed numerous times to push her out, worrying that she is a danger to herself and the president. The deal seems to be that she’s so scarily devoted to Trump that she worries her colleagues, which is saying something. But scary levels of devotion, it perhaps unsurprisingly turns out, are a register that really works for our president, and all this has paradoxically ensured her continued employment in the White House. Maybe all it takes to achieve job security in this admin is to do what Harp did and write creepy letters to Trump in which you refer to him as your “Guardian and Protector in this Life.”AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementIf all this is public knowledge and has been for some time, one wonders why members of Trumpworld were so rattled by Ossoff’s mention of Natalie. And they were rattled: White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote a post in response that began, “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.” Another White House staffer called Ossoff a “cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid cosplaying as Barack Obama.” Trump also snapped at a reporter who asked about the remarks. Part of it may be that Ossoff is starting to look like a contender for the presidential race in 2028. Another part may be that there’s a difference between newspaper and magazine stories about Trump’s “human printer” and a clip that can travel around social media when a senator mentions Natalie by name. Team Trump may figure that nobody reads anymore, but they do watch videos, and the natural response to this one is to ask: Who’sNatalie?Get the best of news and politicsSign up for Slate's evening newsletter.Thanks for signing up! You’ll also receive updates on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team.It’s safe to say that the Trump administration is failing on many fronts: Its economic policy has worsened inflation, its foreign policy has landed America in another seemingly endless war, and its healthcare policy is rejecting decades of research-backed vaccine guidance. In Donald Trump’s goals of tormenting the nation’s immigrants, though, the administration is clearlywinning. Sure, there have been plenty oflosses in courtand in thebattle of public opinion, but deportations for fiscal year 2026 still managed toexceed 350,000, on track to beat the Obama administration’s record. Trump also notched decisive victories at the Supreme Court overtemporary protected status,legal permanent residents, and his invocation of theAlien Enemies Act. On top of this, the president has successfully secured the most funding in U.S. history for the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection, a sum that will outlast his second term, to the tune of approximately $200 billion. Meanwhile, Democrats not only failed to stop this funding; they allowed it to pass with basically no congressional oversight baked in. We’re finally starting to get a sense of what Trump is spending thisenormouspot of money on, and, well, it’s ugly, but it’s also terrifyingly effective.The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which awarded $170 billion to DHS, ICE, and CBP, is the president’s signature policy bill. It was, among other things, intended to help fulfill this wish of Trump’s: deport 1 million immigrants within his first year in office. One year later, after ICE agents killed two American citizens in Minnesota and inflicted violence against thousands of protesters across the country, congressional Republicans decided to award the agency even more money, as Trump’s goal remained unmet. In June, they passed another $70 billion funding package for DHS through the Secure America Act. Critically, both of these spending bills were passed via reconciliation so Senate Republicans could move them forward with only 51 votes, instead of the typical 60 required for budget negotiations; the bills also featured scant congressional oversight and lacked guidelines dictating how the funds should be allotted.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementThis is an intoxicating amount of money already being abused by an administration that has, for the past 20 months,abused federal lawand the courts to fulfill its extremist agenda. Just consider what the country’s top law-enforcement agencies have been buying with their new loot. Last year, under former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, the agency allocated $464 million for a no-bid contract to purchase 10 airplanes for deportation flights. However, the planes, some of which are luxury business jets, havebarely been usedbecause the agency “did not have the staff necessary to operate them.” Because springing for and maintaining a fleet of its own is costly, ICE has historically outsourced its deportation flights to private companies or used military and Coast Guard vessels. You might say that this is not a very effective use of money, and you’d be right. But, waste aside, the threat of this fleet remains.AdvertisementThen there are the recent headlines announcing ICE’s plan to spend $20 million on electric-shock glovesthat will deliver“a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds.” One expert told the Associated Press that he envisions these gloves being used when officers encounter resistance, particularly as they try to remove a person from a car or house, or into and out of detention centers. As we’ve seen this year, it’s easy to imagine this violence being inflicted onanyonewhom ICE officers decide to target, no matter their immigration status.AdvertisementThere’s more. This month, we also learned that Our Rescue, an anti-human-trafficking organization whose founder was accused of sexual exploitation himself, was awarded a $158 million no-bid contract to provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children.According to NPR, it’s unclear if Our Rescue has lawyers on staff, though its CEO, Derek Benner, previously worked for ICE. Meanwhile, nearly 100 legal nonprofits who have historically been hired by the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the federal agency charged with overseeing migrant children held by the U.S. government, have watched their contracts expire, without any renewal offers. This is a recipe for disaster for immigrant children who lack permanent legal status; they have beenleft without legal representation in complex asylum cases.AdvertisementAdvertisementThis is simply what has been uncovered in recent weeks, but there’s also the $700 million spent by DHS toconvert warehousesall over the country into detention facilities; this initiative has drawn large-scale protests from local residents, even in GOP-majority districts. Again, many of these facilities sit unused, but they remain a threat, as they are still owned by the federal government. We’ve seen in places like the Dilley Immigration Processing Center for family detention, in Texas, and Delaney Hall Detention Facility, in New Jersey, that the administration knows how to warehouse human beings under tortuous conditions. Last week, theNew York Times reportedthat an immigrant had died at Delaney Hall from lack of medical care, the third such case in less than a year.AdvertisementAdvertisementThat’s not to mention the massive uptick in investment insurveillance apparatus, a move often fueled by artificial intelligence. These devices collect information about immigrants, citizens and protesters.AdvertisementRelated From SlateJessica PishkoIf You Want to Know How Trump 2.0 Is Really Going, I Suggest a Visit to the Dying Trump “Superstore”Read MoreMeanwhile, lawmakers have not touched U.S. immigration policy in any substantive way that could limit the administration’s agenda; instead, these legislators empower Republicans to throw as much money as they can at DHS while they still retain power in Congress and the White House. When Democrats tried to intervene earlier this year, only after massive public outcry following the deaths of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, they failed to force Republicans to agree toguardrails for immigration agents, like a ban on masks and establishing use-of-force standards. Republicans simply waited until the dust settled, dropping their new funding bill in June, when they again used reconciliation to bypass Democrats andaward DHS an additional $70 million, an amount that will support the agency through the end of Trump’s second term. Weeks later, an ICE officer killedLorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who had been living and working in the U.S. for decades.AdvertisementAdvertisementEven if Democrats are successful in this year’s midterm election cycle—currently, they’re projected to onlynarrowly win the House—there isn’t much they can do to stop DHS, ICE, or CBP. Not only has funding for those agencies already been approved through 2029, but Democrats have shown that when push comes to shove, they’re not interested in duking it out with the GOP. Last year, Democrats all over the country organized to highlight how the Trump administration was allowing federal subsidies for the Affordable Care Act to expire, a move that would force healthcare costs to skyrocket for thousands of Americans. Instead of holding the line as they leveraged a government funding bill to force Republicans to negotiate on the healthcare issue, eight Senate Democrats broke rank to vote with the GOP, without securing any agreement for healthcare costs. And last week,Democrats quietly agreedto Republicans’ stopgap government funding bill. As midterm elections near, they’ve chosen not to use this moment to foreground the administration’s horrific abuses, let alone force the GOP to course-correct.AdvertisementIf Democrats manage to win a majority in the House, they could leverage committee posts to initiate investigations and call Trump officials forward to force them to publicly testify under oath. This is a squarely reactive strategy, however. Democrats will not be in a position to proactively prevent the president’s immigration agenda from killing more people, harming more communities, and ripping families apart.Popular inNews & PoliticsThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyTrump Just Dealt a Huge Blow to America’s Standing in the WorldThe reality is that Democrats would need to persuade a handful of Republicans, particularly in the Senate, to join them in passing substantive immigration reform. But given how Republicans have typically fallen in line behind Trump, despitedismal approval ratingsand34 people’s deaths in ICE custody—a 22-year high—that may be a pipe dream. “Up until this point, we have really seen most Republicans align with President Trump’s policies,” Adriel Orozco, senior policy counsel at the American Immigration Council, told me. “I can’t really imagine seeing Republicans, even if they lose one of the chambers, stepping up to challenge the president on some of these immigration policies.”One of the only remaining levers available is in the hands of the American people. If ICE, CBP, and DHS continue to behave egregiously, unnecessarily shocking innocent people with electric gloves, throwing lawful immigrants into deadly detention centers, and killing more Americans with their cars and guns, public outcry will be absolutely vital in forcing the White House’s hand. It’s the one thing that so far seems capable of scaring this administration into some semblance of complying with thelaw.Sign up for Executive DysfunctionDelivered every Thursday morning.Thanks for signing up! title: Mickey Mouse, Welcome to the Resistance
content: The MediaMickey Mouse, Welcome to the ResistanceDisney’s lawsuit against Trump’s FCC is a battle for the First Amendment.ByNitish PahwaFollow NitishSigned Up For Email AlertsError Signing Up For Email AlertsCloseEnter your email to receive alerts for this author.Thanks for signing up! You canmanage your newsletter subscriptionsat any time.You're already subscribed to the aa_Nitish_Pahwa newsletter. Please try again, ormanage all your newsletter subscriptions here.Please enable javascript to sign up for newsletters.Email address:Sign UpBy signing up, you agree to ourPrivacy PolicyandTerms.Sign inorcreate an accountto better manage your email preferences.CloseUnsubscribe from email alertsAre you sure you want to unsubscribe from email alerts forNitish Pahwa?Yes, unsubscribeAug 18, 20263:39 PMDavid Pashaee/Middle East Images via AFP via Getty ImagesCopy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Sign up for the Slatestto get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.The fight against the Trump administration’s media crackdowns just leveled up a notch. On Tuesday morning, Disney, ABC, and the network’s eight affiliate stations collectively filed a federal lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission, arguing that the agency is violating the broadcaster’s First Amendment rights—and requesting that the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia halt the FCC’s ongoing regulatory actions against ABC.“The Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts,” the complaint reads up top.It’s rare for any TV news outfit to call out its own regulators in such an unabashed manner. But, as Disney’s lawyers make clear, this was a long time coming. The filingkeeps a diligent recordof public statements made by President Donald Trump and FCC Chair Brendan Carr over the past two years, as they repeatedly excoriated ABC’s political coverage while threatening to revoke the licenses that allow it to operate over the public airwaves.More recently, Carr made amove toward realizing this power grabin April, when he formally asked that Disney submit early renewal applications for ABC’s eight licensed regional affiliates—even though all those stations’ contracts remain in effect until 2028 or later. The FCC had framed this historically unprecedented order as part of a long-running investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity, and inclusion policies. The agency’s request also landed immediately after the president had, once again, excoriated ABC’s political coverage,aiming special ireat the Trump-critical hosts ofThe ViewandJimmy Kimmel Live!In the months since theFCC’s initial letter, the alarming threat it presented to ABC’s press freedoms only became more apparent. Disney was willing to submit the premature renewal applications, and aflood of more than 150,000 commentsto the FCC, from a swath of cross-partisan advocates, demonstrated overwhelming public support for ABC. Last month, however,leaks from the FCC indicatedthat Carr was ready to make binding rulings that would changeThe View’s programming structure and bring ABC’s broadcast licenses closer to total revocation. Hence, Disney writes, it had “no choice” but to take legal action against this “existential threat.” The message is clear: Disney is ready for battle, and it is waging this war not just on its own behalf, but for the sake of American journalism as a whole.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisement“If the Administration gets its way, the message to every media company in the country will be unmistakable: tell only the stories the Administration deems favorable, or face the coercive machinery of the federal government,” the lawsuit states.It’s a remarkable, bold stance for Disney to take at this moment, just two years after itsettled a weak personal lawsuitfrom Trump over host George Stephanopoulos’ technically true utterance that the then candidate had been found “liable for rape” in a federal case filed by E. Jean Carroll. (Not that ABC News was the only media outlet that hasattempted to appease Trump.) But this year, the vibe once again seems to have shifted—this time away from supplicating the reelected president.Trump’s approval isat record lowsthese days, and his attacks on the pressaren’t helping himregain any momentum. Disney also came to understand the sheer scale of American liberals’ anger when it ill-advisedly suspended Jimmy Kimmel from the air last September. To recap: In response to a factually shaky quip the late-night host had made on air about Charlie Kirk’s alleged assassin, broadcast giants Nexstar and Sinclair blocked Kimmel’s show from their ABC affiliate channels (with Carr’s vocal encouragement), leading Disney executives to temporarily, suddenly halt production onJimmy Kimmel Live!altogether. Trump celebrated the decision, but the broader backlash was immediate and immense, with Disney adultstaking to the streets in protestand pledging to boycott the corporation’s theme parks and streaming services. Kimmel was then quickly reinstated.AdvertisementAdvertisementStill, the government again pursued Kimmel in April, after a wannabe presidential assassin breached the White House Correspondents’ dinner. Melania Trump pointed to a pre-dinnerJimmy Kimmel Live!sketch in which the host joked about the first lady having “a glow like an expectant widow”—a nod to the president’s flailing health that his wife reframed, ludicrously, as incitement of violence. By that point, however, some things had changed at Disney: It had anew CEO, and it had gottenthousands of supportive commentsfrom the public when Carr began probingThe Viewover its choices of political guests. Plus, the House of Mouse was already changing up its rhetorical tack to mount an abundant self-defense on free speech and free press grounds. Even as ABC played ball by submitting license renewals on the FCC’s hastened timeline, it claimed to do so “under protest in response to an unlawful, arbitrary, and unconstitutional order.” The broadcaster additionally cited Americans’ continuous deluges of supportive comments when it asked the regulatory agency, in June, todrop its license order. And it further defied the administration when itrefused to broadcastTrump’s election-denying July 16 address, a slight that Carr claimed would be factored into his decision.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementRelated From SlateLizzie O’LearyDisney Finds Its SpineRead MoreThe belligerent, blatant nature of Trump and Carr’s anti-ABC vendetta is a motif of the new lawsuit, which quotes various interviews, social media posts, and documents in making the case that 1) the president has consistently called for ABC to lose its licenses on no other pretense than his perception of bias, and 2) Carr is less an independent government regulator than a Trump lackey who makes his censorious desires rather open, as in a March tweet threatening that broadcasters covering the Iran invasion would “lose their licenses” if they didn’t “correct course.”Popular inSlateWhy Did Trump Lose It Over Natalie Harp—and Who Is She, Anyway? Unfortunately, I’ve Learned Too Much.This Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyTrump Just Dealt a Huge Blow to America’s Standing in the WorldThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyDonald Trump Has Finally Wielded His Presidential Power for GoodThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyThe Quiet Decision Microsoft Made That Devastated Thousands of NonprofitsDisney’s counsel likewise points out that this top-down crusade is already having a chilling effect on the type of guests shows likeThe Viewmight invite on. “Since the Bureau’s inquiry began, ABC must now evaluate any invitation to a political candidate for its potential consequences, including whether it might later be cited by the Commission as a basis for non-renewal,” they write. As such,The Viewhas for now stopped bookinganycandidates for office as guests and is not airing certain clips that may even depict a politician of whom Trump disapproves.AdvertisementDisney’s legal team warns too that whatever happens to ABC will not be limited to that particular newsroom: “Other news organizations throughout the country are also watching and waiting to see the extent to which ABC and the Stations will be punished, as promised, for coverage that the Administration has deemed unfavorable—because if it happens to ABC, they could be next.” After all, most media properties are nowhere near as well resourced and lucrative as Disney. With this lawsuit, the corporation is sending a message: It’s ready to deploy those resources to fight this thing as long as it takes, with the hope that federal judges will heed all the evidence of Trump and Carr’s censorious intent and stop this crusade. Because if they don’t recognize the constitutional stakes here,everymedia company in America will be atarget.Get the best of news and politicsSign up for Slate's evening newsletter.Thanks for signing up! Have a workplace problem big or small?Send it to Laura Helmuth and Doree Shafrir here. (It’s anonymous!)Dear Good Job,I work for a private company that provides support to various law enforcement agencies. Through my job, I’ve learned some disturbing information about a relative’s new boyfriend.Popular inAdviceThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyI Read My Son’s Texts From His Ex-Girlfriend. Uh-Oh.My Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life HellThis relative is a single parent of a young child and has begun dating a man I happen to know is a target of an ongoing investigation for sexual crimes involving young children. He currently has no publicly available criminal record. I’m literally losing sleep over this. On the one hand, I am under heavy-duty confidentiality agreements, plus anything that alerts this man that the law is on to him could compromise the investigation. On the other hand, I don’t know how I would live with myself if my own little relative became his victim and I didn’t say anything for the sake of his potential conviction and my career. Advice?—TornDear Torn,Ugh, what a horrible situation all around. Unfortunately, you can’t say anything to your relative about this man, because it could jeopardize the investigation and possibly also put your own job at risk. But what youcando is make sure that she’s aware, generally, of best practices when it comes to romantic partners and her children. When my son was in preschool we had a woman come give a safety presentation, and she emphasized that one of the most dangerous people for young kids is a parent’s new partner. It’s so depressing, but it’s real. I’m not sure how close you are with this relative, but perhaps you could take her to lunch or coffee and just suss out how mindful she is about keeping her kids safe. I really hope that the relationship fizzles out before this even remotely becomes an issue, and/or the investigation is made public. I’ll be thinking of you and your relative and hoping for the best.—DoreeClassic PrudieMy friend “Carla” has this habit of asking what my plans are without telling me why she’s asking. title: My Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life Hell
content: Good JobMy Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life HellAdvice byDoree ShafrirAug 18, 20261:00 PMPhoto illustration by Slate. Photo by Mariia Vitkovska/iStock/Getty Images Plus and Nenad Cavoski/iStock/Getty Images Plus.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Copy LinkShareShareCommentGift StoryOnly Slate Plus members can gift Slate stories.Become a memberto share 10 free articles a month.Good Jobis Slate’s advice column on work. Have a workplace problem big or small?Send it to Laura Helmuth and Doree Shafrir here. (It’s anonymous!)Dear Good Job,I have a co-worker who scream sneezes and it enrages me to no end every time it happens. I’ve joked about it with her that it scares me so much, and asked, does she have to scream? She says she can’t help it. Do you have any mindset shifts for me to practice acceptance of an incredibly performative and annoying habit?—I’m Jumpy!Dear I’m Jumpy,This sounds really distracting! I’m so curious how this habit of hers developed, but in terms of the more immediate issue, I think you have two options. You could start wearing noise-cancelling headphones, although I’m not sure how feasible that is at your workplace (and will also mean that you’re blocking out everyone else, which may not be ideal). The other option is to start practicing radical acceptance, and for this I actually think that meditation could help because it forces you to block out everything around you and really focus for a certain amount of time. If you’re able to start doing meditating, say, every morning, I’m confident that the practice will help you redirect some of your anger over the sneezing and, hopefully, come to just block it out.Semi-related, I often play tennis in a public park that always has a ton of other stuff going on—from kickball games to dogs barking to helicopters flying overhead to the occasional fight. It’s gotten to the point where I don’t even notice the chaos anymore while I’m playing because I need to be so focused, but when players from private clubs play against our team, they inevitably complain about how loud and distracting our park is, and I just smile inwardly and use it against them. I tell you this because I think just generally, learning how to focus and not getting flustered by distractions is a really important skill in many aspects of life, not just sneezing co-workers or tennis matches. I’m confident you will be able to learn to tune her out!AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementGet work advice—submit a question!Please keep questions short (<150 words), and don‘t submit the same question to multiple columns. We are unable to edit or remove questions after publication. Use pseudonyms to maintain anonymity. Your submission may be used in other Slate advice columns and may be edited for publication.Thanks! Your question has been submitted.Dear Good Job,*Your letter signoffYour pronounsYour email (optional and confidential—please include if you're open to Good Job following up)SubmitDear Good Job,I have a very stressful job at a non-profit that supports people living in poverty. I work directly with our clients. Our organization can help directly with one aspect of what our clients need and only provide information for resources about other aspects. I am very good at my job. Where I can help, I do help, and in that sense my job is fulfilling. But I feel powerless to do anything about the many other areas where they need help besides give them information and encourage them to contact the other agencies. This has made me depressed and I feel pretty defeated a lot of the time. Recently a friend of mine asked why I didn’t just make the calls to other agencies on behalf of my clients. It would be against the rules of our organization, where I’m paid to do a certain kind of work only. We also cannot share personal information with clients, so I can’t follow-up with them on my own. But my friend’s comment did make me start to wonder if maybe I could set up something “off books” with a burner email address and a Google phone number to follow-up and check-in with clients to remind them to contact these other agencies. I would ask them if they wanted me to do this first. I don’t think this would break any rules. What do you think?—Want to Help MoreDear Want to Help More,AdvertisementUh, please do not do this.Let me be more clear: DO NOT DO THIS.Popular inAdviceThis Content is Available for Slate Plus members onlyI Read My Son’s Texts From His Ex-Girlfriend. Uh-Oh.My Co-Worker’s Annoying Habit Is Making My Life HellI think I’ve made my point, but I also want to say that I know you are coming from a good place here! So this is not in any way meant to make you feel bad. I know it’sbecauseyou care so much about your clients that you want to help them in any way you can, but your solution to go “off books,” followed by “I don’t think this would break any rules,” is a huge red flag. If you have to go off books, you are, by definition, breaking rules! This could have catastrophic consequences for your clients, and yourself. I know it’s really hard to focus only on the area that you’re supposed to be helping them in, but for their sake, and for yours, I think you need to be able to compartmentalize a bit. You’re helping them in this specific way, and there are other people, and agencies, that can help them with other aspects of their lives. Your getting involved, off the books no less, will likely cause more harm than good.AdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementAdvertisementI also worry that you are going to end up depleting your own well of empathy by trying to solveallof their problems. You can’t solve everyone’s problems, and you can’t solve all the problems of any one person. That’s a lesson that’s worth learning both on and off the job.—DoreeClassic PrudieI lost my husband when I was six months pregnant. Whatever good will my in-laws had for me evaporated when I decided to move back home and have my baby with my family around. My mother-in-law accused me of being a coward and “stealing” her only grandson. It got worse when I met and married an old high school friend the next year. He was raising his daughter and her half-sister alone because the mother was unstable and the other father was in prison. We found solace and support in each other.My in-laws couldn’t understand or forgive that.Never miss new Slate Advice columnsGet the latest from Prudie and our columnists in your inbox each weekday, plus special bonus letters on Saturdays.Thanks for signing up! title: Japan’s Annual Penis Festival Is Unlike Anything Else
content: JPGJapan’s Annual Penis Festival Is Unlike Anything ElseKanamara Matsuri has been an annual tradition since 1969, and besides being known for its fun, it raises money for a good cause.BybyKenneth BachorBuzzFeed News Photo EditorandbyKo SasakiBuzzFeed ContributorPosted onApril 7, 2023, 4:38 pmcommentTwitterFacebookLinkAttendees at Kanamara Matsuri in Kawasaki, Japan, on April 2, 2023In early April, scores of revelers gather in the city of Kawasaki, about 30 minutes south of Tokyo, to celebrate Kanamara Matsuri – Japan’s infamous penis festival, with a name translating roughly to Festival of the Steel Phallus. Kanamara Matsuri’s main festivities have taken place on the first Sunday of April since 1969 (yes, seriously).At the festival centering on the um,organand fertility, attendees get to erect gigantic penis statues on handheld shrines, enjoy penis-shaped lollipops, buy penis-shaped candles, and (obviously) dress as penises. There’s a seemingly endless array of phallic merch!“Amazing. So fun, so unique, such a different experience,” one Australian tourist who went to this year’s gatheringtold Euronews. “It’s so weird coming from Australia to see something like this, but it looks like everyone’s having a great time.”In the past,an estimated50,000 people from around the world have gathered annually for the festival, with numbers shrinking in recent years due to COVID. Besides being visually unique, the festival has taken on a positive message: raising awareness about safe sex and gathering profits from merch sales to fund HIV research. (In recent years, Japan has seen arise in rates of sexually transmitted diseaseslike syphilis, with more than 50%more patients treated for the diseasein 2022 than in 2021, per Japanese news source the Mainichi.) The event has also been an inclusive space for Japanese LGBTQ communities.But what about the festival’s origins? During Japan’s Edo Period, from 1603 to 1867, Kawasaki was known for having quite the nightlife scene, as it was a popular center for trade and commerce. The city’s Kanayama Shrine, built in roughly 698 CE, features a statue of a steel penis and became a place for sex workers to pray for protection against sexually transmitted infections and for others to pray for fertility. This history, combined with one particular local folktale involving a toothed demon and a steel penis – quite the combo – led to the modern version of Kanamara Matsuri.BuzzFeed News last attended Kanamara Matsuriin 2019. We decided to go back post-COVID and the festival is still going strong, with revelers partying extra hard.Kenneth BachorBuzzFeed News Photo EditorKo SasakiBuzzFeed Contributor
